0.title: Jeremiah: The Weeping Prophet
0.overview:
Jeremiah is the book of a man who was sent to tell his own nation that it was finished, and to keep telling them for forty years while they laughed at him, beat him, tried him for his life and threw him into a pit. It is also the book in which God promises a new covenant (a new binding bond with his people), a righteous King from David's line, and a day when he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (31:34). Judgment and hope run side by side through all fifty-two chapters, and both come from the same God.

Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a village a few miles from Jerusalem. The word of the LORD came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 627 BC, and he was still prophesying when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, and after it (1:1-3). He lived through the last five kings of Judah: Josiah, the reforming king; Shallum (also called Jehoahaz), carried off to Egypt after three months (22:11; 2 Kgs 23:31-34); Jehoiakim, who cut up and burned Jeremiah's scroll column by column (36:23); Coniah (also called Jehoiachin), hurled into exile (22:24-26); and Zedekiah, who asked Jeremiah for a word from God in secret and never had the courage to obey it.

Assyria collapsed, and Babylon rose in its place and defeated Egypt at Carchemish about 605 BC (46:2). Judah's kings tried to survive by playing the great powers against each other. Jeremiah's message was that the real threat was not Babylon but the LORD, whom they had abandoned, and that Babylon was the rod in his hand. These nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years (25:11). The seventy years are most simply counted from about 605 BC to the first return about 538 BC; some count from the temple's fall in 586 to its rebuilding in 516. Daniel read the number and prayed (Dan. 9:2).

The charge against Judah is set out in the second chapter: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (2:13). They worshipped other gods on every high hill, oppressed the poor, and assumed that the temple would protect them anyway (7:4). Underneath all of it lay a problem no reform could reach: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? (17:9).

Jeremiah did not want the job, and God answered his protest with a promise: Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you (1:8). His commission was to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10): four words of demolition and two of building, and the building words come last. He was told not to marry (16:2), so that his lonely life became a sign of the coming ruin. He was put in the stocks (20:2), arrested as a deserter (37:13), and lowered into a cistern where he sank in the mud (38:6). After the city fell he was taken to Egypt against his will (43:6-7). The book never tells us how he died.

Jeremiah lets us see inside his own heart. He argues with God, curses the day he was born, and tries to stop preaching, and finds he cannot: the word is a burning fire shut up in my bones (20:9). Yet the same man says your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (15:16). His prayers teach every weary servant of God that honesty with God is not unbelief, and that faithfulness is measured by obedience, not by results.

The book is not arranged in date order. Chapter 1 is the call. Chapters 2-25 are mainly warnings to Judah: sermons, visions, acted parables and Jeremiah's own anguished prayers. Chapters 26-29 show him in conflict with priests and false prophets, and include his letter to the exiles. Chapters 30-33 are a book of comfort (30:2). Chapters 34-45 tell the story of the siege, the fall of Jerusalem and the chaos after it. Chapters 46-51 are oracles (messages of judgment) against the nations, ending with the fall of Babylon (51:64). Chapter 52 is a historical appendix.

Who wrote the book down? Baruch son of Neriah was Jeremiah’s scribe and friend, who wrote at his dictation and read the scroll in the temple (ch. 36); he went with Jeremiah to Egypt (43:6). The Greek translation of Jeremiah is about an eighth shorter and arranges the oracles against the nations differently; both forms were known among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Hebrew text, followed by the ESV, is most likely the fuller edition that Jeremiah and Baruch completed (36:32).

Through all of it runs one conviction: God's word will be done. I am watching over my word to perform it (1:12). His word is like fire and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (23:29). When the king burned the scroll, God simply had it written again, with more added (36:32). What God says about judgment happens, and what God says about mercy happens too.

And the mercy is astonishing. To the exiles God says, I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (29:11), spoken to people who would spend seventy years far from home. It was a promise to the exiles as a people, not a promise of an easy life for each of them, and many who heard it died in Babylon; yet for everyone in Christ the same God works all things for good (Rom 8:28). With Babylon's army at the walls, Jeremiah buys a field in his home village as a sign that the land has a future (32:15), and prays, Nothing is too hard for you (32:17). The last verses of the book show a king of David's line brought out of prison to eat at the king's table every day of his life (52:31-34): a small light left burning for David's house.

That light leads to Christ. Jeremiah promised a righteous Branch for David, whose name would be The LORD is our righteousness (23:5-6). He promised a new covenant in which God would write his law on their hearts (31:33), the only answer to the deceitful heart. On the night before he died, Jesus took the cup and said, This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's promise in full to show that it has come (Heb 8:8-12). Jesus drove the traders from the temple with Jeremiah's words, a den of robbers (Matt 21:13; Jer 7:11); some thought he was Jeremiah come back (Matt 16:14); Matthew hears Jeremiah's Rachel weeping at Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18). Jesus too wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), warned that its temple would fall, and was rejected by its priests. But where Jeremiah could only announce the new covenant, Jesus made it, in his own blood.

Jeremiah is a book for anyone tempted to trust in religion instead of God, for anyone who must keep saying unpopular truth, for anyone living through the collapse of what they thought was secure, and for anyone who needs to hear that God's plans for his people run through the ruins to a future and a hope. Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth (9:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Man and His Times
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A priest's son from Anathoth (v. 1) receives the word of the LORD from Josiah's thirteenth year (v. 2) to the captivity of Jerusalem under Zedekiah (v. 3): about forty years, ending in the ruin of the city.
verseByVerse.theology: God's word comes to a real man, in named years, under named kings: the message of this book is anchored in history.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, to whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, and until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah. The book begins with a name, a father and a village. Jeremiah is a priest's son from Anathoth, a small place within sight of Jerusalem, not a member of the temple establishment in the capital. Anathoth was the town to which Solomon had banished the priest Abiathar (1 Kgs 2:26), and Jeremiah’s family may well have been of that line, priests long kept at a distance from the Jerusalem temple. He is an outsider, and he will spend his life telling the capital what it does not want to hear.

In the days of Josiah. The date matters. Josiah was the last good king of Judah, the one who did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the way of David his father (2 Kgs 22:2). Jeremiah's ministry begins as a national reform is gathering pace: Josiah had begun purging the idols the year before (2 Chr 34:3), and the great reform came five years later (2 Kgs 22:3). He is called in the best years, and he will watch them end.

Until the captivity of Jerusalem. Forty years of preaching, and the summary of how it went is in the last phrase of verse 3: until the captivity of Jerusalem. Under Jehoiakim the Babylonian empire had already closed in (2 Kgs 24:1). The thirteenth year of Josiah is about 627 BC; the fifth month of Zedekiah’s eleventh year is the summer of 587 BC (some reckon 586), when the Babylonians burned the temple and the city (2 Kgs 25:8-9).

Faithfulness, not results. Judged by results, he failed. Judged by faithfulness, he is one of the great men of the Bible. Those are not the same measure, and confusing them has wrecked more ministries and more Christians than open sin has.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, from about 627 BC to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 and beyond. Anathoth was a priests’ town about 3 miles north-east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Before I Formed You in the Womb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God knew and appointed Jeremiah before he was born (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he is only a youth (v. 6), and is told to go and speak, with the promise of God's presence (vv. 7-8). Then the LORD touches his mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations to tear down and to build (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The call rests on God's prior choice, God's presence and God's words, not on the prophet's ability.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the word of the LORD came to me. The narrator's voice becomes the prophet's own. What follows is Jeremiah telling you what happened to him.

Before I formed you in the womb. Four verbs, and God is the subject of every one. He formed, he knew, he consecrated, he appointed. And all four happened before Jeremiah had done anything at all, before he had any character to commend him or any failure to disqualify him.

I knew you. This is more than knowing facts about him. It means knowing him personally and setting his love on him. Before there was a person to know, God knew him. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them (Ps 139:16).

Others called from the womb. The same pattern is claimed by the servant of Isaiah (Isa 49:1), and by Paul, who described God as the one who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace (Gal 1:15). John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb (Luke 1:15).

What follows for us. Two things follow for anyone reading. God deals with unborn children as persons he knows, names and has purposes for. And your significance is not something you are building. It was settled before you existed, by God, and no failure of yours can overturn it.

A calling needs a Caller. Our culture talks a great deal about vocation, but it usually means something inward: find your passion, discover what you were born to do, and go after it. The trouble is that a calling you invent for yourself has nobody behind it. When it goes wrong, as Jeremiah’s ministry would by every outward measure, it has nothing to say to you except that you chose badly. Os Guinness argued in The Call that the very word assumes a Caller: you cannot be called by no one. Verse 5 puts the Caller first. Before Jeremiah had a passion, a gift or a single sermon, God knew him and appointed him. That lifts two burdens our culture lays on the young: the pressure to manufacture a meaningful life from scratch, and the fear that one wrong turn will waste it. And the One who calls goes with those he calls, which is the whole point of verse 8. Jesus told his friends, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16), and he does not drop those he has chosen.

What about a child who dies before birth? Parents who have lost a pregnancy often come to this verse with an ache, and it speaks to them gently. A child carried for a few weeks and never held was known by the God who formed it, and is not forgotten. Scripture does not tell us all we would like about such little ones, but it gives ground for hope: when his infant son died, David said, I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Sam 12:23), and the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ. Such a child may be entrusted to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Gen 18:25), and whose Son took little children in his arms (Mark 10:16). A miscarriage is a sorrow, not a sin, and no mother should hear this verse as blame.

Does “before I formed you in the womb I knew you” mean souls exist before their bodies? No. It means God chose and set Jeremiah apart before his life began; the knowing is God’s, not the soul’s. It speaks first of Jeremiah’s unique call as a prophet, but it rests on a truth that holds for all God’s people: he chose us in him before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4). And it shows that God knows and forms each person in the womb (Ps 139:13–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ah, Lord GOD! The response is not enthusiasm but dismay. Ah, Lord GOD! is a cry, not a greeting. And the objection is in two parts: I cannot do this, and I am too young to be taken seriously.

I do not know how to speak. Both are probably true. That is the point. Moses said the same thing at the burning bush (Exod 4:10), and God's answer was not a compliment about his hidden potential but a question, Who has made man's mouth?, and a promise: I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak (Exod 4:11-12).

Not self-esteem but God. In these calls God never says, you are better than you think. He says, I will be with you. Confidence for service does not come from a higher estimate of yourself; it comes from a higher estimate of God.

For I am only a youth. And youth is not a disqualification in Scripture. Paul told a young minister, Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity (1 Tim 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to me, "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not say, ‘I am only a youth.’ God does not argue with the objection; he forbids it. Then he replaces the two halves of Jeremiah's excuse with two commands that put the responsibility where it belongs. Where you go is not your decision, and what you say is not your decision either.

Freedom in obedience. That is a hard word and a liberating one: no freedom to choose the audience or edit the message, and no burden of inventing something worth saying.

Do not be afraid of them. God names the real problem. It is not inability; it is fear. Jeremiah will be beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern and accused of treason, so the fear is not irrational. The remedy given is not a promise that they will listen, or that he will be liked. It is a presence: I am with you.

For I am with you to deliver you. That is the same word the risen Christ left with his church when he sent it into the world: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20), a presence he keeps by the Spirit he gives. And it is what Paul heard in Corinth when he was afraid: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you (Acts 18:9-10). Is there a conversation you are avoiding because of what the person might say back? The promise is the same for you: he goes with you into it, and he has already forgiven the times you stayed silent.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. And the LORD said to me, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. See, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. The objection was about a mouth, so God touches his mouth. Isaiah's lips were touched with a coal from the altar to deal with his guilt (Isa 6:7). Here the touch is a commission: the words themselves are put into his mouth.

Sweet and bitter. Ezekiel was made to eat a scroll (Ezek 3:1-3), and John in Revelation ate a little scroll that was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter (Rev 10:10). That is Jeremiah's life in a sentence. The word of God is sweet to receive and bitter to carry.

Over nations and over kingdoms. A village boy is set over nations and over kingdoms, not with an army but with a message. The empires of his day would have laughed. They are gone, and his words are still being read.

To pluck up and to break down. Six verbs: four tear down, two build. That is the proportion of this book, and it is honest about what the word of God must do in a place that has gone wrong. You cannot plant in ground that has not been cleared. Paul describes his ministry the same way: weapons with divine power to destroy strongholds (2 Cor 10:4-5).

To build and to plant. But the two constructive verbs are not an afterthought, and later God takes them up again: so I will watch over them to build and to plant (31:28). The book that begins with demolition reaches a new covenant at its centre (31:31-34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Two Visions: the Almond and the Boiling Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two visions. An almond branch: God is watching over his word to perform it (vv. 11-12). A boiling pot tilted from the north: disaster let loose (vv. 13-14), the northern kingdoms at Jerusalem's gates (v. 15), and judgment for forsaking the LORD (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God watches over his word to do it, and the first thing it will do here is bring an army from the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Jeremiah, what do you see?" And I said, "I see an almond branch." Then the LORD said to me, "You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah, what do you see? The first vision is almost domestic: a branch in blossom, the sort of thing anyone might notice on a walk. God asks him what he sees, because God is about to teach him to read ordinary things.

I see an almond branch. The answer turns on a play on words that English cannot carry: the Hebrew word for almond sounds like the Hebrew word for watching. The almond is the first tree in the land to blossom, flowering in late winter while everything else still looks dead, which is probably why its name sounds like ‘the wakeful one’. Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says, I am the watching God, and what I am watching over is my word. God is awake over what he has said.

I am watching over my word to perform it. That is the sentence to hold for the next fifty-one chapters. Not one syllable of what God says in this book will fall to the ground unattended. So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose (Isa 55:11). Has he said, and will he not do it? (Num 23:19).

For prophet and nation. It cuts both ways, which is exactly why it is here. For a prophet who will preach for forty years and see almost no response, it means his labour is not wasted. For a nation that has heard the warnings and shrugged, it means the warnings are not empty words.
verseByVerse.note: Wordplay: “almond” (shaqed) sounds like “watching” (shoqed) (ESV note). The almond is among the first trees to blossom in spring.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me a second time, saying, "What do you see?" And I said, "I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north." Then the LORD said to me, "Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land. For behold, I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north, declares the LORD, and they shall come, and every one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, against all its walls all around and against all the cities of Judah. And I will declare my judgments against them, for all their evil in forsaking me. They have made offerings to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north. The second vision is a cooking pot at the boil, tilted so that what is inside is about to pour out over Judah, from the north.

Out of the north. Babylon lay to the east, but the desert was in between, so its armies marched round and came down from the north; that is the road every invader took. Within Jeremiah's lifetime Babylon would come down it.

I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north. The one doing it is God: I am calling. Babylon thought it was pursuing its own ambitions. It was being summoned. The thrones set in the gateway are the picture of a conquered city, with foreign officials sitting where Judah's elders used to give judgment.

For all their evil in forsaking me. And the reason is given plainly, so that no one can call the disaster meaningless. It is not bad luck or merely the politics of empires. It is forsaking me, and the shape that forsaking took: worshipping the works of their own hands. They made something, then bowed to it. Every generation does, and the objects change.

Does God do evil? The word can mean “evil” or “disaster”. God brings calamity as judgment on sin (Isa 45:7), but he never does moral evil or tempts anyone to it (Jas 1:13). The disaster from the north was the just punishment of a people who had forsaken him.
verseByVerse.note: The kingdoms of the north turn out to be Babylon and its allies (25:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — An Iron Pillar and Bronze Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is told to get ready, speak, and not be dismayed (v. 17). God makes him a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls against the whole land (v. 18): they will fight, but not prevail, for God is with him (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not promise the prophet an easy audience; he promises to make him able to stand and to keep him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, dress yourself for work; arise, and say to them everything that I command you. Do not be dismayed by them, lest I dismay you before them. And I, behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dress yourself for work. In Hebrew this is "gird up your loins": gather the long robe, tie it at the waist, get ready to move. It is the posture of a man about to run or to fight.

Lest I dismay you before them. Then a warning with a sting in it: lest I dismay you before them. Fear of the audience is not a small weakness to be indulged in a preacher; it is the thing that will break him in public. If he will not fear God more than the crowd, God will let the crowd frighten him. The cure for the fear of people is not courage summoned from inside. It is the fear of God, which crowds out every lesser fear, and it is God who gives it.

A fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls. Three images follow, all defensive and immovable: a walled city, an iron pillar, walls of bronze. God does not remove the opposition, and he lists exactly who it will be: the palace, the civil service, the clergy and the public. Instead of removing them, he makes the man able to stand.

Strength for the calling. Ezekiel received the same kind of hardening (Ezek 3:8-9). God gives what the calling requires, and he gives it to the person who has just said he cannot do it. Every Christian who has kept quiet out of fear has a better word than a scolding: the one who never once flinched from the Father's word went to the cross for cowards, and his Spirit makes the fearful bold.
verseByVerse.note: The same picture of readiness is used in Job 38:3 and 1 Peter 1:13.

verseByVerse.quote: They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, declares the LORD, to deliver you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall not prevail against you. The chapter ends with the promise it has been building toward, and it is worded with great care. God does not say they will not fight him; he says plainly that they will. What he promises is that they shall not prevail.

What the promise covers. Read Jeremiah's life before deciding what that promise covers. He was put in stocks, left to sink in a muddy cistern, imprisoned, accused of desertion, ignored by a king who burned his scroll, and finally carried off to Egypt. He was not protected from any of it. He was preserved through all of it, and the word he carried outlived every one of his opponents.

The same promise to the church. Jesus said of his church, the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt 16:18), and told his disciples, In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33). If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31).

Not delivered, so that we would be. And there is one prophet of whom this promise was not made in that form. Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem and was preserved; Christ wept over the same city (Luke 19:41) and was handed over to it. He had the words of God in his mouth in a way no prophet ever had, speaking only what his Father gave him (John 12:49), and when they fought against him, he did not call for deliverance. He was the prophet Moses promised (Acts 3:22), and he was not delivered, so that we would be.

1.title: The Call of Jeremiah: I Am Watching Over My Word
1.overview:
Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, received the word of the LORD from the thirteenth year of Josiah until Jerusalem went into captivity: about forty years of preaching that ended with his country in ruins (vv. 1-3).

God tells him that he knew, consecrated and appointed him before he was born (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he cannot speak and is only a youth; God forbids the excuse and promises, I am with you to deliver you (vv. 6-8). God touches his mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations to tear down and to build (vv. 9-10).

Two visions follow: an almond branch, because God is watching over his word (vv. 11-12), and a boiling pot tilted from the north, an invasion God himself is summoning (vv. 13-16). Finally God makes Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls: they will fight him and will not prevail (vv. 17-19).
1.theology:
God's call rests on his own prior choice, not on the one called (vv. 4-5; Ps 139:16; Gal 1:15), and he deals with the unborn as persons he knows and appoints. Fitness for service is not self-confidence but God's presence and God's words (vv. 6-9; Exod 4:11-12; Matt 28:20).

The word of God does demolishing work before it builds (v. 10; 2 Cor 10:4-5), and the building is promised (31:28). God watches over his word to perform it, so that neither warning nor promise falls to the ground (v. 12; Isa 55:11; Num 23:19).

God governs the nations that punish his people: the invader from the north is summoned by him (v. 15). Fear of man is the prophet's real danger, and the remedy is the fear of God (v. 17). God does not remove opposition but makes his servant able to stand and preserves him through it (vv. 18-19; Matt 16:18). The prophet greater than Jeremiah was not delivered from those who fought him (Acts 3:22; Luke 19:41), so that we would be.
1.examples: Jeremiah's forty years of faithful preaching, ending in national ruin, are a standing rebuke to judging a ministry by its results. And when a calling feels too large, God's answer to "I can't" is never "you are better than you think" but "I am with you".

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Devotion of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Jeremiah to Jerusalem with a memory of Israel's early devotion (vv. 1-3), then asks what wrong their fathers found in him (vv. 4-5). They stopped asking where the LORD was (v. 6), defiled the land he gave them (v. 7), and every kind of leader failed together (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The question of verse 5 is a lover's question as well as a judge's: what did I do, that you should leave me?

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown. Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem. The first sermon of the book does not open with an accusation. It opens with a memory, and it is God's memory.

I remember the devotion of your youth. He is thinking of the exodus and the wilderness years, and he describes them the way a husband describes the early days of a marriage. There was a time when they followed him anywhere, into a land not sown, with no crops and no guarantees, simply because he was going that way.

A long memory for the good. That is a remarkable thing for God to say about the wilderness generation, because the books of Exodus and Numbers are full of their grumbling. He remembers the love, and does not rehearse the complaints. Grace has a long memory for the good.

The firstfruits of his harvest. Firstfruits were the portion given to God and reserved for him alone; anyone else who ate them was guilty. That is what Israel was to him: set apart, his own, protected by his jealousy so that whoever touched them answered for it.

A husband’s memory. Before a word of accusation, hear the tone. This is not a landlord evicting a tenant. It is a husband remembering a honeymoon, and it is about to become one of the saddest chapters in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless? They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the clans of the house of Israel. The address widens. Jeremiah is standing in Jerusalem, but the summons goes to all the clans of the house of Israel, the northern tribes included, a century after Assyria scattered them. The whole family was in the wilderness, and the whole family is now called to answer.

What wrong did your fathers find in me? Then the question at the heart of the chapter, and God is the one asking it. Not, what did you gain by leaving, but what fault did you find? He invites them to produce the grievance, the thing he did that justified it. There is none.

Went after worthlessness, and became worthless. And then: went after worthlessness, and became worthless. The word is the same on both sides. You become what you worship. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8). Paul says the same of the human race: they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images, and their foolish hearts were darkened (Rom 1:21-23). Worship is never neutral. Whatever you give yourself to is shaping you into its own likeness right now.

Where is the LORD? The failure was not a decision to reject God. It was a question they stopped asking. Nobody said, “Where is the LORD?” The rescue was still in the history books and had gone out of the conversation. That is how faith is usually lost: not in a crisis of belief, but in a slow silence.

A land of deserts and pits. And look at what they had stopped remembering: not a pleasant journey but deserts, pits, drought and deep darkness, a land where no man dwells. Moses had told the same people to remember the God who brought you water out of the flinty rock (Deut 8:15). The worse the road had been, the more there was to be grateful for, and the more complete the forgetting.

verseByVerse.quote: And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination. The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I brought you into a plentiful land. God gave them a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity (Deut 8:9), and the gift became the occasion of the forgetting. Prosperity is often harder on faith than poverty, because it removes the daily sense of need.

You defiled my land. The possessives matter: my land, my heritage. God gave them the land and never stopped owning it. What they defiled was not their property but his inheritance. Everything a believer has is held on the same terms.

Four failed leaders. Then the leadership, four groups, and every one has failed. The priests never asked where God was. The scholars who handle the law did not know its author. The shepherds (the ESV notes the word may be rendered "rulers") broke the covenant themselves. And the prophets preached another god entirely. When a nation collapses spiritually, it is rarely the people who fall first.

Those who handle the law did not know me. And the first failures are failures of knowing. It is entirely possible to handle Scripture professionally, every day, and not know the God who wrote it. The question for anyone who teaches is not how much of the text he has mastered, but whether he still asks where the LORD is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No nation changes its gods, but God's people have exchanged their glory (vv. 9-11). Heaven is called to be appalled at two evils: the forsaken fountain and the broken cisterns (vv. 12-13). The lions have roared and the land is waste (vv. 14-16), a ruin they brought on themselves, and running to Egypt and Assyria for water will not mend it (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin is never only a rule broken. It is a greater good abandoned for a lesser one, and heaven itself is summoned to be appalled at the exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend. For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing. Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see. God takes them to court, and the case rests on a survey. Send west to Cyprus, send east to Kedar, and ask a simple question: does anyone do this?

I still contend with you. And the lawsuit runs across generations: with your children's children I will contend. A God who is still contending three generations on has not given up on the defendants.

Has a nation changed its gods? The survey is almost comic: other nations keep faith with deities that do not exist, while Israel breaks faith with the one who does. Israel traded their glory, the living God himself, their honour and their boast, for something that does not profit. It is not only wicked; it is a spectacularly bad deal.

The civilisation that changed its gods. Verse 11 has an unexpected modern ring. The nations round Israel stayed loyal to their gods, and the modern West may be the first civilisation in history to walk away from the God who shaped it. Many people see that as a coming of age. Jeremiah would ask what we exchanged him for. A culture does not stop worshipping when it stops believing; it moves its devotion elsewhere, and the things we have made ultimate are mostly good gifts asked to do a god’s work: the self, success, the nation or the cause, romance, health and youth. None of them has been proved worthless, exactly. They have simply been asked to carry a weight they cannot hold, which is why verse 13 calls them broken cisterns. The surprise is in verse 9. God has not given up on the defendants; he will contend with their children’s children. The God the West has walked away from is still pleading with it, and Christ is still the fountain at the end of the empty road.

verseByVerse.quote: Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate, declares the LORD, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be appalled, O heavens, at this. Heaven is called as witness, and told to be horrified. Sin has become so normal on earth that the proper horror has to come from heaven.

My people have committed two evils. Here is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward, and it is one of the clearest definitions of sin in Scripture. Not one evil, but two.

The fountain of living waters. The first is leaving. God is the fountain of living waters: a spring, moving, fresh, free, endlessly replenished, requiring no work from anyone but a cupped hand. In a hot country that is not poetry; it is life.

Broken cisterns that can hold no water. The second is the substitute. A cistern is a pit cut out of rock to hold rainwater. Cutting one is brutal labour, months of it. The water it holds is still and stale at best. And these are broken cisterns, cracked, so that the digger is left with a dry hole he spent his strength on.

Never be thirsty again. Jesus stood in the temple and answered this verse directly: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37), and he meant the Spirit whom those who believed were to receive. To a woman drawing water he said, whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:14). And at the end of the Bible the offer still stands: To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (Rev 21:6). The fountain is free; only the cisterns cost.

In everyday life. That is the pattern of every sin: a real spring abandoned, and enormous effort spent on a leaking substitute. Nobody works harder than someone trying to get from a career, a relationship, a bottle or an image what only God gives. And the cistern always leaks, which is why it must be dug again next year.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew usage “living water” is running water from a spring, as opposed to water stored in a tank.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is Israel a slave? Is he a homeborn servant? Why then has he become a prey? The lions have roared against him; they have roared loudly. They have made his land a waste; his cities are in ruins, without inhabitant. Moreover, the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head. Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, when he led you in the way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is Israel a slave? Three questions and a scene of ruin. Israel was God's son, not anyone's slave, so why is he being carried off like plunder? The lions are the empires, and the roaring has already begun: towns burned, fields wasted, villages emptied.

The men of Memphis and Tahpanhes. Memphis and Tahpanhes are Egyptian cities, and the shaved crown is the mark of a slave or a mourner. The ESV notes that have shaved is in Hebrew "grazed". The allies Judah courted have treated her like pasture. Jeremiah’s hearers would probably think of 609 BC, when Pharaoh Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo, deposed his son and put Judah under tribute (2 Kgs 23:29-35).

Have you not brought this upon yourself? Verse 17 refuses every comfortable explanation. The cause is not the empires, not bad luck, not God’s neglect: they brought it on themselves by forsaking the LORD. Not every sorrow is of this kind, and Scripture never says it is; but there is a kind of pain that is simply our own choices coming back on us, and this was it.

When he led you in the way. And the last clause makes it worse: when he led you in the way. They were not lost when they left. They were being led, the way a father leads a small child, and they let go of his hand. Moses had described that wilderness care: the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went (Deut 1:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And now what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates? Your evil will chastise you, and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the LORD your God; the fear of me is not in you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To drink the waters of the Nile. The water image returns, now as foreign policy. Judah's politics swung between the two superpowers, drinking first from the Nile and then from the Euphrates, buying protection with tribute and treaties. Every generation has its version of this: the fear that God is not enough, and the search for a stronger friend.

Your evil will chastise you. God does not need to invent a punishment; the sin brings its own. The psalm shows God doing this as a judgment: So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels (Ps 81:12). Sometimes the severest thing God does is let a person have what he insisted on.

The fear of me is not in you. The verse ends at the root of it all: the fear of me is not in you. Every other failure in the chapter grows out of that absence. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Prov 1:7), and a people without it will run to Egypt and Assyria because they are more afraid of the empires than of him. What a person fears most is what he ends up obeying.
verseByVerse.note: The Nile is “Shihor” and the Euphrates “the River” in Hebrew (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Choice Vine Gone Wild
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people threw off God's yoke and bowed to idols on every high hill (v. 20). God's choice vine turned wild (v. 21), and no soap removes the stain (v. 22). They deny it, though they run like a wild animal in heat (vv. 23-25). They will be shamed like a caught thief, calling a tree their father and crying to God only in trouble (vv. 26-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry is both a slavery that cannot be broken by willpower and a stain that cannot be scrubbed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "For long ago I broke your yoke and burst your bonds; but you said, 'I will not serve.' Yes, on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed down like a whore. Yet I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine? Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will not serve. God broke the yoke in Egypt, and the freed slave answered, I will not serve: not him, at least. And then he bowed anyway, on every hill and under every tree, to whatever local shrine was at hand. Nobody serves nothing. The yoke thrown off is always replaced.

A translation note. The King James Version reads I will not transgress here. The Hebrew words for “serve” and “transgress” differ by one similar-looking letter, and the scribes' marginal reading gave “transgress”; most modern translations, with the Greek Old Testament, read I will not serve. Either way, the people's words were contradicted on every hill.

I planted you a choice vine. The gardener chose the best stock and planted it himself, and what came up was wild. The fault cannot be traced to the seed or the gardener.

Though you wash yourself with lye. Now the image changes to laundry, and it settles the question of self-improvement. Lye and soap were the strongest cleaners available. Scrub as hard as you like: the stain of your guilt is still before me. The stain is before him, and that is the problem: what matters is not whether we feel clean but what God sees.

The one open door. This verse leaves only one door open, and the New Testament opens it: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). The stain that no effort removes is removed by confession and by the blood of Christ, and by nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: How can you say, 'I am not unclean, I have not gone after the Baals'? Look at your way in the valley; know what you have done— a restless young camel running here and there, a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves; in her month they will find her. Keep your feet from going unshod and your throat from thirst. But you said, 'It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at your way in the valley. The denial is answered with evidence: Look at your way in the valley. The valley is most likely the Valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem, where children were burned to Molech (7:31). Do not tell me what you believe; look at what you have done.

A restless young camel running here and there. The images are deliberately undignified: a young camel bolting in every direction, a wild donkey in heat that nobody needs to chase because she comes to them. Idolatry is not sophisticated. It is compulsive.

Who can restrain her lust? And the chapter is honest about addiction: Who can restrain her lust? The question expects the answer nobody, and certainly not the animal herself. Anyone who has tried to break a habit by willpower alone knows the verse from the inside. The God who broke the yoke in Egypt (v. 20) is the one who breaks this one too, by his Spirit, his word and the help of his people.

It is hopeless. God pleads with them to stop wearing out their shoes and their throats chasing what will not feed them. The reply is the saddest line in the chapter: It is hopeless. Not defiance, but despair: I am too far gone; this is who I am now. Many people are held in something they hate by exactly that sentence, and it is a lie, because the God who is still pleading in this verse has not called it hopeless.

verseByVerse.quote: "As a thief is shamed when caught, so the house of Israel shall be shamed: they, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets, who say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their back to me, and not their face. But in the time of their trouble they say, 'Arise and save us!' But where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise, if they can save you, in your time of trouble; for as many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a thief is shamed when caught. The shame of a thief is not remorse for stealing; it is the shame of being caught. That is the shame coming to Judah, and the list runs from the palace down, much the same list as verse 8. The failure runs through the whole society, and each group is named.

Religion in good times and bad. Two sentences that between them describe most religion. In good times they say to a tree, “You are my father,” and to a stone, “You gave me birth”: they treat what they have made as if it had made them. In bad times they cry, Arise and save us!, to the God on whom they have turned their backs.

They have turned their back to me, and not their face. God notices the posture: they have turned their back to me, and not their face. A wandering child still faces his father; a settled rebel has turned his back. It also shows what repentance is. Turning round is all that is required, and it is the one thing they will not do.

Where are your gods that you made for yourself? The irony is sharp: your gods that you made for yourself. Call them, God says. See if they stand up. Isaiah put it the same way: Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? (Isa 44:10). There was a god for every town, and not one of them able to move.

In everyday life. The test still works. When the diagnosis comes, or the job goes, or the marriage cracks, you find out very quickly which of the things you serve can stand up and help, and that the God you had turned your back on is still the one who can.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's discipline taught them nothing, and they killed the prophets (vv. 29-30). He asks whether he has been a wilderness to them (v. 31); a bride does not forget her attire, yet his people have forgotten him (v. 32). With the blood of the poor on their skirts they still claim innocence (vv. 33-35), and Egypt will shame them as Assyria did (vv. 36-37).
verseByVerse.theology: The final defence of a guilty people is not argument but denial, and God answers it by bringing them to judgment for the denial itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me, declares the LORD. In vain have I struck your children; they took no correction; your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravening lion. And you, O generation, behold the word of the LORD. Have I been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness? Why then do my people say, 'We are free, we will come no more to you'? Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you contend with me? They are arguing with him, and he asks why. Then two sentences of terrible summary: the discipline achieved nothing, and the messengers sent to explain the discipline were killed. A nation that will neither feel a warning nor hear an explanation has closed both doors.

Have I been a wilderness to Israel? The question of verse 5 returns, sharper. Have I been barren ground to you, the dark place you had to escape? God asks to be shown the evidence for the way he is being treated.

We are free, we will come no more to you. And the answer his people give is the oldest lie about God there is: We are free, we will come no more to you. Freedom is defined as distance from him. It is exactly what the serpent suggested, and what every generation repeats.

Can a virgin forget her ornaments? A bride does not forget her dress; it is the most precious thing she owns and the day is the biggest of her life. Yet God's people have forgotten him days without number.

Forgetting, not atheism. It is not an accusation of atheism but of forgetting, and forgetting does not feel like rebellion. It feels like being busy. God measures it in days: how many have gone by, with no thought of him at all?

The Bridegroom who does not forget. Paul uses the same marriage language of the church: he had betrothed the Corinthians to one husband, Christ, and feared they would be led astray (2 Cor 11:2-3). The bride who forgot is answered by a Bridegroom who does not forget, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25). His faithfulness, not hers, is what holds the marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: "How well you direct your course to seek love! So that even to wicked women you have taught your ways. Also on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor; you did not find them breaking in. Yet in spite of all these things you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
How well you direct your course to seek love! Two charges together, and their pairing is the point. They have become expert at pursuing love in all the wrong places, so accomplished that even wicked women could learn from them (v. 33). And there is blood on their clothes: the lifeblood of the guiltless poor, people who had done nothing.

Idolatry and injustice. Idolatry and injustice arrive together, always. A people who will worship anything will eventually sacrifice anyone. The prophets never separate the two, and neither should we.

You did not find them breaking in. The phrase you did not find them breaking in is legal language. The law allowed a householder to strike a burglar caught at night: If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him (Exod 22:2). The poor who were killed were not burglars, so there was no such excuse for their deaths. They were simply in the way.

I am innocent. With blood on the hem, the claim is I am innocent. And God names what he will judge: not only the sin, but the denial of it.

The one obstacle. That is a sobering line, and also a hopeful one. It means the one thing standing between this people and mercy is the sentence they keep repeating. The next chapter will show God pleading for one word of acknowledgement (3:13), and it is the same word the New Testament asks for. Insisting that we are innocent is the one attitude in which forgiveness cannot be received.

verseByVerse.quote: How much you go about, changing your way! You shall be put to shame by Egypt as you were put to shame by Assyria. From it too you will come away with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you will not prosper by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How much you go about, changing your way! The chapter ends with restless diplomacy: first Assyria, now Egypt, always looking for a better arrangement. They will come home from Egypt with your hands on your head, the posture of prisoners and mourners. Assyria’s shaming lay a century back: King Ahaz had paid the Assyrian king for help, and he came and afflicted him instead of strengthening him (2 Chr 28:20).

With your hands on your head. It is the gesture Tamar made when she walked out disgraced (2 Sam 13:19). A nation that had courted every available power would end with the same gesture: used, and sent away.

The LORD has rejected those in whom you trust. The reason is given last and it is final: the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust. Every refuge that is not God is a refuge God has already rejected. Better to learn that before the crisis than during it.

Looking back on the chapter. Judah kept switching allies because none of them satisfied: the cistern of verse 13 again, dug in a new place each time. The only fixed point in the chapter is the one they left: the God who remembered the devotion of their youth and was still contending for them.

2.title: Two Evils: The Fountain and the Broken Cisterns
2.overview:
God sends Jeremiah to Jerusalem with a memory of the early days, Israel's devotion as a bride (vv. 1-3). Then he asks what wrong they found in him, that they went after worthlessness and became worthless; they stopped asking where he was, defiled the land he gave them, and their leaders all failed (vv. 4-8).

Israel exchanged its glory for what does not profit (vv. 9-11). Heaven is called to be appalled at two evils: forsaking the fountain of living waters, and digging broken cisterns (vv. 12-13). The ruin is self-inflicted, and running to Egypt and Assyria will not mend it (vv. 14-19).

The freed slave bowed to idols anyway; the choice vine turned wild; no soap removes the stain (vv. 20-22). The people deny it and call their case hopeless (vv. 23-25), call a tree their father and cry to God only in trouble (vv. 26-28). A bride who could never forget her dress has forgotten God (vv. 29-32), and with the blood of the poor on their clothes they plead innocence (vv. 33-37).
2.theology:
Sin is defined here in two steps: forsaking God, the fountain of living waters, and constructing substitutes that cannot hold what they promise (v. 13). Christ answers the first half by offering living water freely (John 4:14; 7:37; Rev 21:6).

Worship shapes the worshipper: those who go after worthlessness become worthless (v. 5; Ps 115:8; Rom 1:21-23). Prosperity and forgetfulness, not argument, are how faith is usually lost (vv. 6-7, 32). Leaders fail first (vv. 8, 26).

Sin carries its own punishment (v. 19; Ps 81:12), cannot be washed out by self-improvement (v. 22; 1 John 1:9), and is most dangerous when denied: God judges the claim I have not sinned (v. 35). Idolatry and injustice always travel together (vv. 33-34).
2.examples: The chapter's pictures stay with a reader because they are ordinary: a husband remembering a honeymoon, a man cutting a tank in rock beside a free spring, lye and soap on a stain that is before God and not before us, a bride who could never forget her dress. Each says the same thing from a different side: the fault was never in the God they left, and he is still calling them back.
