verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Would You Return to Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law forbids a divorced wife who has married another to return to her first husband, yet God asks his unfaithful people to return (v. 1). The rains have been withheld and they refuse to be ashamed (vv. 2-3), while still speaking warmly of God (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Affectionate words to God alongside unchanged behaviour are not repentance; and yet the impossible invitation to return is the one God makes.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD. Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will he return to her? The chapter opens with a point of law. Under Deuteronomy, a man who divorced his wife could not take her back once she had married someone else: her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD (Deut 24:4). The door is shut by God's own statute.

And would you return to me? And then, in the same breath, God asks, would you return to me? That is the astonishing thing in this chapter, and everything else stands under it. What the law forbids, love offers. God is not pretending the marriage was undamaged or the adultery small (many lovers is his own phrase), and still he opens a door the law had bolted. How he can do this without ceasing to be just is the question the whole Bible answers at the cross.

Where have you not been ravished? The invitation does not pretend to forget: every hilltop has a shrine, and she has been at all of them. Like an Arab in the wilderness pictures a desert raider crouched beside a caravan route, watching the road for whoever comes along. Israel is not a victim ambushed by temptation but the one lying in wait for it.

You have the forehead of a whore. The drought was a message, and it was missed. Moses had warned that turning to other gods would make the LORD shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain (Deut 11:16-17). The irony was sharp: Baal was worshipped in Canaan as the god of storm and rain, and it was the LORD who held the showers back. The forehead of a whore is a face that has lost the capacity to blush. Shame is painful and it is a mercy; a conscience that can still be embarrassed is still alive. The danger point in any life is not doing wrong but reaching the stage of doing it without a flicker of shame.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, you have spoken. The words are lovely: My father, you are the friend of my youth. Warm, intimate, theologically correct, and quite compatible with having done all the evil that you could. Religious language is not repentance. It is possible to call God Father in one breath and keep every arrangement he hates in the next, and this verse exists to stop us doing it comfortably.

Will he be angry forever? The theology inside their question is true: He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever (Ps 103:9). But they are using it as a licence to go on sinning. God will say almost those words himself, I will not be angry forever (v. 12), to people who return. The same truth is comfort to the penitent and presumption in the mouth of someone who has done all the evil that you could.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Faithless Israel and Treacherous Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets two sisters side by side, Israel already exiled and Judah who watched and learned nothing, and sends the call to return northward (vv. 6-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Watching judgment fall on someone else and learning nothing is worse than the sin that brought it; and the way back is one honest admission.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore? And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it. She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sisters. Now a history lesson with two sisters in it. Israel is the northern kingdom, already destroyed by Assyria a century before Jeremiah preached. Judah is the southern kingdom, still standing, listening to this sermon.

After she has done all this. God's I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me' is the language of a patient husband waiting at the window, and it is how God describes his own long-suffering. And her treacherous sister Judah saw it: Judah had a front-row seat at her sister's funeral.

Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear. She watched the deportations, the ruined towns, the end of a nation, and drew no conclusion at all. Judah did not fear. There is no education in watching judgment fall on someone else if you have decided in advance that it cannot happen to you.

A decree of divorce. The decree of divorce is the legal image of verse 1 made concrete. Isaiah uses the same image of Zion's own exile and asks the pointed question, Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away?, before giving the answer: for your transgressions your mother was sent away (Isa 50:1). The exile of the north was not God abandoning a faithful wife. It was the consequence of a marriage she had already left.

verseByVerse.quote: Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She took her whoredom lightly. That is how nations and people fall, not by deciding sin is good but by deciding it is small. And Judah did return, but in pretense.

In pretense. This is said in the days of King Josiah, during the great national reform: the idols were smashed, the temple repaired, the Passover kept. It was genuine at the top, and it never reached the heart of the people. A reformation of behaviour without a change of heart is what God calls pretence, and he can tell the difference.

Not with her whole heart. Isaiah describes the same condition: this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me (Isa 29:13). And this book will later promise the cure that God himself supplies, I will give them a heart to know me, so that they shall return to me with their whole heart (24:7). What Judah could not produce under Josiah, God undertakes to give.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah. Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More righteous than treacherous Judah. A shocking verdict: exiled Israel is called more righteous than Judah. Israel sinned with no warning example in front of her; Judah sinned having watched the consequences, while holding the temple, the law, the priesthood and the promises. The more light, the greater the guilt.

Proclaim these words toward the north. And Jeremiah is told to face north, toward a people scattered into Assyria a hundred years ago, a lost cause by every reckoning, and preach to them. The reasons given are all about God: I am merciful, I will not be angry forever. Not, you are not as bad as you think. The ground of the invitation is his character, which is the only ground any of us has.

Only acknowledge your guilt. That is the whole requirement. Not make restitution first, not clean yourself up, not produce a period of good behaviour to prove you mean it. Say what is true; that is the door. Joel says it the same way: return to me with all your heart, rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:12-13). Hosea gives the words to use: Take with you words and return to the LORD (Hos 14:2). And John says it to the church: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9).

How do I acknowledge my guilt? It is simpler than we fear and harder than we like. Be specific. Not “I haven’t been great lately”, but the thing itself: I lied to my manager about the report; I have been cold to my wife for a week. Vague confessions keep the sin and shed only the discomfort. Say it to God without excuses. Leave out the “but” that explains why it was not really your fault. David found relief at exactly that point: I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity (Psalm 32:5). Tell the person you wronged. Where someone else was hurt, go to them, say what you did, and put right what can be put right. Tell a trusted Christian friend when a sin keeps returning: confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed (James 5:16). Then believe the pardon. Do not keep confessing the same forgiven sin as if God had not heard. You come not to an accuser but to a Father, and we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Shepherds After My Own Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return, O faithless children: God promises to gather a remnant one from a city and two from a family, and to give shepherds after his own heart (vv. 14-15). The ark will not be missed; Jerusalem will be the LORD's throne, all nations will gather to it, and Judah and Israel will come home together (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is small in its beginnings, pastoral in its care, and larger than Israel at its end.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion. "'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One from a city and two from a family. The promise attached to the repeated call is deliberately modest: one from a city and two from a family. God is not predicting a national landslide but a remnant, a small number who return, gathered person by person out of places that will not come as a whole. Revival is talked about in national terms; it usually arrives one and two at a time, and God calls that homecoming.

For I am your master. The ground of the call is a claim: for I am your master. The Hebrew word can also mean “husband”, as the King James Version takes it (I am married unto you), and it shares its root with the name Baal, which means “lord” or “owner”: the LORD claims the title the idol had usurped. They had left, but they had not stopped being his. Their unfaithfulness did not cancel his right to them, and it is that right, not their merit, that gives him the right to call them back.

Shepherds after my own heart. Chapter 2 exposed shepherds who transgressed against me (2:8). Here is the remedy: not better management but men whose hearts match God's, and whose work is feeding. The phrase echoes what God said of David, a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22). The risen Christ still gives the shepherds and teachers to his church (Eph 4:11), and behind every faithful one stands the good shepherd himself.

How is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. But the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. Faithful Christians differ here, and those who look for a future return to the land do so out of reverence for God's promises; this commentary follows the apostles, who read such promises as gathered up in Christ (2 Cor 1:20; Acts 15:14-17).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again. At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark of the covenant of the LORD. The ark was the most sacred object in Israel's worship, the throne of God's presence at the centre of the holy of holies, and it will not be missed. Not destroyed and mourned; simply not needed. That is not a downgrade but a promotion: a sign becomes unnecessary when the thing it signified has arrived in person. The ark itself drops out of the record; it was probably lost when Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC, and the temple rebuilt after the exile stood without it.

The throne of the LORD. The whole city becomes the throne room, not one gold box inside one room. All nations gather, not Israel alone. And the heart itself changes: they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart, which is exactly what chapter 31 will call the new covenant. The divided kingdoms come home together, the family reunited.

All nations shall gather to it. Isaiah saw the same gathering: all the nations shall flow to it, saying Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD (Isa 2:2-3). And the last pages of the Bible complete the thought about the ark. John sees the holy city and reports, I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22). The box that once marked God's throne is not missed, because God himself is present without one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God longed to be called Father, but Israel left like a treacherous wife (vv. 19-20). Weeping rises on the bare heights, God promises to heal their faithlessness, and the people come back confessing their sin (vv. 21-25).
verseByVerse.theology: God heals faithlessness rather than merely forgiving it, and the confession that follows is the fruit of that healing, not a way of earning it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
How I would set you among my sons. This is God speaking about his own hopes, and it is almost unbearable to read. He wanted to treat them as children, to give them the best land there was, to hear them call him Father.

A grieving God. Scripture is not embarrassed to show God like this. How can I give you up, O Ephraim?, he says through Hosea; My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hos 11:8). Whatever else the judgment in this book is, it is not the cold act of a God who never wanted anything else.

As a treacherous wife leaves her husband. And verse 20 ends with the marriage picture again. Not a tenant breaking a lease, but a wife walking out. The offence is measured by the intimacy it violated, which is why sin against God is never merely rule-breaking.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. "Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice on the bare heights. The bare heights were the scene of the idolatry in verse 2. Now the same hills carry a different sound: weeping. The place of the sin becomes the place of the sorrow over it. And the cause is named in the right order: they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. The crooked road is the symptom; the forgetting is the disease.

I will heal your faithlessness. This is the gospel of this chapter. God promises not merely to forgive the faithlessness, but to heal it. He treats the disloyalty as a disease in his people rather than only a debt against himself, and he undertakes the cure.

That is the only reason anyone returns at all. If the invitation were simply "come back and do better", it would sink the very people it calls, who have already proved they cannot. The God who is wronged will himself restore their ability to love him, and for the Christian reader that healing is the work of the Spirit he has given, who pours God's love into the heart and makes a faithless people steady (Ezek 36:26-27; Rom 5:5).

Behold, we come to you. And they answer. The ESV notes that a delusion is in Hebrew "commotion": all that noise on the hilltops, and nothing in it. Repentance always includes seeing that what we left God for was worthless. And they put their hope in a new place: Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel. Not in the hills, not in the alliances, not in a better religious programme, but in a person. It is the confession Jonah made from inside the fish, Salvation belongs to the LORD! (Jonah 2:9), and it is where every true return ends up.

verseByVerse.quote: "But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shameful thing. The confession is complete and it is costly. The shameful thing is a scornful name for Baal, the Hebrew word for shame put where the idol's name would go (11:13 sets the two side by side). They add up what idolatry took: the livestock, the harvests, the children given to Molech. Sin is finally accounted for not as pleasure but as loss.

Let us lie down in our shame. Set let us lie down in our shame beside verse 3, you refuse to be ashamed. The capacity to blush has come back. In a returning people shame is not despair; it is the sign of a conscience coming back to life.

We and our fathers. And they do not minimise: we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, the exact reverse of the people who said I am innocent in chapter 2 (2:35). This turn comes after the promise to heal, not before it; the kindness is what makes the confession possible. Nor does the returning life become flawless afterwards. The obedience Israel never gave, Christ gave in his people's place, and it is counted as theirs (Rom 5:19), so each new failure has the same way back as this one: confession and the mercy God promised.

3.title: Return, Faithless Israel: I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
3.overview:
The law says a wife who has left her husband for another cannot return, yet God asks his adulterous people, would you return to me? (v. 1). The hills show where they have been, the rains have been withheld, and they have lost the ability to blush (vv. 2-3). They still use affectionate words about God while doing all the evil they can (vv. 4-5).

In Josiah's days God contrasts two sisters: faithless Israel, whom he divorced and exiled, and treacherous Judah, who watched it happen, did the same, and returned only in pretence (vv. 6-10). So Israel is judged the more righteous of the two (v. 11), and the call goes north: Return, faithless Israel, on one condition: Only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12-13).

God promises a remnant, faithful shepherds, a city that is itself his throne, and a reunited people (vv. 14-18). He speaks of how he longed to be called Father, promises I will heal your faithlessness, and the people come back confessing their sin (vv. 19-25).
3.theology:
The invitation to return goes beyond what the law allows (v. 1; Deut 24:1-4): grace opens a door justice had shut, at a cost only the cross explains. Religious language and partial reform are not repentance (vv. 4-5, 10), and those who know more are more to blame (v. 11).

The one condition of return is honest acknowledgement of guilt (v. 13; Joel 2:12-13; 1 John 1:9).

God gathers a remnant one by one (v. 14), gives shepherds after his own heart (v. 15; Acts 13:22; Eph 4:11), and will make the ark unnecessary because the presence it signified has come (vv. 16-17). God promises to heal faithlessness, not merely pardon it (v. 22), and the confession of vv. 24-25 follows that promise rather than earning it.
3.examples: The chapter's pictures are easy to carry away: a door the law had bolted, opened by love; a face that has forgotten how to blush; Judah in a front-row seat at her sister's funeral, learning nothing. They warn against a reform that is genuine at the top and never reaches the heart, and they steady anyone discouraged when revival comes one from a city and two from a family.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>"If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — If You Return, Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A true return is to God himself, with idols put away and oaths sworn in truth, and it opens blessing to the nations (vv. 1-2). Judah is told to break up its fallow ground and circumcise its heart, before wrath burns (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Real return is to a person, not to a programme, and it reaches the heart or it is not return at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver, and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To me you should return. Chapter 3 ended with the people saying Behold, we come to you (3:22). Chapter 4 tests it. The sentence turns on a single phrase: to me you should return. Not to religion, not to the temple, not to better behaviour. To me.

And do not waver. It is possible to reform a life without returning to God, and the two look alike for a while. The conditions given are concrete: remove the idols, and do not waver: no half-return, no shrine kept in the garden just in case.

As the LORD lives. The oath formula As the LORD lives was the ordinary way to swear in Israel, and it was being said constantly by people serving other gods. God attaches three conditions: in truth, in justice, and in righteousness. His name on the lips of someone living a lie is not devotion; it is perjury.

Nations shall bless themselves in him. Look where it leads. If Israel returns honestly, nations shall bless themselves in him. That is God’s promise to Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through him (Gen 12:3), surfacing in a sermon about repentance. A people genuinely right with God becomes the means of blessing to everyone else. The world has more at stake in the church's repentance than it knows.

The gospel beforehand. Paul calls that promise to Abraham the gospel beforehand, fulfilled when the nations are justified by faith in Abraham's offspring, who is Christ (Gal 3:8, 16). Israel's honest return was always meant to open onto that wider blessing, and in Christ it does.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Break up your fallow ground. Fallow ground is land left unploughed so long it has hardened over. It is not barren; it is compacted. Seed thrown on it bounces. The command is not to sow harder but to break the ground first. Hosea said it too: Break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD (Hos 10:12).

Sow not among thorns. Many people are trying to sow good seed on hard ground: more services, more resolutions, more reading, on a heart that has not been broken up in years. And sow not among thorns: clearing what chokes the seed is part of the work, as the parable of the sower says of cares and riches.

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD. Circumcision was the mark in the body that a man belonged to God’s covenant people, and every man in Judah had it. The mark of belonging is worthless if the heart is untouched.

Who circumcises the heart? Here is a difficulty the whole Bible answers. The people are commanded to circumcise their own hearts. In Deuteronomy God promises, the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deut 30:6), and in this book he will promise to write his law on it (31:33). Both are true: God commands what only he can give, and the command is how people come to ask him for it. Paul completes it: a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom 2:29), and it is done in Christ, a circumcision made without hands (Col 2:11). So the Christian does not break up his own heart by willpower; the Spirit now in him does the ploughing through the word. Where his heart is still hard in places, as it will be, Christ's own wholehearted obedience is counted as his (Phil 3:9), and the way back is confession, not despair.

How do I break up hard ground? Fallow ground is usually not one great sin but a corner of life you stopped letting God near. Find the field. Ask where you have grown hard: the subject you change when it comes up in a sermon, the relationship you have quietly written off, the habit you no longer even call sin. Pray, Search me, O God, and know my heart! (Ps 139:23). Turn the soil with the word. Read a passage that speaks to that very area, slowly, and let it say what it says. Name it to God plainly. Hardness thaws in confession, not in vague regret: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Pull one thorn. Cancel the subscription, make the call, close the tab. Let others in. We are to exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). None of this earns a soft heart. It is how you ask for one, from the God who has promised, I will give you a new heart (Ezek 36:26), and who ploughs gently because his Son was broken for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Alarm from the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trumpet sounds and God brings disaster from the north (vv. 5-13), yet even as the besiegers close in, Jerusalem is called to wash her heart and be saved (vv. 14-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is announced in detail, the false comfort is exposed, and in the middle of the siege the door is still open.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I bring disaster from the north. The tone changes without warning, like an air-raid siren in the middle of a sermon. These were the orders given when an invader crossed the border: families in the open country left their farms for the walled towns, and a standard, a signal pole raised on a height, pointed the refugees toward Zion. And the terrible clause in the middle of the panic: for I bring disaster from the north. The invasion is not an accident of history that God will use. He is bringing it.

The call fulfilled. This is the vision of Jeremiah's call arriving on schedule. As a young man he had been shown a boiling pot and told, Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land (1:14). What was a picture then is a trumpet now. God's warnings have dates attached.

verseByVerse.quote: A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant. For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A destroyer of nations has set out. Nebuchadnezzar is never named; he is simply a destroyer of nations who has set out. This is not a threat about what might happen if things do not improve. It has started.

Lament and wail. The right response to the news is not a strategy meeting but mourning. There is a kind of trouble that calls for grief before it calls for plans, and a church that has lost the ability to lament will meet such trouble with activity instead.

Has not turned back from us. And the pronoun at the end matters: has not turned back from us. The prophet does not stand outside the verdict pointing: he counts himself among the people under it.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Courage shall fail both king and officials. The four groups again: king, officials, priests, prophets. Not one of them will have anything to say. The prophets, in particular, will be astounded: the men who had been predicting peace will be the most surprised people in the city.

Surely you have utterly deceived this people. Jeremiah's protest is startling, and the Bible records it without softening it. He hears the message of the official prophets, It shall be well with you, and he lays the responsibility at God's door.

Does God deceive? Not as Scripture teaching that God lies. God's own answer comes later in the book: he never sent those prophets, and they have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (6:14). But the prophet feels something real here: God sometimes judges people by giving them what they insist on. When people insist on comfortable preaching, God may let them have it, and the comfortable preaching becomes part of the judgment. The sermon you most want to hear may be the most dangerous one available.

A lying spirit. Scripture shows that kind of judgment elsewhere. When Ahab wanted only favourable prophets, Micaiah saw heaven's court decide it, and told the king, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets (1 Kgs 22:23). And Paul says of those who refuse the truth, God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false (2 Thess 2:11). God does not deceive the honest. He hands those who wanted to be deceived over to what they chose.

Protest as faith. Jeremiah says this to God, not about him behind his back. Honest protest addressed to God is a form of faith; the psalms are full of it.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them." Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not to winnow or cleanse. A farmer wants a light breeze to winnow grain, separating wheat from chaff. What is coming is the desert wind that strips the field bare: not to winnow or cleanse. This is not corrective discipline any more. It is judgment.

Woe to us, for we are ruined! Dust on the horizon like a storm front, chariots like a whirlwind, horses faster than eagles, and then the voice of the people themselves, the first time they see it clearly: woe to us, for we are ruined!

Swifter than eagles. Habakkuk describes the same army in the same terms: Their horses are swifter than leopards, and their horsemen fly like an eagle swift to devour (Hab 1:8). Two prophets watching one invasion from different vantage points, and neither sees any way to outrun it.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you? For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may be saved. In the middle of the siege report, an invitation. The army is on the road and God is still saying that you may be saved. Mercy runs later into the story than anyone expects.

Wash your heart from evil. And the diagnosis again goes to the inside: wash your heart, and the question, how long will wicked thoughts lodge within you? The word suggests a guest who has settled in. Sins that were once visitors become residents, and the difference is how long they were allowed to stay.

The call to wash echoes Isaiah's opening sermon, Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes (Isa 1:16), and like every such command it drives the hearer to the one who can actually do it. Paul writes to converts who had been everything this chapter describes: But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Cor 6:11).

From Dan and from Mount Ephraim. Dan is the northern border; Ephraim is the hill country just above Jerusalem. The report is a relay of dispatches as the enemy moves south, and the distance is closing between sentences.

Warn the nations. The surrounding peoples are told too. What happens to Jerusalem is not a private family matter; the whole region is meant to learn from it what kind of God the God of Israel is.

verseByVerse.quote: Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD. Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like keepers of a field. A quiet, awful image. Besieging armies ring the city the way watchmen sit around a field at harvest: patient, settled, waiting for what is inside to be ready.

Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. The verdict is the one already given in 2:17: they have brought this on themselves. It needs saying plainly, because people will do almost anything to avoid it. Not every disaster is deserved; the book of Job is in the Bible to prevent that conclusion. But some are, and pretending otherwise makes repentance impossible. It has reached your very heart, the place the whole chapter has been pointing to.

What one sows. Paul states the principle for the church without exception: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7). The bitterness in Judah's mouth was the taste of her own harvest.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet is in anguish as crash follows crash (vv. 19-21), and God names the cause: a people foolish, clever at evil, who do not know him (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who preaches the judgment is broken by it; God's word is never delivered from a safe distance.

verseByVerse.quote: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war. Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?
verseByVerse.commentary:
My anguish, my anguish! This is why Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet. He is not reading a bulletin. He is doubled over. He announces the disaster, and the announcement tears him apart. There is no satisfaction in him at being proved right, no relish in the doom of people who have dismissed him for years.

No relish in judgment. That is the test of anyone who handles the severe parts of Scripture. Hell, judgment and wrath can be preached with a certain enjoyment, and when they are, something has gone badly wrong. The prophet who tells the truth about judgment should be the one most obviously wounded by it.

My heart is beating wildly. He can feel his own heartbeat; he cannot sit still or stay quiet. He calls the ruined homes my tents, my curtains. These are not other people's losses to him. And then the cry every sufferer knows: How long?

He wept over it. And that anguish points beyond Jeremiah. Six centuries later another man came toward the same city, which again lay under sentence, and he wept over it, saying, Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! (Luke 19:41-42). The prophet's breaking heart was a preview of the heart of God made flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: "For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They know me not. God answers the prophet’s How long? with a diagnosis. The problem is not intelligence; it is that they know me not. And then the bitter irony: they are experts at evil and amateurs at good. Every culture has this shape: brilliant at what harms it, helpless at what would heal it.

Wise as to what is good. Paul's hope for the Roman church is the precise reversal: I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil (Rom 16:19). Judah had it backwards, and the gospel does not simply make people cleverer. It turns their competence the right way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — I Looked on the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four times he looks and sees creation undone (vv. 23-26). The land will be desolate, yet God will not make a full end (vv. 27-28). The city paints her face for lovers who seek her life, and cries out like a woman in labour (vv. 29-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is creation running backwards, and even there God sets a limit: not a full end.

verseByVerse.quote: I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light. I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro. I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled. I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without form and void. Four times Jeremiah says I looked, and what he sees is Genesis played backwards. The first phrase is quoted from the creation account: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2). Then God said, “Let there be light.” Here the light has gone out.

All the hills moved to and fro. Day three of creation gave dry land; here the land itself is unsteady. The earth staggers like a drunken man, says Isaiah of the same day (Isa 24:20).

There was no man. Days five and six are undone: the birds gone, and humanity, the crown of the creation week, simply absent.

Sin unmakes the world. This passage is terrifying, and it makes a theological point that no amount of moralising could. Sin is not a private matter between a person and God with no wider consequence. It unmakes the world. Creation itself is dragged down by it, groaning, subjected to futility and waiting to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:20-21).

Which is why salvation in the Bible is never merely the rescue of souls out of a doomed world. It is new heavens and a new earth, and the same God who spoke the first light will speak again.
verseByVerse.note: The four visions run the creation week in reverse: light, land, people and birds, and last the fruitful land with its cities.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end. "For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet I will not make a full end. These words keep this book from being despair: yet I will not make a full end. They will be repeated (5:10, 18). However far the judgment goes, God draws a line beyond which it will not go, and he draws it himself. A remnant, a surviving few, will come through, and through them the promises will run on.

Days cut short. Jesus says the same of the worst days: if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short (Matt 24:22).

I have not relented. Three verbs of settled intent: spoken, purposed, not relented. Elsewhere God does relent when people turn (18:7-8), which is exactly why this is so grave. The door in verse 14 is open, and the people are not walking through it.

verseByVerse.quote: At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them. And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In vain you beautify yourself. With the army at the gates, the city is doing her make-up: scarlet, gold, painted eyes, still trying to attract the very nations whose armies are coming. The alliances she trusted have turned murderous, and she is still dressing for them. Painting the eyes with dark kohl was what Jezebel did as Jehu rode into Jezreel (2 Kgs 9:30), and it did not save her either. People do this. Faced with ruin, we reach for the thing that ruined us.

A woman in labor. The chapter ends with the cry of a woman in her first labour: pain that cannot be postponed, and hands stretched out for help. In Scripture that image is not always the end: labour pains lead somewhere, and Paul uses the same picture for a creation in the pains of childbirth (Rom 8:22). But nothing of that comfort is offered here. The chapter closes on the cry, and leaves the reader inside it.

4.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
4.overview:
If Israel returns, it must be to God himself, putting away idols and swearing truly, so that the nations are blessed (vv. 1-2). Judah is told to break up hard ground rather than sow among thorns, and to circumcise their hearts (vv. 3-4).

Then the alarm sounds: an army is coming from the north, every leader's courage fails, and a scorching wind arrives to judge, not to winnow (vv. 5-13). Even so, God calls Jerusalem to wash her heart and be saved (vv. 14-18).

The prophet breaks down at what he must announce, and God names the cause: a people clever at evil who do not know him (vv. 19-22). In four visions creation is undone (vv. 23-26), yet God will not make a full end (v. 27), and the chapter closes on the cry of a city in labour (vv. 28-31).
4.theology:
Repentance is return to God himself, not reform of behaviour (v. 1), and it must reach the heart: the command to circumcise the heart (v. 4) is what God elsewhere promises to do (Deut 30:6; Jer 31:33) and does in Christ.

God governs the invading army: he brings the disaster (v. 6). Comfortable preaching can itself be part of judgment (v. 10; 6:14). Mercy is still offered while judgment is arriving (v. 14), and honest protest may be addressed to God (v. 10).

Sin unmakes the world: judgment is creation running backwards (vv. 23-26; Gen 1:2; Rom 8:20-22), so salvation must include a renewed creation. And God limits his own judgment: yet I will not make a full end (v. 27).
4.examples: Some hearts are like ground so hard that good seed simply bounces, and some lives carry the outward mark of belonging to God’s people with nothing beneath it in the heart. Wicked thoughts arrive as visitors and, if they are allowed to stay, become residents. And when ruin comes, people still reach for what ruined them, like a city doing her make-up while the army stands at the gate.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her.<sup>2</sup>Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely.<sup>3</sup>O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.<sup>4</sup>Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.<sup>5</sup>I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds.<sup>6</sup>Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.<sup>7</sup>"How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of whores.<sup>8</sup>They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife.<sup>9</sup>Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD; and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?<sup>10</sup>"Go up through her vine rows and destroy, but make not a full end; strip away her branches, for they are not the LORD's.<sup>11</sup>For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous to me, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>They have spoken falsely of the LORD and have said, 'He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine.<sup>13</sup>The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them. Thus shall it be done to them!'"<sup>14</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them.<sup>15</sup>Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD. It is an enduring nation; it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say.<sup>16</sup>Their quiver is like an open tomb; they are all mighty warriors.<sup>17</sup>They shall eat up your harvest and your food; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; your fortified cities in which you trust they shall beat down with the sword."<sup>18</sup>"But even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make a full end of you.<sup>19</sup>And when your people say, 'Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' you shall say to them, 'As you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.'"<sup>20</sup>Declare this in the house of Jacob; proclaim it in Judah:<sup>21</sup>"Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not.<sup>22</sup>Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass; though the waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass over it.<sup>23</sup>But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away.<sup>24</sup>They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and keeps for us the weeks appointed for the harvest.'<sup>25</sup>Your iniquities have turned these away, and your sins have kept good from you.<sup>26</sup>For wicked men are found among my people; they lurk like fowlers lying in wait. They set a trap; they catch men.<sup>27</sup>Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich;<sup>28</sup>they have grown fat and sleek. They know no bounds in deeds of evil; they judge not with justice the cause of the fatherless, to make it prosper, and they do not defend the rights of the needy.<sup>29</sup>Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?"<sup>30</sup>An appalling and horrible thing has happened in the land:<sup>31</sup>the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Search the Streets for One Just Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God offers to pardon Jerusalem for one just man, and the search fails: the city swears falsely and has hardened its face (vv. 1-3). The great are no better than the poor, and the predators wait (vv. 4-6). How can I pardon you? God asks a people he fed to the full (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God offers to spare a whole city for one just man, and the search fails.

verseByVerse.quote: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her. Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See if you can find a man. God sends Jeremiah on an errand through the capital, and the terms are extraordinary. Find one man who does justice and seeks truth, and the whole city will be pardoned.

Starting at one. Abraham once bargained God down over Sodom, from fifty righteous to ten: For the sake of ten I will not destroy it (Gen 18:32). Here God does not wait to be bargained with. He starts at one, and he offers it about his own city, with the temple in it and a king of David's line on the throne.

The search fails. The search fails. Ezekiel was given the same errand with the same result: I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none (Ezek 22:30). And the psalm had already said why: They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one (Ps 14:3).

One just man, not spared. Hold on to the shape of this verse, because the gospel is built on it. God is willing to spare a city for the sake of one righteous man. There was no such man in Jerusalem. So God provided one, and he did not spare him (Rom 8:32). Because the one just man, Christ, was not spared, the city of God, his people, is spared.

Yet they swear falsely. Zephaniah, prophesying in the same years, pictured God searching Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph 1:12), and what the search finds is not a shortage of religion but of honesty. The name of God is still in every mouth. Religious language survives long after religion has died. Using God's name to guarantee a lie is not a sign of faith; it is the very sin being charged. The city was short of truth, and Jesus names what God is looking for in the same terms: the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him (John 4:23).

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They felt no anguish. Three refusals, and the middle one is the most frightening: struck, and they felt no anguish. Pain is a mercy when it makes us stop. What is described here is a people who took the blows and felt nothing, whose faces have gone harder than rock. Hardness is not caused by one great sin; it is built by many small refusals.

Do not your eyes look for truth? Jeremiah frames the complaint carefully: O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? He appeals to God's own character. God is not fooled by the oath formula; the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7). Amos had watched the same pattern well over a century before, with a refrain after every disaster God sent: yet you did not return to me (Amos 4:6). Discipline that is received and not heeded does not soften a heart; it hardens it further.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God. I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are only the poor. Jeremiah tries to rescue his own people with a very modern explanation. The problem is education and circumstance; these are the poor, and nobody taught them. So he goes uptown, to the educated and the powerful, and finds exactly the same thing: They all alike had broken the yoke.

They all alike had broken the yoke. The verdict dismantles a comfortable theory. Sin is not a poverty problem or an education problem, and the well-taught are not less guilty but more.

Doesn’t education make people better? It is one of the deepest hopes of the modern world, and an honourable one. Socrates argued that no one does wrong knowingly: show a person the good clearly enough and he will choose it. Teach more, and people will behave better. Jeremiah ran the experiment in Jerusalem, and the great were no better than the poor. Modern history has run it again. Of the officials who met at Wannsee in January 1942 to organise the murder of Europe’s Jews, more than half held doctorates. But knowing the good and loving it are different things, and Paul puts the gap in one sentence: For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing (Rom 7:19). (On where that evil comes from, see the note on Genesis 3:1–7.) If education could save us, the gospel would be good news only for the clever. Instead it comes to the poor and the great on the same terms, because what we need is not better information but a new heart, and a Saviour who knows the worst about us and loves us still.

A leopard is watching their cities. The leopard is the worst image: not hunting, watching, waiting by the gate for whoever steps outside. Hosea used the same animals and put God himself behind them: So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way (Hos 13:7). The predators are not random; the verse gives the reason, because their transgressions are many, and the wild beasts outside the walls are God’s answer to the rebellion inside them.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of whores. They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD; and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can I pardon you? This is not a rhetorical shrug. It is the question of a judge who wants to acquit and cannot find grounds. God is not looking for an excuse to condemn; he is looking for a way to forgive, and the chapter has just shown that the way is not in them.

When I fed them to the full. The sequence matters: when God fed them to the full, they committed adultery. The generosity came first, and the betrayal was fuelled by it. Full stomachs and idle afternoons have ruined many who would have stood firm in hunger.

Jeshurun grew fat. Moses had predicted exactly this in his last song: But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him (Deut 32:15). And the first charge in the verse is the root of the rest: they have sworn by those who are no gods. A man who breaks faith with God will not long keep faith with his neighbour.

Each neighing for his neighbor’s wife. The image of verse 8, well-fed stallions neighing, is coarse on purpose. Men with time, money and appetite, behaving like animals in a field, and the object is specifically his neighbor's wife: the woman down the street, whose husband they know. Sin here is not abstract; it has an address.

Shall I not punish them? The question of verse 9, Shall I not punish them for these things?, will be asked again word for word in verse 29. It deserves an honest answer. A God who looked at predatory men, betrayed marriages and abandoned children and did nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent. Wrath is not the opposite of love. Indifference is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vine is stripped but not ended (vv. 10-11). The people say God will do nothing and the prophets are wind (vv. 12-13), so God makes his word fire and brings a nation of unknown speech to devour everything they trust (vv. 14-17). Even then he will not make a full end, and the exile is given its reason (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Practical atheism, the belief that God will do nothing, is answered by a judgment shaped exactly like the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up through her vine rows and destroy, but make not a full end; strip away her branches, for they are not the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But make not a full end. The vineyard of chapter 2 is pruned savagely, and the invaders, who think they are looting, are being given limits they know nothing about: make not a full end. Even the destruction is on a leash.

For they are not the LORD’s. And look at the reason given for what is cut away: for they are not the LORD's. The branches stripped off are the ones that were never his. Jesus describes his Father as the same kind of vinedresser: Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away (John 15:2). Judgment removes what does not belong; it does not uproot the vine.

verseByVerse.quote: For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous to me, declares the LORD. They have spoken falsely of the LORD and have said, 'He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine. The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them. Thus shall it be done to them!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will do nothing. Here is the creed of Judah, and of most people who have never formally denied anything: He will do nothing. Not “There is no God”. Simply that he is not going to act, so his opinion need not affect any decision. It is atheism that keeps its religion. Ask what difference it would make to tomorrow if that sentence were true; for many of us the honest answer is very little.

The same creed elsewhere. Zephaniah heard the same creed: those who say in their hearts, 'The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill' (Zeph 1:12). And Peter hears its modern form in scoffers who ask Where is the promise of his coming? because all things are continuing as they were (2 Pet 3:4). Delay is mistaken for absence, in every generation.

The prophets will become wind. And these men call the preachers wind. Jeremiah heard this about himself for forty years. The insult contains its own answer, which comes in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My words in your mouth a fire. They called his words wind. God calls them fire. Later Jeremiah will say the word is a burning fire shut up in my bones when he tries not to speak it (20:9), and God will ask whether his word is not like fire, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (23:29).

The word of God does something wherever it lands. A congregation that treats preaching as background noise is not thereby safe from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD. It is an enduring nation; it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say. Their quiver is like an open tomb; they are all mighty warriors. They shall eat up your harvest and your food; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; your fortified cities in which you trust they shall beat down with the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A nation whose language you do not know. The detail that would frighten an ancient city most: you will not be able to talk to them. No negotiation, no pleading, no diplomacy: soldiers in your streets whose orders you cannot understand.

The covenant curse. It was the curse Moses had written into the covenant centuries earlier, almost word for word: The LORD will bring a nation against you from far away, a nation whose language you do not understand (Deut 28:49). Nothing in Jeremiah's warning was new. Judah had simply stopped believing the old words meant what they said.

They shall eat up. Four times they shall eat up, and the list moves from food to children to livelihood to defences. Everything a family works for, in order. And the last phrase names the real casualty: your fortified cities in which you trust. What falls is not only the wall but the thing the heart was leaning on.

Their quiver is like an open tomb. One image sits before the list: Their quiver is like an open tomb. Every arrow in it is a grave already dug.

verseByVerse.quote: "But even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make a full end of you. And when your people say, 'Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' you shall say to them, 'As you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Why has the LORD our God done all these things? The limit is restated, I will not make a full end, and then God writes the answer the exiles will need. They will ask why, and the answer is to be given plainly: the punishment has the same shape as the sin. You served foreign gods at home; now you will serve foreigners abroad. God lets the sin itself become the punishment, so that its true nature is finally visible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — Eyes That Do Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people with eyes that do not see will not fear the God whose sand holds back the sea (vv. 20-22). Their stubborn hearts never thank him for the rain (vv. 23-25); the rich trap their neighbours and refuse justice to the fatherless (vv. 26-29); and the people love the lies their prophets tell (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The sea obeys its limits and the people do not; and the lies they are told are the lies they want.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare this in the house of Jacob; proclaim it in Judah: "Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not. Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass; though the waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who have eyes, but see not. The eyes and ears work; what fails is the seeing and hearing. This is the condition Isaiah was sent to describe and Jesus applied to his own generation: people who look straight at the evidence and see nothing. It is not a failure of intelligence but of the will.

Disciples too. Jesus put the same question to his own disciples when they missed what he had just done in front of them: Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? (Mark 8:18). The failure can live in people who follow him.

Do you not fear me? Stand on a beach and watch the Atlantic throw itself at the shore, and then notice what stops it: sand. Not granite cliffs, but grains. The sea has more power than every army in history and it turns back at a line of sand, because God drew the line. Israel’s neighbours told stories of gods who had to battle the sea as a monster of chaos (in the Canaanite myths Baal fights Yam, whose name means “Sea”); the LORD does not fight it at all, he simply sets its limit. The most violent thing in creation keeps the boundary God set, and his people will not.

Thus far shall you come. God reminds Job of the same boundary, speaking of the sea: and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed' (Job 38:11). The ocean hears that sentence and stops. Judah had heard far more, and kept going.

verseByVerse.quote: But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away. They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and keeps for us the weeks appointed for the harvest.' Your iniquities have turned these away, and your sins have kept good from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do not say in their hearts. Look at what they fail to say, and where: in their hearts. And it is about rain: the autumn rain to soften the ground, the spring rain to swell the grain, the weeks kept for harvest, God's fingerprints on the ordinary year. Gratitude for weather is a better test of faith than most people expect.

The witness of the rain. Paul used exactly this argument with pagans who had never read a page of Scripture: God did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons (Acts 14:17). If the rain testifies to the Gentiles, it testifies all the more to the people who were told who sends it.

Your sins have kept good from you. Not every hardship is caused by sin, and this book will not let us say that it is. But some good things are absent from a life because sin has kept them out, and it takes honesty to consider whether that is the case.

verseByVerse.quote: For wicked men are found among my people; they lurk like fowlers lying in wait. They set a trap; they catch men. Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek. They know no bounds in deeds of evil; they judge not with justice the cause of the fatherless, to make it prosper, and they do not defend the rights of the needy. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They lurk like fowlers. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, but the picture is clear enough. Bird-catchers crouch, wait and spring a net, and what they catch is men, among my people. Their houses are cages full of trapped birds, and that is how the wealth was made. Therefore they have become great and rich: their prosperity is evidence against them, not a sign of God’s blessing.

The fatherless and the needy. And the two groups they refuse are always the same two: the fatherless and the needy, the people with no one to take their case. God notices who cannot get a hearing, and he counts the failure to defend them as a deed of evil in its own right, not merely an omission.

To make it prosper. The phrase to make it prosper matters too. Justice for the fatherless was meant to be active: taking up their case until it came out well. That is the God of Israel's own way with the helpless, who took up his people's cause when they were slaves in Egypt (Deut 10:18-19). For the Christian the same Spirit who brought him from death to life now moves him to take up such cases, and where he has walked past them, as everyone has, there is forgiveness to come back to and the help of the Spirit to begin again.

The question of verse 9 returns unchanged, now with the evidence assembled.

verseByVerse.quote: An appalling and horrible thing has happened in the land: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
My people love to have it so. The surprise is where the blame lands. The preachers lie. The clergy take their orders from the liars. And then: my people love to have it so.

Supply and demand. The false prophets are not an occupying force. They are supplying a demand. A people who want to be told that everything is fine will always find someone to tell them. That is as true of a modern church choosing its teachers, or a person choosing what to read and listen to, as it was in Jerusalem.

What will you do when the end comes? The last line is the question the whole book presses: what will you do when the end comes? Comfortable religion is judged by what it leaves you holding at the end, and the question is best answered before the end asks it.

5.title: Search Her Squares: Find One Just Man
5.overview:
God sends Jeremiah through Jerusalem to find one man who does justice and seeks truth, promising to pardon the whole city for his sake, and the search fails among poor and great alike (vv. 1-9).

Because the people say He will do nothing, God makes his words fire and brings a nation whose language they cannot understand, though even then he will not make a full end (vv. 10-19).

The sea keeps the boundary God set, but this people does not: they never thank him for the rain, they trap the needy, and they love the lies their prophets tell (vv. 20-31).
5.theology:
God offers to pardon a city for one righteous man and finds none (v. 1; Ezek 22:30; Ps 14:3), and the gospel answers that search with the one just man God provided. Sin is not a matter of class or education (vv. 4-5).

God's wrath is the response of love to those who prey on others and betray them, not the opposite of love (vv. 9, 29). His word is fire, never without effect (v. 14; 23:29). Judgment is limited by God himself (vv. 10, 18) and shaped to fit the sin (v. 19).

Creation obeys the boundaries God sets and his people do not (v. 22). False teaching flourishes because people want it (v. 31), and comfortable religion is tested by what it leaves a person holding at the end.
5.examples: The theory that better education would fix the human heart is tested among the educated and powerful, and it fails. He will do nothing is atheism that keeps its religion: God is confessed and then ignored. It is common among people who would never deny God aloud. And false teachers rarely impose themselves: they supply what a people already loves to hear.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin, from the midst of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms out of the north, and great destruction.<sup>2</sup>The lovely and delicately bred I will destroy, the daughter of Zion.<sup>3</sup>Shepherds with their flocks shall come against her; they shall pitch their tents around her; they shall pasture, each in his place.<sup>4</sup>"Prepare war against her; arise, and let us attack at noon! Woe to us, for the day declines, for the shadows of evening lengthen!<sup>5</sup>Arise, and let us attack by night and destroy her palaces!"<sup>6</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts: "Cut down her trees; cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her.<sup>7</sup>As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil; violence and destruction are heard within her; sickness and wounds are ever before me.<sup>8</sup>Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land."<sup>9</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts: "They shall glean thoroughly as a vine the remnant of Israel; like a grape gatherer pass your hand again over its branches."<sup>10</sup>To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it.<sup>11</sup>Therefore I am full of the wrath of the LORD; I am weary of holding it in. "Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged.<sup>12</sup>Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.<sup>13</sup>"For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely.<sup>14</sup>They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.<sup>15</sup>Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I punish them, they shall be overthrown," says the LORD.<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it.'<sup>17</sup>I set watchmen over you, saying, 'Pay attention to the sound of the trumpet!' But they said, 'We will not pay attention.'<sup>18</sup>Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them.<sup>19</sup>Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.<sup>20</sup>What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me.<sup>21</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"<sup>22</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth.<sup>23</sup>They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!"<sup>24</sup>We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor.<sup>25</sup>Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side.<sup>26</sup>O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.<sup>27</sup>"I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways.<sup>28</sup>They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly.<sup>29</sup>The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed.<sup>30</sup>Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alarm sounds again and enemy commanders camp round the city like shepherds round a pasture, eager to attack (vv. 1-5). God orders the siege against a city full of oppression, yet still warns her (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The siege is described in detail and the warning is still open: even here God says Be warned, not farewell.

verseByVerse.quote: Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin, from the midst of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms out of the north, and great destruction. The lovely and delicately bred I will destroy, the daughter of Zion. Shepherds with their flocks shall come against her; they shall pitch their tents around her; they shall pasture, each in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin. Jeremiah was from Benjamin, and his own people are the first told to run. Tekoa and Beth-haccherem, on the hills south of the city, were beacon stations: the warning system is working perfectly, and it is carrying bad news. There is a pun as well: blow the trumpet is tiqʿu in Hebrew, and it sounds like Tekoa.

Blow the trumpet in Tekoa. Tekoa had a history. It was the home town of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa (Amos 1:1), the herdsman God sent north with a warning to Israel more than a century earlier. Israel ignored him and was destroyed. Now the beacon on Tekoa's hill is lit for Judah.

The lovely and delicately bred. The ESV notes another possible rendering, "I have likened the daughter of Zion to the loveliest pasture", which fits the shepherds in the next verse. Either way the contrast is between what she is, lovely and sheltered, and what is about to happen to her. These shepherds are enemy commanders, their flocks are armies, and each takes his own section of wall the way a shepherd takes his own patch of grass.
