verseByVerse.note: Beth-haccherem means “house of the vineyard”; it is usually placed on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Prepare war against her; arise, and let us attack at noon! Woe to us, for the day declines, for the shadows of evening lengthen! Arise, and let us attack by night and destroy her palaces!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us attack by night. Now we hear the soldiers talking among themselves, and it is chilling because of the eagerness. Frustrated that the light is going, they decide to attack at night instead.

Whose orders? There is a gap between what the soldiers think and what is really happening. They believe they are pursuing their own ambition; the very next verse gives the orders from above: For thus says the LORD of hosts. Men who think they are acting entirely on their own account are often carrying out a sentence they know nothing about. And their target is precise, her palaces, the grand houses of the people the next verse accuses of oppression.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: "Cut down her trees; cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her. As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil; violence and destruction are heard within her; sickness and wounds are ever before me. Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. The orders come from God, not from the invading general. The trees around the city are felled for the siege ramp, the mound of earth raised against the wall: the beginning of the end. And the charge is oppression: not idolatry this time, but the treatment of people. In the prophets, worship and justice are never separated for long.

So she keeps fresh her evil. A good well keeps its water fresh; Jerusalem keeps her evil fresh, constantly replenished. And sickness and wounds are ever before me: God is not detached from what the city does to its weak. He is looking at the injuries, continuously.

Be warned, O Jerusalem. After all that, a warning rather than a verdict: Be warned. The siege ramp is going up and God is still speaking as though it might be stopped. This is the pattern of the book, and it repays noticing every time, because it tells us what God is like.

Lest I turn from you in disgust. The danger named before the ruin is lest I turn from you in disgust. The first and worse thing is God withdrawing himself; the desolation comes second. Hosea put it in one line: Woe to them when I depart from them! (Hos 9:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What remains of Israel will be gleaned, picked over a second time (v. 9); their ears are closed and God's word is scorned (v. 10). The prophet is full of God's wrath (vv. 11-12). Everyone is greedy, and prophet and priest heal the wound lightly with Peace, peace, unable to blush (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: A wound treated lightly is the classic failure of false religion: comfort offered where surgery is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "They shall glean thoroughly as a vine the remnant of Israel; like a grape gatherer pass your hand again over its branches." To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall glean thoroughly. Gleaning is the second pass over a vine, the careful hand going back along branches already picked. Applied to an army it means thoroughness: what the first sweep missed the second will take.

Their ears are uncircumcised. The prophet's despair is practical: who is left to talk to? In chapter 4 the problem was uncircumcised hearts; here it is the ears that are uncircumcised: closed over, so that they cannot listen. And the diagnosis ends with a phrase that should stop any reader: they take no pleasure in it.

They take no pleasure in it. This is the deepest measure of a spiritual condition: not whether a person can argue with the Bible, but whether it gives them any pleasure. A believer's love for the word waxes and wanes, but total distaste for it ought to be taken seriously.

An appetite for the word. The blessed man is the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD (Ps 1:2), and the psalmist says How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Appetite for the word is not a personality trait. It is a sign of life, and it can be asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I am full of the wrath of the LORD; I am weary of holding it in. "Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged. Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am full of the wrath of the LORD. Jeremiah, who wept in chapter 4, is here full of the wrath of the LORD and tired of containing it. A man who feels only anger at a corrupt society has stopped loving it; a man who feels no anger has stopped taking its victims seriously.

Both husband and wife shall be taken. The list that follows spares nobody: children, young men, married couples, the elderly. Judgment on a nation always lands on the whole household, which is one reason it is so grievous and why God delays it so long.

I am weary of holding it in. This is the same exhaustion Jeremiah will confess in his darkest chapter, where the word is a fire shut up in his bones (20:9). He did not choose this message and could not keep it down. And the details of the sentence are the covenant curses coming true: You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it (Deut 28:30), and the same verse foresaw wives taken by other men, as verse 12 says here. Moses had spelled out precisely what these verses announce.

Judgment and the children. Can a just God sweep up children in judgment? The whole nation fell under the judgment it had chosen, and a city’s fall strikes the young with the old. God takes no pleasure in it (Lam 3:33), and the judgment of each soul’s eternal destiny rests with him who does right (Gen 18:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the least to the greatest. Two phrases take in everyone: from the least to the greatest, and from prophet to priest. When the leadership is corrupt there is nowhere left to appeal.

Peace, peace. Verse 14 has been quoted ever since, because it describes a permanent temptation. The wound is real. The treatment is a clean bandage over an infected cut and a reassuring word: Peace, peace.

Why heal lightly? Because it is what the patient wants, because the true diagnosis is unbearable to deliver, and because the healer gets thanked for it in the short term. Micah heard the same men: yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us" (Mic 3:11).

The wound or the feeling. The test for any preaching, counselling or friendship is whether it deals with the wound or only with the feeling about the wound. A gospel that never mentions sin is a bandage over an infection, and its kindness is an illusion that costs the patient everything.

What peace really is. When we say we are at peace, we usually mean we feel calm. The false prophets dealt in that kind of peace: a feeling produced by not looking at the wound. Peace in the Bible, shalom, is first a state of affairs, things actually put right, beginning between us and God. You can feel calm while the infection spreads, and you can have real peace while you still hurt. So God’s peace never comes by ignoring the wound. It came by someone taking it: upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5). The prophets of Jerusalem said the injury was slight; the gospel says it was so deep that the Son of God bore it, and that it is truly healed. This week, when you reach for calm, ask not “Do I feel settled?” but “Is the wound dealt with?” Bring Christ the sin you would rather bandage, name it, and rest in the peace he has made (Rom 5:1). See Peace.

Peace and security. Paul saw the same false peace at the end of history: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman (1 Thess 5:3). The reassurance sounds kindest just before the disaster falls.

verseByVerse.quote: Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I punish them, they shall be overthrown," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not know how to blush. Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No. Not that they refused; they had lost the ability. Shame is a nerve ending, and a conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does. The loss is quiet and is usually mistaken for maturity or confidence.

They shall fall among those who fall. Paul describes the end of the same process: people whose consciences are seared (1 Tim 4:2). And the sentence that follows is flat: they shall fall among those who fall. There will be no special category for religious leaders; the men who assured everyone of peace go down with the people they reassured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — Ask for the Ancient Paths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls his people to ask for the ancient paths and find rest, and they refuse, ignoring the watchmen too (vv. 16-17). The nations are called to witness the fruit of their devices, and costly offerings will not turn it aside (vv. 18-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The old way is not nostalgia but the road that leads home, and refusing it is a decision, not an accident.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it.' I set watchmen over you, saying, 'Pay attention to the sound of the trumpet!' But they said, 'We will not pay attention.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand by the roads, and look. Four commands, and they are the cure for everything this chapter has described. Stand: stop moving long enough to think. Look: consider the roads in front of you. Ask: for the old paths, which means asking someone who knows them. Walk: because knowing the way home and standing at the junction is not the same as going.

The ancient paths. This is not nostalgia for an older decade. The ancient paths are the ways God gave the people he had brought out of Egypt and made his own, older than the fashion of any era. They were never a ladder up to him but the road home with him, and the promise attached is not success but rest: find rest for your souls.

Find rest for your souls. Jesus takes that exact phrase and offers it in his own name: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt 11:29). The ancient path, it turns out, is a person. He walked it without one false step, in the place of people who had said We will not walk in it, and his obedience is counted to those who come to him (Rom 5:19). The walking that follows is not by willpower: those who belong to him walk by the Spirit (Gal 5:16), and when they stray the same voice still calls them back to the road.

Why does more choice leave us less at rest? We live at more crossroads than any generation before us. Careers, cities, partners, beliefs, even identities are now ours to choose, and to keep choosing, and we were promised that this would make us free. In some ways it has. But the psychologist Barry Schwartz, in The Paradox of Choice, gathered evidence that beyond a certain point more options leave people more anxious and less satisfied, always wondering about the road not taken. A life of endless junctions is exhausting, because nothing is ever settled. Jeremiah’s word is neither “choose whatever feels right” nor “never choose at all”. It is ask: there is a good way, older than our moods, and rest is found by walking in it. That sounds like a loss of freedom until you notice who is on the road. The one who offers rest for the soul did not leave us to find the way by ourselves; he came out to the crossroads to fetch us. Rest is not in keeping every option open. It is in belonging to him.

How do I ask for the ancient paths? Take the four verbs into the next real crossroads: a job offer, a move, what to do with money, a marriage under strain. Stand. Do not decide in the rush; take an evening to stop and pray before the momentum chooses for you. Look. Write the roads down honestly, including where each is likely to lead in five years, not just how it feels this week. Ask. Open the Scriptures first, since Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Ps 119:105), and then ask an older believer who has walked that way: Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith (Heb 13:7). The newest advice is not always wrong, but the oldest has been tested. Walk. Once the good way is clear, take the first step this week, while it is still clear. And when you find you have wandered, do not stand at the junction despising yourself. The path is a person, who said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6), and he walks it with you.

We will not pay attention. The refusal itself is not a failure of information. It is a decision. The watchmen are the prophets, whose job was to see trouble early and shout. What they refuse is an alarm, which seems a strange thing to resent until you remember that an alarm wakes people who would rather sleep on.

Refusing him who warns. Hebrews draws the line from this refusal to ours: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven (Heb 12:25). The watchmen of Jeremiah's day spoke for God; the voice now is the Son's.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them. Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit of their devices. The nations are called as witnesses, and the sentence is described as the fruit of their devices: what grew from the seed they planted. God's judgment is often the ripening of what people have themselves sown.

As for my law, they have rejected it. The charge is specific: as for my law, they have rejected it. Judah was not a people who lacked the law but a people who had it and threw it aside.

verseByVerse.quote: What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frankincense that comes from Sheba. Expensive imported incense, the best available, and God says it is no use to him. Frankincense came by caravan from Sheba in south-west Arabia, and fragrant cane, probably brought from as far away as India, was one of the spices of the holy anointing oil (Exod 30:23). The prophets say this repeatedly (I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams, Isa 1:11; I hate, I despise your feasts, Amos 5:21; I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, Hos 6:6), and it is never an attack on worship as such. It is the refusal to accept worship as a substitute for obedience. Generous giving and faithful attendance can both be ways of trying to buy God off.

Stumbling blocks. The road they refused to walk becomes a road they cannot walk: God lays stumbling blocks on it. Grace refused long enough turns into obstacles, and whole families go down together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A cruel nation comes from the north with a sound like the sea, and terror is on every side (vv. 22-26). Jeremiah is made a tester of metals, and the refining fails: Rejected silver they are called (vv. 27-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The metal is tested honestly and fails; only a better refining, and a better price, can save such people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sound of them is like the roaring sea. Sound before sight: an army heard before it is seen, like surf. Cruel and have no mercy is not propaganda; it is the plain character of ancient warfare, and God is telling his people the truth about what is coming rather than letting them imagine a manageable version.

The same words against Babylon. Hold this description in mind, because the book will use it again. Near the end, the same words are turned on Babylon herself: a people from the north, they are cruel and have no mercy, riding against you, O daughter of Babylon! (50:42). The God who sends an army from the north against Zion will, in time, send one against Zion's destroyer. No nation God uses to judge others is itself exempt from judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor. Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side. O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hands fall helpless. For the first time the people are not arguing. The bravado of chapter 5 is gone. It took the sound of that army, roaring like the sea, to silence it.

Terror is on every side. The phrase becomes a refrain in this book, and later a nickname thrown at Jeremiah himself (20:10). Here it is simply life under siege: going to the field, walking the road, become impossible.

Mourning as for an only son. Among the deepest griefs the ancient world could name was the loss of an only son: the end of a family line and every hope with it. Zechariah saw where that mourning would finally be directed: when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child (Zech 12:10). The grief God prescribes for Jerusalem's ruin becomes the grief of Jerusalem's repentance, when it recognises the Son it rejected. John saw that verse fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways. They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A tester of metals. A new picture for the prophet's work. He is an assayer: the man who takes a sample, heats it, and reports what the metal actually is. Preaching tests people. The same word that softens one heart hardens another, and how people react shows what they are.

They are bronze and iron. The sample comes back as base metal. Bronze and iron are useful and they are not silver, which is what this refining was meant to produce.

Going about with slanders. One phrase names what the assayer found among the people: going about with slanders. The corruption is not only in the temple and the courts. It is in ordinary conversation, the steady traffic of reputations damaged in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed. Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In vain the refining goes on. Refiners used lead to draw impurities out of silver. Here the process is run to the limit: the bellows roar, the lead burns away, and nothing pure emerges. The fire is the long series of disasters God has already sent. Suffering refines some people and hardens others, and the difference is not in the fire but in what is put into it.

A refiner who does not fail. Malachi promised a different refiner, who does not fail: He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and refine them like gold and silver (Mal 3:3). Where the fire of disaster could only expose the metal, he will actually purify it.

Rejected silver. The chapter ends with the assayer's certificate: metal that failed the test, put aside. It is exactly why the New Testament's language about redemption lands with such force. Peter tells Christians they were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:18-19). Rejected silver cannot buy anything. But rejected people can be bought back, by a price that does not come from the furnace at all.

6.title: Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
6.overview:
The alarm sounds again and enemy commanders camp around Jerusalem, yet God, who orders the siege against a city full of oppression, still says Be warned (vv. 1-8).

No one will listen. Everyone is greedy, and prophets and priests heal the wound lightly with Peace, peace where there is none (vv. 9-15).

God calls them to ask for the ancient paths and find rest for their souls, and they answer We will not walk in it (vv. 16-21). A cruel nation approaches with a sound like the sea, and Jeremiah, made a tester of metals, finds only rejected silver (vv. 22-30).
6.theology:
God directs the armies that punish his people (v. 6), and warns even while the siege ramp rises (v. 8). Spiritual deadness shows itself as an inability to hear and a distaste for God's word (v. 10).

False ministry treats a deep wound lightly and calls it peace (v. 14); true ministry names the wound. The remedy is the old way God gave, and the rest it promises is fulfilled in Christ's invitation (v. 16). Worship offered as a substitute for obedience is rejected (v. 20).

Judgment is often the ripening of what people themselves sowed (v. 19). Suffering refines some and hardens others (vv. 27-29), and those who fail the test are bought back, if at all, by a price that does not come out of the furnace: the blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).
6.examples: A clean bandage over an infected wound, with a reassuring word, is still the most tempting kind of ministry, because everyone thanks the healer for a while. A conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does, and the loss is usually mistaken for confidence. And it is possible to stand at the junction knowing the way home, and still not walk it.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD:<sup>2</sup>"Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place.<sup>4</sup>Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'<sup>5</sup>"For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another,<sup>6</sup>if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm,<sup>7</sup>then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.<sup>8</sup>"Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail.<sup>9</sup>Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known,<sup>10</sup>and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations?<sup>11</sup>Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.<sup>13</sup>And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer,<sup>14</sup>therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.<sup>15</sup>And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.<sup>16</sup>"As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you.<sup>17</sup>Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?<sup>18</sup>The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.<sup>19</sup>Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?<sup>20</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."<sup>21</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh.<sup>22</sup>For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices.<sup>23</sup>But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'<sup>24</sup>But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.<sup>25</sup>From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day.<sup>26</sup>Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers.<sup>27</sup>"So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.<sup>28</sup>And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips.<sup>29</sup>"'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'<sup>30</sup>"For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.<sup>31</sup>And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.<sup>32</sup>Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere.<sup>33</sup>And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.<sup>34</sup>And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the temple gate Jeremiah calls the worshippers to amend their ways and stop trusting the chant the temple of the LORD (vv. 1-4). God names what amendment means: justice, protection for the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, no innocent blood and no other gods (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A building, however holy, guarantees nothing; God attaches his promise to repentance and to the treatment of the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand in the gate of the LORD’s house. The place is chosen deliberately: the temple gate, on a day when crowds are streaming in to worship. Jeremiah is to preach to religious people on their way to a service. That is a harder assignment than preaching to pagans. Everyone coming through those gates believes they are doing the right thing, and the worship is commanded.

What it cost. This sermon is told again in chapter 26, where we learn what it cost: priests and prophets seized him and said, You shall die! And the parallel account adds the instruction that made it so dangerous: speak to all the cities of Judah that come to worship in the house of the LORD all the words that I command you to speak to them; do not hold back a word (26:2). The easiest way to survive a sermon like this is to leave out the paragraph that will cost you. Jeremiah was told in advance not to. Chapter 26 also dates the sermon: in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim (26:1), about 609 BC, just after good King Josiah had been killed in battle at Megiddo, when the reform he had led was already unravelling under his son.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 26 dates the sermon to the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign (26:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place. Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amend your ways and your deeds. The offer is unchanged from chapter 4: change, and you may stay in the land. God is naming a condition, not an unavoidable fate, and the condition is your ways and your deeds: conduct, not ceremony.

The temple of the LORD. Then the chant, three times, like a slogan at a rally. It was their confidence: God lives here, and he will never let this city fall, because his own house is in it. God calls it deceptive words, though every word of the chant was true. What made it deceptive was what they were doing with the truth: using it as a reason to feel safe while living as they pleased.

Our own chants. This is the easiest error in the world to repeat. A denomination, a confession, a conversion experience, a baptism, a family heritage: all good, all capable of becoming a chant that shields a person from the question of how he actually lives. Jesus finished the Sermon on the Mount on this note: the man who hears and does not do is building on sand, and great was the fall of it (Matt 7:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm, then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you truly execute justice. The list of what amendment would look like repays a slow reading. It begins with justice one with another: ordinary dealings between neighbours. Then three groups: the sojourner, the immigrant with no family network; the fatherless; the widow. In that society these three had no one to take their case. God names them every time, and makes his continued presence with the nation turn on how they are treated.

Innocent blood. Then comes innocent blood, and only last the matter of other gods. A modern reader expects a religious checklist; God gives a mostly social one, without making devotion to him any less important. He refuses to let the two be separated. A church that is orthodox on Sunday and indifferent to the vulnerable on Monday has failed the half of the test that God put first. And the word truly comes twice, because justice can be done only for show.

To your own harm. Idolatry is to your own harm: the false gods damage the people who serve them. And the promise at the end reaches back to the beginning: the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever. The land was given before any condition was laid down. The gift had not been withdrawn; it was still on offer to a generation that had done nothing to keep it. That is the order for the Christian reader too. We take up the cause of the stranger and the widow because God first took up ours, and the Spirit he has given is the one who turns that mercy outward (Gal 5:22).

What this looks like. The promise of the land belonged to Israel, but the New Testament carries the concern straight over: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas 1:27). It is usually less dramatic than we fear. Deal straight. Justice one with another starts with the invoice you send, the reference you write and the tenant you rent to. Learn one name. Get to know one newcomer: the family from overseas at the school gate, the student far from home, the colleague whose English is still halting. Have them round for a meal. Visit. Put the widow from church in your diary, not just your prayers, and the single parent who has not had an evening off in months. Speak up. When someone with no one behind them is being pushed aside, at work or in a council office queue, be the person who takes their case. We do this not to keep our place with God but because we were the strangers once: you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph 2:19). Christ found us with no one to plead for us, and pleaded for us himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — As I Did to Shiloh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They break the commandments and then claim deliverance in God's house, as if it were a robbers' den (vv. 8-11). So they are sent to look at Shiloh, where God's name first dwelt: the same will be done to this house (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The place God chose can be destroyed by God: Shiloh is the precedent, and the temple is not exempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail. Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known, and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will you steal, murder, commit adultery? Read that list against the Ten Commandments: stealing, murder, adultery, false swearing, other gods. God lists them like the detailed charges in a court case. Then they go from the sin straight to the service, saying We are delivered! and going out to do it all again. The language of rescue is being used as an insurance policy.

Only to go on doing all these abominations. This is the sting. Worship had become the thing that made the sin sustainable. Confession without any intention to stop is not repentance; it is a way of keeping the sin going.

Continue in sin that grace may abound? Paul met the same logic in the church and answered it the same way: Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it? (Rom 6:1-2). Grace that is used as permission to keep sinning has been misunderstood at the root. The cross that forgives sin is also the death of the old life that loved it.

verseByVerse.quote: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A den of robbers. A den is not where robbers rob. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe and divide the takings. That is what the temple had become: they did their damage in the city and came here to be secure.

Christ in the temple. Six centuries later Jesus walked into the same courts, overturned the tables and quoted this verse: My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers (Matt 21:13). He was charging that generation with Jeremiah's indictment, and, like Jeremiah, he went on to predict that the building would come down (Mark 13:2).

A house of prayer for all the nations. Mark gives the fuller form: Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers (Mark 11:17). Jesus joined Isaiah's promise of what the temple was for (Isa 56:7) to Jeremiah's verdict on what it had become. And he did more than repeat Jeremiah: he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21). The meeting place of God and the nations would no longer be a building but himself.

Behold, I myself have seen it. The last clause removes every hiding place. He who formed the eye, does he not see? (Ps 94:9). The worshippers imagined that what happened in the city stayed in the city. God saw both, and how they were connected.
verseByVerse.note: Luke records the same saying (Luke 19:46).

verseByVerse.quote: Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go now to my place that was in Shiloh. God sends them on a field trip. Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations before the temple was built. In Eli's day the ark was carried out of Shiloh into battle as a lucky charm, and the ark of God was captured (1 Sam 4:11). The psalm records the end of it: He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind (Ps 78:60).

The ruins were about twenty miles north, close enough to walk to. That is what God does to a holy place that is treated as a lucky charm.
verseByVerse.note: Shiloh had been destroyed, probably by the Philistines after the battle of 1 Samuel 4.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer, therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In which you trust. The house in which you trust will go the way of Shiloh. Misplaced trust is not protected by being religious trust. If anything it is treated more severely, because it uses God's own gifts as a shield against him.

When I called you, you did not answer. The history that led here is a conversation that only went one way: when I called you, you did not answer. Isaiah gives the same reason for the same sentence: because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen (Isa 65:12). Judgment in Scripture is rarely sudden. It is the end of a long, unanswered call.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the offspring of Ephraim. Ephraim is the northern kingdom, gone a century before. Judah had watched it happen (3:8) and concluded that it could not happen to them, because they had the temple. God says the precedent stands.

Cast out of my sight. The phrase cast you out of my sight has an old shape. The first human beings were sent out of God's garden, and He drove out the man (Gen 3:24). Exile in the Bible is always a small repetition of Eden lost: removal from the place where God had made himself present. And that is why the promise of return, when it comes, is always more than a promise of land: it is a promise of God’s presence again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Do Not Pray for This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for the people, while whole families bake cakes for the queen of heaven (vv. 16-18). They harm themselves more than they provoke God, and his wrath will fall on land and people (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The forbidding of intercession is deeply solemn, and even it is framed by the fact that sin destroys the sinner first.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not pray for this people. This verse is aimed at the intercessor rather than at the guilty. Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for his own nation. The prohibition comes three times in this book (11:14; 14:11), which suggests he kept doing it anyway; in chapter 14 he is still pleading (14:7-9, 19-22).

What does it mean? Not that God has stopped being merciful; the same book will promise a new covenant. It means that a point can be reached where judgment is settled and further pleading will not turn it aside; and it means God is telling his prophet in advance, so that when the city falls Jeremiah will not think his prayers failed.

Sin that leads to death. John writes something in the same territory: There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that (1 John 5:16). These are not verses to wield against people we have given up on. Nobody can know how another person stands with God. They are warnings about how serious sustained refusal is, and they are rare precisely because the normal command is to pray for everyone.

Should I stop praying for someone hardened? No. Jeremiah received a direct word from God about a nation whose sentence was already fixed; no one today receives such a word about a son, a friend or a country. Our standing command is to pray for all people (1 Tim 2:1), even for those who persecute us (Matt 5:44), and many parents have prayed for years over a child who seemed beyond reach and seen that child come home. And the prophet who was told to stop interceding points to an Intercessor who was never told to stop. Christ prayed for the men who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and he always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cakes for the queen of heaven. It is a family scene, and that is what makes it terrible: children collecting kindling, fathers at the fire, mothers making the dough. Everyone has a job, and the whole household is at work on idolatry. It is cosy. It is also a very effective way to hand a religion to the next generation. The queen of heaven was probably the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar, known in Canaan as Astarte, a goddess of love and fertility, and the cakes seem to have been made in her image (44:19).

The queen of heaven returns. The queen of heaven does not go away. Decades later, after the city has burned, the survivors in Egypt will defend this exact practice to Jeremiah's face: we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven, because then we had plenty of food, and prospered (44:17). A religion taught around the family fire outlasts even the ruin it caused.
verseByVerse.note: The “queen of heaven” was probably the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar (Astarte).

verseByVerse.quote: Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame? Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is it I whom they provoke? A question that corrects how we picture God’s anger. The damage of sin falls first on the sinner: Is it not themselves? His anger is not wounded pride; it is the response of love to people destroying themselves and their children.

Upon man and beast. And the land itself suffers with the people, as it did in the un-creation vision of chapter 4. Human sin never harms human beings only.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sacrifice was never the first word: at the exodus God called his people to obey his voice, and they went backward (vv. 21-24). He sent prophets day after day, each generation did worse, and Jeremiah too will go unheard, for truth has perished (vv. 25-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Sacrifice was never meant to replace obedience, and centuries of persistent preaching have met a stiffened neck.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat the flesh. The tone is bitterly ironic. In the burnt offering the whole animal was burned to God; in other sacrifices the worshippers ate part of the meat. God says: put them all together and eat the lot yourselves. If the sacrifices mean nothing, they may as well be dinner.

What came first. Read carelessly, this sounds like a denial that God gave the sacrificial law, which would contradict Leviticus. Read in its own terms, it is about what came first and what it was for. The founding word came in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt: rescue first, and then not a manual of offerings but a relationship, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. The sacrifices were given inside that covenant to serve it, never to replace it.

One voice in the prophets. The prophets say this in one voice. To obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (Hos 6:6). Bring no more vain offerings, and instead learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause (Isa 1:13, 17). Let justice roll down like waters (Amos 5:24).

Obedience today. The modern equivalents are attendance, giving, service and the right doctrinal words: all good, and all able to be offered instead of obedience. And none of us obeys that voice perfectly either. The one who did was the Son, who could say I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), and his obedience is counted to those who trust him (Rom 5:19). That does not make obedience optional; it makes it the glad answer of people already claimed, with a way back when they fail.

verseByVerse.quote: But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Backward and not forward. This is the whole history in four words. There is no standing still in this book. A people either walks in the way it is shown or drifts back from it.

Walked in their own counsels. The alternative to God's voice is named exactly: walked in their own counsels. Not a rival god this time, but their own judgment. Proverbs puts the choice the same way: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding (Prov 3:5). Every drift backward starts with a person deciding he can find the way without being told.

verseByVerse.quote: From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day. Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers. "So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persistently, day after day. Persistently, and day after day, for centuries: that is God's patience measured in messengers, not one warning ignored but a stream of them across generations, each one a mercy. A stiffened neck is the picture of an animal that will not turn its head to the rein. And They did worse than their fathers: each generation had the added evidence of what the previous one had suffered, and went further anyway.

But they will not listen to you. Here is a commission almost no one would accept: preach, and they will not listen. God tells his servant the outcome in advance, and still sends him. Jeremiah is not sent to be effective; he is sent to be faithful. Anyone serving in a hard place, a stagnant church, an indifferent family, is standing where Jeremiah stood, and the standard by which the work will be judged is the one given here.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips. "'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truth has perished. Truth has perished: not merely that people tell lies, but that truth itself has died out of public life, so that no one expects it in a courtroom, a market or a temple. A society can survive a great deal of wickedness; it cannot survive the death of truth, because nothing can then be repaired.

Cut off your hair and cast it away. Cutting the hair was a public sign of grief, and the bare heights were the hilltops where the idols were worshipped: hold the funeral at the scene of the sin.

Did not accept discipline. One charge explains the rest: did not accept discipline. Discipline, Hebrews says, seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it (Heb 12:11). The pain was never the problem. The refusal to be trained by it was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They have defiled the temple and burned their children at Topheth, which God never commanded (vv. 30-31). The valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and the voices of bridegroom and bride will fall silent (vv. 32-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned gives its name to the place of judgment, and the sound that ends is the sound of weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their detestable things in the house. The idols are inside the temple now. The building they chanted about had been furnished with the very things that made it uninhabitable for God.

To burn their sons and their daughters. This is the lowest point of the book. In a ravine outside Jerusalem, parents were burning their children alive as offerings. The law had forbidden it plainly: You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech (Lev 18:21). Kings Ahaz and Manasseh had each burned a son as an offering (2 Kgs 16:3; 21:6), and Josiah had defiled Topheth so that no one could do it again (2 Kgs 23:10); after his death the fires were evidently lit once more.

Nor did it come into my mind. Then comes a phrase that is almost unbearable: God says the thought never entered his mind. Whatever these people told themselves about pleasing a god, it had no connection whatever to the God who was speaking. Religion cut loose from what God has said does not drift toward kindness.

The Valley of Hinnom. Two things follow. First, every generation should ask what it does to its own children and calls necessary. Second, see where this valley leads. The Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom in Hebrew, Gehenna in Greek) became the New Testament word for hell itself; the name of a real ravine where children burned became the name for final judgment, the place Jesus described as one where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched (Mark 9:48).

Did God not foresee it? No; he knows all things (Ps 139:4). It means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.

What do we sacrifice our children to? It is tempting to feel a great distance from this verse. But ask why loving parents in Jerusalem did. Molech worship was a bargain: give the god what is most precious, and he will secure the harvest, the city, the family’s future. The parents were not monsters; they were frightened people trying to buy security. Every idol makes that bargain sooner or later, and it always asks for the children. The father who gives his best years to the company and his leftover evenings to his son is making an offering. So is the parent who needs a child’s results to prove the family a success, or the home where the adults’ freedom always comes first. We do not use fire. We still make our children pay for our gods. The God of the Bible is the opposite. When he asked Abraham for his son, he stopped the knife (see the note on Genesis 22:1–2), and then he did what no idol would ever do. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32) is the one God who gives his child instead of taking ours.
verseByVerse.note: The name Topheth is probably linked to a word for a hearth or fireplace.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere. And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Valley of Slaughter. The punishment takes the shape of the crime, as in 5:19. The valley where they killed their children becomes the valley where their own dead are buried, so many that the graveyards overflow into it. The renaming is God's verdict written on the map.

Said twice. Jeremiah will stand in this valley again, holding a clay flask, and repeat the renaming there: this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter (19:6). God said it twice, in two places, so that nobody could claim to have missed it.

None will frighten them away. To be left unburied was a terrible disgrace in that world, and there will not even be anyone left to wave off the birds.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of the bride. The chapter ends not with an image of violence but with silence. No laughter in the streets, and no weddings. Of all the sounds God could name as the mark of a living community, he chooses the voices of a bride and bridegroom: the sound of people betting on a future.

What judgment takes away. This is what judgment takes away, and it is how John describes the fall of Babylon at the end of the Bible: the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more (Rev 18:23).

The voices restored. But this is the God who later says to these same exiles that he will bring back into this ruined land the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride (33:11), because his purpose was never the silence. Jeremiah preached in the temple gate that the house would fall. It did. And the one who quoted this sermon in the same courts, Jesus, went out and was himself put to death, so that the wedding could be held after all: the Bible ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9).

7.title: The Temple Sermon: Do Not Trust in Deceptive Words
7.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to the temple gate to preach to worshippers on their way in: amend your ways, and do not trust the chant the temple of the LORD (vv. 1-7). They break the commandments and then claim deliverance in God's house, so they are sent to look at the ruins of Shiloh: the temple will go the same way (vv. 8-15).

Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them while whole families bake cakes for the queen of heaven (vv. 16-20). Obedience, not sacrifice, was God's first word, and centuries of prophets went unheard (vv. 21-29). Because they burned their children at Topheth, the valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and the voices of bridegroom and bride will fall silent (vv. 30-34).
7.theology:
Religious privilege guarantees nothing: true words about God's house became deceptive words when used as a shield for unrepentance (vv. 4, 8; Matt 7:26-27). God ties his presence to repentance and to justice for the weakest (vv. 5-7), and refuses to let worship and ethics be separated (vv. 9-11).

Shiloh proves that God will destroy a place he chose when it is treated as a lucky charm (vv. 12-15). Sacrifice was given inside the covenant to serve obedience, never to replace it (vv. 21-23). Sin's damage falls first on the sinner (v. 19), and God's wrath is love's response to people destroying themselves and their children.

Prayer for a people can be forbidden when refusal has hardened (v. 16; 1 John 5:16), and faithfulness, not results, is the standard for the messenger (v. 27). Jesus took this sermon up in the same courts and went to his death outside its walls, so that the wedding joy silenced here might be restored (33:11).
7.examples: The hardest congregation is the one already on its way into church, and the most dangerous words are true ones used as a shield. A den is not where the robbery happens but where robbers feel safe afterwards, and any place of worship can become one. And a family with a job each, working together at the fire, can hand on idolatry as warmly as faith.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>"At that time, declares the LORD, the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be brought out of their tombs.<sup>2</sup>And they shall be spread before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped. And they shall not be gathered or buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground.<sup>3</sup>Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them, declares the LORD of hosts.<sup>4</sup>"You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD: When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return?<sup>5</sup>Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They hold fast to deceit; they refuse to return.<sup>6</sup>I have paid attention and listened, but they have not spoken rightly; no man relents of his evil, saying, 'What have I done?' Everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong into battle.<sup>7</sup>Even the stork in the heavens knows her times, and the turtledove, swallow, and crane keep the time of their coming, but my people know not the rules of the LORD.<sup>8</sup>"How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie.<sup>9</sup>The wise men shall be put to shame; they shall be dismayed and taken; behold, they have rejected the word of the LORD, so what wisdom is in them?<sup>10</sup>Therefore I will give their wives to others and their fields to conquerors, because from the least to the greatest everyone is greedy for unjust gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely.<sup>11</sup>They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.<sup>12</sup>Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among the fallen; when I punish them, they shall be overthrown, says the LORD.<sup>13</sup>When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered, and what I gave them has passed away from them."<sup>14</sup>Why do we sit still? Gather together; let us go into the fortified cities and perish there, for the LORD our God has doomed us to perish and has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD.<sup>15</sup>We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.<sup>16</sup>"The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan; at the sound of the neighing of their stallions the whole land quakes. They come and devour the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it.<sup>17</sup>For behold, I am sending among you serpents, adders that cannot be charmed, and they shall bite you," declares the LORD.<sup>18</sup>My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me.<sup>19</sup>Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people from the length and breadth of the land: "Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her King not in her?" "Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and with their foreign idols?"<sup>20</sup>"The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved."<sup>21</sup>For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me.<sup>22</sup>Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bones of Judah's leaders and people will be taken from their tombs and spread unburied before the stars they worshipped, and the survivors will prefer death to life (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: The gods they served become the witnesses of their shame, and the living envy the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be brought out of their tombs. And they shall be spread before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped. And they shall not be gathered or buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them, declares the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bones shall be brought out of their tombs. Five times the bones, tolling through the sentence: kings, officials, priests, prophets, people. The groups the book keeps naming, now listed as skeletons. Death has levelled the hierarchy, and the invaders will loot the graves.

Which they have loved and served. Five verbs describe their devotion (loved, served, gone after, sought and worshiped), and then the bones are laid out under those same stars. The gods they gave their lives to will watch them rot, and do nothing, because they were only ever lights in the sky. This worship of the host of heaven had flourished under Manasseh, who built altars for it in the temple courts, and Josiah had torn those altars down (2 Kgs 21:5; 23:4-5, 12); the bones laid out under the stars expose a devotion the reform never uprooted.

Idols as audience. This is the logic of this passage: idols do not merely fail to save; they become the audience of the disaster. Whatever a person has given himself to will be standing there at the end, mute.

Death shall be preferred to life. For the survivors, life becomes worse than death. Scripture does not moralise about that or soften it. It is a plain statement of what exile will feel like from inside.

Longing to die. John sees the same condition at the end of history: people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them (Rev 9:6). A world that has lost God does not simply lose comfort; it can lose the will to live. Scripture names that darkness honestly, but it is not the last word: the same book that records it carries God's promise of a future and a hope (29:11).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People who fall get up again, but this people holds to deceit and never asks what it has done (vv. 4-6). The birds keep their seasons; God's people do not know his rules (v. 7). The scribes have made the law a lie, and the false peace of chapter 6 is preached again (vv. 8-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The instinct to get up after a fall has died, the birds, who keep their seasons, shame them, and even the Scriptures have been turned into a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD: When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return? Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They hold fast to deceit; they refuse to return. I have paid attention and listened, but they have not spoken rightly; no man relents of his evil, saying, 'What have I done?' Everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong into battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When men fall, do they not rise again? Two questions drawn from ordinary life, and both expect the answer yes. A man who trips gets up. A traveller who takes a wrong turning goes back. Nobody lies in the road on principle, and nobody keeps walking the wrong way once he knows.

Perpetual backsliding. The word perpetual is the sting. Not a fall but a way of life; not a wrong turning but a direction. And they are holding tight to the wrong thing: they hold fast to deceit, clinging to the thing that is destroying them.

What have I done? God says he has been listening: leaning in, waiting to catch one sentence. And the sentence he is listening for is short: What have I done? Four words, and nobody says them.

God is not waiting for an explanation, a defence or a plan for improvement. He is waiting for the question people ask when they finally see their own behaviour from outside.

Two men who asked it. Two men in Luke asked it. The younger son in the far country came to himself and rehearsed his sentence: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you (Luke 15:17-18). The man at the back of the temple would not look up and prayed, God, be merciful to me, a sinner! (Luke 18:13). Neither offered a defence. Each simply asked, in his own words, “What have I done?”, and each was received.

Like a horse plunging headlong into battle. Instead, everyone goes his own way, like a horse plunging headlong into battle. A warhorse in a charge cannot be reasoned with, cannot stop and will not turn. It is the perfect picture of momentum: a life with speed, direction and no brakes.

verseByVerse.quote: Even the stork in the heavens knows her times, and the turtledove, swallow, and crane keep the time of their coming, but my people know not the rules of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the stork in the heavens knows her times. Now look up. The migrating birds leave and return on time, every year, without instruction. The ESV notes that one of the bird names is uncertain, and that rules may be rendered "just decrees". The point does not depend on the details: creatures with no reasoning keep God's calendar, and people made in his image do not know his ways. Isaiah said it with farm animals: The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know (Isa 1:3).

They keep the time of their coming. The birds come back, which is exactly what Judah would not do: they refuse to return. A bird obeys the instinct to come home that God built into it. God's people had his own word calling them home, and ignored it.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie. The wise men shall be put to shame; they shall be dismayed and taken; behold, they have rejected the word of the LORD, so what wisdom is in them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law of the LORD is with us. The claim was perfectly true and completely hollow. They had the scrolls; Josiah's reform had rediscovered the book. Owning the Scriptures had become their proof that all was well with them.

The lying pen of the scribes. The charge is aimed at the professionals: the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie. God does not accuse them of losing the text but of turning it into something false, by the way they explained it, applied it and used it to approve what the nation wanted to do.

How the pen lies. Verses arranged to bless what God condemns, comfort detached from repentance, technical study that never asks for obedience: the pen is lying while every letter it copies is accurate. Anyone who teaches the Bible should read verse 8 once a year.

Twisted Scriptures. Peter warns of the same thing in the church: there are passages which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures (2 Pet 3:16). And Paul asks, with the scribe named alongside the wise man: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? (1 Cor 1:20). Learning that has walked away from God's word has not become neutral. It has become foolish, however many qualifications it holds.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will give their wives to others and their fields to conquerors, because from the least to the greatest everyone is greedy for unjust gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among the fallen; when I punish them, they shall be overthrown, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sermon repeated. These three verses repeat 6:13-15 almost word for word, and the repetition is the message. The sermon has already been preached; nothing has changed; so it is preached again, unaltered. Ezekiel used another image for the same men, prophets who say 'Peace,' when there is no peace and then whitewash the flimsy wall the people have built, so that it looks sound (Ezek 13:10).

A preacher who has to say the same thing twice to the same people is not necessarily failing. Jeremiah did it, and it was God's idea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — No Grapes on the Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God finds no fruit on his vine (v. 13). The people shut themselves in to die, having looked for peace and found terror (vv. 14-15), as the enemy's horses are heard and serpents are sent that cannot be charmed (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest God looked for is not there, and the remedies people reach for are poison and panic.

verseByVerse.quote: When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered, and what I gave them has passed away from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No grapes on the vine. God comes to his vineyard at harvest and finds nothing: no grapes, no figs, not even green leaves. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, but the picture is unmistakable. And what I gave them has passed away from them: judgment often begins not with a blow but with good gifts quietly taken away.

Nothing but leaves. Jesus acted out something very like this verse on the road into Jerusalem, seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, and when he came to it he found nothing but leaves (Mark 11:13). And he told a parable about the patience that comes before the sentence: an owner who came seeking fruit on it and found none, and a vinedresser who pleaded, Sir, let it alone this year also (Luke 13:6-8). God's inspection of his vineyard is never hasty. By Jeremiah's day it had been going on for centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do we sit still? Gather together; let us go into the fortified cities and perish there, for the LORD our God has doomed us to perish and has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD. We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do we sit still? The people speak, and it is almost repentance. They name the cause correctly, because we have sinned against the LORD, and then act on despair rather than on that knowledge, shutting themselves into walled towns to die. Knowing your sin without hope produces a giving up that looks like humility and is not. The God they have sinned against is the one who still says return.

We looked for peace, but no good came. This is what the Peace, peace preaching of verse 11 finally delivers. People were promised healing and handed terror. False comfort is not a harmless kindness; there are casualties, and they are the ones who believed it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan; at the sound of the neighing of their stallions the whole land quakes. They come and devour the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. For behold, I am sending among you serpents, adders that cannot be charmed, and they shall bite you," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan. Sound again before sight: cavalry heard from Dan, the proverbial far north. The enemy is inside the country.

Adders that cannot be charmed. Snake charmers were a familiar sight, and their whole trade was managing danger. These serpents cannot be charmed. There is a point at which the techniques that have always worked stop working.

The serpents in the wilderness. Many Christians have heard an echo here of the wilderness, where God once sent serpents among his rebellious people, and then gave the remedy himself: Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live (Num 21:8). No charm, no technique: a look of trust at what God had provided. Jesus took that scene as a picture of his own death: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14-15). Where no charmer can help, the lifted-up Son still can.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Is There No Balm in Gilead?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet's joy is gone. The people ask whether the LORD is not in Zion, and God asks about their idols (vv. 18-19). The harvest is past and they are not saved; the prophet is wounded with their wound and asks why there is balm and a physician, yet no healing (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The medicine exists and the doctor is available; what is missing is any willingness to be treated.

verseByVerse.quote: My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me. Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people from the length and breadth of the land: "Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her King not in her?" "Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and with their foreign idols?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
My heart is sick within me. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of the first line is uncertain. What comes through is plain enough: joy gone, grief arrived, heart sick. He has been preaching this judgment for chapters, and it is making him ill.

Is the LORD not in Zion? Then the people cry out the belief they have always relied on: Is the LORD not in Zion? He lives here; this cannot be happening. And God answers with a question: then why the carved images? Their confidence rested on his presence while their affections rested elsewhere. You cannot claim a God as your security and treat him as optional.

verseByVerse.quote: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me. Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The harvest is past. A haunting sentence, and it is the people's own. In an agricultural year there is a window: the grain ripens, the harvest is gathered, and after that nothing more will grow. The window has shut, the barns are not full, and winter is coming.

The day of salvation. Opportunity has a season, as everyone knows in farming, in health, in relationships. Paul makes the same point with urgency rather than gloom: now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2). The sentence in Jeremiah is what it sounds like to say it too late.

For the wound of the daughter of my people. Jeremiah does not stand outside their loss: in verse 21 their wound is his wound, and he makes no distinction between them. That shared wound points past Jeremiah. Isaiah describes one who does not merely grieve over his people's injury but carries it: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isa 53:4). The prophet's broken heart is the faint outline beforehand; the Servant who takes the wound into himself is the reality.

Is there no balm in Gilead? Gilead, east of the Jordan, was known for a medicinal resin traded across the region. Is there no balm? Of course there is. Is there no physician? There is. Then why is this patient not healed?

Why she is not healed. The answer the whole book has been giving: because she will not be treated. The wound has been bandaged lightly by men who called it peace, and the physician who could actually heal it has been refused. Jesus said, Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Mark 2:17). The one thing that keeps a person from the doctor is the conviction that nothing much is wrong.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis already pictures traders carrying balm from Gilead down to Egypt (Gen 37:25).

8.title: Is There No Balm in Gilead?
8.overview:
