The tombs of Judah's kings, officials, priests, prophets and people will be opened and their bones spread before the sun, moon and stars they worshipped, unburied; the survivors will prefer death to life (vv. 1-3).

Men who fall get up, and migrating birds come home, but this people backslides perpetually, and no one asks What have I done? (vv. 4-7). They have the law, yet the scribes' pen has made it a lie, and the false peace of chapter 6 is preached again (vv. 8-12).

God finds no fruit, the people shut themselves in to die, and the enemy is heard from Dan (vv. 13-17). The harvest is past and they are not saved, and Jeremiah, wounded with their wound, asks why there is balm in Gilead and yet no healing (vv. 18-22).
8.theology:
Idols cannot save and end as witnesses of their worshippers' ruin (vv. 1-2). Repentance begins with a question almost no one asks: What have I done? (v. 6). Creation keeps God's order while his people do not (v. 7; Isa 1:3).

Scripture can be turned into a lie by the way it is taught, without a word being altered (v. 8), and comfort preached over an untreated wound destroys those who believe it (vv. 11, 15; Ezek 13:10).

Opportunity has a season, and it can close (v. 20; 2 Cor 6:2). The remedy exists, for there is balm and there is a physician (v. 22), and the barrier is the refusal to be treated (Mark 2:17). The prophet does not stand outside the grief he announces (vv. 18, 21).
8.examples: Whatever a person gives himself to will be standing there at the end, as silent as the stars over the bones of their worshippers. A life can become a warhorse in a charge, all speed and direction with no brakes, and the four words that would stop it, What have I done?, are the ones hardest to say. And a teacher can quote every letter of Scripture accurately and still teach a lie with it.

For they are all adulterers, a company of treacherous men.<sup>3</sup>They bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood and not truth has grown strong in the land; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not know me, declares the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Let everyone beware of his neighbor, and put no trust in any brother, for every brother is a deceiver, and every neighbor goes about as a slanderer.<sup>5</sup>Everyone deceives his neighbor, and no one speaks the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies; they weary themselves committing iniquity.<sup>6</sup>Heaping oppression upon oppression, and deceit upon deceit, they refuse to know me, declares the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do, because of my people?<sup>8</sup>Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceitfully; with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush for him.<sup>9</sup>Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?<sup>10</sup>"I will take up weeping and wailing for the mountains, and a lamentation for the pastures of the wilderness, because they are laid waste so that no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard; both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled and are gone.<sup>11</sup>I will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals, and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant."<sup>12</sup>Who is the man so wise that he can understand this? We are utterly shamed, because we have left the land, because they have cast down our dwellings.'"<sup>20</sup>Hear, O women, the word of the LORD, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach to your daughters a lament, and each to her neighbor a dirge.<sup>21</sup>For death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces, cutting off the children from the streets and the young men from the squares.<sup>22</sup>Speak: "Thus declares the LORD, 'The dead bodies of men shall fall like dung upon the open field, like sheaves after the reaper, and none shall gather them.'"<sup>23</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches,<sup>24</sup>but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD."<sup>25</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will punish all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh—<sup>26</sup>Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who dwell in the desert who cut the corners of their hair, for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Oh That My Head Were Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet longs to weep day and night for his people, and in the same breath to escape them (vv. 1-2). Their tongues are bows, no neighbour or brother can be trusted, and they refuse to know God (vv. 3-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet weeps for his people and longs to escape them at once, and the sin he grieves is a collapse of truth between neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that my head were waters. This is the verse most often linked with Jeremiah's title, the weeping prophet. The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible it is the last verse of chapter 8, which fits: it is the answer to the question about the balm of Gilead. There is no cure, so there are tears.

Day and night. Look at the scale he wants. Not a few tears but a head turned to water, eyes become a spring that never runs dry, weeping day and night. He is saying that the grief he already feels is inadequate to what he is looking at.

The same tears. The psalmist knew the same tears: My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law (Ps 119:136). Paul knew them for his own nation: I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart (Rom 9:2). And on the last approach to Jerusalem, when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it (Luke 19:41). Christ stood where Jeremiah stood, looked at the same city, and cried.

Some said Jeremiah. Some of Jesus' contemporaries made the connection: asked who people said he was, the disciples reported that some said Jeremiah (Matt 16:14). They may have seen in him the same tears over Jerusalem, the same word against the temple, the same rejection by priests and townsfolk. The likeness is a real one, not a hidden message, and it points one way: Jeremiah wept over a judgment he could only announce; Christ wept over the city and then bore judgment himself.

Our own tears. It is a fair question whether any of us weep over anything but our own losses, and the first answer to it is not guilt but the sight of Christ, whose tears were shed over people exactly like us.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 9:1 is 8:23 in the Hebrew numbering, so the Hebrew verse numbers of chapter 9 run one behind the English.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that I had in the desert a travelers' lodging place, that I might leave my people and go away from them! For they are all adulterers, a company of treacherous men. They bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood and not truth has grown strong in the land; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not know me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that I had in the desert a travelers’ lodging place. Immediately comes the opposite wish: a rest house on a caravan road, anywhere away from these people. The same man wants to weep for them and to be rid of them. Anyone who has loved a difficult family, church or city recognises both, often in one day. Scripture does not tidy the prophet's emotions into consistency.

They bend their tongue like a bow. A bow is drawn deliberately, aimed, and released to wound at a distance. That is the tongue here: not careless talk but speech used as a weapon. The ESV notes an alternative reading of the middle clause; either way, falsehood has become the strong thing in the land.

They do not know me. The root is named last: they do not know me. Not that they do not know about him: they do not know him.

verseByVerse.quote: Let everyone beware of his neighbor, and put no trust in any brother, for every brother is a deceiver, and every neighbor goes about as a slanderer. Everyone deceives his neighbor, and no one speaks the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies; they weary themselves committing iniquity. Heaping oppression upon oppression, and deceit upon deceit, they refuse to know me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put no trust in any brother. This is what a society looks like when truth has collapsed: a standing instruction to trust nobody. Not enemies, but neighbor and brother. The people you live beside and the people you are related to.

When trust goes. Trust is what ordinary life quietly runs on. When it goes, everything costs more: every agreement needs a lawyer, every statement needs verification, every relationship carries a guard. The verse describes a nation living that way, and it is describing the fruit of the lying they were so proud of.

Micah’s collapse. Micah described the same collapse in the same terms, Put no trust in a neighbor; have no confidence in a friend, for a man's enemies are the men of his own house (Mic 7:5-6), and Jesus took Micah's words for what faithfulness to him would sometimes cost: a person's enemies will be those of his own household (Matt 10:36). Where truth has died, even the family stops being a refuge.

They have taught their tongue to speak lies. This is trained behaviour, practised until it is fluent.

They weary themselves committing iniquity. Sin is hard work. Keeping the accounts straight, remembering what was said to whom, maintaining the version of yourself that different people are shown: it is exhausting, and the exhaustion is invisible from outside. The gospel's offer of rest lands precisely here, addressed to exactly these people: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28). The labour of keeping a double life going is among the heaviest loads there is, and the invitation does not require it to be tidied up first.

They refuse to know me. The second time in four verses. Ignorance of God in this book is not a gap in education; it is a decision maintained daily, and it is the reason the neighbours cannot trust each other.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — I Will Refine Them and Test Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will refine his people, whose tongues speak peace and plan ambush (vv. 7-9). He weeps for the emptied land and will make Jerusalem a ruin (vv. 10-11), and he gives the reason himself: they forsook his law for the Baals, and will be scattered (vv. 12-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the judgment is refining work, and its cause is stated plainly so that no one need guess.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do, because of my people? Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceitfully; with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush for him. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what else can I do? The refining image returns from chapter 6, where the metal failed the test. But listen to the middle of the sentence: for what else can I do, because of my people? That is the language of a parent at the end of the options, and it is astonishing on the lips of God. He is not confessing weakness; he is showing what this has cost him. Judgment here is what remains after prophets, warnings, droughts and mercies have all been refused.

In his heart he plans an ambush. The arrow again, and now exactly how it works: speaks peace aloud, plans an ambush inwardly. This is the sin of the double heart, friendliness as cover, and the damage is worse than open hostility because the victim never sees it coming. David had been on the receiving end of it: His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart; his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords (Ps 55:21).

Shall I not avenge myself? The question of 5:9 and 5:29 is asked once more. A God who watched neighbours ambush one another and shrugged would not be kind.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will take up weeping and wailing for the mountains, and a lamentation for the pastures of the wilderness, because they are laid waste so that no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard; both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled and are gone. I will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals, and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will take up weeping and wailing. Now it is God who weeps. Jeremiah wanted a head of waters in verse 1; here the LORD takes up the lament himself, for empty pastures, no cattle lowing, roads with nobody on them. (The Hebrew reads I will take up; the Greek Old Testament has a command, take up weeping, which some translations follow.) Whatever else the judgment in this book is, it is not the act of a God who feels nothing. He grieves the loss of his own creation, and he says so before it happens.

A lair of jackals. Jackals move in when people move out. The city of David becomes a den for scavengers.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the man so wise that he can understand this? To whom has the mouth of the LORD spoken, that he may declare it? Why is the land ruined and laid waste like a wilderness, so that no one passes through? And the LORD says: "Because they have forsaken my law that I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice or walked in accord with it, but have stubbornly followed their own hearts and have gone after the Baals, as their fathers taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is the man so wise? It is the question that gets asked after every catastrophe: why? And God does not leave it to be guessed at, argued over or turned into philosophy. He answers it himself, in plain words, immediately. Hosea closes his book the same way: Whoever is wise, let him understand these things, because the ways of the LORD are right, and the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them (Hos 14:9). Wisdom here is the willingness to accept God's explanation of what has happened.

As their fathers taught them. Four verbs of the same movement: forsaken, not obeyed, not walked, followed their own hearts. And as their fathers taught them adds how it spread. Idolatry is handed down like a trade, and the chain has to be broken by somebody or it runs on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink. I will scatter them among the nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bitter food and poisonous water. Bitter food, poisoned water, scattering: the food and the dwelling place of exile. And the phrase whom neither they nor their fathers have known makes the loneliness of it concrete: strangers, foreign speech, no family memory of the place.

A root bearing bitter fruit. The bitterness has a history. Moses warned of a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit (Deut 29:18), a heart turning from the LORD to serve other gods. The bitter food and poisoned water of the sentence are that root's own harvest. Judah planted it, and God lets them eat what grew.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Call for the Mourning Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mourning women are summoned to teach a people to weep, and daughters are to learn laments, for death has climbed in at the windows and the dead lie like ungathered sheaves (vv. 17-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief on this scale needs trained mourners and lessons: a generation must be taught how to mourn.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Consider, and call for the mourning women to come; send for the skillful women to come; let them make haste and raise a wailing over us, that our eyes may run down with tears and our eyelids flow with water. For a sound of wailing is heard from Zion: 'How we are ruined! We are utterly shamed, because we have left the land, because they have cast down our dwellings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Call for the mourning women. Professional mourners were a real institution: skilled women who led the wailing at a funeral and drew the grief out of a family that could not find it alone. The purpose is that our eyes may run down with tears: this is a people who need help to cry. Numbness is itself a sign that something is wrong, and there are seasons when the honest thing for a church to do is teach its people to lament rather than hurry them past it.

How we are ruined! The lament is quoted as though from the far side of the event: exile spoken of in the past tense while the city still stands.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O women, the word of the LORD, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach to your daughters a lament, and each to her neighbor a dirge. For death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces, cutting off the children from the streets and the young men from the squares. Speak: "Thus declares the LORD, 'The dead bodies of men shall fall like dung upon the open field, like sheaves after the reaper, and none shall gather them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach to your daughters a lament. Now the mourning becomes something to be taught: teach to your daughters a lament. It is a devastating picture of what is coming: grief that will last long enough that the next generation will need to know the songs.

Death has come up into our windows. Death is pictured as a burglar climbing in at the window. Doors can be barred; windows were where a thief got in. And it takes the children from the streets and the young men from the squares, exactly the places where a healthy town makes its noise. The silence of 7:34 arrives.

Like sheaves after the reaper. A harvest image turned inside out. Behind the reaper the sheaves lie in rows, waiting to be gathered, and no one comes. It is the picture of 8:20 completed: the harvest that was past is now a harvest of the dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Let Him Who Boasts Boast in This
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let no one boast in wisdom, might or riches, but only in knowing the LORD who delights in steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23-24). Those circumcised only in the flesh will be punished with the nations, for Israel is uncircumcised in heart (vv. 25-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Against a chapter of ruin stands the one thing that lasts: knowing the God who delights in steadfast love, justice and righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom. After twenty-two verses of ruin, the chapter turns. Three boasts are forbidden, and they are the three things human beings have always traded on: brains, strength and money.

Still the three. They are still the three today. Qualifications, capability, security. None of them is condemned as a possession; the wise man is not told to become stupid or the rich man to become poor. It is the boasting that is forbidden: resting your identity and your confidence there.

All three failing. All three have just been shown failing. The wise men were put to shame (8:9), the mighty could not hold the wall, and the rich lost their fields to conquerors (8:10).

That he understands and knows me. One boast is permitted, and it is not an achievement: that he understands and knows me. The chapter has said twice that they do not know me and refuse to know me; here is the cure, offered as the one thing to be proud of.

Steadfast love, justice, and righteousness. What is to be known is not raw power but character: steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. God delights in those three, which means they are the three his people should practise, as people who first received them from him. Micah put a similar list as a command (Mic 6:8); here it is a description of God himself.

Boast in the Lord. Paul quotes this verse twice, both times in shortened form: Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (1 Cor 1:31; 2 Cor 10:17). He uses it in a letter to a church obsessed with clever speakers, powerful personalities and money: the same three boasts, in a Greek city, six centuries later.

Nothing except the cross. And in the same chapter Paul says who the Lord is in whom we boast. Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), and he became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1:30). What the wise, the mighty and the rich of Jerusalem could not supply is given in a crucified Saviour, whose righteousness is counted as ours, which is why Paul would boast in nothing except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal 6:14).

In everyday life. If the competence, the strength and the security were removed, what would be left to say about yourself? Verse 24 gives the only answer that survives.

How do I boast in the Lord? Boasting is not only talk; it is what you lean on when you need to feel that you count. Notice your boasts. Listen to what you mention early when meeting someone new, and what you rehearse at 2 a.m. when you feel small: the degree, the salary, the results, the house. Receive them as gifts. Thank God for each by name, and ask Paul’s question of it: What do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor 4:7). Put the knowing first. Guard the time in which you actually come to know God, in his word and in prayer, as carefully as you guard your work; it is the one thing verse 24 lets you be proud of. Practise what he delights in. Show steadfast love, justice and righteousness wherever you have influence. Boast in weakness too. When the strength fails, say so, and say who holds you, as Paul learned: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). You can let the other boasts go because in Christ you have something better. Paul counted everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8), and he cannot be taken from you.

This is eternal life. Jesus defined life itself by the same boast: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). Knowing God is not a religious extra laid on top of a successful life. It is the life, and it is the only possession that death cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will punish all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh— Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who dwell in the desert who cut the corners of their hair, for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcised merely in the flesh. The chapter ends by putting Judah in a list with Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab. Several of those nations practised circumcision as a custom; Judah had it as the sign of God’s covenant with them. Those who cut the corners of their hair are desert tribes who trimmed the hair at the temples, probably as a religious custom; Israel was forbidden to do it (Lev 19:27), and the same tribes are named this way again in 25:23. God says that at the level that matters they are indistinguishable, because Israel is uncircumcised in heart.

Circumcision of the heart. It is the theme of 4:4 and 6:10 brought to its conclusion, and Paul draws the line straight through to the church: circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom 2:29). Every external mark of belonging, whether baptism, membership, family faith or church attendance, comes under this verse’s warning. The mark is good. It settles nothing about the heart it is meant to signify.

9.title: Let Him Who Boasts Boast in This
9.overview:
Jeremiah longs to weep day and night for his people, and in the next breath to escape them, for no neighbour or brother can be trusted and they refuse to know God (vv. 1-6). God himself takes up weeping over the land he must judge, and he names the reason plainly: they forsook his law for the Baals (vv. 7-16).

Mourning women are summoned to teach the people to lament (vv. 17-22). Then the chapter turns: let no one boast in wisdom, might or riches, but only in knowing the LORD who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23-24), for outward marks without a circumcised heart settle nothing (vv. 25-26).
9.theology:
Grief over sin is a mark of the faithful, and it is shared by God himself (vv. 1, 10; Ps 119:136; Rom 9:2; Luke 19:41). Refusing to know God (vv. 3, 6) destroys trust between neighbours, and sin is exhausting labour (v. 5).

Judgment is what remains when every mercy has been refused (v. 7), and its cause is stated plainly rather than left to speculation (vv. 12-14). Idolatry is handed down by teaching (v. 14).

The one permitted boast is knowing God, whose delight is in steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23-24; Mic 6:8), quoted by Paul against boasting in wisdom, power and wealth (1 Cor 1:31; 2 Cor 10:17). Outward marks of belonging to God’s people settle nothing without a circumcised heart (vv. 25-26; 4:4; Rom 2:29).
9.examples: Anyone who has loved a hard family or church will know the wish to weep for people and to be rid of them on the same day. Where speech becomes a bow, drawn and aimed, or friendliness becomes cover for an ambush, trust drains away and ordinary life grows costly. And brains, strength and money are still the three boasts, each of which this chapter watches fail.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Learn Not the Way of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's people are not to learn the nations' ways or dread the signs of the sky (vv. 1-2). Their idols are trees carved, plated and nailed upright, scarecrows that can neither harm nor help (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The gods of the nations have to be nailed upright and carried home; they can neither harm you nor help you.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "Learn not the way of the nations, nor be dismayed at the signs of the heavens because the nations are dismayed at them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Learn not the way of the nations. The danger named here is imitation: not their crimes first, but their way, the assumptions everyone around you holds without examining them. And the specific example is fear of the signs of the heavens: eclipses, comets, the movement of planets read as omens. The pagan world lived under the sky in dread.

The remedy for dread. The remedy God gives is not more information about astronomy. It is that the heavens belong to the God who addresses Israel as his own house (v. 1), so they carry no message of doom for his people. Every age has its version of dread, read off the charts and the headlines, and believers absorb it simply by breathing the air.

Do not be conformed. Paul gives the same instruction to Christians in the capital of the pagan world: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2). The pressure is not dramatic. It is the slow shaping of what feels normal, and it is resisted not by a list of forbidden things but by a mind the Spirit is renewing through the word, among God's people.

Is this a ban on Christmas trees? No. Jeremiah describes the making of an idol: a tree cut down, carved, overlaid with silver and gold, and nailed so that it will not fall (vv. 3–5), and then worshipped. A decorated tree that no one worships is not this. The warning is against bowing to anything made by human hands.

verseByVerse.quote: for the customs of the peoples are vanity. A tree from the forest is cut down and worked with an axe by the hands of a craftsman. They decorate it with silver and gold; they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it cannot move.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that it cannot move. Now the mockery, done simply by describing the process: a tree is cut in the forest; a carpenter shapes it; a metalworker plates it; and finally it is nailed down so that it cannot move, because otherwise it would fall over. The ESV notes that vanity here may be rendered "vapor" or "mist": something that looks substantial and vanishes.

Isaiah’s version. Isaiah told the joke at greater length: a man cuts a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner, and out of the rest he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it, saying Deliver me, for you are my god! (Isa 44:15, 17). The wood that cooked the meal becomes the deity.

verseByVerse.quote: Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like scarecrows in a cucumber field. A scarecrow in a vegetable patch: upright, human-shaped, dressed, motionless, and frightening only to birds. The ESV notes that where the English reads Their idols, the Hebrew simply has "They". A god you have to transport is not a god. The psalm makes the same list and adds the sting: Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8).

Do not be afraid of them. This is the conclusion, and the reason the passage exists. Israel was tempted to worship these things partly out of fear that they might be real. God's answer is that they can neither hurt nor help you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — There Is None Like You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is none like the LORD, King of the nations (vv. 6-7). Idols are costly wood without breath, but the LORD is the true and living God, maker of heaven and earth and master of the storm, and the portion of Jacob (vv. 8-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The satire turns into a hymn: the maker of the world against the things that had to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might. Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For this is your due; for among all the wise ones of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is none like you, O LORD. In the middle of the satire, worship breaks out. The Bible argues not only by exposing the counterfeit but by displaying the real thing, and beside a nailed-down scarecrow the living God needs only to be described.

Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? The answer should be no one, and yet the whole book is the evidence that people manage not to. And note the title: King of the nations, not only of Judah. The peoples who bow to blocks of wood are already his subjects.

The song of the redeemed. The question outlives Jeremiah. At the end of the Bible the redeemed stand beside the sea of glass and sing it, now as praise rather than rebuke: Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you (Rev 15:3-4). What Jeremiah asked as a challenge, heaven sings as a certainty.

A textual note. The Greek Old Testament lacks verses 6-8 and 10, and a Dead Sea Scroll fragment shares that shorter form. The Greek Jeremiah is shorter than the Hebrew throughout, by about an eighth, and many scholars think the book circulated in two editions. Our English Bibles follow the Hebrew, and every truth in these verses stands again in verses 11-16.

verseByVerse.quote: They are both stupid and foolish; the instruction of idols is but wood! Beaten silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz. They are the work of the craftsman and of the hands of the goldsmith; their clothing is violet and purple; they are all the work of skilled men. But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instruction of idols is but wood. A block of wood has nothing to teach. And the list of costs is deliberate: silver shipped from Tarshish, gold from Uphaz, violet and purple cloth, skilled craftsmen. Tarshish was a distant port at the far western edge of the known world, probably in Spain; Uphaz is otherwise unknown, perhaps another name for Ophir, the proverbial source of gold. Enormous investment, real artistry, imported materials, and the finished product still has to be carried. Modern idols are also expensive and beautifully made, and cost and craftsmanship have never been evidence of divinity.

The true God, the living God, the everlasting King. Three titles in one line: the true God, against the false; the living God, against things with no breath in them; the everlasting King, against gods that will perish. This is the sentence the chapter is built around.

From idols to the living God. Those three titles describe the whole of conversion. Paul writes of Gentiles who turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thess 1:9). The movement is always the same: away from what was made, toward the one who makes; away from what has no breath, toward the one who is alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to them: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Written in Aramaic. The ESV notes something remarkable about this verse: it is in Aramaic, not Hebrew. Aramaic was the international language, the speech of diplomacy and trade. So here is a sentence God gives his people to say to the nations, in the nations' own language.

The gods who did not make the heavens. The test it applies is creation. Did your god make this? If not, he is a creature at best and a piece of furniture at worst, and he will not outlast the world he did not make.
verseByVerse.note: It may have been meant as a ready-made reply for the exiles to give their captors.

verseByVerse.quote: It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is he who made the earth. Power, wisdom, understanding, and then weather. Thunder is his voice; lightning and rain arrive together; and the wind is kept in storehouses, as if God had a barn for gales. The people were tempted to worship storm gods. Jeremiah says the storm runs errands for the LORD.

The hymn repeated against Babylon. Near the end of the book the same hymn is repeated almost word for word in the oracle against Babylon (51:15-19). Babylon was the great city of astrology and carved gods, and God answers it in the very words he first gave his own people against the idols of their neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no breath in them. This is the decisive charge. In Genesis God breathed into man and he became a living creature; here men breathe over their gods and nothing happens. Life flows only from God to his creatures, never from men to their gods.

The true image. The New Testament carries the contrast to its end. Men make images of God and nothing lives in them; God has given the true image of himself, his Son, the image of the invisible God, by whom all things were created (Col 1:15-16). The idol is carried by its makers; the Son upholds the universe by his word (Heb 1:3).

Paul in Athens. Paul argued the same way in Athens: we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man (Acts 17:29). And to Corinth: an idol has no real existence, for there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor 8:4, 6).

The portion of Jacob. The comparison ends with relationship rather than argument. God is the portion of Jacob: the share, the inheritance, what the family actually owns. And, astonishingly, the possession runs both ways: Israel is his inheritance. The idol-worshipper owns an object. The believer is owned by, and owns, a person.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The besieged must gather their bundles, for God is slinging them out (vv. 17-18). The tent is down and no one is left to pitch it, because the shepherds never inquired of the LORD (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Exile reduces a household to a bundle and leaves no one to pitch the tent again, and behind it stand shepherds who never asked God anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Gather up your bundle from the ground, O you who dwell under siege! For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I am slinging out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and I will bring distress on them, that they may feel it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gather up your bundle. From hymn to evacuation in one line. This is what a refugee does: the whole life of a household reduced to a pack.

That they may feel it. The picture is a sling: stones whirled and flung far away. And the stated purpose is almost gentle in its severity: that they may feel it. A people who did not feel the earlier blows (5:3) will feel this one. Pain is being used to bring feeling back.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me because of my hurt! My wound is grievous. But I said, "Truly this is an affliction, and I must bear it." My tent is destroyed, and all my cords are broken; my children have gone from me, and they are not; there is no one to spread my tent again and to set up my curtains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is an affliction, and I must bear it. Who speaks here? The prophet and the people are hard to separate, which is the point: he carries their grief as his own (8:21). And the response is neither denial nor collapse: this is an affliction, and I must bear it. There is a kind of faith that consists simply in shouldering what cannot be changed, without pretending it is light.

My tent is destroyed. The nation pictured as a tent: poles down, guy ropes snapped, and my children have gone from me, and they are not. Worst of all, no one is left to help put it back up.

verseByVerse.quote: For the shepherds are stupid and do not inquire of the LORD; therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered. A voice, a rumor! Behold, it comes!— a great commotion out of the north country to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a lair of jackals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds do not inquire of the LORD. The shepherds are the nation’s leaders again (2:8), and the charge is precise: they do not inquire of the LORD. Not that they consulted him and disobeyed, but that it never occurred to them to ask. Leadership that does not ask God anything will scatter the people it is meant to gather. Chapter 23 will return to these shepherds with a promise of a better one.

A voice, a rumor! In a siege the news arrives before the army, and by the time it reaches Jerusalem there is nothing to do but believe it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–25 — The Way of Man Is Not in Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet confesses that man cannot direct his own steps and asks to be corrected in justice, not anger (vv. 23-24), and prays against the nations that devoured Jacob (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet who has watched a nation steer itself into ruin asks for correction rather than for exemption.

verseByVerse.quote: I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps. Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way of man is not in himself. After watching a nation navigate itself into catastrophe, the prophet states the lesson as a confession. We can choose, plan and walk, and we cannot finally set the course of a life. Proverbs says it without the ruins in view: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Prov 16:9). The psalm says it warmly: The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way (Ps 37:23). This is either a frightening sentence or a freeing one, depending on who is holding the map.

The captain of my soul. In the 1870s the poet William Ernest Henley, who had already lost a leg to tuberculosis and was lying in hospital fighting for the other, wrote a poem that ends, “I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul.” It is a brave poem, and it has become the anthem of the modern self: plan your path, own your story, let nobody else write it. Jeremiah has just watched a whole nation try to captain itself, and he concludes the opposite: it is not in man who walks to direct his steps. We still choose, plan and walk; but nobody controls the diagnosis, the market, the war or the phone call at midnight, and a person who must be captain will live either in anxiety or in denial. The gospel offers something better than control. On the night before he died, the one man who truly could have taken charge of his own fate prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42), and walked into the hands of his enemies for us. Because he gave up control, we can. Freedom is not in being the captain of your soul but in entrusting it to the one who gave everything to bring it home.

Correct me, O LORD, but in justice. He does not ask to be spared correction: he says Correct me. He asks that it be measured, in justice; not in your anger. He has just watched what unrestrained judgment looks like.

Discipline for our good. A believer can pray this honestly. O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger (Ps 6:1). And the New Testament gives the answer the prophet could not yet see: God disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10). For those in Christ the correction is never the anger; the anger fell on Christ at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Pour out your wrath on the nations that know you not, and on the peoples that call not on your name, for they have devoured Jacob; they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pour out your wrath on the nations. The chapter ends with a hard prayer, and it is honest about what the invaders did. God used Babylon, and Babylon will answer for how it behaved; the last chapters of this book are given to exactly that. Being an instrument in God's hand is no defence for cruelty.

A twin in the Psalter. The prayer has a near twin in the Psalter. A psalm of Asaph, lamenting a defiled temple, uses almost the same words: Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name! For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his habitation (Ps 79:6-7). When grief has no language of its own, Scripture lends it one.

May a Christian pray like this? Such prayers hand vengeance to God instead of taking it, as Paul commands (Rom 12:19), and ask that cruelty not have the last word. But the Christian prays them under the cross, beside the command to pray for enemies (Matt 5:44), knowing that God's answer to the nations includes mercy: the King of the nations will be worshipped by all nations (Rev 15:4).

10.title: Scarecrows in a Cucumber Field
10.overview:
Israel is told not to learn the way of the nations or dread the signs of the heavens, for their idols are trees carved, plated and nailed upright, like scarecrows in a cucumber field (vv. 1-5).

Against them stands the LORD, King of the nations, the true God, the living God and the everlasting King, who made the world, commands the storm, and is the portion of Jacob (vv. 6-16).

Then the siege: the people must gather their bundles, the tent is down with no one to pitch it, and the shepherds never inquired of the LORD (vv. 17-22). Jeremiah confesses that man cannot direct his own steps, asks to be corrected in justice rather than anger, and prays against the nations that devoured Jacob (vv. 23-25).
10.theology:
Idolatry is exposed simply by describing how an idol is made: gods that must be manufactured, fastened upright and carried are neither to be feared nor trusted (vv. 3-5; Ps 115:4-8). Believers absorb the fears of their culture unless taught otherwise (v. 2).

The living God is known as Creator, and creation is the test he gives the nations (vv. 11-13; Rev 4:11). He is his people's portion, and they are his inheritance (v. 16).

Human beings cannot direct their own steps (v. 23; Prov 16:9). The right prayer is for correction in justice, not for exemption (v. 24; Ps 6:1), and for those in Christ discipline is never wrath (Heb 12:10). Nations God uses to judge remain accountable for their cruelty (v. 25).
10.examples: A god that has to be nailed down so it will not topple over is a scarecrow, frightening only to birds, and modern idols, however costly and well made, are no different. The storms people once worshipped run errands for the living God. And leaders to whom it never occurs to ask God anything will scatter the people they were meant to gather.
