The young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine,<sup>23</sup>and none of them shall be left. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their punishment."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Hear the Words of This Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is sent to preach the covenant God made when he brought Israel out of Egypt, with its curse and its promise, and he answers So be it, LORD (vv. 1-5). He proclaims it in the streets: God warned their fathers persistently, and they did not obey (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant came with blessing and curse attached, and the prophet says amen to both before preaching either.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Cursed be the man who does not hear the words of this covenant that I commanded your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. So shall you be my people, and I will be your God, that I may confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as at this day." Then I answered, "So be it, LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear the words of this covenant. This chapter is a covenant lawsuit: God charges his people with breaking the agreement he made with them, and it opens by reading that agreement aloud. The setting is probably the years after the book of the law was found in the temple in Josiah’s eighteenth year (621 BC), when the king read it to the people and they pledged themselves to the covenant (2 Kgs 22:8; 23:2-3); Jeremiah is sent to press that same covenant on the towns. The curse Jeremiah must announce comes from Deuteronomy, where the whole nation said amen to it: Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say, 'Amen' (Deut 27:26).

Terms they agreed to. Judah had agreed to the terms, and that is the force of everything that follows. God is not imposing something new; he is enforcing what they swore.

Christ became a curse for us. Paul quotes the same curse and draws the conclusion: all who rely on keeping the law are under it (Gal 3:10). Then he gives the way out: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). The covenant Jeremiah preached ended in a curse Judah had sworn to; the new covenant he would announce rests on the One who bore it.

From the iron furnace. Two things stand together here. The iron furnace is Egypt: a furnace for melting metal, the place of heat and slavery from which God dragged them. Rescue came first. Then the terms: Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. Obedience is the response to redemption, never the price of it.

So shall you be my people. At the centre is the sentence that runs through the whole Bible. That is what a covenant is for. It appears again at the heart of the new covenant in chapter 31, and again at the end of Revelation. The relationship is the point; the commandments describe what it looks like.

So be it, LORD. Jeremiah's reply is an amen. He is standing where Israel stood at the foot of the mountain, agreeing to a covenant that carries a curse, and he says amen to it before he preaches a syllable of it. That is what makes him able to preach judgment without cruelty.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem: Hear the words of this covenant and do them. For I solemnly warned your fathers when I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, warning them persistently, even to this day, saying, Obey my voice. Yet they did not obey or incline their ear, but everyone walked in the stubbornness of his evil heart. Therefore I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do, but they did not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear the words of this covenant and do them. The covenant is not to be read in the temple to the devout but shouted in the streets of the towns. Hear and do them: in this book hearing is never complete until it produces action.

Warning them persistently. The warning has been continuous for the nation's whole history, so nobody can say the terms were unclear.

All the words of this covenant. Read the last sentence slowly, because it is precise. God brought on them all the words of this covenant: the very words they had agreed to. The disaster is not an outburst; it is the contract being honoured. God keeps his word in judgment as faithfully as in blessing, and that is a strange comfort: a God whose promises hold is a God whose warnings hold too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah has conspired to return to the old idolatry (vv. 9-10). Disaster will come that they cannot escape, and their many gods will not save them; Jeremiah is again told not to pray for them (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry has become organised, and the gods multiplied for every street cannot answer a single emergency.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the LORD said to me, "A conspiracy exists among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, who refused to hear my words. They have gone after other gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant that I made with their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A conspiracy exists. A conspiracy is organised, agreed and quiet: not scattered individuals slipping into sin but a settled arrangement among the leading men of the nation to go their own way while keeping the appearances. Sin usually becomes respectable by consensus: once everyone who matters does it, it feels less like rebellion than common sense.

They have turned back. This is not a new idea but a going back. Josiah's reform had pushed the idols out of sight; the moment the pressure eased they came back, because the heart had never changed. Reform imposed from above is always this fragile, and it is why the promise of chapter 31 has to be about hearts: a law written within by God himself, the work the New Testament gives to the Spirit (2 Cor 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD, Behold, I am bringing disaster upon them that they cannot escape. Though they cry to me, I will not listen to them. Then the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they make offerings, but they cannot save them in the time of their trouble. For your gods have become as many as your cities, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem are the altars you have set up to shame, altars to make offerings to Baal. "Therefore do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer on their behalf, for I will not listen when they call to me in the time of their trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though they cry to me, I will not listen. Two terrible phrases: that they cannot escape, and Though they cry to me, I will not listen. This is not God refusing a repentant sinner; it is God refusing a nation that has cried out in every emergency for generations while serving other gods in between. Prayer offered as a fire extinguisher, by people who want rescue but not God, is not prayer.

They cannot save them. They will try the gods they have been funding all along, and they cannot save them in the time of their trouble. Every substitute god is fine until there is trouble. That is what trouble is for, in the mercy of God: it shows which of the things we serve can act. And idolatry multiplies, a god for every town and an altar on every street, because no single idol ever delivers.

Therefore do not pray for this people. The prohibition of 7:16 returns, and it will come a third time (14:11), which suggests Jeremiah kept praying: a man forbidden to intercede who could not stop.

What this is not. It bears saying again: it is not a licence to write people off; no one but God knows how another person stands with him. It is the most solemn warning Scripture gives about the point at which persistent refusal becomes settled, and the fact that it grieved the man commanded to obey it is part of the message.

Can prayer change anything? Yes, and this verse shows it: God does not forbid what makes no difference. Moses prayed and Israel was spared (Exod 32:11-14); later God says even Moses and Samuel could not turn this judgment now (15:1), which shows how settled it had become, not that prayer is useless. God ordains his people's prayers along with the outcomes, and our part is to pray as he commands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's beloved comes to his house with sacrifices that cannot avert the doom (v. 15). The green olive tree he planted and named will be set on fire because of Baal worship (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The one who planted the tree is the one who burns it; sacrifice offered by a faithless worshipper buys nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: What right has my beloved in my house, when she has done many vile deeds? Can even sacrificial flesh avert your doom? Can you then exult? The LORD once called you 'a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit.' But with the roar of a great tempest he will set fire to it, and its branches will be consumed. The LORD of hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you, because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah have done, provoking me to anger by making offerings to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What right has my beloved in my house? The tone is that of a betrayed husband watching his wife arrive at his house with a gift. My beloved: the affection has not gone. And the questions are sharp: what business have you here, and do you imagine that meat on an altar will cancel this? The Hebrew of this verse is difficult and translations differ in detail, but the questions are clear.

Can sacrificial flesh avert your doom? The answer the whole prophetic tradition gives is no. Sacrifice was never a payment that let the worshipper keep the sin. That is the difference between the gospel and religion: religion offers God something so that we may keep the sin we love; the gospel puts that sin to death, and gives us God.

A green olive tree. An olive tree lives for centuries and takes years to come into full bearing, and God himself had given Judah that name. Now the same tree is set alight in a storm: not a weed grubbed up, but a beautiful tree burned.

The olive tree in Romans. Paul takes up the same picture. Some branches of God's olive tree were broken off for unbelief, Gentiles were grafted in by faith, and God is able to graft the broken branches in again (Rom 11:17-24). The tree Jeremiah saw burned was not finished: its root held, and in Christ it bears fruit from every nation.

The LORD of hosts, who planted you. The one who decrees the fire is the LORD of hosts, who planted you. He is not a stranger to the orchard. Everything that is lost here is his own work, which is why judgment costs God something.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — A Gentle Lamb Led to the Slaughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God reveals to Jeremiah that his own townsmen of Anathoth are plotting to kill him; he had been like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter (vv. 18-19). He commits his cause to the God who tests hearts, and God declares their punishment (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's own townsmen want him dead, and the words he uses about himself will be used of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD made it known to me and I knew; then you showed me their deeds. But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes, saying, "Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name be remembered no more." But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. Now the chapter turns from the nation to the man, and this is the first of the passages usually called Jeremiah's confessions: his own prayers, complaints and terrors, preserved in the book. He had walked among them unsuspecting, like a tame lamb following the man with the rope, and God is the one who tells him.

Let us destroy the tree with its fruit. Their plan has three parts, and the third is the cruellest. Destroy the tree with its fruit, so nothing of his work survives. Cut him off from the land of the living. And that his name be remembered no more: erase him, as if he never spoke.

The Lamb who knew. So Jeremiah's words about himself echo, without his knowing it, the picture Isaiah gave of his Lord, the servant of the LORD: like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). It was the passage the Ethiopian was reading when Philip explained to him that it spoke of Jesus (Acts 8:32-33). The prophet was a lamb who did not know; Christ was the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and he knew exactly what was planned and walked into it anyway.

To you have I committed my cause. The last clause governs the rest. He does not organise a defence or repay them; he hands the case over.

Let me see your vengeance. The request for vengeance troubles Christian readers, and it should be read for what it is: a man refusing to take revenge and asking the righteous Judge to act instead. That is the opposite of personal retaliation, and it is the same instinct Peter records of Christ, who continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23). The God appealed to is the one who tests the heart and the mind (compare Ps 7:9; Rev 2:23), which means Jeremiah is inviting a judgment that will examine him as well.
verseByVerse.note: “Heart and mind” is literally “kidneys and heart”: the inner feelings and the will.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, and say, "Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand"— therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will punish them. The young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine, and none of them shall be left. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their punishment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men of Anathoth. Now the names: his own village, three miles from Jerusalem, the priestly town where he grew up. These are the people who taught him, the families he knew, probably his own relatives; chapter 12 will say his brothers and his father's house dealt treacherously with him. Why priests should turn on a priest’s son is not said. The message was reason enough; some suggest too that Josiah’s reform, which closed the country shrines and brought their priests to Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:8-9), had cost families like theirs, and that Jeremiah was seen as its spokesman.

Do not prophesy, or you will die. Their terms are simple: stop preaching or be killed. Not a theological argument, a threat.

No prophet in his hometown. It is the oldest pattern in Scripture. No prophet is acceptable in his hometown, said Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, where they tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:24). He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The hardest audience is usually the one that knew you as a child.

The year of their punishment. God answers the threat against his servant personally, and the sentence includes a phrase that softens nothing: the year of their punishment. There is a date on it.

When family turns against you. Preaching the covenant faithfully made Jeremiah hated in his own village, and God took that hatred as aimed at himself. Anyone who has lost family or friends over their obedience to Christ is standing in a long line, and the Lord of hosts has noticed.
verseByVerse.note: Abiathar, the priest Solomon banished, had been sent home to Anathoth (1 Kgs 2:26), and Jeremiah's priestly family may have been of his line.

11.title: The Words of This Covenant
11.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to proclaim the covenant God made when he brought Israel out of Egypt, with its curse and its promise, and he answers So be it, LORD (vv. 1-8). Judah has conspired to return to its old idols, and disaster is coming that their many gods cannot avert (vv. 9-14).

The green olive tree God planted will be set alight (vv. 15-17). Then God reveals a plot: the men of Jeremiah's own town, Anathoth, mean to kill him, and like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter he commits his cause to the God who tests hearts (vv. 18-23).
11.theology:
The covenant carried blessing and curse, and Judah had said amen to both (vv. 3-5; Deut 27:26). Rescue came before commands: obedience is the response to redemption (v. 4). Judgment here is God keeping his word, not losing his temper (v. 8).

Prayer used as an emergency service by people who serve other gods is not prayer (v. 11), and substitute gods fail precisely when trouble comes (v. 12). Sacrifice never buys permission to keep the sin (v. 15).

Jeremiah's words about himself, a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, fit Christ even more truly than they fit him (v. 19; Isa 53:7; John 1:29). Faced with plots, he commits his cause to the God who tests the heart rather than taking revenge (v. 20), and his own townspeople are his fiercest opponents (vv. 21-23).
11.examples: Sin is usually made respectable by everyone agreeing to it, and reform imposed from above lasts only while the pressure does. Prayer can be used as a fire extinguisher by people who want rescue but not God. And the hardest audience is often the people who knew you as a child; anyone who has paid that price for following Christ stands in Jeremiah's line.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive?<sup>2</sup>You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.<sup>3</sup>But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you. Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and set them apart for the day of slaughter.<sup>4</sup>How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field wither? For the evil of those who dwell in it the beasts and the birds are swept away, because they said, "He will not see our latter end."<sup>5</sup>"If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan?<sup>6</sup>For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; they are in full cry after you; do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you."<sup>7</sup>"I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies.<sup>8</sup>My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has lifted up her voice against me; therefore I hate her.<sup>9</sup>Is my heritage to me like a hyena's lair? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the wild beasts; bring them to devour.<sup>10</sup>Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled down my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness.<sup>11</sup>They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart.<sup>12</sup>Upon all the bare heights in the desert destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the land to the other; no flesh has peace.<sup>13</sup>They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing. They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger of the LORD."<sup>14</sup>Thus says the LORD concerning all my evil neighbors who touch the heritage that I have given my people Israel to inherit: "Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them.<sup>15</sup>And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them again each to his heritage and each to his land.<sup>16</sup>And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, 'As the LORD lives,' even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people.<sup>17</sup>But if any nation will not listen, then I will utterly pluck it up and destroy it, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Conceding God's righteousness first, Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper, though God planted them and they keep him far from their hearts (vv. 1-2). He offers his own heart for testing and asks for judgment on a people who think God will not see their end (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet brings his hardest question to God rather than about him, and concedes God's righteousness before arguing.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive? You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteous are you, O LORD. This is the second of Jeremiah's confessions, the private laments in which he pours out his struggle to God. Before he asks anything he settles the question of who is in the right: Righteous are you, O LORD. Whatever the answer turns out to be, God is not the defendant.

Yet I would plead my case. Then he argues anyway, and the phrase is legal language: he wants to lay the matter out as an advocate would. The complaint is addressed to God, not circulated behind his back, and that is the difference between lament and cynicism.

Why does the way of the wicked prosper? The question itself is the oldest one believers ask. Job asked it: Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? (Job 21:7). Habakkuk asked it more sharply: why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? (Hab 1:13). And Asaph nearly lost his faith over it until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end (Ps 73:17).

You plant them. Jeremiah's version has a personal edge. He has just learned that his neighbours want him dead (11:21). The wicked in view are the men who threatened him, and they are doing well. And he does not soften it: You plant them. Their success is not in spite of God; it comes from his hand. That is harder than saying evil men flourish by luck, and it is the truth this book keeps insisting on.

Near in their mouth and far from their heart. This sentence pins the whole problem. His name is in their conversation, their oaths, their worship, and nowhere near the centre of them. That is what enrages the prophet: not open atheism, which at least is honest, but a religion that keeps God on the lips and out of the life, and prospers doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you. Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and set them apart for the day of slaughter. How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field wither? For the evil of those who dwell in it the beasts and the birds are swept away, because they said, "He will not see our latter end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, know me. Having described men whose hearts are far from God, he offers his own for inspection: you know me, and test my heart toward you. This is the same appeal as 11:20, and it costs something: a man who asks God to examine him has given up the right to be selective about what is found. It is also the only safe ground from which to complain about anyone else. Most of our indignation at others would not survive it.

Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter. Then comes the prayer that makes modern readers wince: that God set them apart for slaughter as a shepherd separates animals for the butcher. Two things keep this from being mere vindictiveness. First, he asks God to do it rather than doing it himself; the prayer is a refusal to take revenge. Second, these men have plotted murder and will shortly preside over the ruin of a nation. To feel nothing about that is not holiness. The psalms are full of such prayers, and the New Testament records the souls under the altar asking, how long before you judge (Rev 6:10).

The vengeance fell on him. Still, Christians read it through a later word. One greater than Jeremiah prayed for those who drove the nails, and the vengeance this prayer asks for fell on him instead, for all who trust him.

How long will the land mourn? The damage falls on the land before it falls on the state: dead grass, animals and birds gone. Human sin bends the creation it lives in, as chapter 4 showed. And the root of it is one sentence they say to themselves: He will not see our latter end. Not that God does not exist, but that he will not be watching when the account comes due. It is the creed of 5:12 in different words, and it is the belief that makes any wickedness possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–6 — How Will You Compete with Horses?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers with harder questions: if footraces weary you, how will you race horses (v. 5)? And even Jeremiah's own family has betrayed him, however friendly their words (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not soothe his servant with easy words; he tells him the race gets harder, warns him about his own family, and stays with him in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan? For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; they are in full cry after you; do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How will you compete with horses? God answers, and he does not answer the question. There is no explanation of why the wicked prosper; that will wait for a cross and an empty tomb. Instead he asks two questions of his own, and they are bracing rather than comforting. You are out of breath from a footrace, and cavalry is coming. You are unsteady on open ground, and ahead is the thicket of the Jordan, the dense scrub along the river where lions lived.

What is God doing? He is telling his servant that this is the easy part. Anathoth was only a village; Jerusalem is still to come. And implicit in the questions is a promise: he is not being asked to find the strength himself. The one asking is the one who said I am with you to deliver you (1:8) and who makes prophets into iron pillars (1:18).

For the weary. There is pastoral wisdom here for anyone worn out by a small trouble. God's cure is not usually to remove it but to grow the person who is carrying it, and for the Christian he does that by his Spirit, who strengthens the weary from within (Eph 3:16). Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1).

Isn’t God supposed to make life easier? Much modern spirituality assumes so. God, if he is there, is there to help us feel better: to lower our stress, mend our relationships and smooth the road to the life we have already chosen. When the road gets harder, we conclude that either we have done something wrong or he has. God’s answer to Jeremiah cuts across it. He does not promise a lighter load. He promises a stronger runner. That sounds harsh only if comfort is the highest good, and almost no one, looking back, believes it is. The people we most admire were not made in easy years. Paul could say that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope (Rom 5:3-4). And God never asks his servants to run a race he has not run himself. The Son did not have life made easier: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8). The God of the Bible is not a therapist who keeps us comfortable. He is a Father who is making us like his Son, and the Son has run the hardest stretch of the course ahead of us.

Even your brothers. Here is the first of the harder things: his own family, in full cry after you, the language of a hunt.

Though they speak friendly words to you. The final instruction is the cruellest kindness in the chapter: do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you. David knew it: it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it, but my companion, my familiar friend (Ps 55:12-13). Of the Lord himself it is written that not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5), and he who knew that loneliness promised those who lose family for his sake a hundredfold household of brothers, sisters and mothers among his people (Mark 10:29-30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — I Have Forsaken My House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God laments that he has given the beloved of his soul to her enemies (vv. 7-9). Shepherds have trampled his vineyard, no one lays it to heart, and those who sowed wheat reap thorns (vv. 10-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is God's own bereavement: he calls the people he is handing over the beloved of his soul.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has lifted up her voice against me; therefore I hate her. Is my heritage to me like a hyena's lair? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the wild beasts; bring them to devour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have forsaken my house. The voice changes, and it takes a moment to realise who is speaking. This is God, describing what he is doing, and every line is a wound. My house: the temple. My heritage: the people and the land, what he chose for himself out of all the earth. And then, unbearably, the beloved of my soul, handed over to enemies.

The beloved of my soul. Read verse 7 before saying that God is detached from the judgment in this book. He is giving away what he loves, in the language of a man surrendering his wife to men who will hurt her.

His own beloved Son. It foreshadows something later. There came a day when God gave his own beloved Son into the hands of his enemies, and that time the giving was not judgment on the one given but redemption for the ones who took him.

Therefore I hate her. Now the line that stops the reader: therefore I hate her. The relationship has reversed: his own inheritance roars at him like a lion. The word hate in covenant language is not a mood but a verdict, the formal rejection of a party who has broken the treaty. It sits in the same book as I have loved you with an everlasting love (31:3), and both are spoken to the same people.

Go, assemble all the wild beasts. Vultures circle and scavengers are called in to the carcass at God's own summons. The armies of Babylon are the beasts, and they come at his whistle.

verseByVerse.quote: Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled down my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart. Upon all the bare heights in the desert destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the land to the other; no flesh has peace. They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing. They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard. Shepherds, that is rulers, again, and they did not merely fail to protect the vineyard; they trampled it. Chapter 23 will bring these shepherds into court. Twice God calls it my portion, the share he took for himself: it is his loss they have caused.

No man lays it to heart. The land mourns to God, and no person does: the fields have more sense of what has happened than the people who farm them. It is possible for a community to live through something catastrophic and simply not register it, and so do individuals with their own souls.

The sword of the LORD. This is Babylon's blade, and God calls it his own. The invaders are instruments, which is why chapter 25 can turn and judge the instrument.

They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns. Good seed in, thorns out; exhausting labour and nothing to show. The ESV notes that where the English reads their harvests, the Hebrew has "your". It is the harvest of chapter 2 in the end: cisterns dug at enormous cost that hold no water. Sin never produces what it advertises, and the bill for the labour still arrives.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will uproot the evil neighbours who seized his heritage, and Judah too, and then have compassion and bring each home (vv. 14-15). If the nations learn to swear by the LORD's name, they will be built up among his people; if not, they will be destroyed (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same hand that uproots replants, and the offer of a place among God's people is extended to the very nations that corrupted them.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning all my evil neighbors who touch the heritage that I have given my people Israel to inherit: "Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them. And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them again each to his heritage and each to his land. And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, 'As the LORD lives,' even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people. But if any nation will not listen, then I will utterly pluck it up and destroy it, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All my evil neighbors. The nations who moved in on Israel's land, Edom, Moab, Ammon and the rest, are now addressed. God calls them my evil neighbors, who touch the heritage that belongs to him. Whatever Judah deserved, the neighbours who profited by her fall are not innocent. In Jehoiakim’s reign raiding bands of Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites joined the Chaldeans against Judah (2 Kgs 24:2), and Edom later gloated over Jerusalem’s fall (Obad 10-14; Ps 137:7).

I will pluck them up. The same verb falls on both: I will pluck them up, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them. Being God's does not mean being spared.

I will again have compassion on them. Here the chapter turns. Chapter 1 gave six verbs, four of them destructive and two constructive, and this is the pattern working out: the same hand that pulls up will plant again. And each to his heritage and each to his land reaches beyond Judah to the nations as well.

Built up in the midst of my people. This is easy to read past. The nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal, the very source of the corruption this book has spent twelve chapters describing, are offered a place: not on the edge, but built up in the midst of my people. The condition is real: diligently learn the ways of my people. Learning runs in the opposite direction from before, and the people who once exported idolatry now have to be taught the fear of God by the nation they corrupted.

The gospel’s shape. This is the gospel's shape, centuries early. Paul describes Gentiles as a wild olive shoot grafted in among the others who share the root's nourishment, with a warning not to be arrogant toward the natural branches (Rom 11:17-18). James summed up the council in Jerusalem the same way: God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name (Acts 15:14).

But if any nation will not listen. The offer is genuine and it is not automatic. The condition that governs Judah governs the nations too: listening. The chapter that began with a question about God's fairness ends by showing him opening his household to his enemies, on the same terms he has been offering his own people since chapter 3.

12.title: Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper?
12.overview:
Jeremiah brings God his hardest question, first conceding that God is righteous: why does the way of the wicked prosper (vv. 1-4)? God does not answer it. He asks two questions of his own, warning his servant that the race will get harder and that his own family has turned on him (vv. 5-6).

Then God laments what he is doing: he has given the beloved of my soul into enemy hands, and his vineyard lies trampled (vv. 7-13). Finally the nations who seized Israel's heritage will themselves be uprooted, and then shown compassion: if they learn the ways of God's people, they will be built up among them (vv. 14-17).
12.theology:
Complaint brought to God, with his righteousness conceded first, is an act of faith rather than rebellion (v. 1; Job 21:7; Hab 1:13; Ps 73:17). Religion in name only keeps God in the mouth and far from the heart (v. 2), and the creed that makes any wickedness possible is that God will not see how it ends (v. 4).

God's answer to a weary servant is not to lighten the load but to make him stronger: the race gets harder and he must grow (v. 5; Heb 12:1). Asking God for vengeance is a way of refusing to take it (v. 3).

Judgment costs God: he hands over the beloved of my soul (v. 7), language that reaches its deepest meaning when he gave his own Son into the hands of enemies for our salvation (Romans 8:32). The uprooting is followed by compassion (v. 15), and the nations that corrupted Israel are offered a place among God's people on the same condition of listening (vv. 16-17; Rom 11:17-18; Acts 15:14).
12.examples: Honest lament begins by conceding that God is in the right, and then brings him the question anyway. A believer out of breath from a footrace, with cavalry coming, is not told the race will be easy but that God is with him in it. And the nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal are offered a place in the household, which is the gospel's welcome seen from far off.

Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A linen loincloth, worn unwashed and hidden by the Euphrates, is dug up ruined (vv. 1-7). Its meaning is the pride of a people God made to cling to him (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: God made his people to cling to him as closely as clothing; pride ruined that closeness, like a garment left to rot by a foreign river.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD to me, "Go and buy a linen loincloth and put it around your waist, and do not dip it in water." So I bought a loincloth according to the word of the LORD, and put it around my waist. And the word of the LORD came to me a second time, "Take the loincloth that you have bought, which is around your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a cleft of the rock." So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go and buy a linen loincloth. Jeremiah's preaching now becomes theatre. He is told to buy a piece of clothing, wear it, and never wash it. Linen was the fabric of priestly garments, and this is the most intimate article of dress there is, worn against the skin under everything else.

Acted sermons. Prophets were regularly asked to act out their message. It makes the word visible, and it costs the messenger his dignity: a man walking round Jerusalem in a garment he is forbidden to wash becomes the sermon.

Go to the Euphrates and hide it there. The second instruction is stranger than the first, and expensive. The Euphrates is the river of Babylon, hundreds of miles away: the direction from which the armies come, and the place to which the people will be carried. He obeys without recorded comment: So I went and hid it.

Obedience before explanation. Obedience in this book is rarely explained in advance. God tells him what to do and only later tells him what it means, which is how most obedience works.

Did Jeremiah walk to the Euphrates and back twice, hundreds of miles? Some think so; others think the place was Parah, a few miles from Anathoth, whose name sounds like the river’s (Josh 18:23), or that it was a vision. Many think the likeliest reading is a real journey to Parah, chosen because its name pointed to the Euphrates and Babylon; it cannot be settled. The meaning is the same: a people that clung to God had been ruined by pride.
verseByVerse.note: Perath may be the Euphrates or a nearby place (Parah) with the same sounding name.

verseByVerse.quote: And after many days the LORD said to me, "Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there." Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth was spoiled; it was good for nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, the loincloth was spoiled. The journey is made a second time, and the prophet kneels in the mud by a foreign river digging up his own underwear. What he lifts out is rotten: stained, weakened, falling apart. Good for nothing.

It was good for nothing. This is the phrase to carry into the meaning. The cloth is not merely damaged and still usable; it is useless, a garment that can no longer do the one thing a garment does.

By the Euphrates. The ruin happened not in Jerusalem but by the Euphrates. What destroys this people will be their long, deliberate burial of themselves among the nations whose gods they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I spoil the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem. This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart and have gone after other gods to serve them and worship them, shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing. For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will spoil the pride of Judah. Now the meaning, and the target is named: pride, twice. Not first their idolatry or their injustice, but the self-satisfaction underneath both. The linen was proud stuff, priestly and fine. God says he will rot it.

Three habits in order. Three habits are listed, and they run in order: refusing to hear, following their own heart, going after other gods. That is the sequence every time. Stop listening, and you will be led by your own heart; follow your heart long enough, and it will find you a god.

As the loincloth clings to the waist of a man. Here is the tenderness at the centre of a harsh chapter. The point of the sign is clinging. That is what God made them for: to be as close to him as clothing is to skin, in contact all day, unnoticed by others but never apart. Moses gave the same command in plain words: You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him (Deut 10:20).

A people, a name, a praise, and a glory. Four words say what he wanted out of it: a people, a name, a praise, and a glory. Not servants who keep the rules, but a people who are his ornament, the thing he is pleased to be seen wearing. It is the same astonishing idea Paul applies to the church, presented to Christ in splendour (Eph 5:27).

But they would not listen. Then the ending. Clothing that will not stay close to the body is buried in mud by a foreign river and rots.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Every Jar Filled with Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A proverb everyone knows is turned into a sentence on the whole nation (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: A proverb about full jars becomes a picture of a nation staggering and smashed against itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall speak to them this word: 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Every jar shall be filled with wine."' And they will say to you, 'Do we not indeed know that every jar will be filled with wine?' Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will fill with drunkenness all the inhabitants of this land: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And I will dash them one against another, fathers and sons together, declares the LORD. I will not pity or spare or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every jar shall be filled with wine. God gives him a proverb so obvious that the reply is predictable: of course jars get filled with wine; that is what jars are for.

I will fill with drunkenness. The obvious saying turns against them. Yes, every jar will be filled, and you are the jars, and what fills you is not wine but drunkenness: confusion, staggering, the loss of judgment that comes over a whole society when God gives it up to its own choices.

From David’s throne down. The list runs from David's throne down to the ordinary citizen. Nobody is sober.

I will dash them one against another. Full jars smashed together: the sound is of pottery breaking. It is a picture of a nation turning on itself under pressure, fathers and sons together, which is exactly what the last years of Judah looked like, with factions destroying one another while an empire waited outside.

I will not pity or spare. The three verbs of withheld mercy are among the heaviest in the book. They are not God's final word to this people; chapter 31 is. They are his word to a generation that has used his patience as permission.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Give Glory Before the Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An appeal to give glory to God while there is light, and the prophet's hidden tears (vv. 15-17); then a word to the king and the queen mother as Judah goes into exile (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: There is a window of light in which glory can still be given to God, and pride is what keeps a people from using it.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken. Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains, and while you look for light he turns it into gloom and makes it deep darkness. But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride; my eyes will weep bitterly and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear and give ear. After the smashing, an appeal, the pattern of the whole book: the door is still open while the sentence is being announced. And the appeal rests on a relationship that still stands: the LORD your God.

The twilight mountains. The picture is of a traveller caught out in the hills. Anyone who has been on a mountain at dusk knows how fast usable light disappears and how quickly the ground becomes treacherous. Give glory to the LORD your God before that happens.

Walk while you have the light. Jesus used the same image about himself, in the last days before the cross: The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you (John 12:35). Light is a season, not a permanent condition, and the sensible thing is to move while it lasts.

Be not proud. What stands in the way is pride. Pride is what keeps a person from giving glory, because giving glory means admitting whose it is.

My soul will weep in secret. Here is the prophet again, and the tears are not for effect: in secret, where nobody would see them. A man can be angry in public and broken in private, and that combination is the mark of someone who actually loves the people he is warning.

He weeps for your pride, grieving not only the coming disaster but the thing that causes it. And he calls them the LORD's flock, still, in the sentence that describes their captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to the king and the queen mother: "Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head." The cities of the Negeb are shut up, with none to open them; all Judah is taken into exile, wholly taken into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king and the queen mother. A specific message for two people, the king and the queen mother. The queen mother held real authority in Judah, and the pairing points to the young king Jehoiachin and his mother, who were carried to Babylon in 597 BC after a reign of three months.

Take a lowly seat. This is court language reversed: come down from the throne and sit on the floor. The crown has already fallen in God's telling, while it is still on the head.

The cities of the Negeb are shut up. The Negeb is the far south, the part of the country furthest from the invasion route, and even there the towns are sealed with nobody to open them. The repetition, taken into exile, wholly taken into exile, is the sound of a door closing twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–27 — Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lost flock and the cause of the disaster (vv. 20-22); the question of the Ethiopian and the leopard (v. 23); and the exposure of a people who forgot God, ending with How long will it be before you are made clean? (vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Habit has hardened into nature, so the command to do good cannot be obeyed, and the chapter ends with the question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Lift up your eyes and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given you, your beautiful flock? What will you say when they set as head over you those whom you yourself have taught to be friends to you? Will not pangs take hold of you like those of a woman in labor? And if you say in your heart, 'Why have these things come upon me?' it is for the greatness of your iniquity that your skirts are lifted up and you suffer violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is the flock that was given you? The question is put to the leaders, and it is the question every shepherd dreads: where are the sheep? They were given you, entrusted, not owned, and they were beautiful. Now look north and count them.

Those entrusted to us. Anyone with responsibility for others (a pastor, a parent, a teacher, an employer) will one day be asked some version of this, and can face it only by leaning on the good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and loses none of them (John 10:11).

Those you taught to be friends. The allies Judah cultivated will become her masters. The diplomacy of chapter 2, drinking from the Nile and the Euphrates (2:18), ends with the foreign friends installed as rulers. Every compromise made to gain their favour becomes a chain.

Why have these things come upon me? God answers the question before it is asked, as he did in 5:19 and 9:12. He refuses to let the catastrophe be mysterious. The imagery that follows is the public shaming of an adulteress, and it is deliberately hard to read: the prophets use it because unfaithfulness to God’s covenant is not the breaking of a rule but the betrayal of a marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil. I will scatter you like chaff driven by the wind from the desert.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can the Ethiopian change his skin? The whole book leans on this sentence, and it is a question with only one answer. Two things are named that cannot alter themselves. The Ethiopian (in Hebrew a Cushite, from the Nile lands south of Egypt) is named only because his dark skin was his own and unchangeable; the verse has sometimes been misused to belittle black Africans, and it never does. Neither skin nor spots is a fault: the point is only that they cannot be changed. And then the application lands: Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil. You can do good about as easily as a leopard can rearrange its coat.

You who are accustomed to do evil. Weigh the word accustomed. The verse does not say that people are born incapable of any decent act, but that long practice has turned a habit into a nature. What was once chosen is now automatic, and the will that would have to choose differently is the very thing that has been shaped by the choosing.

It cannot. The New Testament says it flatly: the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8:7-8). And Jesus, to a religious man at night: unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). Not may not; cannot. The flesh is human nature without God’s Spirit.

The doorway to hope. This is why moral appeals alone never save anyone, and why the whole book has been pleading with people who cannot do what is being asked. It sounds like despair, and it is the doorway to hope, because it drives the question to the only one who can answer it. What a leopard cannot do to itself, God can do to a person: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek 36:26), and in this book, a law written on the heart (31:33). For the Christian that promise is kept: the Spirit now lives in those who belong to Christ and gives the power to walk in God's ways (Ezek 36:27; Rom 8:4), and when they still fail, it is Christ's perfect obedience in their place, not their own record, that stands for them before God (Rom 5:19).

An Ethiopian in Acts. There is a quiet postscript in Acts. An Ethiopian sits in a chariot reading Isaiah, a man explains Jesus to him, and he goes on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:32-35). He did not change his skin. God changed his heart.

Two creeds about change. Our culture holds two beliefs about change, and they contradict each other. The first says you can become anyone you want: reinvent yourself, break the habit, rewrite your story, and a thousand books and apps will show you how. The second says you should never be asked to change: this is who I am, and to love me is to accept me exactly as I am. Jeremiah’s question overturns both at once. Against the first, he says we cannot change at the root by our own effort; the leopard keeps its spots. Against the second, he says we must be changed, because what we are accustomed to is killing us. Left there, that would be despair. But the gospel holds the two together as no self-help programme can. God receives us as we are: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). And he will not leave us as we are: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17). We are accepted before we change, and so, for the first time, we can.

Like chaff driven by the wind. Chaff is what is left when the grain is gone: weightless, and the desert wind takes it. The ESV notes that you is in Hebrew "them". Either way the image is of a people with nothing solid left to hold them down.

verseByVerse.quote: This is your lot, the portion I have measured out to you, declares the LORD, because you have forgotten me and trusted in lies. I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen. I have seen your abominations, your adulteries and neighings, your lewd whorings, on the hills in the field. Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is your lot. In chapter 10 the LORD was the portion of Jacob (10:16); he was their share. Now their share is exile. A people who would not have God as their portion receive another one, measured by him.

You have forgotten me and trusted in lies. The cause is two things: you have forgotten me and trusted in lies. No one trusts in nothing: when God is forgotten, something false takes his place.

Your shame will be seen. The exposure imagery returns, and it is the punishment fitting the crime: what was done in secret on the hills will be made public. I have seen: the shame was visible to God long before it was visible to anyone else.

Your adulteries and neighings. The word neighings recalls 5:8, where the men of the city were stallions after their neighbours' wives. The language is coarse because the behaviour was, and because the prophets refuse to let sin be described in terms that make it sound manageable.

How long will it be before you are made clean? The chapter ends on a question, and it is left hanging. After verse 23 the reader knows that the city cannot answer it: a people who cannot do good cannot wash themselves either.

God will wash them. The question waits for God, and he answers it later in the same book: I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me (33:8). The one who asks how long is the one who will do the washing, and the cost of it appears at the far end of the story, when the Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world.

13.title: Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin?
13.overview:
A ruined loincloth shows what pride has done to a people God made to cling to him (vv. 1-11). A proverb about full jars becomes a sentence of drunkenness and smashing (vv. 12-14), followed by an appeal to give glory to God before the darkness, and the fall of the king and queen mother (vv. 15-19).

Then the question that explains everything: can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? The chapter ends asking how long before Jerusalem is made clean (vv. 20-27).
13.theology:
God made his people to cling to him as closely as clothing (v. 11; Deut 10:20), to be his people, his name, his praise and his glory, and pride is what rots that closeness (vv. 9, 15-17).

Verse 23 teaches that sinners cannot heal themselves: habit has become nature, so doing good is beyond them (Rom 8:7-8; John 3:3). That drives them to what only God can give, a new heart and a law written within (Ezek 36:26; Jer 31:33), and the closing question, how long before you are made clean, is answered by God himself (33:8).
13.examples: Jeremiah preaches by wearing an unwashed garment round the city and then digging it, rotten, out of the mud of a foreign river. A traveller on a mountain as the light goes, and a leopard invited to rearrange its spots, are the chapter's pictures of urgency and helplessness: move while you can see, and know that you cannot change yourself.
