Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us."<sup>10</sup>Thus says the LORD concerning this people: "They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins."<sup>11</sup>The LORD said to me: "Do not pray for the welfare of this people.<sup>12</sup>Though they fast, I will not hear their cry, and though they offer burnt offering and grain offering, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence."<sup>13</sup>Then I said: "Ah, Lord GOD, behold, the prophets say to them, 'You shall not see the sword, nor shall you have famine, but I will give you assured peace in this place.'"<sup>14</sup>And the LORD said to me: "The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a lying vision, worthless divination, and the deceit of their own minds.<sup>15</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name although I did not send them, and who say, 'Sword and famine shall not come upon this land': By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed.<sup>16</sup>And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, victims of famine and sword, with none to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters. For I will pour out their evil upon them.<sup>17</sup>"You shall say to them this word: 'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered with a great wound, with a very grievous blow.<sup>18</sup>If I go out into the field, behold, those pierced by the sword! And if I enter the city, behold, the diseases of famine! For both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge.'"<sup>19</sup>Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? Why have you struck us down so that there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.<sup>20</sup>We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you.<sup>21</sup>Do not spurn us, for your name's sake; do not dishonor your glorious throne; remember and do not break your covenant with us.<sup>22</sup>Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A drought: the city mourns, the servants and farmers are ashamed, and even the animals suffer (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The land itself preaches: empty vessels, ashamed farmers and animals abandoning their young.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought: "Judah mourns, and her gates languish; her people lament on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goes up. Her nobles send their servants for water; they come to the cisterns; they find no water; they return with their vessels empty; they are ashamed and confounded and cover their heads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her gates languish. The gates were where a town did its business and held its courts; when the gates languish, public life has stopped. People are sitting on the ground, which is the posture of mourning, and the noise of the city has become one long cry.

The drought and the covenant. Drought was not a random misfortune in Israel's understanding. God had said at the start that the land's rain was tied to the covenant: the heavens over your head shall be bronze, and the earth under you shall be iron (Deut 28:23). A sky that gives nothing was a sermon everyone could feel.

They cover their heads. Anyone who has watched a harvest, a business or a body fail will recognise the instinct to cover the head. The sequence is written like a short film: the order given, the walk to the cisterns, the search, the empty jars, the long walk back. And then the faces: ashamed and confounded, heads covered.

They find no water. The detail that matters most is the cisterns. This is the book that defined the nation's sin as digging broken cisterns that can hold no water while abandoning the fountain of living waters (2:13). Now they go to their cisterns and find exactly what the picture warned of. Sin's outcome eventually arrives in physical form, and the empty jar in a servant's hands is the picture of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the ground that is dismayed, since there is no rain on the land, the farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads. Even the doe in the field forsakes her newborn fawn because there is no grass. The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail because there is no vegetation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ground that is dismayed. Even the soil is said to be dismayed. The farmers cover their heads like the nobles' servants: the two ends of society making the same gesture, because the drought does not consult rank.

The farmers are ashamed. There is the shame too. A farmer whose field fails feels it as failure, though he did not make the weather.

The doe forsakes her newborn fawn. Now the animals, and these two pictures are among the most affecting in the book. A doe abandons her newborn, against every instinct she has, because there is nothing to feed it with. Wild donkeys stand on the ridges with their heads up, panting, eyes failing.

Creation groans. Scripture keeps insisting that human sin damages more than humans. The creation that was subjected to futility groans (Rom 8:20-22), and here the groaning is a fawn left in the grass.

A mirror for the nation. It is also, quietly, an argument. The animals have done nothing wrong and are suffering; the people have done a great deal wrong and are complaining. The drought is a mirror held up to a nation that has abandoned its own young in the valley of Hinnom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Act for Your Name's Sake
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people pray well, appealing to God's name (vv. 7-9); God answers that they have loved to wander, and forbids Jeremiah to pray for them (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is theologically perfect, but the feet, the way the people actually live, have not changed direction, and God answers the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake; for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against you. O you hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who turns aside to tarry for a night? Why should you be like a man confused, like a mighty warrior who cannot save? Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though our iniquities testify against us. The people pray, and as prayer it is very good indeed. They do not argue that they deserve help. They concede the evidence, our iniquities testify against us, and then appeal to the one ground that is left: for your name's sake.

The firmest ground. No prayer stands on firmer ground. Moses used it at Sinai, Asaph used it after the temple was sacked, Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake! (Ps 79:9), and Daniel would use it in Babylon: we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy (Dan 9:18).

For your name’s sake. To modern ears this can sound like an appeal to God’s ego, as if he were a celebrity guarding his image. But God’s name is who he has shown himself to be. When he proclaimed it to Moses, it was The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). To pray “for your name’s sake” is to say: be who you said you are. Timothy Keller, in The Reason for God, answered the worry that a God who seeks his own glory must be self-centred by pointing to the Trinity: the Father, the Son and the Spirit have always delighted to glorify one another, so God’s glory is the glory of self-giving love. That love went all the way on the night Jesus prayed, Father, glorify your name (John 12:28), and then went to the cross, so that John can write, your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake (1 John 2:12). Judah’s prayer was refused (v. 10), not because the plea was wrong, but because their feet had not turned. So when your own record testifies against you this week, do not reach for a better record. Turn, and plead his name: “Because you are merciful, and you have said so.”

Like a traveler who turns aside. The titles are exactly right: hope of Israel, savior in time of trouble. And the complaint is vivid. You are behaving like a tourist, someone who stops at an inn, sleeps, and is gone in the morning with no stake in the place. Why are you a visitor in your own country?

Like a mighty warrior who cannot save. Bolder still: like a soldier who has lost his nerve. They are telling God that his reputation is suffering. And they end with the covenant itself, Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name, and a plea a child might make: do not leave us.

Read on its own, this prayer deserves an answer. Which is what makes the next verse so unsettling.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning this people: "They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins." The LORD said to me: "Do not pray for the welfare of this people. Though they fast, I will not hear their cry, and though they offer burnt offering and grain offering, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have loved to wander thus. God does not answer the words. He answers the feet, the way they actually walk.

They have not restrained their feet. They loved it, not merely drifted. Restraining their feet was the one thing repentance would have required, and it was never attempted. Beautiful prayers came out of the same city in which the shrines stayed open.

Words measured against a life. This is the lesson the chapter presses, and it is not that God is deaf. It is that words to God are measured against the direction of a life. The same book has already told us what God is listening for: one honest What have I done? (8:6), and a turning that follows it.

Do not pray for the welfare of this people. This is the third time Jeremiah has been told not to pray for them (7:16; 11:14). Each time it is more specific, and each repetition tells us the prophet had gone on praying.

An Intercessor never silenced. Here the human intercessor is silenced. The gospel gives an Intercessor who never is: Jesus always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and the Father always hears him (John 11:42).

Though they fast, I will not hear. Fasting, burnt offering and grain offering, the full range of religious response, are refused. Isaiah heard the same from God: even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15).

What these verses do not mean. These verses need care. They are not a general statement that God rejects sinners who come to him; the whole Bible says the opposite, and this book will end with a new covenant. They are about a people using worship to force God’s hand while refusing to change course, and they exist to stop anyone treating prayer as a technique.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah pleads that the people were misled; God answers that he never sent those prophets, and that preachers and hearers will fall together (vv. 13-16). Then the commanded tears (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: False comfort kills both the preacher and the congregation, and God orders the weeping over it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said: "Ah, Lord GOD, behold, the prophets say to them, 'You shall not see the sword, nor shall you have famine, but I will give you assured peace in this place.'" And the LORD said to me: "The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a lying vision, worthless divination, and the deceit of their own minds. Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name although I did not send them, and who say, 'Sword and famine shall not come upon this land': By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, victims of famine and sword, with none to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters. For I will pour out their evil upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Assured peace in this place. Jeremiah tries one more argument, and it is a generous one: they were misled. Their preachers told them there would be no war and no hunger, and promised assured peace; the phrase has a confident, official ring to it.

It is the plea of a pastor who knows his people are not chiefly wicked but badly taught.

I did not send them. God's answer is emphatic, and the denial is threefold: not sent, not commanded, not spoken to. Whatever those men were doing, God had no part in it.

The deceit of their own minds. The last phrase names the source. They were not channelling demons; they were saying what they themselves found plausible and agreeable, and calling it the word of the LORD. That is how most false teaching is made: sincere men speaking with no word from God behind them.

By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. The sentence fits the crime exactly: the men who said the sword would not come will fall to it. Teachers are judged by the standard they preached.

The people die too. Here is the hard part of the answer to Jeremiah's plea. The congregation dies with the preachers. Being deceived is not treated as an acquittal, because they chose the men who told them what they wanted: my people love to have it so (5:31).

The listener’s responsibility. That puts a real responsibility on anyone who listens to teaching. Nobody will be able to say at the end that they were only doing what their church told them. But God has not left his people to work it out alone: he gives his word to test teaching by, and his Spirit, who leads believers into the truth (1 John 4:1).

Is sincerity enough? Most people today would say that what matters in religion is not being right but being sincere. It sounds generous, and it guards against arrogance. But we never apply that rule anywhere else. In December 1799 George Washington’s doctors, among the most respected in America, treated his throat infection by drawing off a large part of his blood. They were entirely sincere, and he died. Sincerity is a virtue in the doctor; it does nothing to the medicine. The people of Jerusalem sincerely trusted their prophets, and the prophets very likely believed themselves (v. 14). It did not stop the sword. That is no reason to despise sincere people; it is a reason to care very much about what is true. And here the gospel brings unexpected relief. Our sincerity is always mixed and our faith often weak, so it would be bad news if we were saved by the quality of our believing. We are saved by the one we believe in, who is faithful when we waver and true when every other voice fails: there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall say to them this word: 'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered with a great wound, with a very grievous blow. If I go out into the field, behold, those pierced by the sword! And if I enter the city, behold, the diseases of famine! For both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let my eyes run down with tears. God tells him what to say, and the message is a flood of tears. This is commanded: the weeping is part of the sermon, not a weakness in the preacher. A man who could announce this dry-eyed would be misrepresenting God, because God is not dry-eyed.

The virgin daughter of my people. He calls them the virgin daughter of my people, the tenderest name he has for them, at the moment of her greatest disgrace.

If I go out into the field. Two doors and no way out: outside the walls the war dead, inside them the starving.

Prophet and priest ply their trade. The final line puts the cause beside the effect. The phrase is one for business as usual, and have no knowledge. Religion carried on as a profession by men who do not know God, while the bodies pile up outside. The priest still takes the service; the prophet still gives the address.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second prayer: confession of sin, an appeal to God's name, throne and covenant, and the confession that only the LORD gives rain (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Every word of the confession is right, and still the answer in the next chapter is no: right words are not yet repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? Why have you struck us down so that there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror. We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you. Do not spurn us, for your name's sake; do not dishonor your glorious throne; remember and do not break your covenant with us. Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you utterly rejected Judah? The people pray again, and the questions are raw. Have you utterly rejected us? Does your soul loathe Zion? They quote back the promise of healing that was preached to them (8:15) and set it against what actually arrived.

We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD. Here is the confession God asked for in chapter 3: Only acknowledge your guilt (3:13). It is all here: their own wickedness, their fathers' iniquity, the direct address we have sinned against you.

For your name’s sake. The appeal is to God's name, God's throne and God's covenant: three grounds, none of them their own merit.

Do not break your covenant with us. The covenant they plead was broken, but not by God. His answer, given later in this book, is a new covenant (31:31-34), and Jesus took the cup at his last supper and called it the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). The prayer of verse 21 is finally answered at the cross.

Can the false gods bring rain? The prayer ends with sound theology about the weather. The Baals were rain gods; the whole point of serving them was showers. Now, in a drought, the people say what chapter 10 said: those things are nothing, and rain is yours. Zechariah puts it positively: Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain (Zech 10:1).

A faultless prayer refused. The chapter ends with a faultless prayer: every phrase true, the doctrine exact, the confession explicit. And the first verse of chapter 15 refuses it.

What the refusal teaches. That refusal must be read carefully. It does not teach that God turns away a broken heart: a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 51:17). It teaches that words, even perfect words, are not repentance, and that a nation can learn to say the right things in a crisis while loving to wander (v. 10).

Mercies new every morning. For anyone frightened by this passage, Lamentations, long associated with this same man and written over the ruins, gives the answer: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23).

14.title: The Drought, and Prayers That Are Not Heard
14.overview:
A drought falls on Judah, and the whole land mourns (vv. 1-6). The people pray well, but God answers the direction of their lives rather than their words, and forbids Jeremiah to pray for them (vv. 7-12).

Jeremiah pleads that the prophets misled them; God replies that he never sent those prophets, and commands the prophet's tears (vv. 13-18). The chapter ends with a second, faultless prayer (vv. 19-22), which the next chapter refuses.
14.theology:
Creation suffers under human sin (vv. 4-6; Rom 8:20-22). Prayer that appeals to God's name rather than to human merit stands on the firmest ground there is (v. 7; Ps 79:9; Dan 9:18), yet God measures prayers against the direction of a life (v. 10), and worship used to move God while the course of life is unchanged is refused (vv. 11-12).

False prophecy is the deceit of the preacher's own mind; teachers are judged by the standard they preached, and hearers are not acquitted for having been deceived (vv. 14-16). Yet the mercy that outlasts this refusal is sung over the ruins (Lam 3:22-23), and the broken covenant is answered by a new one sealed in Christ's blood (31:31-34; Luke 22:20).
14.examples: The chapter's sharpest picture is the empty jars carried back from the cisterns, in the book that called sin a broken cistern (2:13). Its sharpest warning is the prayer that would score full marks offered by people whose lives have not changed direction, and by preachers who say what they find plausible and call it the word of the LORD.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go!<sup>2</sup>And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.'<sup>3</sup>I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.<sup>4</sup>And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>"Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare?<sup>6</sup>You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting.<sup>7</sup>I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways.<sup>8</sup>I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly.<sup>9</sup>She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."<sup>10</sup>Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me.<sup>11</sup>The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?<sup>12</sup>Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze?<sup>13</sup>"Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory.<sup>14</sup>I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."<sup>15</sup>O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach.<sup>16</sup>Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.<sup>17</sup>I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation.<sup>18</sup>Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?<sup>19</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them.<sup>20</sup>And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD.<sup>21</sup>I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Though Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God refuses the prayer even if Moses and Samuel made it, and allots the people their destinations because of Manasseh (vv. 1-4). No one will pity Jerusalem, and God is weary of relenting (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest intercessors in Israel's history could not turn this, and the sins of a king two generations back are still working themselves out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go! And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.' I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy. And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My heart would not turn toward this people. This is the answer to the faultless prayer at the end of chapter 14, and it is devastating.

Though Moses and Samuel stood before me. Moses and Samuel are named because they are the two men in Israel's story whose prayers most famously turned judgment aside. Moses stood in the breach at Sinai when the nation deserved destruction, and the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people (Exod 32:14). Samuel said it would be a sin against God for him to stop praying for Israel (1 Sam 12:23). The psalm remembers both: They called to the LORD, and he answered them (Ps 99:6).

The moment has passed. God says that if those two were standing here making that case, his heart would not turn. It is the strongest way of saying that the moment for this generation has passed, and it explains why Jeremiah has three times been forbidden to pray.

Where shall we go? They will ask the practical question people always ask in a crisis: where do we go? The answer is a grim list. It offers no refuge, only a fate assigned to each.

Four kinds of destroyers. Sword, dogs, birds, beasts: on a battlefield the sword kills, and then the animals come for the bodies. It is deliberately without dignity, because that is what the end of a siege looks like.

Because of what Manasseh did. Manasseh had been dead for decades. He reigned fifty-five years, filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood, and, Chronicles records, repented late in his own life (2 Chronicles 33:12-13). Kings does not mention the repentance; it is not denying it but explaining why judgment still came (2 Kings 23:26), while Chronicles shows that even Manasseh could be forgiven. His personal forgiveness did not undo what he had built into the nation.

Forgiven, with consequences. Sin can be forgiven and still leave consequences running through families and institutions for generations. A father restored to God may still watch his children live with what his years of neglect made normal. Grace does not undo the past, but it does not leave him alone in it either: he can pray for them, own what he did, and show them the mercy he has found.

Are there people Christians should stop praying for? God forbade Jeremiah to pray for a nation whose judgment was fixed. Christians are commanded to pray for all people (1 Tim 2:1) and for enemies (Matt 5:44). John speaks of sin that leads to death and does not command prayer for it (1 John 5:16), but we cannot see who is beyond hope, so we keep praying.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare? You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting. I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways. I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly. She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? Three questions, and they are about loneliness rather than punishment. Who will feel sorry? Who will mourn? Who will even stop to ask how you are? A city that has become a warning to others will find the neighbours passing on the other side.

You keep going backward. This is the same charge as 7:24. Then comes a phrase to stop at: I am weary of relenting.

I am weary of relenting. Relenting is what God has been doing for centuries. Every warning not carried out, every disaster postponed, every prophet sent instead of an army was God relenting. He is not saying that mercy has run out in principle; three chapters later he will say that if a nation turns he will relent of the disaster he intended (18:8). He is saying that this generation has treated his patience as leave to go on sinning.

I have destroyed my people. In verse 7 God says I have three times, and the third is I have destroyed my people. God does not distance himself from what is happening, and he does not stop calling them his.

They did not turn from their ways. The reason is stated last, plainly: they did not turn from their ways. Everything in this book comes back to that sentence.

She who bore seven has grown feeble. The promise to Abraham was descendants like the sand of the sea; now the widows are counted that way. Seven sons was the picture of a blessed mother, and this one has lost them all: her sun went down while it was yet day.

Her sun went down while it was yet day. The phrase has comforted and haunted the bereaved ever since, because it names the particular cruelty of losing a child: the light going at noon. Scripture does not hurry past that grief or explain it away; it gives it words, so that those who carry it can bring it to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — A Man of Strife and Contention
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah wishes he had never been born (v. 10); God answers with his care for him, and with the unbreakable iron from the north (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet wishes he had never been born, and God answers him without apology and without contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me. The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me. Now the prophet breaks. This is the third of his confessions, his personal complaints to God. He turns to the woman who gave him birth and wishes she had not. Job said it in his ashes: Let the day perish on which I was born (Job 3:3).

A man of strife and contention. What he cannot bear is what he has become: a man of strife and contention to the whole land. He never wanted to be a man who is always in a quarrel. He is a village priest's son who would have been content to be ignored, and he is the most argued-about man in the country.

I have not lent, nor have I borrowed. The detail about lending is the saddest touch. Debt was the usual reason for a man to be hated in a small society. I have not lent, nor have I borrowed: he has given nobody any of the ordinary grounds for a grudge, and they curse him anyway. He is hated purely for the message.

Disliked for faith. Anyone who has been disliked for their faith rather than for their faults will understand the particular loneliness of this verse.

Have I not set you free for their good? The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, and translations differ. What comes through is that God answers, and that his answer is about his own care: he has been at work for Jeremiah's good and has pleaded for him when enemies pressed.

God answers the outburst. God does not rebuke the outburst, and he does not pretend the pain is unreasonable. He replies. Anyone who has wished they had never been born should notice that: the wish is written down in Scripture, and God answers the man who made it with his care, not his contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze? "Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory. I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can one break iron? The question sounds as if it is about metals, but it is about politics. The iron from the north is Babylon, and nobody breaks it, certainly not Judah with its alliances. It is the answer to every plan for escape that the palace has been making.

Without price. There is no ransom, no tribute paid to buy it back, no compensation. The treasures simply change hands. A nation that trusted its reserves discovers they were never security.

In a land that you do not know. This repeats the sentence of 5:19, and the punishment fits the sin exactly: you served foreign gods at home, so you will serve foreigners abroad. Exile is not random misfortune. They chose foreign masters; now they have them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Your Words Were Found, and I Ate Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet's prayer: God's words were his delight (vv. 15-16), and they have left him alone, asking whether God is like a deceitful brook (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The same words that were his joy have cost him every friendship, and he tells God that he feels like a dry streambed.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach. Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, you know. He prays, and the first words are the ones every sufferer needs. He does not ask God to explain. It is enough that God knows.

In your forbearance take me not away. Then a request that shows how well he understands his own situation. God is being patient with his persecutors, and that patience is the very thing endangering the prophet. In your forbearance take me not away: do not let me be killed while you are being slow to judge them.

For your sake I bear reproach. This is the ground of the appeal. A psalm uses the same words (Psalm 69:7), and Paul hears Christ praying that psalm: The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (Romans 15:3). Jeremiah bore reproach for God's sake; Christ bore it in full, and those who suffer for him share it (Hebrews 13:13). That is what makes the suffering bearable.

Your words were found, and I ate them. This lovely sentence about Scripture comes from a man in the middle of a breakdown. Your words were found may be a memory of the scroll discovered in the temple in Josiah's reign, or perhaps simply of the moment God's word came to him. And I ate them: not admired, studied or filed. Eaten, taken in as food, made part of himself. Ezekiel was given a scroll to eat and found it as sweet as honey (Ezek 3:3). The psalmist said, How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Jesus answered the tempter, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4).

A joy and the delight of my heart. This was the result, and this is the man who has just wished he had never been born. Both are true at once, and anyone who has walked with God through a hard season knows that they can be.

May a believer pray for vengeance on persecutors? Jeremiah hands his cause to God instead of taking revenge (Rom 12:19). Christians may pray for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, while praying for their persecutors to repent (Matt 5:44), as Jesus did (Luke 23:34).

verseByVerse.quote: I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation. Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I did not sit in the company of revelers. Here is the cost of the previous verse. The word that was his joy has taken away his company. He did not join the parties, partly because he could not bring himself to, partly because a man who says what he says is not invited twice.

I sat alone. The hand of God is usually spoken of as protection or power. Here it is what keeps a man out of the room. Faithfulness is often isolating, and Jeremiah does not pretend it is noble or that he enjoys it. He is lonely, and he tells God so, knowing that God's hand is in it.

The idol of being liked. Few things frighten us more than being the person nobody invites. We are social creatures, and our age has turned approval into something we can count: followers, likes, the replies to a post. Many people quietly arrange their lives around not being disliked, saying what the room wants and keeping their convictions where they will not cost anything. Scripture names the trap: The fear of man lays a snare (Prov 29:25). Jeremiah shows what it costs to step out of the snare, and he does not pretend the price is small. But approval is a hard master, because it can be withdrawn at any moment and so must be earned again every day. The way out is not to stop needing approval but to receive it from somewhere it cannot be lost. The one who was despised and rejected by men (Isa 53:3) had first heard his Father say, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17), and those who are in him share that verdict. A person who already has God’s delight can afford to sit alone for a while, and can even afford to love the people who left the room.

Like a deceitful brook. This is among the sharpest things Jeremiah ever says. In a dry country a wadi, a desert streambed, runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in the summer. Travellers died of thirst walking to one because they remembered water there.

Like waters that fail. He is saying to God: I think you might be a stream that dries up. And the accusation lands exactly where this book began: God had called himself the fountain of living waters and the people's idols the broken cisterns (2:13). Now the prophet who preached that sermon asks whether the fountain itself sometimes runs dry.

Scripture keeps the accusation. Scripture writes it down and keeps it. The Bible is not embarrassed by a servant of God accusing God of unreliability, because the God of the Bible is not fragile, and because believers need to know that somebody in the book has felt what they are feeling.

If you are where Jeremiah was. If you are where Jeremiah was, with pain that will not lift and a God who seems to have run dry, this verse is for you. Feeling abandoned is not proof that you are, and saying so to God is prayer, not unbelief. Depression is often an illness as well as a spiritual trial, so do not carry it alone: tell your pastor and a friend, and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up. And remember who hears you: a High Priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), who was himself a man of sorrows, and who does not dry up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — If You Return, I Will Restore You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls his prophet to return, and renews the promise of the bronze wall (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: God calls his own prophet to repent, and then gives him back his commission with the original promise attached.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD. I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer. God's answer is not what a modern reader expects, and it is exactly right. He does not comfort first. He calls his prophet to repent.

If you return, I will restore you. The word Jeremiah has been preaching to the nation is now addressed to him. His complaint went past lament into accusation. God does not call him to repent of his pain or his tears, which he never rebukes, but of the bitter words that had begun to call God false. He treats him as an adult: turn, and you will be restored to your place, standing before me as a servant stands before a king.

You shall be as my mouth. He is to sort his speech. Self-pity and bitterness are worthless; God's word is precious; and the promise attached is staggering: you shall be as my mouth.

They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. This is the rule for every minister since. The pressure of an audience is constant, and the temptation is to be shaped by the people you are speaking to until you are saying what they would have said anyway. That is how the false prophets of chapter 14 were made. The prophet is to change his hearers; they are not to change him. No servant of God keeps this rule perfectly; the one who did, who always did what pleased the Father (John 8:29), is the one whose faithfulness covers those who fail at it, and the way back for them is the one offered here: return, and be restored.

A fortified wall of bronze. God gives him back his call, in the words of the first chapter (1:18-19). A bronze wall; opposition that does not prevail; I am with you.

Repeated, not improved. Two things stand out. The promise is repeated rather than improved, because it was always sufficient and the man had simply lost sight of it. And it is given after the rebuke, not instead of it. God's way with his exhausted servants is neither to ignore their sin nor to withdraw his promise, but to call them back and then hand them the same commission again.

Back to work. Jeremiah went back to work, and kept at it until the city fell and after.

15.title: A Deceitful Brook, and the Bronze Wall
15.overview:
God answers the faultless prayer of chapter 14: even Moses and Samuel could not turn his heart toward this generation (vv. 1-9).

Then the prophet breaks. He wishes he had never been born (vv. 10-14), and he asks whether God, whose words were his delight, has become a brook that fails (vv. 15-18). God calls him back, restores him, and renews the promise of the bronze wall (vv. 19-21).
15.theology:
There is a point at which even the greatest intercessors would not turn God's heart (v. 1), and forgiven sin can still leave consequences running for generations (v. 4). God's long patience is real, and people can take it for granted until it ends (v. 6; compare 18:8).

God's word is food and delight to those who receive it (v. 16), and it can isolate the one who carries it (v. 17). Scripture keeps a prophet's accusation that God may be a brook that fails (v. 18), because faith may speak honestly to God. And God calls his weary servant back from accusation, then restores him with the same promise he was first given (vv. 19-21; 1:18-19).
15.examples: Two of the chapter's pictures stay with a reader: the light going at noon for a mother who has lost her children, and a wadi that runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in summer. Between them stands a man who ate God's word with joy and lost every invitation because of it.

They shall not be lamented, nor shall they be buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. They shall not be buried, and no one shall lament for them or cut himself or make himself bald for them.<sup>7</sup>No one shall break bread for the mourner, to comfort him for the dead, nor shall anyone give him the cup of consolation to drink for his father or his mother.<sup>8</sup>You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and drink.<sup>9</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will silence in this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.<sup>10</sup>"And when you tell this people all these words, and they say to you, 'Why has the LORD pronounced all this great evil against us? What is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?'<sup>11</sup>then you shall say to them: 'Because your fathers have forsaken me, declares the LORD, and have gone after other gods and have served and worshiped them, and have forsaken me and have not kept my law,<sup>12</sup>and because you have done worse than your fathers, for behold, every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen to me.<sup>13</sup>Therefore I will hurl you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.'<sup>14</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it shall no longer be said, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,'<sup>15</sup>but 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' For I will bring them back to their own land that I gave to their fathers.<sup>16</sup>"Behold, I am sending for many fishers, declares the LORD, and they shall catch them. And afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.<sup>17</sup>For my eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from me, nor is their iniquity concealed from my eyes.<sup>18</sup>But first I will doubly repay their iniquity and their sin, because they have polluted my land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and have filled my inheritance with their abominations."<sup>19</sup>O LORD, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth and say: "Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit.<sup>20</sup>Can man make for himself gods? Such are not gods!"<sup>21</sup>"Therefore, behold, I will make them know, this once I will make them know my power and my might, and they shall know that my name is the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three prohibitions make Jeremiah's life a sign: no marriage (vv. 1-4), no funerals (vv. 5-7), no feasts (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's private life is confiscated and made into the sermon: no marriage, no funerals, no parties.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place. For thus says the LORD concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning the mothers who bore them and the fathers who fathered them in this land: They shall die of deadly diseases. They shall not be lamented, nor shall they be buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. They shall perish by the sword and by famine, and their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not take a wife. In a society where marriage and children were the whole of a man's future, his security in old age and his name after death, God forbids his prophet both. Jeremiah is to be single and childless, not by preference but by command, and the whole town will see it.

The cost of the calling. This is the cost of the calling at its sharpest. He has already lost his village (11:21) and his family (12:6); now he is denied the family he might have made. Ezekiel would face something similar when God took his wife and forbade him to mourn: Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead (Ezek 24:17).

They shall die of deadly diseases. And here is the reason, which turns the command from cruelty into mercy. Children born in Jerusalem now will die in the siege. God is sparing his servant the sight of his own family starving.

A calling for a crisis. Paul reasoned in the same direction for a different crisis: the appointed time has grown very short, so let those who have wives live as though they had none (1 Cor 7:29). And Jesus spoke of those who renounce marriage for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:12). Singleness is never second-class in Scripture, and here it is part of the prophet’s message.

For the single and childless. The command was Jeremiah's alone; it tells no one else to stay unmarried. But for those who are single or childless without having chosen it, he is company: a man with no wife and no children whom God called, kept and used. And the Lord Jesus himself lived unmarried.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah’s unmarried life was itself a sign of coming judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Do not enter the house of mourning, or go to lament or grieve for them, for I have taken away my peace from this people, my steadfast love and mercy, declares the LORD. Both great and small shall die in this land. They shall not be buried, and no one shall lament for them or cut himself or make himself bald for them. No one shall break bread for the mourner, to comfort him for the dead, nor shall anyone give him the cup of consolation to drink for his father or his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not enter the house of mourning. The second prohibition takes away the ordinary duties of a neighbour. He may not go to funerals. In a village culture that is not a minor absence; it is a public insult, and it is meant to be noticed and asked about.

My steadfast love and mercy. And the reason is the most frightening sentence in the chapter: I have taken away my peace from this people, my steadfast love and mercy. Peace, steadfast love and mercy are covenant words, the things God had bound himself by solemn promise to show, and now he withdraws them.

Not the last word. But the same words come back later, in Lamentations, when the city has actually fallen: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end (Lam 3:22). What is withdrawn from a generation is not lost from the world.

The cup of consolation. Every custom of comfort is listed and cancelled: the burial, the lament, the mourning rites, the meal brought to the bereaved, the cup of consolation pressed into the hand of a man who has lost his mother.

No one shall lament for them. The horror here is not only death but the collapse of the community that normally carries people through it. There will be too many dead and too few living to sit with them.

Cut himself or make himself bald. Gashing the body and shaving the head were mourning rites for the dead that the law forbade (Lev 19:28; Deut 14:1); the people had adopted them.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and drink. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will silence in this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of feasting. And the third prohibition takes the other half of social life. No funerals, and now no weddings or celebrations either. He may not sit down and enjoy an evening with his neighbours.

Alone among his people. Jeremiah has already said that he sat alone (15:17). This is the command behind it. A man who tells the truth in such a time will find himself outside both the grief and the gladness of his people.

The voice of the bridegroom. Verse 9 repeats the sentence that closed the temple sermon (7:34), and it is the sound of a civilisation ending: no laughter, and no weddings. Jeremiah's enforced absence from the feasts is a preview. He stays away from them now because soon there will be none.

Before your eyes and in your days. And there is mercy hidden in the timing: before your eyes and in your days. God tells him plainly that he will live to see it, so that when it comes he will not think God has lost control.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people will ask what their iniquity is; the answer covers two generations, and the sentence is shaped like the sin (vv. 10-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A people can be so far gone that they cannot name a single sin, and the sentence simply gives them what they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when you tell this people all these words, and they say to you, 'Why has the LORD pronounced all this great evil against us? What is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?' then you shall say to them: 'Because your fathers have forsaken me, declares the LORD, and have gone after other gods and have served and worshiped them, and have forsaken me and have not kept my law, and because you have done worse than your fathers, for behold, every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen to me. Therefore I will hurl you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is our iniquity? God predicts the reaction, and it is not defiance but blank incomprehension. What is our iniquity? They genuinely cannot think what they have done.

A conscience without feeling. This is the condition the whole book has been describing from a different angle. A conscience that has lost feeling (6:15), a people who never ask What have I done? (8:6), religion carried on as a trade (14:18). The end of that process is not a guilty nation pleading for mercy but a puzzled one asking what the fuss is about.

You have done worse than your fathers. The answer covers two generations. The fathers forsook God; and you have done worse than your fathers (compare 7:26). Their upbringing explains a great deal and excuses nothing, because each generation could see where the sin of the last had led.

Refusing to listen. And how it happened is stated exactly: every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen. Not one national decision, but thousands of private ones.

Day and night. The sentence is shaped like the sin, as in 5:19. You wanted other gods; you shall have them day and night, in a country where they are the only ones on offer. God's severest judgment is often to give people what they insisted on, in quantities they never wanted.

In practice. The cure is to ask their question while it can still be answered. Read Scripture as a mirror rather than a weapon, and ask a friend who knows you well what you have stopped noticing in yourself. Then confess it plainly, because the God who names our sin does so in order to forgive it: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — A New Exodus, and Fishers and Hunters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A promised homecoming greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), but first the fishers and hunters (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Even while announcing the hunt, God promises a rescue that will make the exodus a second-best story.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it shall no longer be said, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' For I will bring them back to their own land that I gave to their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The days are coming. And then, without warning, hope, and on a scale that is easy to miss. The exodus was the foundation of Israel's whole identity. Every oath, every feast, every creed began there: the God who brought us out of Egypt. It was the story that defined them.

Out of the north country. God says that the rescue he is planning will be so much greater that people will stop swearing by the exodus and start swearing by this. The Red Sea will become the second-best story about him.

A new thing. Isaiah said the same in his own way: Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing (Isa 43:18-19). And the saying is repeated later in this book (23:7-8), attached there to the coming of a righteous Branch.

A greater exodus. Christians can hardly read it without looking further. There is a rescue that makes even the return from Babylon a rehearsal: a greater exodus, out of a deeper slavery, led by Jesus, who kept the Passover the night before he died to accomplish it.

How is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. But the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. Faithful Christians differ on whether a future return to the land is also promised, and those who expect one share the same hope in the same Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am sending for many fishers, declares the LORD, and they shall catch them. And afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks. For my eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from me, nor is their iniquity concealed from my eyes. But first I will doubly repay their iniquity and their sin, because they have polluted my land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and have filled my inheritance with their abominations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am sending for many fishers. Before the homecoming, the round-up. Fishermen drag a net through the water and take everything in it; hunters go after what escaped the net, into the hills and the rock crevices where refugees hide. Between them, nobody gets away.

Fishers of men. Many think Jesus had this image in mind and turned it inside out: Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Matt 4:19). The same picture of men caught in a net serves judgment here and salvation there, and the difference is who is doing the sending and what he does with the catch.

My eyes are on all their ways. The reason no one escapes the hunters is not the skill of the hunters. My eyes are on all their ways. There is no cleft of the rock out of God's sight, which is terrible here and is the same fact that makes him a refuge two verses later.

I will doubly repay. This does not mean twice what they deserved. Many think double here means a full equivalent, the complete penalty their sin deserved, as when Isaiah says Jerusalem has received double for all her sins (Isaiah 40:2).

The carcasses of their detestable idols. The idols are called carcasses, dead things whose presence defiles a place like an unburied body. It is the language of contamination, and the land God calls my inheritance has been filled with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — To You Shall the Nations Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet worships, and sees the nations coming to renounce the lies they inherited (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of judgment the prophet sees Gentiles arriving from the ends of the earth to renounce the lies they inherited.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth and say: "Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit. Can man make for himself gods? Such are not gods!" "Therefore, behold, I will make them know, this once I will make them know my power and my might, and they shall know that my name is the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My strength and my stronghold. The prophet answers the announcement of judgment with worship, and the titles he uses are a soldier's: strength, stronghold, refuge in the day of trouble. David piled up the same words: The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer (Ps 18:2). The man forbidden to marry, to mourn or to feast still has the LORD himself.

To you shall the nations come. And then his eyes lift to the horizon and he sees something no one else in the chapter is looking at: to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth. Not Judah restored, but the nations arriving.

Nothing but lies. Listen to what they say when they come. Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit. That is a whole conversion in one sentence: a verdict on the religion they were raised in, named as inherited, named as a lie, named as worthless. Paul describes the lie, that people exchanged the truth about God for a lie (Rom 1:25), and the turning: they must turn from these vain things to a living God (Acts 14:15).

Isn’t my faith just where I happened to be born? It is one of the most common objections, and it deserves respect. Most people hold roughly the religion of their parents, and a sceptic reasonably asks whether a belief that tracks your birthplace can be more than an accident. But look at what these converts do. They do exactly what the objection asks: they examine what they were handed and call it a lie. And the argument cuts every way. The secular confidence of a modern Western graduate is also very typical of where and when he was born, and how anyone came to a belief does not settle whether it is true. That has to be weighed on other grounds. The gospel itself has always spread against inheritance: its first believers were Jews and pagans who left what their fathers taught, and it now grows fastest where hardly anyone’s grandparents were Christians. Scripture never lets faith be a family heirloom. Those who receive Christ are born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13). No one is a Christian by birth. Everyone who is one has been born again.

Can man make for himself gods? They have seen for themselves what chapter 10 taught, that idols are man-made. Can man make for himself gods? The question answers itself once it is asked out loud.

The nations streaming in. Isaiah saw the same procession: all the nations shall flow to it (Isa 2:2). It is one of the great surprises of the prophets that the books most full of judgment on Israel are also the books that see the world coming in.

I will make them know. God answers the prayer, and three times he says know. The judgment that is falling on Judah is itself part of how the nations will come to know him. The disaster is not only an ending; it is an announcement, and people who never heard of the LORD will learn his name from what he does with his own people.

16.title: A Life Made into a Sign
16.overview:
Jeremiah's own life becomes the sermon: God forbids him to marry, to mourn at funerals or to sit at feasts, because death and silence are coming on the city (vv. 1-9). The people cannot even name their sin, and they will be given the other gods they wanted (vv. 10-13).

Then, without warning, a promise of a homecoming greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), but first the fishers and hunters (vv. 16-18). The prophet answers with worship, and sees the nations coming from the ends of the earth to know the LORD's name (vv. 19-21).
16.theology:
A servant's life may itself be made into the message, at great personal cost (vv. 1-9; Ezek 24:16-18), and singleness can be a calling rather than a deprivation (1 Cor 7:29-31; Matt 19:12). God can withdraw his peace and steadfast love from a generation (v. 5), though his mercies do not fail in themselves (Lam 3:22).

Hardened people lose the ability to name their own sin (v. 10), and judgment often consists of being given what was insisted on (v. 13). Yet God promises a rescue greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), and he will be known by the nations, who come renouncing their inherited lies (vv. 19-21; Isa 2:2-3).
16.examples: The chapter is full of absences: a man the whole town watches not marrying, a cup of consolation with no one left to hand it over, a guilty people who cannot think of a single thing they have done. Against them stands one great arrival, the nations coming from the ends of the earth and calling the religion they inherited a lie.
