verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Sin Engraved on the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah's sin is engraved on heart and altar, remembered by the children, and will cost them their heritage (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The record of sin is cut into the very place where God means to write his law.

verseByVerse.quote: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of their altars, while their children remember their altars and their Asherim, beside every green tree and on the high hills, on the mountains in the open country. Your wealth and all your treasures I will give for spoil as the price of your high places for sin throughout all your territory. You shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave to you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Written with a pen of iron. The image is of an inscription cut into stone with the hardest tools available: an iron stylus, a diamond point. Not written in ink, which fades, but engraved, which lasts.

The tablet of their heart. And the surface it is cut into is the tablet of their heart. That phrase belongs to the covenant. God wrote his law on tablets of stone, and he had asked for it to be kept on the heart. What is engraved there instead is the record of their sin, so deep that it has become part of them, not a stain on the surface.

Toward the new covenant. Hold this verse beside the promise this book is moving toward: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (31:33). The new covenant is not a better set of rules. It is God writing something new on the same heart. For that, the old record of sin had to be removed, and it was, at the cross.

The horns of their altars. The second surface is worse: the horns of their altars. The horns were where the blood of the sin offering was smeared, the place of atonement. Their sin is carved into the very furniture of forgiveness. Religion practised without repentance does not remove guilt; it records it.

While their children remember. What the children remember is what the parents did. Not the Passover, not the law read at the feast, but where the shrines were and what happened there. In any household, children learn most surely from what the adults actually do.

You shall loosen your hand. The sentence of 15:13-14 is repeated with one new phrase: You shall loosen your hand from your heritage. It is the picture of fingers being prised off something held tight. They will not hand the land over; it will be taken out of their grip.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two portraits: the man who trusts in man, a shrub in a salt land (vv. 5-6), and the man who trusts in the LORD, a tree planted by water (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Two lives are told as two plants, and the difference is not circumstance but where the roots go.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD. He is like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see any good come. He shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, in an uninhabited salt land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cursed is the man who trusts in man. This is one of the great passages of the book, built as a pair of portraits. The first begins with Cursed, and the definition has three parts: he trusts in man, he makes flesh his strength, and his heart turns away from the LORD. The ESV notes that strength is in Hebrew "arm": the muscle you lean on.

Whose heart turns away from the LORD. The three go together. Trusting human resources is not a neutral method that happens to fail; it is a heart turning away from God. Whatever we lean on has our heart.

What it does not mean. This is not a warning against using doctors, savings or friends. It is about where the weight rests. The question is what you would still have if the arm you are leaning on gave way tomorrow.

Like a shrub in the desert. The picture is of scrub in the Judean wilderness: grey, stunted, only just alive. It is not that such a life collapses dramatically. It survives, and never flourishes. Shall not see any good come is almost worse than disaster: a life in which nothing good is ever quite noticed.

An uninhabited salt land. And an uninhabited salt land is soil where nothing will grow again, the ground around the Dead Sea. Misplaced trust does not only fail to feed you; it ruins the ground for anything else.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh his strength” is literally “flesh his arm” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD. He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD. The second portrait says it twice on purpose: he trusts in the LORD, and whose trust is the LORD. He is not trusting God to deliver a particular outcome; God himself is what he is resting on.

Like a tree planted by water. Psalm 1 has the same tree, like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season (Ps 1:3), but Jeremiah adds the weather, and after chapter 14 we know why. The heat comes. The year of drought arrives. The point is not that the believer is exempt from the drought that scorched the whole country; it is that his roots are somewhere the drought does not reach.

Does not fear when heat comes. Two words describe him in the crisis: he does not fear, and he is not anxious. Anyone who has tried to argue himself out of anxiety knows that this cannot be produced by effort. It is the fruit of where the roots are. And the tree did not plant itself: it is planted, and kept watered by God's Spirit through his word and prayer. Roots grow slowly, in ordinary weather, long before they are tested.

It does not cease to bear fruit. And the last clause: it does not cease to bear fruit. Not merely survives; keeps producing, in the drought year, for other people's benefit.

How do I put my roots down? Trust is not a feeling you summon at 2 a.m.; it is a habit of leaning, formed in ordinary weather. Go to the stream daily. Read a passage of Scripture before you pick up the phone, and pray one of its sentences back to God; that is how roots reach water. Name the arm. When the redundancy rumour starts or the test results are late, ask what you are actually leaning on: the savings, the boss’s good opinion, your own competence. Say it to God, and tell him that he is your trust. Act on it in one decision. Give generously when the budget is tight, or tell the truth when a lie would protect you, because your security does not rest on the outcome. Keep company with the planted. Ask believers who have come through a drought how they were kept. And remember who does the planting. Christ trusted his Father perfectly when every human arm failed him; He trusts in God; let God deliver him now (Matt 27:43) was flung at him on the cross, and God answered by raising him from the dead. Joined to him, you are rooted and built up in him (Col 2:7), planted in the one who has already come through the worst heat there is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The deceitful heart and the God who searches it (vv. 9-10); a proverb on unjust riches (v. 11); and the throne and the fountain of living water (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody can read his own heart; God reads it, and the diagnosis drives us back to the fountain abandoned in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? "I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart is deceitful above all things. Few sentences explain this book better, and it should be taken a word at a time. The heart in Scripture is not the emotions but the control centre of a person: mind, will and affections together, the part of you that decides. It is deceitful above all things: it lies, and its most practised victim is its owner. It is desperately sick, beyond the reach of any human cure. The King James Version has desperately wicked; the Hebrew word means incurably ill, and both renderings describe the same disease.

Who can understand it? Then the question: who can understand it? Not you, about yourself. That is the uncomfortable point. The instrument you would use to examine your heart is the heart, and it is the thing under suspicion. This is why sincerity is not a defence: a person can be entirely sincere and entirely deceived, because the deceiver lives inside.

I the LORD search the heart. The question is answered in the next breath, and the answer is God. I the LORD search the heart, and the ESV notes that mind is in Hebrew "kidneys", the innermost parts. He does not guess at us from the outside; he reads what we cannot read.

Good news for the believer. That could be the most frightening sentence imaginable, and for the believer it is the opposite, because the God who reads it has dealt with what he finds. The right response is the psalmist's, and it takes courage: Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! (Ps 139:23).

Why a new heart is needed. And the diagnosis makes the promise later in this book necessary. A heart this sick cannot be managed, educated or made well by good resolutions. It has to be replaced: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (31:33); I will give you a new heart (Ezek 36:26).

Does this still describe a Christian? A believer has been given a new heart, yet remaining sin still deceives, which is why Christians do not treat their feelings as the final word about themselves. That cuts both ways. A heart that flatters you cannot be trusted, and neither can a heart that condemns you: whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20). Assurance rests on Christ and his promise, not on reading your own heart correctly.

Is judgment by works? Each person’s deeds show what is in the heart, and God judges them truly (Rom 2:6). The one who is saved is saved by grace through faith, not by works (Eph 2:8–9), but saving faith always bears fruit, which God sees.
verseByVerse.note: “Mind” is literally “kidneys” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Like the partridge that gathers a brood that she did not hatch, so is he who gets riches but not by justice; in the midst of his days they will leave him, and at his end he will be a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A proverb on wealth. A single proverb dropped into the middle of the chapter, and it fits the theme: here is the heart's deceit at work in how a man gets his money.

Like the partridge. The picture is a bird sitting on eggs that are not hers. The proverb draws on what was commonly said of the partridge; its point is the man, not the bird's habits. She keeps them warm, defends them, does all the work of a mother, and when they hatch they run off to their own kind. She is left with a bare nest and nothing to show for the sitting.

They will leave him. So it is with money gained unjustly. It looks like a clutch of eggs; the man broods over it; and in the midst of his days they will leave him. Not even at the end, when everyone's wealth departs, but halfway through, while he still had plans for it.

At his end he will be a fool. And the verdict is not that he is wicked, which he is, but that he is stupid: at his end he will be a fool. Injustice for profit is a bad investment.

verseByVerse.quote: A glorious throne set on high from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary. O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who turn away from you shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A glorious throne set on high. After the wilderness scrub and the empty nest, worship. The temple is not first a building but a throne room, and it has been set on high from the beginning. Whatever happens to the city, that throne is not vacated.

Written in the earth. Those who turn away from God shall be written in the earth: their names are scratched in dust, which the next wind or footstep erases. Their sin, by contrast, is engraved with an iron pen (verse 1), and the names of God’s people are written in heaven. The ESV notes that where the English has you, the Hebrew has "me".

The fountain of living water. And the chapter reaches back to the book's first great image: they have forsaken the fountain of living water (2:13). Everything in between, the cisterns, the drought, the empty jars, the shrub in the salt land and the tree by the stream, has been about water, and here the source is named again.

Christ the fountain. Jesus stood in the temple courts on the great day of the Feast of Booths and cried out, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). The fountain that Judah abandoned came to Jerusalem in person.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah prays to be healed, answers the taunts, and hands his persecutors to God (vv. 14-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who asked whether God was a failing brook now asks to be healed, and knows who alone can do it.

verseByVerse.quote: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise. Behold, they say to me, "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!" I have not run away from being your shepherd, nor have I desired the day of sickness. You know what came out of my lips; it was before your face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heal me, O LORD. The prophet prays, and the wording shows what he believes about God. Heal me... and I shall be healed. He does not say, help me to heal, or heal me so that I can recover. If God does it, it is done; if God does not, nothing else will.

The wound brought to God. This is the man who asked in chapter 8, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22), and who accused God of being a brook that fails (15:18). Now he brings the wound to the only physician there is. Watch that progression in a person's life: from complaint about the absence of healing to a request for it.

Where is the word of the LORD? This is the taunt of people who have heard the warnings for years and watched nothing happen. It is the mockery Peter predicted for the last days: Where is the promise of his coming? (2 Pet 3:4). They take the delay as proof that it will never come, and the challenge has a swagger to it: Let it come! Within a few years it came.

I have not run away. He denies two things, and both matter. He has not run away from being a shepherd to this people, though everything in his circumstances invited it. And he has not desired the day of sickness: he has not wanted the disaster he preaches, which is the accusation people always make against the man who warns them.

You know what came out of my lips. His defence is simply that God heard him: You know what came out of my lips. A minister's real record is not the reputation he has among his hearers but what God heard him say.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster. Let those be put to shame who persecute me, but let me not be put to shame; let them be dismayed, but let me not be dismayed; bring upon them the day of disaster; destroy them with double destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not a terror to me. A remarkable prayer, and an honest one. Be not a terror to me: he asks God not to become the thing he is afraid of. When judgment is falling all around, the hand that sends it is the same hand he is sheltering under, and that is a hard place to stand.

Refuge from the God who permits. Everyone who trusts God through a disaster knows this tension. The God who is my refuge is also the God who permitted the thing I need refuge from. Jeremiah does not resolve it; he prays it.

What it means to take refuge in God. We usually picture a refuge as a place away from the danger: a cellar in a storm, a harbour out of the wind. Jeremiah’s refuge is stranger. The storm coming on Jerusalem is God’s own judgment, and the shelter he runs to is God (16:19; 17:17). He flees to God from God. That sounds impossible until you stand at the cross. There the storm of God’s judgment against sin fell in full on his own Son, so that for everyone hidden in Christ the one place it cannot reach is God himself: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). That changes what we do when trouble comes. When we suspect God is behind a hard providence, our instinct is to keep our distance from him and shelter in something else: busyness, a screen, a drink, a grievance. Jeremiah shows the other way. Take the fear straight to the God you are afraid of, and say with him, you are my refuge in the day of disaster.

Destroy them with double destruction! His prayer for judgment on his enemies returns, sharper than before. Read it as the prayer of a man who has been forbidden to defend himself and has handed the case over (11:20): everything he wants done to his enemies he asks God to do, which means he will do none of it himself.

Praying since Calvary. Christians pray differently since Calvary, where the one who was persecuted asked for his enemies' forgiveness. But the instinct underneath, to leave the judging to God and say so out loud, is one the New Testament commends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — The Sabbath at the Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A sermon at the gates on the Sabbath (vv. 19-23), with two futures running through those gates (vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole future of the city is hung on one visible, weekly act of trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus said the LORD to me: "Go and stand in the People's Gate, by which the kings of Judah enter and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem, and say: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates. Thus says the LORD: Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem. And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers. Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck, that they might not hear and receive instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go and stand in the People’s Gate. Another open-air sermon, and the location is chosen for traffic: the gate the royal household uses, and then every other gate in the city. Everyone entering will hear it.

Keep the Sabbath day holy. And the subject is the Sabbath. After chapters about idolatry, injustice, false prophets and a deceitful heart, God sends his prophet to talk about carrying loads on a Saturday.

What the Sabbath was for. It can look trivial until you see what the day was for. The Sabbath was the public sign of the covenant, God’s bond with Israel. It was a weekly, visible statement that this people belonged to God, that their lives were not their own and that their provision did not depend on their own unbroken effort. A man who stops trading one day in seven is saying, out loud, that God feeds him. Bringing a burden in through the gate on that day was not a technicality; it was a public refusal of the trust described in verse 7.

A palace in time. Benjamin Franklin advised a young tradesman, “Remember that time is money,” and most of us have absorbed the lesson so well that an unproductive hour feels faintly guilty. Phones make every evening a working evening, and rest is valued chiefly as recovery, so that we can produce more on Monday. The Jewish thinker Abraham Joshua Heschel, in The Sabbath, argued that a technical civilisation is very good at conquering space and very poor at hallowing time, and he called the Sabbath “a palace in time”: a day that is not for getting anything. That is why the day was so threatening to Jerusalem’s traders, and why it is threatening to us. A person who cannot stop has made his work his saviour; he is quietly convinced that if he stops, everything, including himself, will fall apart. The Sabbath answered that fear every week, and the gospel answers it at the root. On the day Jesus’ body lay in the tomb, his work finished, the women who loved him did nothing: On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment (Luke 23:56). Our rest is grounded in a work already done, and none of it ours.

Call the Sabbath a delight. Isaiah put the invitation warmly: call the Sabbath a delight, and then you shall take delight in the LORD (Isa 58:13-14).

Yet they did not listen. The verdict on the fathers is in the language of 7:26, and the wording is telling: they stiffened their necks that they might not hear. They did not fail to hear by accident; not hearing was the aim.

Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exod 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and they keep it with great blessing; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Heb 4:9–10), so that no one may bind another’s conscience about days (Rom 14:5). The Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a law with rules about work. Faithful Christians differ here, and bear with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But if you listen to me, declares the LORD, and bring in no burden by the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy and do no work on it, then there shall enter by the gates of this city kings and princes who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their officials, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And this city shall be inhabited forever. And people shall come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the Shephelah, from the hill country, and from the Negeb, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and bringing thank offerings to the house of the LORD. But if you do not listen to me, to keep the Sabbath day holy, and not to bear a burden and enter by the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem and shall not be quenched.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two futures. Now the two futures, and both of them run through the same gates.

But if you listen to me. If they listen: kings of David's line riding in, officials, crowds, and a city inhabited forever. The promise is enormous and it hangs on something small enough to see from the street. God often puts the weight of great things on one small, visible act of obedience, because that is where trust can be seen.

Bringing thank offerings. Pilgrims from every region, with the whole range of offerings, and the list ends with thank offerings, the sacrifice that is not required by guilt but brought because someone is glad. That is the picture of a country put right with God: roads full of people who want to be there. The regions are named so as to cover the whole country: Benjamin to the north, the Shephelah foothills to the west, the hill country around the city, and the Negeb desert to the south. The entire land is pictured on its way to worship.

A fire in its gates. And the other future: fire in the gates, spreading to the palaces, unquenchable. That is exactly what happened when Babylon took the city (52:13).

Christ, lord of the Sabbath. For Christians the Sabbath command comes through Christ, who said The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and called himself lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28). Hebrews says that there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, entered by resting from our own works as God did from his (Heb 4:9-10).

The question for us. So the question the chapter finally asks is the question of verses 5 and 7 in a practical form. Is your life arranged to say that God provides, or does it say that everything depends on your unbroken effort? The answer is visible in a diary, which is why God sent a prophet to stand at a gate and watch what people carried through it. No one's diary answers it perfectly. Christ trusted the Father without a lapse, and his rest is offered to those who have not: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

17.title: The Heart Is Deceitful: Two Trees and a Sabbath
17.overview:
Judah's sin is engraved on heart and altar (vv. 1-4). Then two portraits, a shrub in a salt land and a tree planted by water (vv. 5-8), and the diagnosis that explains the whole book: the heart is deceitful above all things, and only God can search it (vv. 9-13).

Jeremiah prays to be healed and saved (vv. 14-18), and is sent to the city gates to preach the Sabbath, with two futures set before the city (vv. 19-27).
17.theology:
Sin is engraved on the heart where God intends to write his law (v. 1), and religion without repentance records guilt rather than removing it. Trust is the dividing line between two lives (vv. 5-8): misplaced trust is a heart turning away, and trust in God bears fruit precisely in the drought.

The heart cannot be read by its owner, only by God (vv. 9-10), which is why it must be replaced, not reformed (31:33). God alone heals and saves (v. 14). The Sabbath was the visible weekly sign that life and provision come from God (vv. 21-27), fulfilled in Christ, lord of the Sabbath, and in the rest that remains for his people (Heb 4:9-10).
17.examples: The chapter works in sharp pictures: sin cut with a diamond point into the horns of the altar, the very furniture of forgiveness; grey scrub in a salt land, alive and never flourishing, beside a tree whose roots reach water the drought cannot touch; a partridge brooding over eggs that run off to someone else. Its last picture is the plainest: a diary that says either that God provides or that everything depends on me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Down to the Potter's House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah watches a potter rework a spoiled vessel (vv. 1-4), and God applies it to Israel (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: God sends his prophet to a workshop to watch a craftsman start again with spoiled clay.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will let you hear my words." So I went down to the potter's house, and there he was working at his wheel. And the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go down to the potter’s house. God's word does not always arrive in a temple or a vision. Here it is scheduled for a workshop, and the prophet has to go down there to receive it. The ESV notes that I will let you hear my words may be rendered “will cause you to hear”: the potter's shed is the place God has chosen to speak.

There he was working at his wheel. Much of what God teaches is learned by watching ordinary work done well. The scene is domestic and unhurried: a man at a double wheel, kicking the lower stone, hands wet, shaping the clay on the upper one. Jeremiah stands and watches, and the sermon is the craftsman's hands.

He reworked it into another vessel. The pot goes wrong, with a stone in the clay, an uneven wall or a wobble, and the potter does not throw the lump away. He collapses it and starts again, making something else of it, as it seemed good to the potter to do.

Two truths at once. Two things are true at once, and the chapter needs both. The potter has complete authority over the clay: the clay does not vote on what it becomes. And the potter does not discard spoiled clay: he reworks it. The God who is about to say terrifying things is first shown as a craftsman who will not throw the clay away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can I not do with you as this potter has done? The interpretation is given as a question, and it is a question about rights. Can I not do with you as this potter has done? Israel had been arguing for chapters that God could not really destroy the temple, could not hand over his own city, would not do this to his people. The potter's wheel answers all of it.

We are the clay. Scripture uses the image both ways. Isaiah turns it into prayer: we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand (Isa 64:8), which is the comforting use. And he turns it into rebuke: Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"? (Isa 29:16).

What it does not mean. The point is not that people are inert lumps with no responsibility; the next six verses make that impossible to conclude. It is that God does not answer to the clay for what he does with it, and that the one who has this freedom is a craftsman who reworks spoiled clay.

Who gets to say what I am? To modern ears the potter is almost an insult. The deepest conviction of our culture is that no one has the right to define me but me: I am not clay, I am the potter, and my life is a pot I am throwing myself. It sounds like freedom, and there is something noble in refusing shapes others chose for us. But notice what it costs. If I am my own maker, I am also my own guarantor. Every failure is a flaw in the only craftsman there is, and a spoiled pot has no one to rework it. Jeremiah’s picture is more humbling and far kinder. You did not make yourself, so you do not have to hold yourself together. You belong to hands that are skilled, patient and unwilling to throw spoiled clay away. And in Christ those hands are at work again: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). Being shaped by someone who loves you is not the end of freedom; it is the end of having to be your own god.

Jars of clay. Paul adds the note that keeps the image from crushing anyone: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Cor 4:7).

The potter in Romans 9. Paul takes up the potter in Romans 9:20–21 to show God’s sovereign right over his creatures. Jeremiah’s potter reworks the clay as the nation responds (vv. 7–10), and some think that excludes election, God’s free choice of those he saves. Both are true: Jeremiah speaks of how God deals with nations in history, Paul of his sovereign mercy to individuals; and in both, the clay has no right to accuse the potter. And Paul's argument ends in mercy: the Potter makes vessels of mercy, prepared beforehand for glory (Rom 9:23), and in Christ he remakes spoiled clay.

Does God change his mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jer 18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rule behind every prophecy (vv. 7-10), a call to return (v. 11), and the people's answer (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Warnings are conditional by design; they are offered so that they need not be carried out.

verseByVerse.quote: If at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom, that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it. And if at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom that I will build and plant it, and if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it. Now, therefore, say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: 'Thus says the LORD, Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way, and amend your ways and your deeds.' "But they say, 'That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pluck up and break down. Everything turns on this paragraph, because it tells you how to read every threat in the prophetic books. The verbs are the ones from Jeremiah's call, pluck up, break down, destroy (1:10), and they are now shown to be conditional.

A warning, not a forecast. A prophecy of judgment is not a weather forecast. It is a warning given so that it need not come true. God says what he intends to do so that the people will turn and he will not have to do it.

The case of Nineveh. Jonah is the case study. He preached that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown, with no conditions attached; the city repented; and God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it (Jonah 3:10). Jonah was furious precisely because he knew this principle in advance.

I will relent of the good. And the rule runs the other way too, which is less often quoted. A promise of blessing is not a charm that survives rebellion. Judah's whole delusion was that the promises to David and to Zion had made them permanently safe, whatever they did.

Steadfast, not indifferent. Nothing here makes God changeable (see the question above): a father who treats a repentant child the same as a defiant one is not steadfast but indifferent.

I am shaping disaster against you. The verb is a potter's: I am shaping disaster. The potter is at the wheel again, and what is taking form on it is judgment, announced while it is still soft, still on the wheel, still capable of being collapsed and remade. Ezekiel puts God's heart in it plainly: I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, so turn, and live (Ezek 18:32).

That is in vain! And the answer chills, because it is not a denial. They do not say the message is false. They say That is in vain!: hopeless, no use, too late. And then they announce that they will do as they please anyway.

Despair and defiance. Despair and defiance have arrived at the same place, as they often do. A person who says "I could never change" and a person who says "I will not change" end up doing exactly the same thing on Monday morning. The answer to both is the scene in the workshop: spoiled clay is not discarded but reworked, and by the potter's hands, not its own. The call to return comes from the God who has just promised to relent when anyone turns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Does the Snow of Lebanon Leave?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nature keeps faith, but God's people have forgotten him, and he will show them his back (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the weather keeps faith better than this people; what nature does by nature they would not do by covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD: Ask among the nations, Who has heard the like of this? The virgin Israel has done a very horrible thing. Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Do the mountain waters run dry, the cold flowing streams? But my people have forgotten me; they make offerings to false gods; they made them stumble in their ways, in the ancient roads, and to walk into side roads, not the highway, making their land a horror, a thing to be hissed at forever. Everyone who passes by it is horrified and shakes his head. Like the east wind I will scatter them before the enemy. I will show them my back, not my face, in the day of their calamity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has heard the like of this? God calls for a survey again, as in 2:10. Go and ask the pagans whether they have ever heard of a people abandoning its own God. The behaviour is not merely wrong; it is unprecedented.

Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Two questions from geography. The snow on the heights of Lebanon does not decide one year to be somewhere else. The cold streams that come off those mountains do not quit. The ESV notes two difficulties in the Hebrew here, but the sense is plain: nature is reliable.

What creation does by instinct. It is the same comparison as chapter 8, where migrating birds kept their calendar. Creation does by instinct what Israel would not do by covenant.

In the ancient roads. The road image returns from 6:16, where they were told to ask for the ancient paths. Here the false gods have tripped them off the highway onto side tracks. Nobody plans to end up lost; they take a turning that looked reasonable.

A thing to be hissed at forever. The nation that was meant to make God known to the world becomes a roadside curiosity, a ruin travellers point at. Israel's calling was to be a witness to God; she will be one either way, by her faithfulness or by her ruins.

Like the east wind. The east wind is the hot desert wind that strips a field. And the last clause reverses the priestly blessing, in which the LORD makes his face shine upon his people: I will show them my back, not my face. The worst part of the judgment is not the wind but the turned back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Let Us Strike Him with the Tongue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A plot against Jeremiah (v. 18), his appeal (vv. 19-20), and a prayer that spares nothing (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The man forbidden to defend himself hands everything to God, including a rage he does not disguise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah, for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us not pay attention to any of his words." Hear me, O LORD, and listen to the voice of my adversaries. Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah. Listen to their reasoning, because it is the reasoning of respectable religion defending itself. We still have priests for the law, sages for counsel and prophets for the word: all three kinds of teacher are still in place. So this one man can be removed without loss. The institution will carry on. Their slogan probably answers Jeremiah’s own warnings that priest, prophet and wise man would all fail together (4:9; 8:8-10). They are saying that the offices he condemned are in no danger at all.

The establishment’s argument. It is the argument every establishment makes against the person who says the establishment has gone wrong.

Let us strike him with the tongue. And the weapon is chosen: let us strike him with the tongue. Not a knife, at this stage, but rumour, insinuation, official statements, the slow discrediting of a man. The psalm knows the method: they whet their tongues like swords and shoot from ambush at the blameless (Ps 64:3-4). And after Jesus raised Lazarus, his enemies did the same: from that day on they made plans to put him to death (John 11:53).

Should good be repaid with evil? He takes it to God and asks him to listen to both sides: hear me, and hear them. The question that follows is the ache of the whole chapter: Should good be repaid with evil?

To turn away your wrath from them. And here is what makes their plot so bitter. The prayers God had forbidden (7:16; 11:14; 14:11) were prayers for these very people. The man they are trying to kill is the man who has been standing between them and God's wrath. They never knew it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore deliver up their children to famine; give them over to the power of the sword; let their wives become childless and widowed. May their men meet death by pestilence, their youths be struck down by the sword in battle. May a cry be heard from their houses, when you bring the plunderer suddenly upon them! For they have dug a pit to take me and laid snares for my feet. Yet you, O LORD, know all their plotting to kill me. Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight. Let them be overthrown before you; deal with them in the time of your anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deliver up their children to famine. This is the hardest passage in the book to read as a Christian, and it should not be softened. Jeremiah asks God to bring famine on their children and widowhood on their wives.

How to read this prayer. Several things need saying, and none of them is that this prayer is a model for ours.

A prayer, not a plan. First, it is a prayer and not a plan. Everything he wants done he asks God to do; he lifts no hand himself, and he goes on living among these people. People who do not pray their rage usually act on it.

The judgment already announced. Second, what he asks for is exactly the judgment God has already announced on the nation (14:12, 16). He is not inventing a punishment; he is asking God to do what he has said, and to do it now, because these men are murdering the messenger.

An honest record. Third, Scripture records it honestly without holding it up as a pattern for us. The Bible is an honest book about its heroes, and this is a man at the end of his strength who has been threatened by his own village, plotted against by the clergy, and forbidden to defend himself.

Forgive not their iniquity. This is the line no Christian can pray, and the reason is not that we are nicer than Jeremiah. It is that we stand on the other side of a cross where the one plotted against said, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34), the prayer this chapter could not reach.

Vengeance handed over. And yet the instinct underneath is one the New Testament keeps: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). Jeremiah's fury is handed over. That is not the last word on prayer, but it is far better than revenge.

Permission to be honest. What this passage gives a suffering believer is permission to be honest. God can be told the truth about what you feel toward people who have wrecked your life, and the telling is safer than the silence.

parallels.desc: Contrast: Christ prays for his killers

18.title: The Potter and the Clay
18.overview:
At a potter's workshop a spoiled vessel is reworked, and so, God says, is Israel in his hand (vv. 1-6). Then the rule that governs every prophecy: warnings and promises depend on how a nation responds (vv. 7-12).

Nature keeps faith, but God's people have forgotten him (vv. 13-17). The religious leaders plot against Jeremiah, and he pours out a prayer against them that Scripture records without commending (vv. 18-23).
18.theology:
God has absolute right over his people as a potter over clay (vv. 5-6; Rom 9:21), and he is a potter who reworks spoiled clay rather than discarding it (v. 4). Prophecies of judgment and promises of blessing are conditional by design (vv. 7-10): warnings are given so that they need not be fulfilled, and promises do not shelter the unrepentant.

Despair and defiance end in the same conduct (v. 12). Opposition to God's word often comes from religious institutions defending themselves (v. 18). Jeremiah's prayer against his enemies hands his rage to God rather than acting on it (vv. 21-23).
18.examples: The chapter's central picture is a craftsman collapsing a spoiled pot and starting again with the same clay, and its sharpest irony is that the man they plotted to kill was the one who had been praying for them.

19.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD, "Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests,<sup>2</sup>and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim there the words that I tell you.<sup>3</sup>You shall say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.<sup>4</sup>Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents,<sup>5</sup>and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—<sup>6</sup>therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.<sup>7</sup>And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.<sup>8</sup>And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds.<sup>9</sup>And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'<sup>10</sup>"Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you,<sup>11</sup>and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended. Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury.<sup>12</sup>Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth.<sup>13</sup>The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"<sup>14</sup>Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people:<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Go to the Valley and Take Witnesses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah takes a flask and the elders to the Valley of Hinnom (vv. 1-2) and announces disaster for the blood shed there (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The sermon is preached at the scene of the crime, with the establishment brought along as witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, "Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests, and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim there the words that I tell you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A potter’s earthenware flask. Chapter 18 was clay on a wheel, soft and workable. Chapter 19 is a finished flask, fired hard in a kiln. The material has changed, and so has the message.

Some of the elders of the people. And this time there is an audience of dignitaries. He is to bring elders of the people and elders of the priests, civic and religious leadership together, the men whose testimony cannot later be dismissed. Whatever happens, there will be witnesses.

The Valley of the Son of Hinnom. The location is chosen with terrible precision. The Valley of Hinnom is where children were burned (7:31). The Potsherd Gate probably takes its name from broken pottery. He will preach about a smashed jar at the gate named for broken pots, in the valley where they burned their children.
verseByVerse.note: The Potsherd Gate led out to the Valley of Hinnom.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents, and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. This is a phrase with a history. God used it when he told the boy Samuel of the fall of Eli's house, at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle (1 Sam 3:11), and again when he pronounced sentence on Jerusalem in Manasseh's day: such disaster that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle (2 Kgs 21:12). It means news so shocking that people flinch when they hear it, and Jeremiah is announcing that the sentence passed under Manasseh has come due.

Because the people have forsaken me. The charge has three parts: forsaking God, profaning the place, and the blood of innocents. And then the specific horror, child sacrifice, with the same phrase as the temple sermon: nor did it come into my mind. God calls those children innocents; he saw every one of them, and their blood is precious in his sight.

Not in God’s name. God's repeated insistence on this matters. A religion that burns children cannot claim any connection to him. When people do appalling things in God's name, the question to ask is whether he ever said it, and Scripture, not sincerity, is where that is settled.

The gods that still ask for children. Every reader recoils from this valley, and rightly. But ask what Baal and Molech were thought to offer: rain, harvests, safety, a future for the family and the nation. Give the god what you love most, and he will secure what you want most. Idols always work that way. They begin by asking for a little and end by asking for everything, and they are hungriest for the people closest to us. We do not burn our children, but we can still lay them on altars: a childhood spent serving a parent’s ambition, a home given up for a career, a child made the proof that we are succeeding. Smaller fires, lit for the same reason. Here is the reversal. The one God who said a sacrifice like this had never even entered his mind (v. 5) is the God who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; see the note on Genesis 22:1–2). The idols take our children to secure our future. The living God gave his Son to secure ours, and that frees parents to love their children instead of using them.

Whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known. One more phrase in the charge: gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known. These were not ancient family loyalties. They were recent imports, and a nation that had the God of the exodus exchanged him for novelties.

Did God not foresee it? No; he knows all things (Ps 139:4). It means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The valley renamed, the plans emptied out, and the horror of the siege (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned is renamed for what will be done in it.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Valley of Slaughter. The new name of 7:32, the Valley of Slaughter, is repeated on the spot. God renames the place for what will happen there. Judgment is fitted to the crime so exactly that the map itself records it.

I will make void the plans. The flask in his hand gives the picture: plans poured out like the contents of a jar. All the policy, the alliances with Egypt and the calculations of the court are poured out on the ground. In Hebrew you can hear the link: the jar is a baqbuq, and make void is baqqoti, perhaps even the sound of liquid gurgling out of a narrow neck.

The counsel of the nations. The psalm sets that against every human strategy: The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples (Ps 33:10). Judah's counsellors were clever. Cleverness against God is simply a longer route to the same valley.

From Hinnom to Gehenna. The Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned, gave its name to Gehenna, which Jesus used for hell (Mark 9:43–47): a place of fire and judgment for those who reject God.
verseByVerse.note: “Make void” (baqqoti) sounds like the word for the potter’s flask (baqbuq) Jeremiah is holding.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds. And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A thing to be hissed at. The city that was meant to be a light to the nations will make passers-by hiss, the sharp intake of breath that travellers give at a ruin.

Foretold at the dedication. And God had said so at the very beginning. When Solomon dedicated the temple, the warning came with it: this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and when they ask why, the answer will be Because they abandoned the LORD their God (1 Kgs 9:8-9). The hissing travellers of Jeremiah's day are the fulfilment of a sentence spoken at the dedication service more than three centuries earlier.

The flesh of their sons and their daughters. Verse 9 is unbearable to read: in the siege people will eat their own children. And it happened. Lamentations, written over the ruins after the siege, records it: The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children (Lam 4:10). It was the curse for breaking the covenant, which Moses had spelled out long before in almost the same words: you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters, in the siege and in the distress (Deut 28:53).

The dreadful symmetry. The symmetry is dreadful. They gave their children to the fire in this valley as an act of religion; in the siege they will eat them to stay alive. Sin runs its course to the end, and the end is always worse than the beginning promised.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — So Will I Break This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The flask is broken before the witnesses, and the whole city will become like Topheth (vv. 10-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's clay could be reworked; a fired flask smashed on the rocks cannot, and that is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you, and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended. Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury. Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you shall break the flask. The sermon becomes an action. He has carried the jar all the way out to the valley; now, in front of the elders, he throws it down.

So that it can never be mended. And here is why the flask is fired and not wet. Soft clay can be collapsed and reworked (18:4); a kiln-hardened pot smashed on stones is finished. So that it can never be mended.

Soft clay and fired clay. Put the two chapters together and you have the whole message. While the clay is soft, God says: return, and I will rework you. When it has been fired hard by years of refusal, there comes a moment when the pot is thrown down. The difference between the chapters is not a change in God but a change in what the clay has become.

Not beyond God’s repair. And yet the book that says so that it can never be mended also contains the promise that the city will be rebuilt and even this valley made holy (31:38-40). What no human hand can repair, God does not repair either. He makes new. Paul says it of every believer: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come (2 Cor 5:17). The gospel is not the mending of the broken flask. It is a new vessel from the same Potter.

Like a potter’s vessel. Scripture uses this image for the judgment of God’s King too: You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel (Ps 2:9), applied to the risen Christ in Revelation (Rev 2:27). And Lamentations mourns that the precious sons of Zion are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands (Lam 4:2).

Making this city like Topheth. The whole city will become what this valley was: a place of the dead.

The potter’s field. Matthew remembered this valley. The priests used Judas's thirty pieces of silver to buy a potter's field to bury strangers in, and Matthew says this fulfilled what was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet (Matthew 27:7-10). The words come mostly from Zechariah 11:12-13, which puzzles readers; the likeliest explanation is that Matthew joins Zechariah to Jeremiah's potter, field and burial ground (here and 32:6-15) and names the greater prophet, as writers then commonly did. Tradition places that field in this very valley, bought with the price of the Lord's betrayal.

verseByVerse.quote: The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: On whose roofs offerings have been offered. Flat roofs were where families slept in summer and where, it turns out, they had been burning incense to the stars. It was household religion, conducted upstairs, in private, by respectable people. Worship of the sun, moon and stars had spread in Manasseh’s reign, probably under Assyrian influence (2 Kgs 21:3-5). Josiah pulled down the altars on the roof (2 Kgs 23:12), and since his death they had come back. Zephaniah, preaching in the same years, names those who bow down on the roofs to the host of the heavens (Zeph 1:5). Those houses will be as unclean as the valley of burning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — From Topheth to the Temple Court
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah carries the message from Topheth into the temple court (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: He carries the broken-flask message straight from Topheth into the temple courtyard, and it costs him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the court of the LORD’s house. He walks up out of the valley and straight into the temple courtyard, fresh from the broken flask, and preaches it again to the crowd. Nothing is toned down for the religious venue.

The same temple precinct. This is the same temple precinct as the temple sermon of chapter 7. He knows exactly what it costs to say these things here, and the opening verses of the next chapter record the result: the chief officer of the temple has him beaten and put in the stocks overnight.

Refusing to hear my words. The summary is short and the reason is one clause: they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words. Not their idolatry, not the blood, not the injustice, but what lies behind all of them: the refusal to listen.

Everything begins with hearing. That is the thread from chapter 7 to here, and it is the one a reader should take to heart. Everything in Jeremiah begins with hearing. The people who would not hear became people who could not (6:10), and that long refusal was the oven in which the flask was fired hard.

Stephen’s charge. Stephen used the same charge in the same city six centuries later, facing the council that was about to kill him: You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you (Acts 7:51). The neck stiffened against Jeremiah was still stiff against Christ's witnesses. Yet a young man named Saul stood by at that stoning, and the risen Christ met him on the road and bent his neck by grace (Acts 7:58; 9:3-6). No refusal is beyond the reach of the one who calls.

19.title: The Broken Flask
19.overview: Jeremiah takes a fired clay flask and the elders out to the Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned, and announces disaster (vv. 1-9). Then he breaks the flask in front of the witnesses: so God will break this city, so that it can never be mended (vv. 10-13). He walks straight up into the temple court and preaches it again (vv. 14-15).
19.theology:
God distances himself absolutely from atrocity done in his name: child sacrifice never came into his mind (v. 5; 7:31), and judgment is fitted to the sin (v. 6).

The soft clay of chapter 18 could be reworked; the fired flask of chapter 19 is broken beyond mending (vv. 10-11), and the difference lies not in God but in what long refusal has made of the people. What cannot be mended, God makes new (31:38-40). Private religion is not hidden from him (v. 13), and the root of every charge is the refusal to hear his words (v. 15).
19.examples: Jeremiah brings the elders along so that nobody can say later that it was not said, and empties the plans of the court like water from a jar. Then he walks from Topheth into the temple courtyard without softening a word.

They shall fall by the sword of their enemies while you look on. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon. To Babylon you shall go, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely."<sup>7</sup>O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. For the word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long.<sup>9</sup>If I say, "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name," there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.<sup>10</sup>For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! "Denounce him! Let us denounce him!" say all my close friends, watching for my fall. "Perhaps he will be deceived; then we can overcome him and take our revenge on him."<sup>11</sup>But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed.
