For he has delivered the life of the needy from the hand of evildoers.<sup>14</sup>Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me, let it not be blessed!<sup>15</sup>Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, "A son is born to you," making him very glad.<sup>16</sup>Let that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without pity; let him hear a cry in the morning and an alarm at noon,<sup>17</sup>because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb forever great.<sup>18</sup>Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Beaten and Put in the Stocks
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pashhur has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks (vv. 1-2); released, Jeremiah renames him and announces his exile (vv. 3-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first physical violence against Jeremiah is ordered by the man in charge of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer, who was chief officer in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Then Pashhur beat Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper Benjamin Gate of the house of the LORD. The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, "The LORD does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first violence. Chapter 19 ended with Jeremiah preaching in the temple court. This is what happened next, and it is the first recorded violence against him.

Pashhur the priest. The persecutor is not a mob, not the Babylonians, not the palace: the priest, chief officer in the house of the LORD, the man responsible for order in the temple. He has the prophet beaten, probably flogged (the law set forty lashes as the limit, Deut 25:3), and clamped overnight in stocks. The word suggests the body twisted into a fixed, painful position. It was done in a public gateway, where everyone going in to worship could see him.

Religious persecutors. Religious institutions can be the most efficient persecutors, because they have authority, premises and the confidence of being on God's side. The apostles were flogged by the council for preaching and left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41). Paul took the thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Cor 11:24). Hebrews sums up the line Jeremiah stands in: Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment, of whom the world was not worthy (Heb 11:36, 38).

The next day. He comes out of the stocks stiff, bleeding and still preaching. His first act is to rename his jailer.

Terror on Every Side. It is the phrase the book has used for the coming siege (6:25), and in a few verses it will be what his enemies whisper about him (20:10). Pashhur will not merely witness the terror; he will be it, to himself and to everyone near him.
verseByVerse.note: “Terror on every side” (Magor-missabib) becomes Jeremiah’s nickname for Pashhur.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They shall fall by the sword of their enemies while you look on. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon. He shall carry them captive to Babylon, and shall strike them down with the sword. Moreover, I will give all the wealth of the city, all its gains, all its prized belongings, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies, who shall plunder them and seize them and carry them to Babylon. And you, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house, shall go into captivity. To Babylon you shall go, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A terror to yourself. This is a terrible sentence. The man who inflicted fear will become the thing he cannot escape, because it is inside him. And he will watch his friends die: not spared, not blinded, but made to look on.

All the wealth of the city. There are four words for what the city owned, wealth, gains, prized belongings and treasures, and one thing happens to all of it: God gives it into the hand of their enemies.

There you shall die. The sentence is personal and specific: you will go, you will die there, you will be buried there. For a man whose identity was bound up with the temple in Jerusalem, dying in Babylon is the complete undoing of his life.

You have prophesied falsely. And the last clause names the real crime. Not the beating: you have prophesied falsely. Pashhur had been telling people what they wanted to hear, and the men who believed him will die in exile beside him. Comfortable preaching has casualties, and they include the preacher.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Fire Shut Up in My Bones
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last of the confessions: complaint (vv. 7-8), the fire in his bones (v. 9), betrayal (v. 10), and confidence breaking into praise (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Complaint, compulsion, confidence and praise in seven verses, all of them honest at once.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me. For whenever I speak, I cry out, I shout, "Violence and destruction!" For the word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long. If I say, "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name," there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have deceived me. Straight from the stocks he speaks some of the sharpest words anyone in Scripture addresses to God. You have deceived me. The word is strong: to be talked into something you would not otherwise have chosen.

What does he mean? Not that God lied. He means that when he was called he did not know what it would cost, that God overpowered his objections (you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed), and that the life he was drawn into has made him the joke of the city, every day, to everyone.

The Bible prints this. The Bible prints this. There is no editorial note correcting him, no lightning bolt, no rebuke in the next verse. God can be spoken to like this by a man at the end of his endurance, and the words are preserved in holy Scripture for every believer who has felt them and been afraid to say them.

A laughingstock all the day. He cannot open his mouth without announcing catastrophe, and it has made him ridiculous. The word that was a joy and the delight of my heart (15:16) is now a reproach and derision. Both are true of the same word in the same man's life.

I will not mention him. So he tries the obvious solution: resign, and never speak in God’s name again. And he finds he cannot, because the word he has swallowed burns. God had told him that his words would be a fire in the prophet's mouth (5:14), and later asks, Is not my word like fire (23:29).

A burning fire shut up in my bones. Few descriptions of a calling are so exact. He is not continuing because he feels strong, or because it is going well, or because anyone thanks him. He continues because stopping is worse. Anyone who has ever said, “I cannot keep doing this,” and has kept doing it, knows the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! "Denounce him! Let us denounce him!" say all my close friends, watching for my fall. "Perhaps he will be deceived; then we can overcome him and take our revenge on him." But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed. Their eternal dishonor will never be forgotten. O LORD of hosts, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause. Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD! For he has delivered the life of the needy from the hand of evildoers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terror is on every side! The phrase he gave Pashhur comes back at him: Terror is on every side! They have turned his own preaching into a nickname for him.

All my close friends. And the worst detail is all my close friends, watching for my fall. Not enemies, but the men he ate with, hoping he will slip so they can be rid of him. The psalms know this pain, and so did Jesus, at table with the twelve on the night Judas betrayed him.

As a dread warrior. And then, without transition, faith. The LORD is with me as a dread warrior: the promise of 1:8 and 1:19 held onto in the dark, and pictured as a champion standing at his shoulder.

What has changed. Nothing in his circumstances has changed between verse 10 and verse 11. The whispering continues. What has changed is what he is looking at.

To you have I committed my cause. Verse 12 repeats 11:20, and the ESV notes that mind is in Hebrew "kidneys", the innermost self. The last clause is the discipline of his whole life: to you have I committed my cause. He hands his case over to God.

Sing to the LORD. And he sings. In the space of seven verses: you deceived me, I cannot stop, they are all against me, God is with me, sing to the LORD. That is not inconsistency; it is what a real prayer life looks like from inside a real crisis.

On praying for vengeance. Jeremiah leaves his cause to God (Rom 12:19), and Christians pray both for justice and for their enemies’ repentance (Matt 5:44).
verseByVerse.note: “Mind” in v. 12 is literally “kidneys” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after the praise, Jeremiah curses the day of his birth and the man who brought the news of it, and asks why he came out of the womb to see toil and sorrow (vv. 14-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The praise of verse 13 is followed immediately by the darkest words he ever speaks, and Scripture keeps both.

verseByVerse.quote: Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me, let it not be blessed! Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, "A son is born to you," making him very glad. Let that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without pity; let him hear a cry in the morning and an alarm at noon, because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb forever great. Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cursed be the day on which I was born! And then, immediately after the praise, the darkest words in the book. The order matters: verse 13 sings, verse 14 curses. Whoever assembled this chapter did not tidy it.

Not cursing God. He does not curse God, and he does not curse his mother. He curses a day, a thing that cannot be harmed by it. It is the cry of someone who wants the fact of his own existence undone. Job did the same in the ashes: Let the day perish on which I was born (Job 3:3).

Cursed be the man who brought the news. The messenger who ran to tell his father the happy news, who did nothing but carry good tidings, is cursed too. That is how far the grief reaches: back to the moment of gladness at his birth. The cities that the LORD overthrew without pity are Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24-25), the standing byword for total destruction.

Why did I come out from the womb? The chapter ends there. No answer, no divine reply, no resolution. Just the question: Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow?

Things to say gently. Several things should be said, gently.

Despair, recorded. This is despair, and Scripture neither commends it nor condemns it here; it records it. A man called before birth (1:5) now wishes that birth had never happened, and the book that contains this also contains 1:5. Both belong to the same life.

If you have felt this. If you have ever felt this, you are not outside the company of God's servants. Job said it, and Jeremiah, and neither was cast off. What God does with such words is keep them, and keep the man.

If the darkness goes further. Wishing you had never been born is not the same as wanting to end your life, and Jeremiah never took that step; he lived on, and God went on using him. But if your darkness has reached that point, do not carry it alone. Tell someone today, a pastor, a friend, a doctor, and if you are in danger, call emergency services or a crisis line now. Seeking help is not a failure of faith. When Elijah asked to die, God sent him sleep and food before he sent him a word (1 Kings 19:4-8).

A greater prophet. And there is one more thing. There was a greater prophet who was also mocked all the day, All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me (Ps 22:7), whose close friends betrayed him, whose soul was very sorrowful, even to death, and who asked for the cup to pass (Matt 26:38-39). He did not curse the day he was born. On the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46), so that no one who trusts him will ever be forsaken. He was born for that day, and went through it, so that people who curse their own birthdays might be born again.

20.title: Terror on Every Side: The Prophet in the Stocks
20.overview:
The chief officer of the temple has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks; released, Jeremiah renames him Terror on Every Side (vv. 1-6).

Then the last and sharpest of the confessions: God's word has made him a laughingstock, yet it burns like fire if he holds it in (vv. 7-9); his friends watch for his fall, but the LORD is with him, and he breaks into praise (vv. 10-13). And immediately he curses the day he was born (vv. 14-18). Scripture keeps both, and God keeps the man.
20.theology:
Persecution of God's messengers often comes from religious authority (vv. 1-2; Acts 5:40-41), and false preaching destroys the preacher and those who believed him (v. 6).

Scripture keeps a servant's accusation that God overpowered him (v. 7) without rebuke: God can bear honest speech from exhausted people. A true calling continues not by enthusiasm but because the word burns if withheld (v. 9). Faith and despair occupy the same page (vv. 13-14), and Christ, mocked and betrayed by his friends (Ps 22:6-8; Matt 26:38), chose to be born for the suffering that made Jeremiah wish he had never been born.
20.examples: Jeremiah comes out of the stocks stiff and bleeding and preaches first. He tries to resign and finds he cannot, and he sees his close friends waiting for him to slip. The chapter sets praise in one verse and a cursed birthday in the next, with nothing tidied away.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Inquire of the LORD for us, for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us."<sup>3</sup>Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah,<sup>4</sup>'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.<sup>5</sup>I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath.<sup>6</sup>And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. They shall die of a great pestilence.<sup>7</sup>Afterward, declares the LORD, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people in this city who survive the pestilence, sword, and famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies, into the hand of those who seek their lives. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'<sup>8</sup>"And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.<sup>9</sup>He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war.<sup>10</sup>For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'<sup>11</sup>"And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD,<sup>12</sup>O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'"<sup>13</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?'<sup>14</sup>I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Myself Will Fight Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With Babylon at the walls, Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to enquire of the LORD, hoping for a miracle (vv. 1-2). The answer is the opposite: God himself will fight against the city (vv. 3-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A king asks for a miracle like the old days and is told that the God of the exodus is now on the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, saying, "Inquire of the LORD for us, for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us." Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The book jumps forward nearly twenty years, to about 588 BC. Josiah is long dead, Jehoiakim too; Zedekiah is the last king of Judah, and Nebuchadnezzar's army is outside the walls. This Pashhur is a different man from the priest who flogged Jeremiah in chapter 20.

Inquire of the LORD for us. The irony is plain. For decades the palace has ignored, imprisoned and beaten this man. Now that the siege lines are up, the king sends an official delegation to ask him to pray.

According to all his wonderful deeds. The request is entirely religious and entirely hollow. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds: they are thinking of the night the Assyrian army melted away outside these same walls in Hezekiah's day (Isa 37:36), and they want it done again.

No mention of repentance. What is missing from the request is any mention of repentance. They want the outcome Hezekiah got without the humble trust Hezekiah had. Prayer as a last-resort lever, offered by men who have not changed their minds about anything, is exactly what chapter 14 refused.

I will turn back the weapons of war. The answer is not merely no. God says he will turn back the weapons in their hands: the defenders will be driven back inside, and the fighting will end up in the streets instead of at the walls.
verseByVerse.note: From here on the Hebrew often spells Nebuchadnezzar as Nebuchadrezzar (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath. And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. They shall die of a great pestilence. Afterward, declares the LORD, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people in this city who survive the pestilence, sword, and famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies, into the hand of those who seek their lives. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
With outstretched hand and strong arm. This sentence shocks because of where its words come from. Outstretched hand and strong arm is exodus language: it is how Israel described God's rescue from Egypt, recited at every Passover.

I myself will fight against you. Now the arm is stretched out against them. The God who fought for them fights against them, with three words for his wrath piled up. Zedekiah asked for a repeat of the old wonders; he is told the old wonders are being reversed.

The most sobering possibility. There is no more sobering possibility in Scripture than this: to be on the wrong side of the God you claim as yours.

A great pestilence. Disease in a besieged city, with the water fouled and the dead unburied, needs no explanation. It killed more than the swords did.

He shall not pity them. The king is named, and his fate is spelled out to his own messengers. The three refusals of mercy, no pity, no sparing, no compassion, were used of God in 13:14; here they describe the man he is handing them to. Babylon will not be gentle, and God says so in advance rather than letting them imagine a negotiated peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — Life and Death Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the people, the way of life and the way of death: staying in the city means death, and surrender means life (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The way of life runs out through the gate of surrender, which is why the offer sounds like treason.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war. For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way of life and the way of death. The words are Moses' words. At the end of Deuteronomy he set the same choice before the nation: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life (Deut 30:19). Jesus put it as two gates and two roads, one wide and easy, one narrow and hard (Matt 7:13-14).

He who goes out and surrenders. What is startling here is the content of the two ways. The way of life is surrender. Walk out of the gate, hands empty, and give yourself up to the enemy, and you will keep your life, though nothing else, as a prize of war, the way a soldier keeps his skin when everything else is lost.

Why they called him a traitor. No wonder they called Jeremiah a traitor. This is the sermon that later gets him thrown into a cistern for demoralising the troops (38:4). He is telling a besieged city to give in, and he is telling them so because the siege is God's judgment and resisting it is resisting God.

A hard lesson. There is a hard and useful lesson in it. Sometimes the godly response to a disaster we have brought on ourselves is not to fight for the position we held but to surrender it and accept the loss. The discipline is from God, a Father's discipline and not a sentence of rejection (Heb 12:6), and the life on the other side of it is real. Surrender looks like defeat and is the only way out.

Losing life to save it. Jesus put the same paradox at the heart of following him: whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it (Mark 8:35). The way of life still runs through surrender, now to a King who has gone through death himself and come out the other side.

Persons within the city. The city itself is not being saved. Individuals within it still can be, one at a time, by walking out. Judgment on a community and mercy to persons inside it are not contradictory, and this verse holds them together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Execute Justice in the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the royal house, a call to do justice first thing in the morning (vv. 11-12); and to a city confident in its rock and its walls, I am against you (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Even at this hour the word to the palace is not military but moral: do justice before breakfast.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'" "Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?' I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Execute justice in the morning. With an army at the gates, the word to the royal household is about the courts. Execute justice in the morning means make this the first business of the day, before anything else. Kings and judges heard cases in the morning at the city gate (2 Sam 15:2; compare Ps 101:8), so the command is to make that daily sitting honest and to hold it before the day’s other business crowds it out.

Him who has been robbed. And the concrete duty is named: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Not issue a statement about justice; get the stolen thing back to the person it was taken from.

How the house of David is judged. This is the measure by which the house of David is judged all through the prophets. Not the size of the army or the splendour of the temple, but whether a poor man who has been cheated can get a hearing before lunch. Two chapters on, God promises a son of David who will at last execute justice and righteousness in the land (23:5): the King this house never produced.

Who shall come down against us? Jerusalem sits on rock above its valleys, and the confidence in that geography has become a slogan: Who shall come down against us? Good walls in a good position, and the question is asked as if it had no answer.

I am against you. God's reply comes before the question, in the opening words of verse 13: I am against you. That is the answer to the question. It is not the Babylonians coming down; it is God.

According to the fruit of your deeds. This is the harvest language of 17:10, where God searches the heart and gives each according to his ways. The forest where the fire is kindled is probably the cedar palaces of the royal quarter, which the next chapter addresses directly.

Where the fire will start. The chapter that began with a king asking for a miracle ends with God pointing at the palace and telling him where the fire will start.

21.title: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
21.overview:
With Nebuchadnezzar's army at the walls, King Zedekiah asks for a miracle like the old days, and is told that God himself will fight against the city (vv. 1-7).

To the people God sets the way of life and the way of death, and the way of life is surrender (vv. 8-10). To the house of David the word is still to do justice first thing in the morning, and to a city confident in its walls, I am against you (vv. 11-14).
21.theology:
Prayer used as a last-resort lever by people unwilling to repent is refused (vv. 1-2; compare 14:11-12), and God may turn the language of redemption against his own people: the outstretched arm that freed Israel now fights them (v. 5).

The choice of Deuteronomy is set again, but the way of life now runs through surrender (vv. 8-9; Deut 30:15-19), and judgment on a community and mercy to individuals within it stand together. The first duty of God's appointed king is justice for the robbed and oppressed (v. 12), the duty fulfilled at last by the righteous Branch (23:5).
21.examples: After twenty years of ignoring the prophet, the palace sends an official delegation when the siege lines go up, wanting Hezekiah's outcome without Hezekiah's humble trust. The answer turns their slogan, Who shall come down against us?, into God's own reply: I am against you.

22.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word,<sup>2</sup>and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.<sup>4</sup>For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people.<sup>5</sup>But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.<sup>6</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city.<sup>7</sup>I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.<sup>8</sup>"'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?"<sup>9</sup>And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"<sup>10</sup>Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.<sup>11</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more,<sup>12</sup>but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."<sup>13</sup>"Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages,<sup>14</sup>who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.<sup>15</sup>Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him.<sup>16</sup>He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.<sup>17</sup>But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."<sup>18</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!'<sup>19</sup>With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."<sup>20</sup>"Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.<sup>22</sup>The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil.<sup>23</sup>O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"<sup>24</sup>"As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off<sup>25</sup>and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans.<sup>26</sup>I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die.<sup>27</sup>But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."<sup>28</sup>Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know?<sup>29</sup>O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Do Justice, or This House Becomes a Desolation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The royal charter preached at the palace gate (vv. 1-3), with two futures for the dynasty (vv. 4-5), and the cedar palace burned for a forsaken covenant (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne is held on terms, and the terms are the treatment of people who cannot defend themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word, and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go down to the house of the king. The prophet is sent to the palace, and told to preach at the gate again, the same method as the temple sermon (7:2) and the Sabbath sermon (17:19). He addresses the king, the civil service and the public together, because all three are implicated in how a country is run.

Who sits on the throne of David. The title matters: who sits on the throne of David. Everything that follows is measured against what that throne was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do justice and righteousness. Here is the royal job description, and it is strikingly concrete. Not defend the borders, not maintain the temple, not manage the economy: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Get the stolen thing back. And protect the same three groups God names every time, the immigrant, the orphan and the widow, the people with no family power to protect them.

The charter of the monarchy. This is not a political programme read back into Scripture; it is the charter of Israel's monarchy, and the prophets judge every king by it.

The ideal king. The psalm of the ideal king says the same, and the church has long heard Christ in it: May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor! (Ps 72:4), because he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper, and precious is their blood in his sight (Ps 72:12, 14). The job description Jehoiakim ignored is the one the true Son of David fulfils.

Does this apply to immigrants today? It commands God’s people to do justice to the vulnerable: the resident alien, the fatherless, the widow. Christians must treat foreigners with love and justice (Matt 25:35); how a nation sets its laws of entry is for governments to decide justly.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you will indeed obey this word. The same two futures as chapter 17, and the same door: obedience keeps the dynasty riding through these gates; refusal empties the palace.

I swear by myself. And God binds himself to it: I swear by myself. There is nothing higher to swear by. The promise to David was never a licence for his descendants to behave as they liked.

God’s oath. Hebrews notes the same form of oath when God promised Abraham: since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself (Heb 6:13). The oath that guarantees God's promises is the same oath that guarantees his threats. Both rest on God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city. I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Gilead to me. The palace is compared to the grandest landscapes the region knew: the wooded highlands of Gilead, the cedar summits of Lebanon. Partly this is about the building itself, which was panelled with imported cedar, and partly about how the dynasty looked to everyone: solid, green, permanent.

An uninhabited city. The ESV notes that an uninhabited city is in Hebrew "cities". Either way, what looked like a forest becomes desert.

I will prepare destroyers against you. The image turns from forest to logging camp. God will prepare destroyers, the way a builder lines up his woodcutters, and the cedars the king was so proud of will be firewood.

Built to last. Anything built to show that we are here to stay is, in the end, firewood. And the image fits the building exactly. Solomon's great hall in Jerusalem was called by a forest's name: He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon, built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars (1 Kgs 7:2). When God says like the summit of Lebanon and your choicest cedars, he is describing the royal complex itself, a manufactured forest cut down for fuel.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?" And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city? The ruins will preach. Travellers will ask the question, and the answer will be public and accurate: not bad luck, not the superior power of Babylon's gods, but a broken covenant.

A sermon from the rubble. Israel was called to make God known among the nations. She does it here, from the rubble, and the sermon is true.

Scripted long before. And the conversation between the travellers was scripted long before. Moses had told Israel exactly what the nations would say over its ruins: Why has the LORD done thus to this land?, and the reply, It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers (Deut 29:24-25). Jeremiah's hearers were watching Deuteronomy come true in their own streets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Woe to Him Who Builds by Unrighteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shallum will not return (vv. 10-12). Woe to Jehoiakim, who builds with unpaid labour, set beside his father Josiah, who judged the cause of the poor (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Knowing God is defined, in God's own words, as judging the cause of the poor and needy.

verseByVerse.quote: Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weep not for him who is dead. A funeral instruction that reverses the usual grief. The dead man is Josiah, killed at Megiddo, and the whole country mourned him. God says: stop weeping for the king who died in his own land and start weeping for the one being marched away alive, his son Shallum (verse 11).

Worse than dying at home. There are worse things than dying at home. Josiah was spared what is coming (2 Kgs 22:20); his son was not.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more, but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shallum the son of Josiah. Shallum is Jehoahaz, who reigned three months before Pharaoh deposed him and took him to Egypt. Of the kings named in this chapter, he and Coniah both end their lives in a foreign country.

Fulfilled to the letter. The history confirms the sentence exactly: Pharaoh Neco took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there (2 Kgs 23:34).

He shall return here no more. Twice in one sentence: He shall return here no more, and he shall never see this land again. Exile is not only punishment; it is the specific loss of home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages, who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness. Now Jehoiakim, and the charge is unpaid labour. He is building a palace during a national crisis, and he is doing it with forced work: makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages. And the country was already being squeezed. Pharaoh Neco had put Jehoiakim on the throne and laid a heavy tribute on the land, which Jehoiakim raised by taxing the people of the land (2 Kgs 23:33-35). The palace went up while his subjects were paying for his overlord.

What the law required. The law was emphatic about this: The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning (Lev 19:13), and You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD (Deut 24:15). James says the cry is heard: the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you (Jas 5:4). God notices payroll.

Habakkuk’s woe. Habakkuk pronounced the same woe on the same kind of builder: Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high, to be safe from the reach of harm! (Hab 2:9). A house built on unpaid labour is built on sand, however many cedar beams it has.

I will build myself a great house. Listen to the king's own voice: I will build myself a great house. The details read like an advertisement: spacious rooms, large windows, cedar panelling, expensive red paint.

The house that says who I am. In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen coined the phrase “conspicuous consumption” for spending whose real purpose is to be seen: goods bought less for use than to display standing. Jehoiakim’s vermilion paint is that, three thousand years early, and our version is everywhere: the extension, the car on the drive, the holiday photographs posted so that others will know. We are still competing in cedar. Underneath lies a question of identity: if the house is impressive, then perhaps I am somebody. The trouble is that a self built from display has to be kept up for ever, and someone else usually pays for it, as Jehoiakim’s unpaid neighbour did. Scripture is not against pleasure; Josiah ate and drank and God commends him (v. 15). The moralist and the show-off are both answered here. What finally ends the competition is a King who had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20) and who now says, In my Father’s house are many rooms (John 14:2). Someone whose standing is given, and whose house is being prepared for him, can stop painting the walls to prove a point.
verseByVerse.note: Jehoiakim built a lavish palace with forced labor.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him. He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? The question cuts through everything: kingship is not a building project or a standard of living. Then Josiah is held up, and the description is ordinary. Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? He enjoyed his life, and God does not fault him for it. And twice comes the refrain: it was well with him, and then it was well.

Is not this to know me? And then the sentence that should stop every religious reader: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me?

Knowing God and the poor. God defines the knowledge of himself by the treatment of the poor. Not instead of worship, prayer or doctrine (this book has spent twenty chapters on idolatry), but as inseparable from them. A man who defends the cause of people who cannot pay him knows God; a man who does not, whatever else he knows, does not know him.

The least of these. And the Lord makes the connection personal at the last judgment. The King says to those who fed the hungry and visited the prisoner, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt 25:40). To judge the cause of the poor is not merely to know about God. It is to meet the King who has chosen to stand with them. And it is that King, not Josiah and not us, who has kept this charter perfectly. Those whose neglect of the poor is forgiven for his sake are given his Spirit, who turns eyes and heart from dishonest gain toward the neighbour (Gal 5:22).

What this looks like. Jehoiakim was a king, but the New Testament carries the principle to every believer: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas 1:27). Pay people properly. If you employ anyone, a cleaner, a builder, a junior colleague, pay a fair wage and pay it on time; this woe began with unpaid wages (v. 13). Learn one name. Get to know one person who cannot repay you: the widow on your street, the asylum seeker who has started coming to church, the family your church supports through the food bank. Take up a cause, not just a feeling. Josiah judged the cause of the poor and needy: help someone fill in the benefits form, go with them to the housing office, write the letter they cannot write. Put it in the diary. Give it a regular slot, as you would a prayer meeting, because God counts it as knowing him. And we do it as people whose own cause was taken up when we had nothing to plead. Lamentations says it of God: You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life (Lam 3:58). In Christ he has done exactly that for us.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."
verseByVerse.commentary: Eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain. Attention and affection both fixed on dishonest gain. That is a portrait of a man whose inner life has narrowed to one thing, and the consequences run outward into blood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Burial of a Donkey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiakim's unmourned burial (vv. 18-19), and Judah's cry from the mountains, because she would not listen in her prosperity (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The king who built himself a cedar palace is dragged out of the city gate like a dead animal.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!' With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall not lament for him. The funeral cries of that world are quoted and cancelled. Nobody will mourn him as family (Ah, my brother!), and nobody will mourn him as king (Ah, lord!). The man who spent his reign building a monument will get no ceremony at all.

With the burial of a donkey. A dead donkey is hauled out of the city and left. That is the burial of the king of Judah: dragged and dumped.

No grave to visit. Set it beside the cedar and the vermilion: he built a house to be remembered by, and has no grave anyone would visit.

Repeated after the scroll. The sentence is repeated after he burned Jeremiah's scroll, in even starker terms: his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night (36:30).

Did he have a donkey’s burial? Jehoiakim was to have the burial of a donkey, yet Kings says he slept with his fathers (2 Kgs 24:6). That phrase means simply that he died; it says nothing of honourable burial. Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chr 36:6), but not that he arrived. Scripture does not say how Jeremiah's word was carried out; many think he died around the start of the siege in 598 BC and that his body was thrown out unburied.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed. I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go up to Lebanon, and cry out. The city is told to climb the high places in every direction and shout, north to Lebanon, north-east to Bashan, south-east to Abarim, and everywhere the news is the same. All your lovers are destroyed: the foreign allies Judah has courted since chapter 2 are gone.

I spoke to you in your prosperity. God spoke in your prosperity, while things were going well, when listening would have cost nothing and prevented everything. Good times are when warnings are cheapest to heed and hardest to hear.

The complacency of fools. Proverbs says how it happens: the complacency of fools destroys them (Prov 1:32). And Jesus told of a rich man in exactly this condition, talking to his own soul in his prosperity, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry, until God said, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil. O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds. A bitter joke: the shepherds who were supposed to lead the flock will themselves be herded, and by the wind. And the city nested among the cedars, comfortable, elevated and expensively furnished, will cry out like a woman in labour.

Height and cedar were supposed to keep trouble out. They only made the fall longer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Signet Ring Torn Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Coniah, the signet ring torn off and hurled into exile (vv. 24-28), is written down as childless (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The signet ring of the house of David is pulled off and thrown away, and the line looks finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coniah the son of Jehoiakim. Coniah is Jehoiachin, eighteen years old, three months on the throne, deported to Babylon in 597 BC. Kings gives his age as eighteen (2 Kgs 24:8); most Hebrew copies of Chronicles read eight (2 Chr 36:9), very likely a copying slip, since some ancient copies there read eighteen.

The signet ring on my right hand. A signet ring was a king's identity: it carried his seal, it went everywhere with him, it was never taken off. To call the Davidic king the signet on God's right hand is to say he is God's own authority displayed in the world.

Yet I would tear you off. And God says he would tear you off. The verb is violent. Even so intimate a symbol of the covenant with David is not immune when the man wearing it is faithless.
verseByVerse.note: Coniah is Jehoiachin (Jeconiah).

verseByVerse.quote: and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans. I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die. But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the hand. Four times into the hand, and the last phrase is the ache of every exile: the land to which they will long to return. They will have the longing, but not the return.

The mother who bore you. His mother goes with him, as 13:18 said she would. His release to eat at the king's table is the note on which the book of Kings closes (2 Kgs 25:27-30), a flicker of light at the end of that history, and the appendix to this very book records it too: in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin, Evil-merodach graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison (52:31). The ring was torn off; the man was not forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know? O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
A despised, broken pot. The question echoes the broken flask of chapter 19. A pot that has been smashed is swept up and thrown out without a thought, and that is what happened to the king: a vessel no one cares for.

Why are he and his children hurled? Hear the tone of the question, too. It is almost pity: Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know? Even under judgment, God does not describe the ruin of a young king without feeling. Many Christians have heard in despised an echo of the King who later came through this very line: He was despised and rejected by men (Isa 53:3).

O land, land, land. Three times, like a herald in the street. The land itself is summoned to hear what is about to be said about the house of David.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Write this man down as childless. Enter it in the record: childless. He had sons, but for the purposes of the throne the line stops here. No descendant of Jehoiachin will reign in Jerusalem, and none ever did.

That looks like the end of the promise to David, and for centuries the question stood unanswered.

Zerubbabel the signet. Two things happen afterwards, and they must be held together. First, Haggai takes this very image and gives it back: to Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin's grandson, God says, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you (Hag 2:23). The ring torn off is put back on.

Through Jechoniah to Christ. Second, Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy that runs straight through this cursed name: Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon, and then Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel (Matt 1:11-12), and on to Joseph, the husband of Mary.

Heir without the curse. The line that carried the throne also carried the curse, and the King who finally sat on David's throne came into that family as its legal heir without being physically descended from Jeconiah. What God said stands, and what God promised stands, and the gospel is how both are true at once.

How can Jesus be Jeconiah’s heir? God said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (22:30), yet Matthew traces Jesus through him (Matt 1:11–12). Jesus was Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father, but not his physical descendant; Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31). The throne passed to a Son of David by another branch.
verseByVerse.note: No son of Jehoiachin reigned; on Jesus' descent, see the question above.

22.title: The House of David on Trial
22.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to the palace with the royal charter: do justice, rescue the robbed, protect the immigrant, the orphan and the widow (vv. 1-3). Refuse, and God swears the house will be a desolation (vv. 4-9).

Shallum is deported, never to return (vv. 10-12). Woe to Jehoiakim, who built a cedar palace with unpaid labour, while his father judged the cause of the poor: Is not this to know me? He will have the burial of a donkey (vv. 13-23). Finally Coniah, the signet ring torn off, is written down as childless (vv. 24-30).
22.theology:
The Davidic throne is held on covenant terms, and the test is justice for those who cannot defend themselves (vv. 3-5). God defines the knowledge of himself by the judging of the cause of the poor and needy (v. 16), not as a substitute for true worship but inseparable from it.

God speaks to people in their prosperity, when heeding him is cheapest (v. 21), and grandeur built on injustice ends as firewood and an unmourned burial (vv. 7, 19). Not even the signet ring of David's house is immune (v. 24), yet God gives the signet back to Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23), and the throne passes to Christ: the curse stands and the promise is kept.
22.examples: The chapter judges a king by whether a robbed man can get his property back, and sets cedar panelling and vermilion paint, paid for with wages never handed over, beside a dead donkey dragged out of the gate as the state funeral. It ends with a signet ring torn off a king's hand and, in Haggai, put back on his grandson's.

Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply.<sup>4</sup>I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>6</sup>In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. Then they shall dwell in their own land."<sup>9</sup>Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words.<sup>10</sup>For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.<sup>11</sup>"Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.<sup>13</sup>In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray.<sup>14</sup>But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah."<sup>15</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"<sup>18</sup>For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened?<sup>19</sup>Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked.<sup>20</sup>The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.<sup>21</sup>"I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.<sup>22</sup>But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.<sup>23</sup>"Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away?<sup>24</sup>Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD.<sup>29</sup>Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?<sup>30</sup>Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another.<sup>31</sup>Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.<sup>33</sup>"When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.'<sup>34</sup>And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household.<sup>35</sup>Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>36</sup>But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.<sup>37</sup>Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>38</sup>But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'"<sup>39</sup>therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers.<sup>40</sup>And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to the shepherds, and God's promise to gather the flock himself (vv. 1-4); the righteous Branch and his name (vv. 5-6); and the new-exodus oath (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Against every failed shepherd God sets one King who will do what the house of David was given the throne to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD. Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD. Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply. I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the shepherds. The shepherds are the kings and leaders of chapter 22, and the charge is precise. They did not merely fail to gather; they destroy and scatter. Bad leadership is not neutral.

The sheep of my pasture. And they are the sheep of my pasture. The flock was never theirs. That is the reason the woe is so heavy: they mishandled someone else's property, and the owner was watching.

I will attend to you. There is a grim play on words here. They did not attend to the flock, so God will attend to them, in judgment.

The sin of inattention. Anyone with pastoral responsibility should feel the weight of it: the opposite of caring for people is not cruelty but inattention, and God treats inattention as an evil deed. The one safe place for a shepherd who has failed is under the good Shepherd, who laid down his life for sheep and shepherds alike.

I will gather the remnant of my flock. And now God takes the job himself: I will gather. Ezekiel puts it even more strongly: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out (Ezek 34:11). When human shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock; he comes for them personally.

I will set shepherds over them. Then he gives them shepherds again, a promise fulfilled in the pastors and teachers Christ gives his church, and finally in the chief Shepherd himself (1 Pet 5:4). And success is now measured as a shepherd measures it: neither shall any be missing. Every sheep is accounted for.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to chapter 22. Chapter 22 ended with the royal line written down as childless. Here is the answer, and the timing is deliberate.

A righteous Branch. The righteous Branch is a shoot growing from a stump: a tree cut down to the ground, and one living green shoot coming up out of it. Isaiah had used it: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit (Isa 11:1). The dynasty is a felled tree; God will grow a king out of the stump.

Execute justice and righteousness in the land. And what he will do is exactly what chapter 22 demanded and no king delivered: execute justice and righteousness in the land. The job description is unchanged; at last there is someone to fill it.

The LORD is our righteousness. This name is the summit of the book so far. The king reigning as Jeremiah spoke was Zedekiah, a weak, faithless man whose reign ended in fire. The coming King will be everything he was not, and his name is not about himself at all: our righteousness.

Righteousness reckoned. Think about what that means. The King's name is a statement about his people's standing. He is called what they receive. His righteousness is reckoned as theirs, credited to them as if they had lived his life, which is why they are saved and dwell securely in his days rather than in their own.

What the New Testament says. The New Testament does not quote these verses, but it says in plain prose what they promise. The righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe (Rom 3:21-22). Christ became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21).

A righteousness from outside. Everything Jeremiah has exposed, the deceitful heart, the leopard's spots, the sin engraved with an iron pen, requires a righteousness from outside. Here is his name.

Everyone has a righteousness project. Few modern people use the word righteousness, but almost all of us are working at it. We want to be on the right side of history, a good parent, an ethical shopper, the reasonable one in the argument. Much public life is now a contest of moral standing, in which the surest way to feel righteous is to find someone less righteous and say so loudly. Religious people do it with rules and attendance; secular people do it with causes and opinions. The method differs; the project is the same: to be my own justification. And it is exhausting, because the verdict is never final and someone is always ready to reopen the case. That is why this name is such a surprise. It does not say, the LORD rewards our righteousness, or, the LORD helps us become righteous. It says the King is our righteousness. The verdict is settled by someone else’s life. A person who has received that can stop defending himself, can admit he was wrong without his whole world shaking, and can give others the mercy he no longer has to earn.

The name given to Jerusalem. Later in this book the same name is given to Jerusalem (33:16): the people are called by their King's name, because what he is, they are counted to be in him. Hebrew names often made a statement about God, as Zedekiah's did, so the name need not by itself call the Branch the LORD; yet many Christians have seen here a hint of what the New Testament makes plain, that the King who is our righteousness is himself God come in the flesh.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers have always taken the righteous Branch as the Messiah, the King of David's line still to come: the Targum renders Branch here as Messiah, and the Talmud (Bava Batra 75b) counts the Messiah among those called by the name of God, citing this verse. Most Jewish interpreters take the name as a sentence praising God, not a claim that the King is divine. On the King himself the two readings agree. This commentary sees him in Jesus, descended from David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), in whom God's righteousness is given to his people (1 Corinthians 1:30).
verseByVerse.note: The “righteous Branch” is the Messiah; his name, “The LORD is our righteousness,” plays on King Zedekiah’s name (“the LORD is righteous”).

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The days are coming. The new-exodus oath of 16:14-15 is repeated, and its position here is the point: it comes immediately after the righteous Branch. The greater rescue and the greater King belong together.

A modest return. Christians read this with the knowledge that the return from Babylon, when it came, was modest: some fifty thousand people (Ezra 2:64-65), a small temple, no king. The oath was not yet fully kept. It is kept in Christ’s rescue of his people from a deeper exile than Babylon, the exile of sin and death.

How is this return fulfilled? Its first fulfilment was the return from Babylon. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel; faithful Christians differ here. In this chapter the promise is tied to the Branch, and its scope is his: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. It is fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered sheep from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and it will be complete in the new creation.

A textual note. The ESV notes a small textual difference in verse 8. The substance is unaffected: the God who is bringing them home will be known by that, as he was once known by the Red Sea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Both Prophet and Priest Are Ungodly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Concerning the prophets: Jeremiah shaken by God's words (vv. 9-10), prophet and priest ungodly even in God's house (vv. 11-12), and Jerusalem's prophets worse than Samaria's (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Preaching that comforts people in their sin is not a minor failure; it is the source from which a nation's ungodliness spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words. For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning the prophets. The heading opens a collection that runs to the end of the chapter. Having dealt with the kings, God now turns to the preachers.

My heart is broken within me. Before he says a word against the false prophets, Jeremiah describes what God's word does to him: heart broken, bones shaking, unsteady on his feet like a drunk. Not because of the opposition, but because of the LORD and because of his holy words.

Wrecked by the word. That is the contrast the whole section turns on. Here is a man wrecked by handling the word of God, about to describe men who handle it lightly and sleep well. Anyone who teaches Scripture might ask which of the two he more resembles.

The land is full of adulterers. It is literal (verse 14 will say the prophets themselves commit adultery), and it is also spiritual: a nation unfaithful to the God it was bound to by covenant, as a wife to her husband. The two are rarely separate for long.

Because of the curse the land mourns. And the drought is read for what it is. Because of the curse the land mourns: this is the curse written into the covenant long before, the heavens over your head shall be bronze and The LORD will make the rain of your land powder (Deut 28:23-24). The pastures are dying because the people broke faith, and the ground itself is pictured grieving.

Sin is never as private as it feels. A nation's unfaithfulness reaches its fields.

Their might is not right. Then the verdict on the powerful: Their course is evil, and their might is not right. They hold the influence in the land and they use it wrongly, and strength that has lost its moral right is simply force.

verseByVerse.quote: "Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD. Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both prophet and priest are ungodly. These were the two offices that should have checked each other: the priest teaching the law that had been given, the prophet bringing the word God was speaking now. Each could have called the other back. Instead they agreed, and when those meant to correct one another join in the same wrong, nobody is left to raise the alarm.

Even in my house. Not only in the streets and the high places, but inside the temple, among the men conducting the worship. Corruption at the centre of religion is worse than corruption outside it, because there is nowhere left for a seeker to go.

Like slippery paths in the darkness. Men who gave others no light will walk in the dark on wet stone, and the punishment fits. A psalmist once envied men like these, secure and prosperous, until he went into the sanctuary and saw their end: Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin (Ps 73:18). The false prophets looked as though they were standing on the firmest ground in Jerusalem: the pulpit, the temple, the favour of the court. They were on a wet slope in the dark, and they were being driven.

The year of their punishment. And the date is already set: the year of their punishment. Judgment is not improvised when patience runs out. It is on the calendar.

verseByVerse.quote: In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray. But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah." Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the prophets of Samaria. Samaria is the northern kingdom, destroyed a century before, and its prophets were openly pagan. God calls that an unsavory thing: repellent, but at least undisguised.

A horrible thing. And the men in Jerusalem, who preach in the name of the LORD, are worse: a horrible thing. Their private lives are corrupt and their public message is false, and the two are connected.

They strengthen the hands of evildoers. The phrase to weigh is they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil. That is the effect of their preaching, and it is the exact opposite of a prophet's job. A man goes to church intending to break with something, hears that God is fine with it, and goes home confirmed in it.

Judged by outcome rather than intention, that is more destructive than Baal worship, because it uses God's own name to do it.

Like Sodom to me. Then the comparison no Jerusalemite could hear calmly: like Sodom to me. Isaiah had already addressed the city's leaders that way, Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! (Isa 1:10), and Ezekiel names what Sodom's guilt actually was: pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy (Ezek 16:49). The likeness is not only in the sexual sin. It is a comfortable city that has lost the capacity to be shocked. Sodom had no prophets; Jerusalem had prophets, and they made it Sodom.

I will feed them with bitter food. The bitter food and poisoned water of 9:15 are now served to the preachers, and the reason names them as the source: ungodliness did not seep up from the people to the pulpit; it flowed out from the pulpit into the country.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Visions of Their Own Minds
