verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not listen to prophets who never stood in God's council (vv. 16-20); the test of their fruit (vv. 21-22); and the God who fills heaven and earth (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The test of preaching is not sincerity or eloquence but whether it comes from God and turns people from evil.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD. They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not listen. This is a direct instruction to the congregation. Hearers are responsible for what they sit under.

Filling you with vain hopes. What the false prophets supply is vain hopes. Hope is a gift; false hope is a cruelty, because it uses up the time a person had to repent. A doctor who tells a man with a treatable illness that nothing is wrong has not been kind to him.

Visions of their own minds. The source is named again (14:14): visions of their own minds. This is not plain lying; these men very likely believed their own material. Sincerity is not the test; where the message comes from is: not from the mouth of the LORD.

It shall be well with you. Look at the audiences: people who despise the word of the LORD and people who stubbornly follow their own hearts. To exactly those people they say, It shall be well with you, and they say it continually, the same reassurance over and over. Chapters 27 and 28 show the message being preached in the temple itself: Hananiah promising that within two years the exiles and the temple vessels would be home (28:2-4).

Itching ears. Paul saw the same market forming: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim 4:3). False prophets are not only a supply problem. There is always demand.

A God who only says nice things. The sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton, in Soul Searching (2005), gave a name to the faith they found among many American teenagers and their parents: Moralistic Therapeutic Deism. God wants people to be nice, wants them to feel good about themselves, and otherwise stays out of the way until he is needed. It is an exact description of It shall be well with you. Such a God is very pleasant. He is also useless when it matters, because a God who never warns cannot really rescue, and a God who never names sin cannot really forgive it; there is nothing for him to forgive. False comfort feels kind and leaves people alone with what they have refused to face. The true word does something harder and better. It says the disaster is real, and then it shows the one on whom it fell. The false prophets said, No disaster shall come upon you. In Christ God says something deeper: the disaster came, and it came upon him. Peace built on that is not a vain hope.

How do I know whom to listen to? The voices now come by podcast and feed as well as from the pulpit, and the command still stands. Check the source. Does the speaker open the Bible and let it speak, or use a verse as a launch pad for his own ideas? Be like the Bereans, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so (Acts 17:11). Notice what it does to you. Does it ever confront your sin, or only reassure? Teaching that says It shall be well with you to everyone, whatever they do, fails the test of verse 22. Watch where it points. Do you come away thinking more about Christ and his cross, or about the teacher, your success and your feelings? Choose a church, not just content. Sit under a pastor who knows you and can be questioned, and keep your diet of online teaching smaller than your diet of Scripture itself. And the safeguard is not finally your cleverness. The Good Shepherd says, My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (John 10:27); he keeps his own by his word.

verseByVerse.quote: For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened? Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who among them has stood in the council of the LORD? The test is put as a question: who has stood in the council of the LORD? A true prophet has stood where God's decisions are made and has listened. These men never went in, which is why they can only report their own minds.

A glimpse of the council. Scripture lets us glimpse that room. When four hundred court prophets told King Ahab to go up to battle and triumph, one man stood apart and said, I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left (1 Kgs 22:19). Micaiah had been in the council; the four hundred had only been in the palace. And Amos states the principle: the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7).

Paid attention to his word and listened. Count the words for receiving in the question: stood, to see, to hear, paid attention, listened. Five of them before a single word about speaking. A preacher is first a listener, and a man who speaks more than he listens has reversed the order God requires.

Behold, the storm of the LORD! While they promise fair weather, the storm is already moving. These two verses return almost word for word in the Book of Consolation, the chapters of comfort that begin at chapter 30 (30:23-24). There they guard the promise, reminding the restored that God's anger against evil has not been cancelled; here they are aimed at the men who said no disaster would come. It is the same storm. What differs is whether a person is sheltered from it.

The intents of his heart. And the anger is not a mood. It will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart: it is a settled purpose, which is terrifying for those who oppose it and steadying for those who trust that he will carry out his purposes of mercy just as surely.

In the latter days. The last line is honest about timing: In the latter days you will understand it clearly. Some things only make sense afterwards, and the people telling you otherwise now will not be there to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I did not send the prophets, yet they ran. God flatly denies two things: he did not send them, and he did not speak to them. Yet they ran, and they prophesied. Zeal and output are not evidence of a call. It is possible to be extremely busy in ministry that God never commissioned.

The practical test. And here is the practical test, and it is a wonderfully usable one. Preaching that comes from God turns people from evil. That is its fruit.

The aim of the word. Not that everyone repents; Jeremiah's own ministry is proof that faithful preaching can be widely rejected. But the aim and the tendency of the word is to turn people, and a message whose effect is to leave everyone exactly as they were, comfortable and unchallenged, has already told you where it came from. Deuteronomy gave a test by fulfilment (Deut 18:21-22); Jeremiah adds a test by fruit.

From their evil way. The turning is concrete: from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds. The direction of a life and the particular things done in it. God's word does not stop at general improvement; it names the road and the acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I a God at hand? The false prophets have been behaving as though God were at hand in the smallest sense: a local deity, the resident of the temple precinct, near enough to be managed and too small to see what went on in their houses. A god like that can be quoted freely, because he will not object.

And not a God far away. God insists he is also a God far away: above, beyond, not contained by the building or by anyone's theology of it. They wanted a God close enough to use and not great enough to fear.

Near and far together. Scripture holds both truths together, and in a particular order. I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit (Isa 57:15). God is near because he chooses to come near, not because he is small, and the ones he comes near to are the humble, not the men using his name.

Can a man hide himself in secret places? Think of what was being done in secret places in this chapter: adultery behind closed doors (v. 14), dreams rehearsed in private and passed off in public (v. 25). Can a man hide himself in secret places? The question answers itself. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13).

Do I not fill heaven and earth? This is not a picture of a very large being in a very large room. It means there is no location without him: no study, no bedroom, no pulpit, no private thought.

Where shall I flee? The psalm turns the same truth into comfort: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7). Paul told pagans in Athens that he is actually not far from each one of us (Acts 17:27). To a liar it is terror; to a child it is home. The God who sees the unconfessed sin is the same God who sees the faithfulness nobody else noticed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dreams and God's word: straw and wheat (vv. 25-29), and three frauds God is against (vv. 30-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Dreams and God's word are not two grades of the same thing; they are straw and wheat.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!' How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart, who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard. The God who fills heaven and earth has been listening to the sermons.

I have dreamed, I have dreamed! The repetition mimics them: I have dreamed, I have dreamed! It is the excited claim of a private revelation that cannot be checked. And God traces it to its source, which is the deceitful heart of chapter 17 (17:9): the deceit is in the prophets' own hearts, and they are its first victims.

How long? This is the voice of patience nearing its end. God has let this go on, and he asks how much longer it will be allowed to.

Who think to make my people forget my name. Their dreams have the same effect as Baal did: they make people forget God's name. Ministry that draws attention to the minister's experiences is not neutral; it crowds out the name it claims to serve.

Even as their fathers forgot my name. And the comparison across the generations is sobering. The grandfathers forgot God by bowing to an idol; the grandsons forget him by listening to dreams told in his name. The method differs and the result is the same: idolatry does not require a statue.

Does God give dreams and visions today? He spoke by dreams and visions when Scripture was being given; now he has spoken finally in his Son (Heb 1:1–2), and his word is complete. A dream may stir the conscience, but no believer should treat one as a word from God. Let him who has my word speak my word faithfully (v. 28). Many continuationist Christians believe God still guides by dreams, always to be tested by Scripture; this commentary is cessationist, holding that nothing received today adds to the finished word, and it honours brothers who see it differently.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD. Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream. The ruling is not that dreams must be suppressed. Tell the dream, and call it a dream. What is forbidden is passing it off as the word of God.

Speak my word faithfully. And the requirement laid on the one who has God's word is a single word: faithfully. Not originally, not impressively, not with fresh angles. A messenger's whole excellence is delivering the message as it was given.

What has straw in common with wheat? The comparison settles it: What has straw in common with wheat? Both come off the same field; one feeds people and one does not. Preaching that is mostly the preacher's own material may be pleasant, but nobody lives on straw.

Like fire, and like a hammer. Here is what the real thing does. It burns, as it burned in Jeremiah's bones when he tried to keep silent (20:9); and it breaks rock, which is the only hope for a people whose faces are harder than rock (5:3).

When nothing burns. If preaching never burns or breaks anything, the problem may not be the congregation. The power is not the preacher's to produce: the word does its work in the hands of the Spirit, which is why a preacher's first task is to deliver it faithfully and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another. Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.' Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am against the prophets. Three times God says I am against the prophets, and each names a different fraud.

Who steal my words from one another. The first is plagiarism: they steal my words from one another. Having nothing from God themselves, they recycle each other's material. A prophetic culture can run for years on borrowed phrases with no fresh dealing with God behind any of it.

Who use their tongues. The second is the formula. They have learned the phrase that makes speech sound authoritative and they attach it to their own opinions. The verse is almost comic in its precision: they use their tongues and say, declares the LORD.

Every generation’s version. Every generation has its version, a tone of voice, a way of quoting, a confident "God told me", by which personal judgment is given divine weight.

They do not profit this people at all. The third is recklessness: not only malice but carelessness with other people's souls. And the verdict is quietly devastating: they do not profit this people at all. All that ministry, and nobody was helped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–40 — The Burden of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A joke about the burden of the LORD is banned and turned back on those who make it (vv. 33-40).
verseByVerse.theology: A reverent-sounding phrase had become a joke about God's word, and God takes the joke away.

verseByVerse.quote: "When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.' And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household. Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is the burden of the LORD? This last section turns on a word. The burden of the LORD was a way of speaking about a prophet's message, and a burden is also a load. People had started asking Jeremiah, with a smirk, what today's burden was, treating God's word as a heavy, tiresome thing and the prophet as the man who carries it round.

You are the burden. God takes the joke and returns it: You are the burden, and I will cast you off. The ESV notes a textual variation in the question, but the wordplay is plain enough. You think my word is a weight? You are the weight, and I am putting it down.

You shall mention no more. The phrase is banned, and the ban reaches everyone, prophet, priest, ordinary citizen and his household, because an attitude to God's word is taught at home before it is voiced in public. It is a striking example of God legislating against a piece of religious slang because of the contempt packed into it.

What has the LORD answered? And he gives them the replacement wording, which is humble and expectant: What has the LORD answered? Not, what is today's burden, but what has God said. The change of phrase is a change of attitude.

Every one to his neighbor. The correction happens between neighbours: every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother. Not in the temple, but in ordinary conversation. The way believers talk to each other about God's word, flippant or expectant, weary or hungry, shapes how they receive it.

The burden is every man’s own word. Here is the heart of it: the burden is every man's own word. Everyone had made his own opinion the word from God. And the charge is the gravest in the chapter, you pervert the words of the living God: twisting them until they say something else.

The words of the living God. Weigh the three titles stacked at the end: the living God, not a dead text to be joked about; the LORD of hosts, the commander of heaven's armies; our God, the one who belongs to these very people. They were bending the words of someone alive, powerful, and theirs.
verseByVerse.note: A pun: “burden” and “oracle” are the same Hebrew word (massa).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'" therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers. And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I sent to you. The instruction is repeated, now addressed to how people speak to the prophet himself, and then the case against them is built with the precision of a legal charge. They were told plainly not to say it. They said it anyway.

From contempt to defiance. That moves the offence from attitude to defiance. The first use of the phrase was contempt; its use after an explicit command was rebellion, and verse 38 records the command in God's own voice so that no one can plead ignorance.

I will surely lift you up. The sentence uses their own word against them one last time: they called God's message a burden, so he will lift you up like a load and put it down outside. The ESV notes that the phrase may be rendered "surely forget you", and both readings land. They could not stop saying the word; God will stop remembering them.

The city that I gave to you. And what is cast away with them is a gift: the city that I gave to you and your fathers. Everything they had came from the God they were mocking.

Which shall not be forgotten. Put the last two verses side by side. God will "surely forget" them, and their shame shall not be forgotten.

Remember their sin no more. Now set that beside the promise eight chapters later: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (31:34). Those are the only two outcomes Scripture offers. In the new covenant God forgets the sin and keeps the person. Outside it, he lets go of the person and the shame is never forgotten.

The two belong together. The chapter that gave us the most beautiful name in the book, The LORD is our righteousness, ends with everlasting reproach for those who made his word a joke. The two belong together: the King who is our righteousness is the Word made flesh, and how people handle the word is finally how they handle him.

23.title: The Righteous Branch: The LORD Is Our Righteousness
23.overview:
Against the shepherds who scattered God's flock stands the promise of a righteous Branch for David, whose name is The LORD is our righteousness (vv. 1-8).

Then the prophets: men who never stood in God's council, who strengthened the hands of evildoers, and who passed off their own dreams as his word, which is wheat to their straw, a fire and a hammer (vv. 9-32). The chapter ends by banning the phrase the burden of the LORD, by which they had made his word a joke (vv. 33-40).
23.theology:
Leaders are accountable for a flock that belongs to God, and when shepherds fail, God gathers his people himself and gives them true shepherds under the chief Shepherd (vv. 1-4; John 10:11). The righteous Branch is the King who does what David's house failed to do, and his name declares what his people receive: his righteousness counted as theirs (vv. 5-6).

False prophecy is sincere and energetic, but it comes from the prophet’s own mind (vv. 16, 21), and is tested by its origin and its fruit: God's word turns people from evil (v. 22; Deut 18:20-22). God is near because he chooses to come near to the humble, not because he is small enough to be managed (vv. 23-24). And there are only two ways to be forgotten by God: in the new covenant he remembers the sin no more and keeps the person (31:34); for those who make his word a joke he lets go of the person, and the shame is never forgotten (vv. 39-40).
23.examples: The chapter's images are memorable: a shoot growing out of a stump that everyone had written off, preachers recycling each other's material with nothing fresh from God, and straw and wheat off the same field, of which only one feeds people. Its sharpest warning is the churchgoer who comes intending to break with a sin and goes home confirmed in it.

24.text: <sup>1</sup>After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>5</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.<sup>6</sup>I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up.<sup>7</sup>I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.<sup>8</sup>"But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them.<sup>10</sup>And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Two Baskets Before the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the first deportation, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple, one very good and one rotten, and asks what he sees (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: Two baskets at the temple door, and the sorting is not the one anybody in Jerusalem would have made.

verseByVerse.quote: After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD. One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten. And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The date fixes everything. This is after 597 BC, when Babylon took the young king Jeconiah, the Coniah of chapter 22, along with the court, the skilled workers and the metalworkers. The first deportation has happened, and Jerusalem is still standing with Zedekiah on the throne.

We are the survivors. That situation produced a very natural way of thinking in the city: God has judged those people and spared us. The deportees must have been the sinners. We are the survivors, we still have the temple, and that proves whose side God is on.

Before the temple of the LORD. So the vision is set before the temple, in the very place where that view was preached, and it is a picture of the harvest offering: two baskets of figs brought to God's house.

So bad that they could not be eaten. First-ripe figs, picked in June, were a delicacy, the best of the crop. The other basket is not mediocre fruit but rotten: so bad that they could not be eaten. There is no middle category anywhere in this chapter.

What do you see, Jeremiah? The question is the one from the almond branch and the boiling pot (1:11, 13). God's method with this prophet is to make him look at something ordinary and say what is there, and then to tell him what it means. Jeremiah's answer is simply accurate, and it commits him to nothing, which is why God’s explanation comes as such a shock.
verseByVerse.note: Jeconiah (v. 1), Jehoiachin and Coniah (22:24) are three forms of the same young king's name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — The Good Figs: the Exiles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good figs are the exiles God sent to Babylon. He will bring them back, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The people who lost everything are the good figs, and God promises to give them the one thing they cannot give themselves: a heart to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans. I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up. I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like these good figs. The good figs are the people in Babylon, which reverses everything Jerusalem believed. The men in chains, who lost their homes, their positions and their temple, are the first-ripe fruit. And note the phrase whom I have sent away: God, not Nebuchadnezzar, sent them. Their deportation was not abandonment but transplanting.

Were the exiles better people? Not by nature: Ezekiel, who lived among them, called them a rebellious house (Ezekiel 2:5). They are good figs because God says I will regard them so and sets his eyes on them for good. The difference lies in his choosing and his gift, not in their merit.

Circumstances are not a scoreboard. It is a hard lesson for comfortable believers. Circumstances are not a scoreboard. The people whose lives look broken may be the ones God has his eye on, and the ones still holding the property may be the rotten basket.

Why do we read suffering as a verdict? The social psychologist Melvin Lerner called it the belief in a just world: the deep instinct that people get what they deserve, so that when disaster strikes someone, we half-assume they must have earned it. It is comforting, because it means that if I am careful, it will not happen to me. Modern spirituality has its own version in karma, and the people left in Jerusalem had theirs: the deportees must have been the sinners. God overturns both the moralist, who reads every loss as punishment, and the cynic, who concludes that there is no justice at all (see the note on Job 1:20–22). The good figs are good because of God’s choosing and gift, not because their circumstances looked good. The clearest case is the cross. By the reckoning of a just world, the man dying on it was plainly cursed. In fact he was the beloved Son, bearing a curse that belonged to others. Once you have seen that, you can never again read a life’s worth off its circumstances, your own or anyone else’s.

I will build them up. Listen to the verbs: build, plant, and the refusal of tear down and pluck up. They are four of the six verbs of Jeremiah's call (1:10), and here the two constructive ones stand on their own, with the destructive pair expressly set aside. Ruin is not the last word of this ministry, and the exiles are where the building starts.

A heart to know me. And here is the promise the whole book has been driving toward. Chapter 13 asked whether a leopard could change its spots; chapter 17 said the heart is deceitful and unsearchable. The answer is not better instruction: I will give them a heart to know me.

God gives what he requires. God gives what he requires. Ezekiel says the same: I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh (Ezek 11:19). And the covenant promise follows, as it always does: they shall be my people and I will be their God.

With their whole heart. Notice the order in the last clause. Because he gives the heart, they shall return to me with their whole heart. Their wholehearted return is real, and it is the fruit of his gift rather than the price of it. That is the shape of the new covenant in 31:31-34, and of every conversion since. Paul calls believers a letter from Christ, written with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3): the heart God promised the exiles is given by Christ through his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Bad Figs: Those Who Remain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bad figs are Zedekiah, his officials and those who stayed in Jerusalem or fled to Egypt: a byword among the nations, pursued by sword, famine and pestilence (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Keeping your place in the land turns out to prove nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt. I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them. And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the bad figs. The bad figs are the people still at home with the king, the officials and the temple, plus those in Egypt, probably Judeans who had gone there rather than submit to Babylon. They took their houses, jobs and worship as evidence of God's approval. God calls them uneatable fruit.

Spared is not approved. Being spared a disaster that fell on others proves nothing about your standing with God, and it is most dangerous when it is taken as God’s verdict in your favour.

A reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse. Verse 9 piles up words for public disgrace: a reproach, a byword, a taunt, a curse. (The ESV notes a small textual difficulty in the opening phrase.) The nation called to make God's name known among the nations becomes the story other nations tell as a warning.

The land that I gave to them. Verse 10 brings the book's familiar threefold sentence of sword, famine and pestilence, and the sting is in the last clause, the land that I gave to them. The possession they trusted in is what they lose, because it was always a gift, never something they had earned. Ten verses overturn a whole way of reading what happens to us; anyone tempted to measure God's favour by his circumstances should read them twice.

24.title: Two Baskets of Figs
24.overview:
Soon after the first deportation in 597 BC, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the temple, one of first-ripe figs and one so rotten they cannot be eaten (vv. 1-3).

The good figs, against every expectation in Jerusalem, are the exiles in Babylon. God will set his eyes on them for good, bring them back, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him (vv. 4-7).

The bad figs are Zedekiah, his officials, those who remain in Jerusalem and those living in Egypt. They will become a byword wherever they are driven, pursued by sword, famine and pestilence until they are gone from the land God gave their fathers (vv. 8-10).
24.theology:
God's favour is not read off circumstances: the difference between the baskets lies in his choosing, not in anyone's merit (vv. 5, 8).

And God gives what he demands. The heart that 17:9 called deceitful, and that 13:23 said could no more change itself than a leopard its spots, he will replace with a heart to know him (v. 7), as Ezekiel 11:19-20 also promises and the new covenant of 31:31-34 will spell out.
24.examples: The chapter warns anyone who reads his own survival, or his comfortable circumstances, as God's verdict in his favour. And it comforts anyone whose life has been uprooted: God calls the deportation transplanting, promises building and planting with no tearing down attached, and gives the very heart he asks for.

25.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),<sup>2</sup>which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem:<sup>3</sup>"For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened.<sup>4</sup>You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets,<sup>5</sup>saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever.<sup>6</sup>Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.'<sup>7</sup>Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.<sup>8</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words,<sup>9</sup>behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation.<sup>10</sup>Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.<sup>11</sup>This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.<sup>12</sup>Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste.<sup>13</sup>I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.<sup>14</sup>For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."<sup>15</sup>Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it.<sup>16</sup>They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them."<sup>17</sup>So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it:<sup>18</sup>Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day;<sup>19</sup>Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people,<sup>20</sup>and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod);<sup>21</sup>Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon;<sup>22</sup>all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea;<sup>23</sup>Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair;<sup>24</sup>all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert;<sup>25</sup>all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media;<sup>26</sup>all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Babylon shall drink.<sup>27</sup>"Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more, because of the sword that I am sending among you.'<sup>28</sup>"And if they refuse to accept the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: You must drink!<sup>29</sup>For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name, and shall you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'<sup>30</sup>"You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.<sup>31</sup>The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth!<sup>33</sup>"And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. They shall not be lamented, or gathered, or buried; they shall be dung on the surface of the ground.<sup>34</sup>"Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, and roll in ashes, you lords of the flock, for the days of your slaughter and dispersion have come, and you shall fall like a choice vessel.<sup>35</sup>No refuge will remain for the shepherds, nor escape for the lords of the flock.<sup>36</sup>A voice—the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock! For the LORD is laying waste their pasture,<sup>37</sup>and the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Like a lion he has left his lair, for their land has become a waste because of the sword of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim Jeremiah sums up twenty-three years of preaching, and centuries of prophets sent to call Judah to turn: they have not listened, to their own harm (vv. 1-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of preaching, summarised by the prophet himself in one word: unheard.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem: "For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The date is 605 BC, the year Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the power of the age. It is also the year of the scroll in chapter 36. The world has just changed shape, and Jeremiah has been preaching into it for over two decades.

The first year of Nebuchadnezzar. The double date also marks a shift in whose calendar counts. Judah's years are now measured beside Babylon's. In these same years Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem and took the first captives, among them a young man named Daniel; Daniel's own book dates it In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim (Dan 1:1), probably counting the reign the Babylonian way, which did not number a king's first part-year. While Jeremiah preached this sermon, the exile had already begun.

For twenty-three years. He counts the years aloud: twenty-three, from his call (1:2) to this moment, and he sums up the whole period in a single clause: but you have not listened.

No visible result. Twenty-three years of faithful, costly, unpopular work with no visible result. If ministry is measured by response, this is a failed career; the man himself would have said so in chapter 20. What God asked of him was faithfulness, and the record is that he was persistent for as long as it took.

Found faithful. Paul names the only measure that applies to such a ministry: it is required of stewards that they be found faithful (1 Cor 4:2). Not successful, not popular, not effective by any visible count.

Measured by the numbers. We live under dashboards: sales, followers, grades, attendance, steps. The historian Jerry Muller, in The Tyranny of Metrics (2018), argued that when counting becomes the goal, people begin to work for the number rather than for the thing it was meant to measure, and the work itself quietly bends out of shape. Churches feel this as much as companies. By any dashboard, Jeremiah’s ministry was a disaster: twenty-three years, no measurable response. If our worth is our output, a life like his is wasted, and so, in our worst moments, are ours. Scripture uses a different measure, and it is not lower but higher, because it looks at what numbers cannot see. Jesus’ own ministry ended, by the count, with a handful of women at a cross and his friends in hiding. Yet the Father’s verdict on that work was resurrection. Those joined to him are measured by the same kind of judgment, given by grace: Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.quote: You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets, saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever. Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.' Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All his servants the prophets. And he was not alone: God persistently sent prophets, plural, over centuries (7:25). The same word is used of God's sending and of Jeremiah's speaking. Patience is measured here in messengers.

Turn now, every one of you. Here is the entire prophetic message in three sentences: turn, don't serve other gods, and you may stay. The God who planted them in the land kept sending and kept offering, and the offer at the end is almost startling in its simplicity: Then I will do you no harm. It is mercy held out, not a price set. Everything that follows in this chapter was avoidable to the last week.

The message outlived them. And the message outlived the men who ignored it. After the exile, Zechariah opened his ministry by quoting it back to the returning generation: Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, Return from your evil ways and from your evil deeds.' But they did not hear or pay attention to me (Zech 1:4). The sermon Judah refused became the warning its grandchildren were raised on.

To your own harm. The closing phrase names who loses: to your own harm. As in 7:19, those who provoke God hurt themselves, not him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will send for Nebuchadnezzar, my servant, and silence the land's joy (vv. 8-10). The nations will serve Babylon seventy years, and then Babylon itself will be punished (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire that executes the judgment is called God's servant, and is given a term that expires.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words, behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will send for all the tribes of the north. Two phrases carry the teaching of this chapter. The first is I will send for: God summons the invader like a master calling a servant into the room.

Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant. The second is the title: Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant. A pagan emperor who worshipped Marduk, who will burn God's temple, is called God's servant. He does not know it, he does not intend it, and he will be judged for how he does it (v. 12), and he is still the instrument in God's hand.

A hard and necessary doctrine. That is a hard and necessary doctrine. God governs the powers that hurt his people. That does not make their cruelty less guilty, and it does mean history is not out of control.

I will devote them to destruction. One phrase turns the history of the conquest inside out: I will devote them to destruction. The Hebrew word (herem) means handing something over wholly to God, usually for destruction, as a judgment from which no one may profit. It is the language once used of Jericho, the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction (Josh 6:17), the sentence under which Israel took the land. Now it is pronounced over Israel's own land. The people who entered Canaan under that word will leave it under the same word.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp. This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of mirth. The refrain of 7:34 and 16:9 returns with two homely details added: the sound of the hand-mill grinding grain at dawn, and the little oil lamp left burning at night in every house.

The grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp. Those are the sounds and sights of ordinary domestic life: breakfast being made, a light left on. That is what judgment takes away. Not first the palaces and armies, but the kitchen and the lamp.

The fall of the last Babylon. John hears this list again at the fall of the last Babylon, almost item for item: the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more (Rev 18:22-23). The judgment Jerusalem suffered becomes the pattern for the judgment of the world city that set itself against God.

Seventy years. And here is the number that shaped the next century of faith: seventy years. It is a sentence with an end date attached. The exile will be long, and most who go will die there, but it is not endless. Daniel was reading this verse in Babylon when he worked out that the time was nearly up and began to pray (Dan 9:2). The Chronicler says the land kept its Sabbaths to fulfill seventy years (2 Chr 36:21).

A night with an end. God times his judgments, and he does not forget the people under them. For anyone in a season that seems to have no end, that is something to hold on to: the One who set the length of the night has also set the morning.

How are the seventy years counted? The dates are approximate, and careful readers count in more than one way. From Babylon’s rise to power over the region (about 609–605 BC) to its fall to Cyrus in 539 BC is roughly seventy years, which fits the wording here: these nations shall serve the king of Babylon. From the first deportation (605 BC) to the first return (about 538 BC) is nearer sixty-seven. From the temple’s burning (586 BC) to its rebuilding (516 BC) is almost exactly seventy (cf. Zech 1:12). Seventy is also the span of a human life (Ps 90:10), so the number may be partly a round one: long enough that most who went would not come back.

Seventy weeks. Daniel’s prayer over this number was answered by stretching it: Seventy weeks of years, leading to an anointed one (Dan 9:24–26). Many Christians have seen there the coming of Christ, who brought the deeper return from exile that Babylon’s fall only began. The details of that prophecy are debated; its direction is not.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler ties the seventy years to the Sabbath years the land had been denied (2 Chr 36:21), echoing the warning of Leviticus 26:34-35.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste. I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will punish the king of Babylon. The servant is judged too. Babylon's brutality was real brutality, freely chosen, and being useful to God's purposes is no defence. No one gets to plead that he was only the rod in God’s hand; he answers for the blows he chose to strike. The point is already made in 10:25 and worked out at length in chapters 50 and 51.

Everything written in this book. Here is a glimpse of the book itself: there is a written collection, and God treats what is written in it as what he will do. The scroll is not a record of opinions but a list of what God has decided.

Against all the nations. And the phrase which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations points forward within this very book. The oracles against Egypt, Moab, Edom, Babylon and the rest stand gathered near its end, and verse 13 treats them as already on file.

A note on the text. The ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah (the Septuagint, made by Jewish scholars before Christ) is about an eighth shorter than the Hebrew (the Masoretic Text, the form behind our English Bibles), and it places the oracles against the nations right here, after verse 13, rather than near the end of the book (chapters 46–51). Fragments of both forms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so Jeremiah’s words seem to have circulated in a shorter and a fuller edition, perhaps reflecting the prophet’s own reworking with Baruch (36:32 says many similar words were added). The message is the same in both; English Bibles follow the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
According to their deeds. The phrase that has run through the book about Judah, repaid according to the work of their hands, is now applied to the empire. God uses one standard, and Paul states it as the rule of the final judgment: He will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6).

Many nations and great kings. And it happened as described. On the night Babylon fell, the writing on the wall was read to its king: your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians (Dan 5:28). The empire that enslaved nations was handed to others by the same God who had handed nations to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–29 — The Cup of the Wine of Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah carries the cup of the wine of wrath to the nations: Jerusalem first, then the kingdoms around, and Babylon last (vv. 15-26). None may refuse it, for disaster begins at the city called by God's name (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: God's own city drinks first, which settles for ever the question of whether he judges by favouritism.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This cup of the wine of wrath. A new vision, and an image with a long future in Scripture. The picture works because everyone knows what strong drink does: it takes away balance, judgment and dignity, and the drinker cannot stop what happens next. The wrath of God is pictured not as a fit of temper but as a measured draught that a nation must drink to the bottom.

The cup through Scripture. The image runs through Scripture. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps 75:8). Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem having drunk the cup of staggering (Isa 51:17). Habakkuk warns Babylon that The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you (Hab 2:16). Revelation says the worshippers of the beast will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger (Rev 14:10).

Let this cup pass from me. And then, in a garden, a man knelt and prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). He knew exactly which cup it was, and he drank it to the dregs so that his people would never have to.

verseByVerse.quote: So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. The order of the list is itself the message. Jerusalem drinks first: not Egypt, not Babylon, but the city with the temple in it.

To his own city first. The prophet had to carry the cup to his own city first, to his neighbours, his relatives, the king he served under, and there is no sign that he took any pleasure in it. The man who wept over Jerusalem was the one told to hand it the cup.

verseByVerse.quote: Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people, and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod); Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon; all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea; Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair; all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert; all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media; all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Babylon shall drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations in rings. The list moves outward in rings from Judah: Egypt to the south, the Philistine cities on the coast, Israel’s relatives east of the Jordan (Edom, Moab and Ammon), the Phoenician ports, the desert tribes, the eastern empires, and it ends with all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth.

Babylon comes last. Babylon comes last. The Hebrew calls it Sheshach, a code name; at the height of its power, its name is written in cipher and placed at the end of the queue.

The land of Uz. Two names in the middle of the list stand out. The land of Uz is where Job lived (Job 1:1): the land of the righteous sufferer is under the same cup. And all who cut the corners of their hair are desert peoples marked by a custom Israel was forbidden (Lev 19:27). No culture, no region and no religion is outside the reach of this sentence. Paul's summary is the same: so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God (Rom 3:19).
verseByVerse.note: Sheshach is formed by an ancient letter cipher that swaps the alphabet end for end, so that the consonants of Babel become those of Sheshach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more, because of the sword that I am sending among you.' "And if they refuse to accept the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: You must drink!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drink, be drunk and vomit. The language is deliberately undignified, and Scripture strips the glamour off power like this on purpose. Empires that considered themselves eternal are pictured as a drunk in the street, sick, on the ground, unable to get up. The kingdoms whose armies emptied cities end the verse in their own vomit.

You must drink! Refusal is anticipated and overruled. Nobody escapes God's judgment by declining to acknowledge it, any more than a man escapes a court by refusing the summons.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name, and shall you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the city that is called by my name. Here is the logic of the whole chapter, and it runs the way people least expect: privilege brings judgment first. God begins at the city that is called by my name. If he does not spare the place where he put his own name, on what basis would anyone else be spared?

Judgment begins at home. Amos said it: You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you (Amos 3:2). Peter says it to the church: it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? (1 Pet 4:17).

Responsibility, not immunity. Closeness to God is not immunity. It is responsibility, and it means the searchlight starts at home.

Mercy begins there too. And the argument is also the church's hope, read the other way. If judgment begins at God's house, so does mercy. The one who drank the cup did it outside the walls of that same city, and it is from Jerusalem that forgiveness was first preached to the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–38 — The LORD Will Roar from on High
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God roars from on high and brings an indictment against all flesh (vv. 30-31). Disaster spreads from nation to nation and the slain lie unburied (vv. 32-33), and the shepherds are told to wail, for no refuge remains and the peaceful folds are laid waste (vv. 34-38).
verseByVerse.theology: The local catastrophe opens out into a universal one: God has a case against the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: "You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth. The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD will roar from on high. Two sounds. The first is a lion's roar, which is how prophets describe God going out to judgment. The second is stranger and more chilling: the shout of men treading grapes.

Like those who tread grapes. A winepress shout was a work song, the noise of a harvest celebration. God is pictured shouting it over the nations, and what is being crushed is not fruit. Revelation takes the same image to its end: the angel gathers the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God (Rev 14:19).

Amos’s roar. The roar itself is borrowed from one of the earliest of the writing prophets. Amos opened his book with it: The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn (Amos 1:2). The same voice that went out from Zion against the nations now roars first against his fold, and the shepherds' pastures mourn again at the end of this chapter.

The LORD has an indictment against the nations. Then comes a legal word: God has an indictment, a case with charges. This is not rage; it is a court sitting, and the defendant is all flesh. Everything local in the book, a small kingdom, a siege, a temple, opens here into something universal. The God of Judah is the judge of the world.

With all flesh. Isaiah uses the same courtroom language for the last day: by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many (Isa 66:16). What Jeremiah announces over the nations of his day is a foretaste of that final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth! "And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. They shall not be lamented, or gathered, or buried; they shall be dung on the surface of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disaster is going forth from nation to nation. Disaster spreads like weather, moving from country to country.

They shall not be lamented. The phrase from 8:2 and 16:4 returns, now on a global scale, and with the same three denials: no mourning, no gathering, no burial. The Bible refuses to make judgment sound tidy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, and roll in ashes, you lords of the flock, for the days of your slaughter and dispersion have come, and you shall fall like a choice vessel. No refuge will remain for the shepherds, nor escape for the lords of the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wail, you shepherds. The shepherds are back, the leaders of chapter 23, and now they are told to mourn for themselves. Roll in ashes is the grief of people with nothing left.

You shall fall like a choice vessel. And the comparison recalls the broken flask of chapter 19: you shall fall like a choice vessel. Not a cheap pot, but a good one, the sort a household is proud of. It shatters exactly the same way. Those who had refuges and escape routes, position, money and foreign contacts, find they have run out.

I will rescue my sheep. Ezekiel heard God say the same thing to the same class of men, and add a promise: Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hand, and I will rescue my sheep from their mouths (Ezek 34:10). When the shepherds fall, the sheep are not abandoned. God takes the flock back into his own hands, and later in the same chapter of Ezekiel he promises to set over it one shepherd, his servant David (Ezek 34:23).

verseByVerse.quote: A voice—the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock! For the LORD is laying waste their pasture, and the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the LORD. Like a lion he has left his lair, for their land has become a waste because of the sword of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peaceful folds are devastated. You can hear it before you see it: a voice, a cry, a wail. And what is destroyed is described with an aching phrase, the peaceful folds, the quiet places where sheep were safe. The lion is out of the thicket, as in 4:7, and two causes are named in one breath: the sword of the oppressor and his fierce anger. A human army and God’s anger are at work in the one event, which is how this whole book reads history.

A shepherd who stood between. The chapter ends with shepherds who have no refuge and a flock with no fold. The gospel's answer is not that the roar was empty, but that it fell on a shepherd who stood between it and the sheep: The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

25.title: Seventy Years and the Cup of Wrath
25.overview:
In 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah sums up twenty-three years of preaching and centuries of prophets: the call was always to turn, and Judah did not listen (vv. 1-7).

So God will send for Nebuchadnezzar, whom he calls my servant. The land's joy will fall silent and the nations will serve Babylon seventy years, after which Babylon itself will be repaid (vv. 8-14).

Then Jeremiah is handed the cup of the wine of wrath for all the nations. Jerusalem drinks first, the surrounding kingdoms after it, and Babylon last; none may refuse, for judgment begins at the city called by God's name (vv. 15-29).

Finally God roars from on high and brings an indictment against all flesh, and the shepherds are told to wail, for no refuge remains (vv. 30-38).
25.theology:
The chapter holds together three truths that people find hard to keep together. God governs even the empires that punish his people, and still holds them answerable for their cruelty (vv. 9, 12-14). His judgments are timed and limited, which gave the exiles something to hold on to (v. 11). And judgment begins with those nearest to him (v. 29), because nearness to God is responsibility, not immunity.

Over all of it stands the cup of wrath (vv. 15-28), the cup that Christ asked might pass from him in Gethsemane and then drank for his people.
25.examples:
A minister whose life's work looks fruitless may take heart from a prophet whose twenty-three years were summed up as unheard, and who was still counted faithful.

Judgment, in this chapter, takes away first not palaces but the millstone at dawn and the lamp at night; and the cup handed round the nations is the one Christ accepted in Gethsemane and drained at the cross.
