And all the people gathered around Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>When the officials of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king's house to the house of the LORD and took their seat in the entry of the New Gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Then the priests and the prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."<sup>12</sup>Then Jeremiah spoke to all the officials and all the people, saying, "The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words you have heard.<sup>13</sup>Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you.<sup>14</sup>But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you.<sup>15</sup>Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants, for in truth the LORD sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears."<sup>16</sup>Then the officials and all the people said to the priests and the prophets, "This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God."<sup>17</sup>And certain of the elders of the land arose and spoke to all the assembled people, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said to all the people of Judah: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "'Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.'<sup>19</sup>Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the LORD and entreat the favor of the LORD, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster that he had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves."<sup>20</sup>There was another man who prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land in words like those of Jeremiah.<sup>21</sup>And when King Jehoiakim, with all his warriors and all the officials, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah heard of it, he was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt.<sup>22</sup>Then King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt certain men, Elnathan the son of Achbor and others with him,<sup>23</sup>and they took Uriah from Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, who struck him down with the sword and dumped his dead body into the burial place of the common people.<sup>24</sup>But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Do Not Hold Back a Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign God sends Jeremiah to preach in the temple court without holding back a word (vv. 1-2). The aim is mercy, that they may turn and God relent (v. 3); if they will not listen, this house will become like Shiloh (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The sermon that could save them is the sermon that will cost the preacher his life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD: Stand in the court of the LORD's house, and speak to all the cities of Judah that come to worship in the house of the LORD all the words that I command you to speak to them; do not hold back a word. It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim. The date, about 609 BC, tells you how tense the moment was. Josiah is dead, killed at Megiddo, and his son Jehoiakim is on the throne. The reform that had cleaned out the shrines is unravelling, and the men who ran it are still in post. Jeremiah is sent into the middle of that: into the temple courtyard, at the season when the worshippers of every town in Judah are streaming in.

Do not hold back a word. Then comes the clause that makes the whole chapter dangerous: do not hold back a word. God knows exactly which sentences his preacher will want to leave out. There is always a way to give a congregation ninety percent of a message and keep the ten percent that would cost something, and nobody is told what was cut. The hard line simply does not get said.

It may be they will listen. And here is why the words must not be trimmed. The sermon is not a formality before a verdict already decided; it is God's own attempt to avoid the verdict. It may be they will listen: the offer is real, on the terms God laid down at the potter’s house, that the moment a nation turns, God relents of the disaster (18:7-8). The trimmed sermon is the cruel one, because it withholds the very warning that could have saved them.

Does God change his mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jer 18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.
verseByVerse.note: This chapter tells what happened after the temple sermon recorded in chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law that I have set before you, and to listen to the words of my servants the prophets whom I send to you urgently, though you have not listened, then I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse for all the nations of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will make this house like Shiloh. One word does all the damage in this sermon, and it is a place name.

What Shiloh was. Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations: Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first (7:12). It was not a rival sanctuary or a pagan site. It was the address God himself had chosen. Then Israel carried the ark into battle as a lucky charm, and the day ended with thirty thousand dead and the news that the ark of God was captured (1 Sam 4:11). A dying woman named her baby Ichabod and said The glory has departed from Israel (1 Sam 4:22). By Jeremiah's day Shiloh was a ruin people could walk to and look at.

Not weak, but free. So the claim is not that God is weak but that God is free. He is not a tenant of any building, and he has already once let his own house be levelled rather than let his name be used as a charm by people who would not obey him.

A curse for all the nations of the earth. The promise to Abraham is reversed as well. Jerusalem was to be the place through which the nations were blessed; now it becomes a curse for all the nations of the earth. Privilege abused does not merely lose its blessing. It turns into a curse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — You Shall Die: The Prophet on Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests, prophets and people seize him with a death sentence, and the officials convene a court in the New Gate (vv. 7-11). Jeremiah retracts nothing, renews the offer of mercy, puts himself in their hands, and warns them of innocent blood (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers a death sentence by offering his judges the mercy they are refusing.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the LORD. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the LORD had commanded him to speak to all the people, then the priests and the prophets and all the people laid hold of him, saying, "You shall die! Why have you prophesied in the name of the LORD, saying, 'This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate, without inhabitant'?" And all the people gathered around Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall die! He held nothing back, and the sentence came before he was off the step.

The priests and the prophets. Consider who seizes him. Not the idolaters, not a political faction, not the street mob, but the priests and the prophets: the clergy. Men whose professional existence was bound up with the building he had just said could fall, standing inside that building, laid hands on the man God had sent to them. Nothing in this scene is irreligious. It is a religious riot.

They quote him correctly. They quote him correctly. That detail matters, because it removes the usual excuse. This was not a misunderstanding to be cleared up with a better explanation; they had heard him exactly and they wanted him dead for what he had actually said. Offence at the message is not always a failure of communication.

Another trial. Six centuries later two witnesses would stand in another trial and repeat another saying about the temple: I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days (Matt 26:61). A word against the house is the charge that gets a prophet killed in this city.

verseByVerse.quote: When the officials of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king's house to the house of the LORD and took their seat in the entry of the New Gate of the house of the LORD. Then the priests and the prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the officials of Judah heard. The lynching becomes a trial. The civil officials walk up from the palace, take their seats in the gateway where legal cases were heard, and the mob has to turn into a prosecution. That is a mercy in itself, and it arrives in an ordinary way: God protects his servant here through ordinary civic procedure, men doing their jobs properly.

As you have heard with your own ears. The charge is capital and the evidence is the sermon. As you have heard with your own ears: there is no need for witnesses, because everyone present heard it. The prosecution's whole case is that the defendant said what God told him to say.

No lie needed. Set that beside the other trial. There they were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, and could not find it (Matt 26:59). Jeremiah's judges needed no lies to convict him; Jesus' judges could not convict him without them. Against Jesus, a case had to be invented.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah spoke to all the officials and all the people, saying, "The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words you have heard. Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you. But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you. Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants, for in truth the LORD sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD sent me. His defence opens by repeating the offence. There is no softening and no plea that he had been quoted out of context; he says it again, in front of the court, with his life at stake.

Mend your ways and your deeds. And then, astonishingly, he preaches to them. The men conducting his capital trial are offered the way out. He is not fighting for an acquittal; he is still doing the job he was arrested for. A man with nothing left to protect can afford to love his judges.

Behold, I am in your hands. There is no bargaining here and no bravado either. He does not threaten them with God, and he does not plead. He simply puts himself in their hands: Do with me as seems good and right to you. That kind of composure is not a matter of temperament; it comes from being certain who actually sent him. Christ promised the same help to his witnesses on trial: the Spirit of their Father would speak through them (Matt 10:19-20).

Innocent blood. Even the warning is for their sake, not his. And it is the warning about innocent blood that another court would one day hear and wave away. A governor washed his hands and said I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves, and the answer came back, His blood be on us and on our children! (Matt 27:24-25). Jeremiah's judges took the warning and lived. The others took the blood, and the mercy of God is that the blood they called down on themselves is the only blood in the world that could wash them. That is precisely what Peter preached to that city seven weeks later, at Pentecost (Acts 2:36-38).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The officials and people acquit him, because he has spoken in the LORD's name (v. 16). The elders recall Micah, who said the same of Zion a century earlier, and Hezekiah, who sought the LORD instead of killing him (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone in the room had read the prophets and could remember how a king ought to answer one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials and all the people said to the priests and the prophets, "This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God." And certain of the elders of the land arose and spoke to all the assembled people, saying, "Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said to all the people of Judah: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "'Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.' Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the LORD and entreat the favor of the LORD, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster that he had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man does not deserve the sentence of death. The verdict turns on one test, and it is the right one: has he spoken in the name of the LORD? Not whether he is popular, not whether the message is good for morale, not whether the city's confidence will survive it.

Micah of Moresheth prophesied. The elders save his life with a quotation. A hundred years earlier a country prophet from Moresheth had said this same unthinkable thing about this same city, and the words were still on record; we can still read them at Micah 3:12. Someone in that assembly knew his Bible well enough to recognise that the intolerable sermon had a precedent.

The verse before it. What they may not have quoted is the verse just before it, where Micah names the confidence he was demolishing: Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us (Mic 3:11). That was the belief in the room in Jeremiah's day too. It had not learned a thing in a century.

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Three questions and a conclusion, and the conclusion applies the old case to the hearers. Hezekiah heard his city sentenced to rubble and responded by seeking God's face, and the city stood. Kill this preacher, the elders say, and the disaster we are trying to avoid is one we will have brought on ourselves.
verseByVerse.note: It is rare for one prophet to be quoted by name in another prophet's book; here a sermon from Micah 3:12 saves a man's life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–24 — Uriah, and the Hand of Ahikam
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second precedent cuts the other way. Uriah son of Shemaiah preached the same message, fled to Egypt, and was brought back and killed by Jehoiakim (vv. 20-23). The chapter ends on one man, Ahikam son of Shaphan, whose hand was with Jeremiah (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Two faithful prophets, one buried in a common grave and one spared, and God was not absent from either.

verseByVerse.quote: There was another man who prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land in words like those of Jeremiah. And when King Jehoiakim, with all his warriors and all the officials, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah heard of it, he was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt. Then King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt certain men, Elnathan the son of Achbor and others with him, and they took Uriah from Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, who struck him down with the sword and dumped his dead body into the burial place of the common people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was another man. And now the narrator adds a second case, and it does not comfort anybody.

He was afraid and fled. Uriah preached the same message and ran for his life. It is hard not to feel the sympathy in the telling: he was afraid is not written as an accusation. Jeremiah himself had begged God to let him stop (20:9), and the man who never bolted had no room to despise the man who did.

King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt. The king sent men to Egypt to bring him back, had Uriah executed, and threw his body into the common burial ground. Jehoiakim would not spend an hour listening to a prophet, but he would fund an expedition to silence one. He could reach into Egypt because Pharaoh Neco had put him on the throne (2 Kgs 23:34); a vassal king could probably ask his overlord to hand back a fugitive.

Why this paragraph is here. Why is this paragraph in the chapter at all? Because the Bible refuses to sell faithfulness as a survival strategy. Two men preached the same word from the same God in the same decade. One was acquitted and one was murdered, and the difference was not the quality of their obedience. Some escaped the edge of the sword and some were killed by it, and Hebrews 11 puts both in the same chapter of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the hand of Ahikam. One verse, one name, and the prophet lives.

Ahikam the son of Shaphan. Ahikam was a son of Shaphan the scribe, the man who had read the rediscovered book of the law aloud to Josiah and watched the king tear his clothes (2 Kgs 22). This family keeps appearing at the turning points of the story, on the right side each time, and Ahikam's own son Gedaliah will one day be the governor who shelters Jeremiah after the city falls. Generations of quiet faithfulness turn out to hold up a great deal.

God’s care through human hands. The verse does not say that God protected Jeremiah, though he did. It says the hand of Ahikam was with him. God’s care in this chapter works through human hands: officials who convened a proper court, elders who remembered a text, and one man with standing who used it. God's care for his servants is very often somebody's decision to stand next to them when it is expensive. That role is open to any believer: to stand beside the pastor under attack, the colleague who told the truth, the Christian on trial for his faith, and to spend whatever standing we have for them. We do it as people for whom Christ stood when it cost him everything.

Not given over to the people. And there the chapter leaves a shadow across the page. Jeremiah was not given over to the people to be put to death. Another prophet stood in that same temple, said that same kind of word about that same house, and was tried by that same court, and when the moment came there was no Ahikam. The officials did not acquit him, no elder rose with a precedent, and his own people asked for a murderer instead. He was given over. The high priest had already explained the arithmetic, truer than he knew: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (John 11:50). Jeremiah was spared by a friendly hand; Jesus was handed over by his Father's (Acts 2:23; Rom 8:32), and that is why anyone reading this has a hope beyond a fair trial.
verseByVerse.note: Ahikam's son Gedaliah, and Jeremiah's shelter with him after the fall of the city, appear in chapters 39 to 41.

26.title: The Trial of Jeremiah
26.overview:
At the start of Jehoiakim's reign God sends Jeremiah into the temple court with one condition: he must not hold back a word. If the people will not listen, this house will become like Shiloh (vv. 1-6).

The priests and prophets seize him with a death sentence, and the officials convene a court in the New Gate. Jeremiah retracts nothing, offers his judges mercy and warns them of innocent blood; they acquit him, and the elders back the verdict by recalling Micah and Hezekiah (vv. 7-19).

A darker precedent follows: Uriah preached the same word and was hunted down and killed. Jeremiah survives because the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with him (vv. 20-24).
26.theology:
The warning is the mercy: God sends the sermon so that he may relent, which is why no word may be held back (vv. 2-3). And he is not the tenant of his own house; Shiloh proves he will let a sanctuary fall rather than be used as a charm (v. 6).

Opposition to God's word is often religious, sincere and accurate in what it quotes (vv. 8-9). Faithfulness is not a survival strategy: Uriah and Jeremiah preached the same word, and only one was spared (vv. 20-24).

The whole trial foreshadows another in the same city, the trial of Jesus, where no friendly hand intervened.
26.examples:
Any preacher knows the temptation to give a congregation the ninety percent of a message that costs nothing. This chapter shows what the other ten percent can cost, and why it must still be said.

It also shows how God usually protects his servants: through officials who keep proper procedure, an elder who remembers his Bible, and one person with standing who decides to stand next to you when it is expensive.

27.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Thus the LORD said to me: "Make yourself straps and yoke-bars, and put them on your neck.<sup>3</sup>Send word to the king of Edom, the king of Moab, the king of the sons of Ammon, the king of Tyre, and the king of Sidon by the hand of the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.<sup>4</sup>Give them this charge for their masters: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: This is what you shall say to your masters:<sup>5</sup>"It is I who by my great power and my outstretched arm have made the earth, with the men and animals that are on the earth, and I give it to whomever it seems right to me.<sup>6</sup>Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, my servant, and I have given him also the beasts of the field to serve him.<sup>7</sup>All the nations shall serve him and his son and his grandson, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings shall make him their slave.<sup>8</sup>"'"But if any nation or kingdom will not serve this Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, declares the LORD, until I have consumed it by his hand.<sup>9</sup>So do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your dreamers, your fortune-tellers, or your sorcerers, who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.'<sup>10</sup>For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you, with the result that you will be removed far from your land, and I will drive you out, and you will perish.<sup>11</sup>But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land, to work it and dwell there, declares the LORD."'"<sup>12</sup>To Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke in like manner: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live.<sup>13</sup>Why will you and your people die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning any nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?<sup>14</sup>Do not listen to the words of the prophets who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you.<sup>15</sup>I have not sent them, declares the LORD, but they are prophesying falsely in my name, with the result that I will drive you out and you will perish, you and the prophets who are prophesying to you."<sup>16</sup>Then I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who are prophesying to you, saying, 'Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you.<sup>17</sup>Do not listen to them; serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a desolation?<sup>18</sup>If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts, that the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem may not go to Babylon.<sup>19</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,<sup>20</sup>which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take away, when he took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem—<sup>21</sup>thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem:<sup>22</sup>They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Straps, Yoke-Bars, and the Owner of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Early in Zedekiah's reign Jeremiah puts a yoke on his neck and sends a message home with the envoys of five neighbouring kings (vv. 1-3). The God who made the earth gives it to whom he pleases, and he has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, my servant, until Babylon's own time comes (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire everyone was plotting against is on a lease, and the landlord is the one who made the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD. Thus the LORD said to me: "Make yourself straps and yoke-bars, and put them on your neck. Send word to the king of Edom, the king of Moab, the king of the sons of Ammon, the king of Tyre, and the king of Sidon by the hand of the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Zedekiah is Babylon's appointee, put on the throne after Jeconiah was carried off, and the small nations around Judah are already testing whether a coalition could throw the empire off. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “Jehoiakim” here, probably a copyist’s slip carried over from 26:1; a few Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read “Zedekiah”, as the ESV does, and the Greek omits the verse. The scene itself is unmistakably Zedekiah's: his envoys, his court, his crisis (vv. 3, 12; 28:1), in about 594 BC.

Make yourself straps and yoke-bars. And God's instruction to Jeremiah is to get dressed. He is not to write a letter but to build a wooden yoke, the double bar that goes over an ox's neck with leather straps to hold it, and to wear it. Jeremiah walks the streets of Jerusalem harnessed like an ox.

A message you can see. He has done this kind of thing before: the ruined loincloth (13:1-11) and the smashed flask (19:1-13). A message you can see is harder to forget and harder to argue with, and this one puts the humiliation on the messenger first. Before he asks five kings to accept a yoke, he carries one himself.

By the hand of the envoys. The postal arrangements are ironic. The ambassadors have gathered in Jerusalem to organise a revolt, and God uses the conspirators' own delegation to carry his instruction home to their masters. The summit called to plan resistance leaves with a word from the God of Israel in its diplomatic bag.
verseByVerse.note: The yoke stayed on Jeremiah's neck for some time: in 28:10 he is still wearing it when Hananiah breaks it.

verseByVerse.quote: Give them this charge for their masters: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: This is what you shall say to your masters: "It is I who by my great power and my outstretched arm have made the earth, with the men and animals that are on the earth, and I give it to whomever it seems right to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation first. Before a word about politics, a word about creation. These are pagan courts with their own gods, and the God of Israel does not open by arguing his case or asking for a hearing. He states who made the ground they are standing on.

Ownership follows from making. The logic is simple enough that it cannot be evaded. Ownership follows from making. The one who made the earth, and everything walking about on it, is the one entitled to say who holds which part of it: I give it to whomever it seems right to me. Nothing in that sentence submits itself to a vote.

My great power and my outstretched arm. The phrase is exodus language, the vocabulary of the night Israel came out of Egypt. It is being used here about the God of a small defeated country, addressed to the superpowers of the region. And Nebuchadnezzar himself would eventually be brought to confess it, after hearing that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (Dan 4:25, 34-35).

No authority except from God. Paul draws the line that reaches to every government since: there is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1). No regime, however it came to power and however it behaves, is holding anything it was not handed.

Must Christians submit to any government? Judah was told to submit to Babylon because God had given Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom. Christians are to honour and obey rulers (Rom 13:1–7), but never to obey a command to sin: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), as Daniel and his friends showed under the same Babylon (Dan 3; 6).

verseByVerse.quote: Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, my servant, and I have given him also the beasts of the field to serve him. All the nations shall serve him and his son and his grandson, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings shall make him their slave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My servant. Two words in that sentence would have stopped the room: my servant.

A title for Moses and David. The title belongs to Moses, to David, to the prophets. It is now given to an idolatrous Babylonian king who worships Marduk, has no interest in the God of Israel, and will burn his temple. He is not called righteous and he is not called godly; he is called useful. God uses men who do not know they are being used, and he still calls them to account afterwards. This is the second time the book has said it (25:9), and the shock has not worn off.

Until the time of his own land comes. And now the time limit is read out: three generations, and then Babylon's own turn to be conquered, when many nations and great kings shall make him their slave. The empire that looks permanent has an expiry date already written into the message announcing its power.

The double comfort. That is the double comfort of this chapter for anyone living under something they cannot change. The power over you is real, and it is temporary, and both of those facts are God's doing. To submit to it is not to say that it has the last word. It is to say that God has.

Who are the son and grandson? Nebuchadnezzar’s son Evil-merodach succeeded him (52:31), and after a few short reigns Babylon fell in 539 BC under Nabonidus and his son Belshazzar, who reigned alongside him (Dan 5). They were probably not Nebuchadnezzar’s descendants by blood, though Daniel 5 calls him Belshazzar’s “father” in the ancient sense of predecessor. The phrase most likely means a span of about three generations, and Babylon’s empire did not outlast it: it fell some sixty-five years after Nebuchadnezzar came to the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The terms are stark: refuse the yoke and face sword, famine and pestilence; bear it and stay on your land, and do not listen to the diviners who say otherwise (vv. 8-11). Zedekiah hears the same terms, and the prophets promising independence are disowned (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Submission is the way to live, and the comforting sermon is the one that kills.

verseByVerse.quote: "'"But if any nation or kingdom will not serve this Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, declares the LORD, until I have consumed it by his hand. So do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your dreamers, your fortune-tellers, or your sorcerers, who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.' For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you, with the result that you will be removed far from your land, and I will drive you out, and you will perish. But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land, to work it and dwell there, declares the LORD."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will punish that nation. The threefold sentence of this book, sword, famine and pestilence, now falls on the nations for a political decision, because the political decision is a religious one. Refusing the yoke means refusing the hand that placed it.

Do not listen to your prophets. Verse 9 lists five kinds of religious professional, and every one of them was predicting what the king wanted to hear. Independence sells. It always has, in every court and every pulpit, and the market for it does not care whether it is true.

The anatomy of a comfortable lie. Trace the chain in that last clause, because it is the anatomy of a comfortable lie: they prophesy, you believe, you resist, you are driven out, you perish. The falsehood does not stay in the sermon. It ends up costing the land and the lives of the people who found it encouraging.

The mercy inside the sentence. And there is the mercy inside the sentence. Accept the yoke and you keep your fields, your house and your ordinary life. That is more than justice required.

verseByVerse.quote: To Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke in like manner: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live. Why will you and your people die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning any nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you. I have not sent them, declares the LORD, but they are prophesying falsely in my name, with the result that I will drive you out and you will perish, you and the prophets who are prophesying to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bring your necks under the yoke. Judah receives the same word as Moab, with no easier terms for being God’s covenant people. Judah has the temple, the promises and the line of David, and the instruction is identical: bend your neck and live.

Why will you and your people die? This is not a taunt; it is the question of a God who does not want this. He asks the king outright why he would choose it, in the tone of a man reasoning with someone about to walk off a cliff.

I have not sent them. The disowning is total: I have not sent them. They were using the name, the formulas and probably the same solemn voice, and the God they invoked had no part in any of it.

You and the prophets. And they go down with their congregation: you and the prophets who are prophesying to you. A preacher who tells people what they want does not escape the wreck he talked them into. Within a chapter one of them, Hananiah, will walk up and snap the yoke off Jeremiah's neck (28:10-11), promising the vessels back inside two years (28:3). He will be dead before the year is out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — The Test of a Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The popular prophets promise that the temple vessels will shortly come back from Babylon (v. 16). Jeremiah answers with a test rather than an argument: if they are prophets, let them pray that the great bronze fittings still in Jerusalem are not taken too (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: A true prophet prays; a false one predicts, and the test is whether he will get on his knees.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who are prophesying to you, saying, 'Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you. Do not listen to them; serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a desolation? If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts, that the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem may not go to Babylon. For thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vessels of the LORD’s house. The popular sermon has found its subject, and it is a good one. Nebuchadnezzar had already taken temple treasure away, first under Jehoiakim, with some of the vessels of the house of God, as Daniel puts it (Dan 1:2), and again with Jeconiah (2 Kgs 24:13). The promise going round Jerusalem was that the gold would be back shortly: restoration without repentance, and soon.

Serve the king of Babylon and live. Once more God pleads and offers life. He is arguing for the city's survival while the popular prophets are the ones marching it toward ruin.

Let them intercede with the LORD of hosts. Here is the test, and it is a beautiful one. If these men really have God's ear, let them use it. Stop forecasting and start praying. Intercession is the work of a true prophet (Abraham for Sodom, Moses on the mountain, Samuel for Israel), and a man who only ever announces good outcomes has never once had to plead for one.

The pillars, the sea, the stands. The inventory is deliberate. The pillars Jachin and Boaz, the great bronze sea and the wheeled stands were the immovable landmarks of Solomon's temple, the things a Jerusalemite would have pointed to as proof that some things never change. Those are the items on the removal list.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — Until the Day When I Visit Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Nebuchadnezzar left behind in 597 BC will be carried to Babylon too, and stay there until the day God visits them; then he will bring them back (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is not that nothing will be lost, but that God knows the day he will come for what is his.

verseByVerse.quote: which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take away, when he took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem— thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall be carried to Babylon. What survived the first deportation will not survive the second. The comfort people had drawn from the leftovers was misplaced; the fact that the pillars were still standing proved only that God’s judgment was not yet finished.

Neither optimism nor despair. And the chapter ends by refusing both of the easy positions. The optimists said the vessels would be home within two years; they were wrong. But the despairing, watching the bronze loaded onto carts, would have said they were gone for good, and they were wrong too.

Until the day when I visit them. God keeps the date himself: until the day when I visit them. Not two years, not never, but his day. And it came. Decades later a Persian king who had never read this page gave the order, and Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem (Ezra 1:7), counted out piece by piece to a prince of Judah. God had told them the bowls were coming back, and the bowls came back.

A yoke taken up. Yet the last word of the chapter is still a yoke on a prophet's shoulders, and that image does not rest until another Prophet takes it up. He told the truth about a temple's fall and was killed for it; he stood before a governor and said what Jeremiah said to the nations: You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above (John 19:11). And having borne the weight that breaks men, he says: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt 11:29). Those are the words of the one who first said Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden (Matt 11:28). Babylon's yoke bought survival in a ruined land. His yoke is easy, his burden is light, and it carries you home.

27.title: The Yoke of Babylon
27.overview:
Early in Zedekiah's reign, with the envoys of five neighbouring kings in Jerusalem to plan a revolt, God tells Jeremiah to wear an ox's yoke and send a message home with those same envoys (vv. 1-3).

The God who made the earth has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar until Babylon's own time comes. Nations that bear the yoke will stay on their land; those that refuse, listening to their prophets and diviners, will perish (vv. 4-11). Zedekiah hears the same terms (vv. 12-15).

To the priests and people Jeremiah answers the popular promise that the temple vessels will soon return: what is left will go too, and God will bring it all back on his own day (vv. 16-22).
27.theology:
God's right over the nations rests on creation: he made the earth and gives it to whom he pleases (v. 5). So a pagan emperor can be called his servant without being called godly, and Babylon's lease has its end written into the same message that announces its power (vv. 6-7).

Even the judgment comes with a way through it: those who accept the yoke stay on their land (v. 11). The false prophet flatters and predicts good things; the true one prays for the people (v. 18). And God keeps the date of his own restoration, neither two years nor never, but the day when he visits (v. 22).
27.examples:
A prophet walks through the city in an ox's harness, and a conspiracy's own ambassadors carry God's message home. The scene is a reminder that no summit or strategy is beyond the reach of God's word.

The test of verse 18 still searches anyone who speaks for God: does he only forecast good outcomes, or does he get on his knees and plead for them?

28.text: <sup>1</sup>In that same year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month of the fourth year, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.<sup>3</sup>Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon.<sup>4</sup>I will also bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon, declares the LORD, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."<sup>5</sup>Then the prophet Jeremiah spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD make the words that you have prophesied come true, and bring back to this place from Babylon the vessels of the house of the LORD, and all the exiles.<sup>7</sup>Yet hear now this word that I speak in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.<sup>8</sup>The prophets who preceded you and me from ancient times prophesied war, famine, and pestilence against many countries and great kingdoms.<sup>9</sup>As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."<sup>10</sup>Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke-bars from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke them.<sup>11</sup>And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two years." But Jeremiah the prophet went his way.<sup>12</sup>Sometime after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke-bars from off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Go, tell Hananiah, 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron.<sup>14</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put upon the neck of all these nations an iron yoke to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, for I have given to him even the beasts of the field.'"<sup>15</sup>And Jeremiah the prophet said to the prophet Hananiah, "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie.<sup>16</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD.'"<sup>17</sup>In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Have Broken the Yoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the temple, before priests and people, Hananiah son of Azzur announces in the LORD's name that Babylon's yoke is broken, and that within two years the vessels, the exiles and King Jeconiah will be back (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Every word of the packaging is correct, and the contents are a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: In that same year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month of the fourth year, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon. I will also bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon, declares the LORD, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that same year. The year is about 594 BC. At the beginning of the reign and the fourth year sound contradictory, but the first phrase probably means the earlier part of Zedekiah's eleven-year reign, as in 27:1; the Greek simply reads “in the fourth year”. The timing helps explain why Hananiah was believed. The Babylonian Chronicle records a revolt inside Babylon itself in 595 to 594 BC, and envoys were in Jerusalem planning a coalition (27:3), so the empire may well have looked shaky.

Hananiah the son of Azzur. Everything about this scene looks official. A named man from a known priestly town stands in the temple, with the clergy and the congregation as his audience, using the full formula: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel. If you were grading the delivery you would give him full marks.

I have broken the yoke. And the content is the exact reverse of what God had just said through the man wearing the yoke. It is not a shading of it or a softer version: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon, spoken in the first person as God's own speech. Two men in one city, both saying “thus says the LORD”, are saying opposite things.

Within two years. The lie is generous. The gold comes home, the deportees come home, the rightful king comes home, and it all happens inside two years, soon enough to plan for but not so soon as to be tested next week. Nothing is asked of anybody. There is no repentance, no change, no turning; simply a reversal handed over by God to people who had earned nothing.

The shape of false comfort. That is the shape false comfort always takes. It offers everything the true word offers, minus the repentance, and on a shorter timetable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Amen, and Yet Hear This Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah's first answer is a prayer that Hananiah were right (vv. 5-6). Then the turn: the prophets of old mostly announced war, so a prophet of peace is proved sent only when his word comes to pass (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who wants the comfortable message to be true, and will not say it is.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the prophet Jeremiah spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD, and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD make the words that you have prophesied come true, and bring back to this place from Babylon the vessels of the house of the LORD, and all the exiles. Yet hear now this word that I speak in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amen! May the LORD do so. Of all the things a man in his position might have said, he says amen.

What kind of man. That one word settles the question of what kind of man Jeremiah was. He had been called a traitor for decades, mocked, beaten, put in the stocks, tried for his life, and when a rival announces that the whole burden is lifted, his first instinct is to wish it were so: May the LORD do so. He takes no relish in the bad news and has no investment in being proved right.

A mark of a true messenger. That is one of the surest marks of a true messenger. A man who enjoys announcing judgment has stopped loving the people he is announcing it to, and his relish already gives a false picture of the God who sent the message. Jeremiah's tears run through this whole book for exactly this reason: he never wanted a word of it to be true.

Yet hear now this word. And then the yet. Wishing the promise were true does not allow him to say that it is. He will say what he wishes were true and then say what is, in public, in front of the same crowd, without pretending the two are the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: The prophets who preceded you and me from ancient times prophesied war, famine, and pestilence against many countries and great kingdoms. As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets who preceded you and me. The argument is historical, and it is disarmingly modest. Jeremiah does not claim a superior experience or a better vision; he points at the record. Look at the men God has actually sent across the centuries, he says, and see what they mostly had to say to comfortable nations. It was not congratulation.

What it does not mean. That does not mean a gloomy message proves a prophet true. Scripture is full of promise, and Jeremiah himself will write chapters 30 to 33. The point is narrower: a message which asks nothing of its hearers and confirms what they already want has very little precedent among the men God commissioned.

When the word of that prophet comes to pass. So the burden of proof is placed on the preacher of peace, and the test is the plain one from the law: when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken (Deut 18:22). Wait and see is not scepticism here; it is obedience to an explicit instruction.

A second test. And the law adds a second test, so that the first is never used alone. A sign can come true and the man still be false, if what he teaches leads you away from God: you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams (Deut 13:3). Fulfilment alone never settles it. A prophet is judged by both tests together, which is why the Lord's own summary is You will recognize them by their fruits (Matt 7:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hananiah answers with theatre, breaking the yoke-bars off Jeremiah's neck, and Jeremiah, with nothing to say, goes his way (vv. 10-11). Later the word comes: the wooden bars have been replaced with iron (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Breaking the sign does not cancel the sentence; it only exchanges wood for iron.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke-bars from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke them. And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two years." But Jeremiah the prophet went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hananiah took the yoke-bars. He does not answer the argument. He performs.

A superb piece of staging. It is a superb piece of staging: walk up to the old man in the harness, snap the bars off his neck in front of the crowd, and let the sound of splitting wood be the sermon. Prophecy with props was a known technique (another court prophet once made for himself horns of iron to promise a king his victory, 1 Kgs 22:11), and it works on a crowd, because people remember an action when they have forgotten an argument.

Jeremiah’s method stolen. And he has stolen Jeremiah's own method. The yoke, the loincloth, the smashed flask were all visual sermons; now the visual sermon is turned against the man who wore it, and the audience goes home having watched Babylon's power break in the temple courtyard.

But Jeremiah the prophet went his way. Then Jeremiah simply went his way. That short phrase teaches as much as anything else here. He does not shout, produce a second yoke, or defend his reputation. He has no word from God about this, so he says nothing about it, and walks out of the temple publicly humiliated.

Silence, not weakness. Silence like that is not weakness; it is the discipline of a man who will not manufacture a message to win an argument. He would rather lose the room than invent a sentence God had not given him, and he is willing to look beaten for as long as God leaves him without an answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Sometime after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke-bars from off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Go, tell Hananiah, 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put upon the neck of all these nations an iron yoke to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, for I have given to him even the beasts of the field.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sometime after. The word came sometime after: not that hour, and not while the crowd was still there to see him vindicated. God's servant had to carry the defeat for a while before he was given anything to say, and the delay was not neglect. Vindication on Hananiah's schedule would have been a smaller thing than vindication on God's.

Bars of iron. Here is the answer, and it is devastatingly brief. The gesture worked: the wood really did break. It simply had no authority over the thing the wood stood for. All Hananiah achieved by snapping the sign was to exchange it for a harder one.

A long-reaching principle. That principle reaches a long way past this courtyard. A word from God is not disarmed by being defied, and sin's consequences are not avoided by defying the warning; they grow heavier.

Your truth and my truth. Two men stand in the same courtyard, both sincere, both saying Thus says the LORD, and saying opposite things. The modern instinct is to call it a draw: he has his truth and Jeremiah has his, and who are we to judge? It sounds humble, and it is often meant kindly. But Babylon did not consult anyone’s truth. The iron yoke came whatever the crowd preferred to believe. Some things are true whether or not we like them, and there is a strange cruelty in a tolerance that will not tell a man the bridge is out. The phrase “my truth” turns truth into a possession, something I hold and you cannot touch. Scripture treats truth as something that holds us, and in the end as someone. Jesus did not say that he had a truth for those who liked it. He said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). That is a hard claim, because it will not go away when it is disbelieved. It is also the best news in the world, because the truth that will not bend is the one who bore the yoke for us.

Even the beasts of the field. The terms of chapter 27 are restated with the metal upgraded, and the closing phrase gives away the scale of the claim. Even the wild animals are assigned. A God who allocates the beasts of the field is not negotiating about the borders of Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — You Have Made This People Trust in a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah tells Hananiah to his face that the LORD has not sent him and pronounces the law's sentence on a presumptuous prophet (vv. 15-16). Two months later Hananiah is dead (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: He had two years to be proved right and was given two months.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jeremiah the prophet said to the prophet Hananiah, "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD.'" In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has not sent you. Two charges, and the second is the graver one. The LORD has not sent you: the man had no commission, whatever he sincerely believed. This is the book's standing verdict on the professionals: I did not send the prophets, yet they ran (23:21).

You have made this people trust in a lie. Then: you have made this people trust in a lie. The damage is not to Jeremiah, and it is not chiefly Hananiah's private guilt. A whole congregation has been persuaded to rest its weight on something that will not hold it, and they will still be resting on it when the Babylonians come. False comfort is not a harmless over-optimism; it is a floor built over a hole. The same book says it of the same trade: they healed the wound lightly, saying Peace, peace, when there was no peace (6:14).

This year you shall die. The sentence is the law's own, written centuries earlier for precisely this case: the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak... that same prophet shall die (Deut 18:20). And the charge is named exactly: not error, not enthusiasm, but rebellion against the LORD. Speaking for God without being sent is treated as an act of war against him.

Should false teachers be put to death today? No. Here God himself carries out the sentence; Jeremiah lays no hand on Hananiah. The church bears no sword: it answers false teaching by refuting it from Scripture, warning, and finally refusing fellowship to those who will not turn (Titus 1:9–11; 3:10; 2 John 10), while praying that God may grant them repentance (2 Tim 2:25).

In the seventh month. The end is told in one flat line. Hananiah had promised two years, and he died in the seventh month, two months after he spoke. The proof Jeremiah had told the crowd to wait for arrived quickly: not the failure of the two-year promise, but the death of the man who made it.

A warning that has not expired. The warning has never expired (there will be false teachers among you, 2 Pet 2:1), and the shape has not changed either: full assurance, no repentance, a short timetable. But beyond the two men in the temple stands a third. Hananiah died because he spoke a word God had not given him. Jesus is the Prophet who spoke nothing except what the Father gave him (John 12:49), who went his way in silence when he was contradicted, and who was put to death all the same. Hananiah died for his own lie; Jesus died for ours, and the iron yoke that our lies keep forging was laid on his shoulders, so that the yoke now offered to us is the one he calls easy.
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon, Hananiah's home town (v. 1), was one of the cities given to the priests, the descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:17).

28.title: Hananiah Breaks the Yoke
28.overview:
In the temple, before priests and people, Hananiah son of Azzur announces in God's name that Babylon's yoke is broken and that within two years the vessels, the exiles and King Jeconiah will be back (vv. 1-4).

Jeremiah answers first with a prayer that it were true, then with a warning: a prophet of peace is proved sent only when his word comes to pass (vv. 5-9). Hananiah breaks the yoke-bars off Jeremiah's neck, and Jeremiah walks away in silence until God gives him the reply: wood has been exchanged for iron (vv. 10-14).

Jeremiah tells Hananiah that the LORD did not send him and that he will die this year. Two months later he is dead (vv. 15-17).
28.theology:
The right words in the right place guarantee nothing: Hananiah has the prophet’s formula, the temple and the confidence, and God did not send him (vv. 1-2, 15). False comfort offers everything the true word offers, minus repentance and on a shorter timetable, and its real victims are the people who rest their weight on it.

The true messenger takes no pleasure in judgment (v. 6), tests every word both by whether it comes true and by whether it is faithful to God (vv. 8-9), and can bear public silence while he waits for God's answer (vv. 11-12). And defiance does not cancel God's decree; it hardens it (v. 13).
28.examples:
Hananiah would get full marks for delivery, and he promised everything restored with nothing asked of anybody. That is still the shape of the most attractive false teaching.

Jeremiah's amen is a model for anyone who must bring hard news: wish with all your heart that the comfortable message were true, and still do not say that it is. And his walk out of the temple, beaten and silent, is a comfort to anyone who must wait for God to answer for them.
