He shall not have anyone living among this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, declares the LORD, for he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah writes to the deportees of 597 BC by a royal delegation (vv. 1-3). God, who says he sent them, tells them to build, plant, marry and multiply, and to seek and pray for the welfare of Babylon (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Settle down in the place of judgment, and pray for the good of the city that carried you off.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders of the exiles, and to the priests, the prophets, and all the people, whom Nebuchadnezzar had taken into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. This was after King Jeconiah and the queen mother, the eunuchs, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metal workers had departed from Jerusalem. The letter was sent by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. It said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophecy by post. This time the word comes as a letter: not a sermon in a courtyard or a sign acted out in the street, but a document written to be carried well over a thousand kilometres by road and read aloud to people the prophet would never see again.

The surviving elders. One word in the address carries a weight of grief: the surviving elders. They are being written to as survivors.

Whom Nebuchadnezzar had taken into exile. These are the deportees of 597 BC, the good figs of chapter 24: the skilled and the well-connected, whose absence gutted the city, now sitting in settlements along the irrigation canals of Babylonia trying to work out what God was doing.

By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan. The postal arrangements matter, because God keeps using them. Zedekiah is sending an official delegation to his overlord, and Jeremiah's letter travels in the state pouch. The embassy’s purpose is not stated; it was probably sent to assure Nebuchadnezzar of Zedekiah’s loyalty, perhaps after the plotting with neighbouring kings in chapter 27, which would date the letter to about 594 BC. One of the couriers is a son of Shaphan, the family whose member Ahikam had saved Jeremiah's life (26:24). A royal errand and a faithful family together carry the word of God into exile, and none of the officials involved had any idea they were doing it.
verseByVerse.note: The other courier, Gemariah son of Hilkiah (v. 3), may have been a son of the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's day (2 Kgs 22:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whom I have sent into exile. Before a single instruction, God corrects the record of who did this. Nebuchadnezzar's army marched them out; God says whom I have sent into exile. The pagan empire was the instrument, and the hand on it was his.

Exile as an assignment. That one clause changes what exile is. If Babylon is an accident of geopolitics, then the exiles are simply unlucky and their only sane response is to wait for better luck. If God sent them, then Babylon is an assignment, and there is something to do there.

Build houses and live in them. These are the most ordinary commands imaginable, and in that setting they are radical. Build a house, not a tent. Plant a garden, which means staying long enough to eat the fruit. Marry, and marry off your children, which means accepting that your grandchildren will be born in Babylon.

Neither false hope nor despair. Every one of those instructions kills a hope the exiles were nursing, namely that this would be over soon. And every one of them rules out the opposite error, despair: refusing to live because life is not what you wanted. God does not tell them to like Babylon. He tells them to live, and to put down roots where God’s providence, not their own choice, has placed them.

Multiply there, and do not decrease. This echoes God’s first command to mankind, Be fruitful and multiply (Gen 1:28). God’s purpose for his people is not put on hold while the exile lasts. It continues in captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the command that nobody could have predicted.

Where I have sent you into exile. Babylon had besieged Jerusalem, stripped the temple, taken their king and marched them across a desert in chains. Psalm 137 is the honest sound of a heart in that city. And into that, God says: work for its good, and pray for it.

The welfare of the city. Welfare means the whole flourishing of a place, its peace and safety and prosperity together. They are not merely to tolerate Babylon or avoid trouble in it, but to seek its good actively, and take its needs to God in prayer.

Pray to the LORD on its behalf. This is the Old Testament seed of a hard command the Lord gives his people, that they love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matt 5:44). It is asked here not of a victorious nation being magnanimous but of prisoners of war, about their captors' capital. No prisoner can produce that love by willpower; it grows from the kindness of the God who says I know the plans I have for you, and for the Christian it is the Spirit's own fruit (Gal 5:22).

In its welfare you will find your welfare. A promise is attached: in its welfare you will find your welfare. God ties their good to the good of the pagan city. There is no separate, sealed-off prosperity for the people of God while the place around them rots.

Christians as exiles. Peter writes to Christians in exactly these terms, as elect exiles of the Dispersion (1 Pet 1:1), sojourners and exiles who are to Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable (1 Pet 2:11-12). The church is not to sulk in the culture or dissolve into it. Our citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20), and for that very reason we seek the welfare of the city we are passing through.

How do I seek the welfare of my city? Start where God has sent you, which may be a town you did not choose or a street you hope to leave. Pray for it by name. Pray for the council, the head teacher, the hospital and the people on your road, as Paul urges prayer for kings and all who are in high positions (1 Tim 2:2). Do your work well. The accounts kept honestly, the lessons prepared, the boiler properly fixed: ordinary work is part of a city’s flourishing. Be a neighbour. Learn names, take in the parcel, sit with the lonely man at the bus stop, turn up to the residents’ meeting. Give beyond the church. Support the food bank or the school reading scheme, not only causes that benefit Christians. Timothy Keller built much of his ministry in New York on this verse, arguing that Christians should neither withdraw from their city nor be absorbed by it, but serve it sacrificially as people with another home. That is what Christ did: he wept over the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41) and suffered outside its gate to make a people his own (Heb 13:12). We seek our city’s welfare because he sought ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Seventy Years, and the Plans I Have for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God disowns the exiles' prophets of a quick return (vv. 8-9). The truth is longer and better: after seventy years he will bring them back, for his plans are for their welfare, and they will seek him and find him (vv. 10-14).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise most of its first readers would die before seeing, and it was still the best news in Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets and your diviners who are among you deceive you, and do not listen to the dreams that they dream, for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you in my name; I did not send them, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your prophets and your diviners who are among you. The false prophets were not left behind in Jerusalem. They were deported too, and they set up shop in the camps with the same product: it will be over soon.

The dreams that they dream. The ESV's note here sharpens the accusation. The Hebrew behind the dreams that they dream reads "your dreams, which you cause to dream": it is the people who cause the prophets to dream what they want to hear. The congregation supplies the longing; the preacher manufactures the vision to match. That is how the trade has always worked.

I did not send them. The verdict of chapters 27 and 28 is now posted to Babylon: I did not send them. Distance changed nothing. Wherever God's people are scattered, someone will be telling them what they want to hear in God's name, and the test does not change either.

Why the lie is cruel. And the cruelty of the comfortable lie shows up clearly here. If you believe the exile is nearly over, you will not build a house, plant a garden or raise a family. You will sit on your luggage for seventy years and waste your one life waiting for a boat that is not coming.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place. For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When seventy years are completed. Here is the number, and it is brutal and kind at once. Seventy years is longer than most of the letter's readers had left. The old men weeping by the canals would die in Babylon; their grandchildren would make the journey home. God does not soften that.

I will visit you. But he sets a limit to it. A sentence with an end is a different thing from a sentence without one, and the God who set the term will keep it: I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise. Decades later Daniel would sit with this very page open, having perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years (Dan 9:2), and begin to pray. And the chronicler records the outcome in the driest possible terms: it happened, to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah (2 Chr 36:21).

For I know the plans I have for you. This verse turns up on mugs and graduation cards, and the setting is a prison camp. It is not a promise that your career will prosper or that the hard thing will be brief. It was given to people whose city had been stripped and whose king was in chains, whose temple would burn within a decade, and who were being told to unpack.

Plans for welfare and not for evil. Which makes it stronger, not weaker. The same English word, welfare, has come back from verse 7, and here the ESV notes it may be read as "peace"; the Hebrew is shalom. God's settled intention toward this people is their whole flourishing, and he is pursuing it through seventy years of Babylon rather than in spite of them. A future and a hope is not the absence of exile. It is God's guarantee that exile is not the end of the story he is telling.

How long is seventy years here? The wording is When seventy years are completed for Babylon: the span of Babylon’s dominion, from its rise over the region about 609–605 BC to its fall in 539 BC, roughly seventy years, with the first exiles going home about 538 BC. The figure is approximate rather than a stopwatch, and it was long enough that most of this letter’s first hearers would not see home again.

Is this promise to me? It was spoken to the exiles in Babylon, promising return after seventy years, not instant ease. But God’s promises are all Yes in Christ (2 Cor 1:20), and his purpose for every believer is good: for those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28), even through exile. So read it in two steps. First, it was a promise to a people, the exiles as a whole, about a national return; it does not promise any one person health, wealth, a career or a quick end to trouble, and many who first heard it died in Babylon still trusting it. Second, in Christ it does reach us: the God who planned welfare for exiles has given us a living hope through the resurrection (1 Pet 1:3), and his plans for us include discipline, suffering and waiting (Rom 8:17–18). The future and the hope are finally God himself and the new creation, not a better year. If you are in a hard place now, this verse does not promise it will end soon; it promises that God has not stopped meaning you good in it.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 10-14 echo Moses' promise to a scattered people in Deuteronomy 30:1-5: when they return to the LORD with all their heart, he will gather them from wherever he has driven them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart. I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore your fortunes and gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, declares the LORD, and I will bring you back to the place from which I sent you into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come and pray to me. Consider how the restoration comes. It comes not through a rebellion, a lobbying campaign or a change in Babylonian politics, but through prayer: a people on their knees in a foreign country, calling on a God whose temple was far away across the desert.

Then you will call upon me. And the order in the sentence matters. God announces what they will do before they do it. The seeking is promised, not demanded, which is the same grace as the heart he pledged to give them in the vision of the figs (24:7): God supplies the very response he requires.

You will seek me and find me. The words come from Moses, spoken over the exile centuries before it happened: you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul (Deut 4:29). And they are taken onto the Lord's own lips in the plainest invitation he ever gave: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matt 7:7).

When you seek me with all your heart. The half-hearted search is the one that fails, and not because it lacks effort. A man who wants God as one item among several has not yet wanted God. Yet no one seeks with a perfectly whole heart, and the promise finally rests on the God who gives the heart and who came in Christ to seek the lost (Luke 19:10). But hear what is actually promised to the whole-hearted: I will be found by you. God is not hiding. The exile was never a matter of his becoming unreachable, and the gathering will reach every place they were scattered to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — The Vile Figs Left Behind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king and the kinsmen still in Jerusalem, whom the exiles envy, face sword, famine and pestilence: they are the vile figs of the two baskets, because they would not listen (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who stayed in Jerusalem kept nothing in the end; the ones in chains were the good figs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because you have said, 'The LORD has raised up prophets for us in Babylon,' thus says the LORD concerning the king who sits on the throne of David, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, behold, I am sending on them sword, famine, and pestilence, and I will make them like vile figs that are so rotten they cannot be eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A comparison in their heads. The exiles had a comparison running in their heads, and it was eating them. Our relatives are still at home, they thought. They have the city, the temple, a son of David on the throne, and prophets telling us we will soon join them.

Your kinsmen who did not go out with you. So God answers the comparison directly, and the phrase your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile names the envy precisely.

Like vile figs. And there is the image from the two baskets, sent to the people who were the good figs in that vision. Jerusalem had been told it face to face (Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, 24:8), and now it is written to Babylon so the exiles can stop envying the wrong people.

A hard comfort. The comfort in it is real, if uncomfortable. The ones who look blessed are not; the ones who lost everything are the objects of God's good intentions. That is a hard message to receive without bitterness, and the letter has already told them how: build, plant, pray for Babylon. Envy dies in a garden you are actually tending.

verseByVerse.quote: I will pursue them with sword, famine, and pestilence, and will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them, because they did not pay attention to my words, declares the LORD, that I persistently sent to you by my servants the prophets, but you would not listen, declares the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will pursue them. The verb is pursue. This is not a disaster they may outrun by staying put, which was the whole basis of their confidence. Judgment follows them into every country it drives them to.

A curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach. They will become a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach, and the tragedy is that this is the nation appointed to make God's name known among those same nations. They will still show the nations something about God, but now it is his judgment and not his blessing.

Because they did not pay attention to my words. The reason is given, and it is not obscure. God is not acting on a whim, and there is no hidden reason to puzzle over: they did not pay attention to my words.

That I persistently sent to you. Weigh the adverb persistently. Decades of prophets were sent again and again to a city that had every chance to listen and used none of them. Judgment in this book always arrives late, after a long patience that has been ignored, and that is why it can be announced without apology.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two named liars in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, will be executed by Nebuchadnezzar and become a curse-word, charged with adultery and with lying in God's name (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: God never judged the private life and the preaching separately.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying a lie to you in my name: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall strike them down before your eyes. Because of them this curse shall be used by all the exiles from Judah in Babylon: "The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire," because they have done an outrageous thing in Israel, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in my name lying words that I did not command them. I am the one who knows, and I am witness, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah. Two men are named. The letter does not deal in generalities about false teaching; it identifies the individuals doing it, because the exiles had to know whose meetings to stop attending.

He shall strike them down before your eyes. Their end is Nebuchadnezzar's doing (he will execute them, probably because preaching a quick return home amounted to stirring up revolt against Babylon), and God claims it as his own sentence carried out by a pagan king who thought he was protecting his empire.

Whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire. Their names end up as a proverb for a horrible death. Burning was a known Babylonian punishment (Hammurabi’s laws prescribe it for several crimes, and Daniel’s friends faced the furnace, Dan 3:6), and the Hebrew carries a grim pun: the word for curse (qelalah) echoes the verb roasted (qalah). Men who had built careers on telling people what they wanted became the byword the same people used when they cursed.

An outrageous thing in Israel. Two charges stand in one sentence, and Scripture will not separate them: adultery with their neighbours' wives, and lying in God's name. The man who is willing to invent a message is the same man who is willing to break a marriage; a life that reshapes God's word to suit itself will use other people to suit itself too.

I am the one who knows, and I am witness. And then the quietest and most searching line in the chapter: I am the one who knows, and I am witness. They had done it where no one saw. Someone saw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shemaiah of Nehelam writes to the priest Zephaniah demanding that Jeremiah be put in the stocks for telling the exiles to settle (vv. 24-28). Zephaniah reads the letter to Jeremiah instead, and Shemaiah is shut out of the good God will do (vv. 29-32).
verseByVerse.theology: He campaigned against the promise of restoration, and was excluded from it.

verseByVerse.quote: To Shemaiah of Nehelam you shall say: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have sent letters in your name to all the people who are in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying, 'The LORD has made you priest instead of Jehoiada the priest, to have charge in the house of the LORD over every madman who prophesies, to put him in the stocks and neck irons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reply over his head. Jeremiah's letter provoked a reply, and the reply went over his head. Shemaiah writes to Jerusalem, to the temple authorities rather than to Jeremiah, to get him silenced.

In your name. The phrase in your name sums up the charge against him. Jeremiah writes in the name of the LORD of hosts; Shemaiah writes in his own, and still expects the weight of God behind it.

Every madman who prophesies. He begins by reminding the priest of his job description, which includes policing anyone who prophesies, and he supplies the label in advance: every madman who prophesies. Call the man unbalanced and you need not answer him. It saves the trouble of weighing whether what he said was true.

The stocks and neck irons. The instruments named are specific, the stocks and neck irons, and Jeremiah had been in the stocks before, at the hands of Pashhur (20:2). Shemaiah knows exactly what he is asking for, and he is asking from a safe distance, in a letter, with his own name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth who is prophesying to you? For he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, "Your exile will be long; build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their produce."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A question meant to shame. The question is designed to shame the priest into acting. Why have you not dealt with him? It is the standard move of a man who wants someone silenced and would rather another hand did it.

Jeremiah of Anathoth. And the address is a sneer: Jeremiah of Anathoth. Not the prophet, not the man God sent, but a villager from a small place, whose own townsmen had once plotted to kill him (11:21). Reduce a man to the village he comes from and you need not reckon with his message.

Plant gardens and eat their produce. Here is the charge sheet, and notice what finally provoked the campaign. It was not a threat or a curse. Shemaiah quotes back, accurately, the gentlest sentences in the letter: build houses, plant gardens.

Your exile will be long. That was the intolerable part. The instruction to settle down implied a long exile, and a long exile destroyed the hope he was selling. Men will forgive a preacher a great deal sooner than they will forgive him for taking away a comfortable expectation, and the offence here is not harshness but realism about how long the trouble will last.

verseByVerse.quote: Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet. Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Send to all the exiles, saying, 'Thus says the LORD concerning Shemaiah of Nehelam: Because Shemaiah had prophesied to you when I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the LORD: Behold, I will punish Shemaiah of Nehelam and his descendants. He shall not have anyone living among this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, declares the LORD, for he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zephaniah the priest read this letter. One sentence holds a whole quiet mercy. The priest who was being urged to put Jeremiah in irons instead took the letter to him and read it to him.

How God protects his prophet. Nothing is said about Zephaniah's motives and he is given no speech. But this is how God has been protecting this prophet all along: Ahikam's hand at the trial, the officials who convened a proper court, and now a temple official who declines to act on a poisonous letter and quietly shows it to the man it targets.

Has made you trust in a lie. The two charges are Hananiah's, in the same words: not sent, and has made you trust in a lie (28:15). The offence is never merely that the man was wrong. It is that people rested their weight on what he said.

I will punish Shemaiah of Nehelam. The sentence fits the crime with terrible precision. Shemaiah campaigned against the letter that promised a future and a hope, and the penalty is that he shall not see the good that I will do to my people. He argued the restoration away, and he is left outside it. The penalty reaches his family too: He shall not have anyone living among this people means that no descendant of his would be among those who came home.

The good that I will do to my people. Yet that sentence assumes something, and it is the last word of the chapter. There is good that I will do to my people. The letter that began by telling prisoners to unpack ends by taking that good for granted as the settled future of this battered congregation. God had sent them into exile and God would visit them there, and the visiting was not finished at Cyrus's decree. When John the Baptist was born, his father sang that God has visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68): the Lord himself came into the far country to seek the welfare of the city that killed him, and prayed for it while it did (Luke 19:41–42; 23:34). Every exile who builds, plants and prays for the place God has put him is living on the strength of that day.

29.title: The Letter to the Exiles
29.overview:
Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem to the deportees of 597 BC, sending the letter with a royal delegation. God, who says he himself sent them into exile, tells them to build, plant, marry and multiply, and to seek and pray for the welfare of Babylon (vv. 1-7).

They must not listen to the prophets promising a quick return. After seventy years God will visit them and bring them home, for his plans for them are for welfare and not for evil, to give them a future and a hope; they will seek him with all their heart and find him (vv. 8-14).

The relatives they envy in Jerusalem are the bad figs of chapter 24 (vv. 15-19). Two lying prophets in Babylon will be executed (vv. 20-23), and Shemaiah, who demands that Jeremiah be silenced, will not see the good God will do for his people (vv. 24-32).
29.theology:
Exile is an assignment, not an accident: because God sent them, Babylon becomes a place with work to do in it (vv. 4, 7). So God's people seek the welfare of the city that holds them and pray for it, which is still the church's calling as exiles in this world.

God's good purpose does not mean no hardship; he firmly intends their good and brings it about through the hardship. The plans for welfare were sent to exiles with seventy years of captivity ahead. And grace comes before their seeking: God announces that they will seek him, and promises to be found (vv. 10-14).

False comfort costs the hearer his life, not just his theology (vv. 8-9), and a man’s preaching and his private life are judged together by the God who is witness to both (v. 23).
29.examples:
Building a house and planting a garden in a place you did not choose is an act of faith: it means accepting God's timetable and refusing both false hope and despair. So is praying for the good of the city that carried you off.

The best-loved verse of the chapter, often printed on mugs and cards, was first posted to a prison camp. Read there, it is not a promise of a better year but of a God who has not stopped meaning his people good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Book, and a Day Like No Other
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Jeremiah to write his words in a book, for days are coming when he will restore Israel and Judah (vv. 1-3). First comes terror, men doubled over like women in labour, a day of distress for Jacob, yet he shall be saved out of it (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The worst day in the story, and the promise of rescue is welded to it in the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. For behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore the fortunes of my people, Israel and Judah, says the LORD, and I will bring them back to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall take possession of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Write in a book. After some forty years of preaching in the open air, Jeremiah is told to write it down.

A change of audience. The instruction marks a change of audience. Spoken words reach the people in front of you; a book reaches the ones who are not born yet. What follows in chapters 30 to 33 is largely promise, and promise needs to outlive the preacher: the generation that would need these pages most was the generation that would read them in Babylon, decades after Jeremiah was dead.

It is also how we have them: a man in a besieged city can speak to the exiles, and to us, because God told him to write it in a book.

Israel and Judah. Note who is included: Israel and Judah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had been gone for well over a century (since 722 BC), deported by Assyria, its people scattered and assumed lost. Judah is about to follow. God names both halves of a broken nation and says he will restore the fortunes of both.

They shall take possession of it. Remember that whenever something seems too far gone. The tribes nobody could find were still on God's list, and the promise is specific: they will come back, and they shall take possession of it, not to visit but to hold.

How is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. But the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. Faithful Christians differ here. This commentary reads the land promises as widening in Christ to the whole renewed earth (Rom 4:13; Matt 5:5), because the New Testament treats them that way; dispensational brothers answer that promises made to Israel by name should be kept to Israel by name, and they deserve a careful hearing. Reformed Christians themselves differ over whether Romans 11:26 foretells a large-scale turning of Jews to Christ before the end, as many Puritans believed, or the full number of the elect from Israel saved through history. On either reading, Jewish people are saved as everyone is, by faith in Jesus their Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and Judah: "Thus says the LORD: We have heard a cry of panic, of terror, and no peace. Ask now, and see, can a man bear a child? Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor? Why has every face turned pale?
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have heard a cry of panic. The Book of Consolation opens with screaming.

No peace. Before any comfort is offered, the trouble is described honestly, and the phrase no peace lands on the exact word the false prophets had been handing out for chapters. They said peace; God reports a cry of panic and terror. Real comfort never begins by understating the situation.

Can a man bear a child? The image is deliberately grotesque, and it is the strongest picture of helplessness available. Soldiers, the men who were supposed to defend the city, are doubled over, hands clutching their bellies, in the posture of a woman in labour. Something is happening to them that they can neither stop nor escape, and they have no more control over it than a man could have over giving birth.

Pain with an outcome. And labour is not an image of pointless agony. It is pain with an outcome, terrible and productive at once, which is precisely what this day will turn out to be for Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob; yet he shall be saved out of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book in one verse. One verse, and the whole book is in it.

That day is so great. Take the halves in order. That day is so great there is none like it: it is beyond anything in the nation's memory, and the prophets use that language for the day of the LORD itself: A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation (Zeph 1:15). The Lord Jesus uses the same kind of language for the end, then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now (Matt 24:21), so this verse looks at Babylon and past it.

A time of distress for Jacob. Then it is a time of distress for Jacob. The name may carry a memory. Jacob and Israel are often paired as two names for the nation (v. 10), but Jacob also recalls the schemer who limped away from a night of wrestling with God. The distress is his, and it is deserved.

Yet he shall be saved out of it. And then the hinge of the chapter, one word: yet. Yet he shall be saved out of it. He is not spared it or diverted around it, but saved out of the middle of it. God does not promise his people an easier day than the one that is coming. He promises that the day will not have the last word on them.

Is “the time of Jacob’s trouble” the future Great Tribulation? Dispensationalists read it so. In context it is the terror of the Babylonian conquest (vv. 5–6), followed by the promise of rescue (vv. 8–9), under David their king, fulfilled in Christ. The Lord himself echoes its language for the last days (Matt 24:21), and faithful readers differ on how far the verse looks beyond Babylon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Fear Not, Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will break the yoke, and his freed people will serve him and David their king (vv. 8-9). So, fear not: he is with them to save, and his discipline will be in just measure, never a full end (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The yoke this book has spent chapters fastening on is broken by the same hand that fastened it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass in that day, declares the LORD of hosts, that I will break his yoke from off your neck, and I will burst your bonds, and foreigners shall no more make a servant of him. But they shall serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will break his yoke from off your neck. The yoke is back: the wood Jeremiah wore through the streets, the iron God said would replace it when Hananiah snapped the bars. Now the hand that put it on takes it off. Hananiah broke a yoke and died for it; God breaks this one himself. The closing clause of verse 8 may also be rendered “serve him”, as the ESV notes. Either way, Israel will no longer be at the disposal of foreign masters.

Rebellion and redemption. That is the whole difference between rebellion and redemption. The same yoke, removed by the wrong hand at the wrong time, is a lie; removed by God in his day, it is salvation.

But they shall serve the LORD their God. Freedom here does not mean serving no one; it means a change of master. They stop serving foreigners and start serving God, and a king.

David their king, whom I will raise up for them. David had been dead nearly four hundred years. The promise is of a David God will raise up, and the other prophets say it in the same terms: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23); the people will seek the LORD their God, and David their king in the latter days (Hos 3:5). Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, sang when it finally happened, that God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).
verseByVerse.note: Ezekiel also calls the coming king simply “David”, and says he will be their prince for ever (Ezek 37:24-25).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, nor be dismayed, O Israel; for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. For I am with you to save you, declares the LORD; I will make a full end of all the nations among whom I scattered you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear not. After the labour pains and the pale faces come two words: fear not.

Jacob my servant. And the title attached is tender: Jacob my servant. This is the nation whose guilt is called great and whose sins are called flagrant a few verses later, addressed by God as his servant. The relationship is not suspended while the discipline runs.

Quiet and ease. The promise is domestic and small-scale, which is what frightened people actually need: quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. It is not empire, and not revenge, but sleep without fear.

I am with you to save you. The ground of the comfort is a person: I am with you to save you. Not better circumstances, not a shorter exile, but his presence.

How do I “fear not”? Fear is not beaten by ordering yourself to stop feeling it. God does not say “fear not” and leave it there; he gives a reason, for I am with you to save you, so take the fear to the reason. Name it. At 2 a.m. tell God exactly what you are afraid of: the scan result, the redundancy letter, the child who will not speak to you. Set a promise against it. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Ps 56:3): the psalm assumes the fear will come, and tells you where to put your weight when it does. Look at the cross, not the odds. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom 8:32). A God who has done that will not abandon you halfway. Do the next faithful thing. Make the phone call, keep the appointment, tell the truth in the meeting. You may meet discipline on the way; you will not meet a full end. In Christ, “I am with you” has a name, and he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5).

Of you I will not make a full end. Then comes a distinction the whole Bible runs on. The nations get a full end; his people do not. The difference is not that Judah sinned less, because the next verses say her guilt is great. The difference is the covenant, God’s own promise binding him to this people.

I will discipline you in just measure. And the last clause refuses to make that soft: I will by no means leave you unpunished. God's people are not exempt from discipline; they are exempt from destruction. In just measure means the chastening is measured by a father, not unleashed by an enemy, and that is the reason sin in a believer's life is dealt with rather than overlooked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — No Healing for You, and I Will Heal You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself pronounces the wound incurable and the blow his own, for great guilt (vv. 12-15). Then, with nothing changed in the patient, he promises to heal it, because her enemies said no one cares for Zion (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the case terminal, and then heals it, for no reason found in the patient.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Your hurt is incurable, and your wound is grievous. There is none to uphold your cause, no medicine for your wound, no healing for you. All your lovers have forgotten you; they care nothing for you; for I have dealt you the blow of an enemy, the punishment of a merciless foe, because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your hurt is incurable. God gives the diagnosis, and it is terminal.

No medicine for your wound, no healing for you. Read the list of what is unavailable: no advocate, no medicine, no healing. Earlier in the book Jeremiah had asked, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22), and here is the answer, spoken by God himself. Nothing in the pharmacy touches this.

Why the diagnosis matters. This is the honesty that makes the gospel possible. Until a man believes his condition is beyond treatment, every offer of grace sounds like an optional extra. Judah's problem was never that she lacked good advice.

All your lovers have forgotten you. The lovers are the allies she courted instead of trusting God: Egypt, Assyria, the alliances that chapter 2 pictures as love affairs. They have moved on, as such lovers do.

I have dealt you the blow of an enemy. And then the hardest sentence: I have dealt you the blow of an enemy. It was not Babylon's blow but God's, delivered with the force of a merciless foe. He does not hide behind the army he used or blame the politics of the day. The reason is stated twice, without embarrassment, because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant, and a God who names the cause is a God who can be reasoned with about a cure.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you cry out over your hurt? Your pain is incurable. Because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant, I have done these things to you. Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your foes, every one of them, shall go into captivity; those who plunder you shall be plundered, and all who prey on you I will make a prey. For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD, because they have called you an outcast: 'It is Zion, for whom no one cares!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you cry out over your hurt? The question has an edge to it. Why cry out, as though this were unjust or unforeseen? She had been told, persistently, for forty years.

Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured. And then therefore, which is the last word anyone would expect after that accusation. By ordinary moral reasoning it does not follow: your guilt is great, your sins are flagrant, therefore your enemies will be destroyed. Nothing in the patient has changed between verse 15 and verse 16.

Those who plunder you shall be plundered. The instruments God used are themselves judged. God used Babylon, and being used by God does not make Babylon innocent, a lesson the empire would learn when its own seventy years ran out.

Your wounds I will heal. The incurable is cured, by the only physician who was ever going to do it. And the stated reason is striking: not her repentance, not her improvement, but the contempt of her enemies. They said nobody cares about Zion. God will not leave that sentence standing about his own people.

How the wound is healed. How he heals a wound he inflicted, without pretending the guilt away, is the question this chapter raises and does not answer. The answer comes from the wounds of another: he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5). The blow of an enemy fell, in the end, on him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — The Prince Who Dares Draw Near
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The city will be rebuilt on its mound, full of thanksgiving (vv. 18-20). Their prince will be one of themselves, brought near by God, when no one would dare approach of himself, and they shall be his people (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: One of their own, brought near by God to do what no one would dare attempt on his own account.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have compassion on his dwellings; the city shall be rebuilt on its mound, and the palace shall stand where it used to be. Out of them shall come songs of thanksgiving, and the voices of those who celebrate. I will multiply them, and they shall not be few; I will make them honored, and they shall not be small.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city shall be rebuilt on its mound. The promise gets specific and unglamorous: tents, dwellings, a city rebuilt on its mound, on the same rubble heap, on the old site. God promises not a better location but this one, restored.

Have compassion on his dwellings. And the word governing it is compassion. The God who dealt the blow of an enemy has compassion on the houses of the people he struck, which is a combination only the cross finally explains.

Songs of thanksgiving. Out of the tents comes singing. The last several chapters have been full of the sound of mourning, lament and the cry of panic; now the noise coming from the ruins is thanksgiving and celebration.

I will multiply them. Both halves of each promise are stated, negative and positive: multiplied and not be few, honoured and not be small. God answers their fear of dwindling away directly. The few who are left, who felt like nothing, are told they will not stay few.

verseByVerse.quote: Their children shall be as they were of old, and their congregation shall be established before me, and I will punish all who oppress them. Their prince shall be one of themselves; their ruler shall come out from their midst; I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me, for who would dare of himself to approach me? declares the LORD. And you shall be my people, and I will be your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their children shall be as they were of old. This promises a restoration that reaches backwards, repairing what the generations had lost, and a congregation established before me, which is to say a worshipping people who can come before God again.

Their prince shall be one of themselves. Here is the summit of the chapter. The ruler will not be a foreign governor but one of their own, and his defining act is not military or administrative. It is priestly: I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me.

Who would dare of himself to approach me? Then God asks a question that stops every religious project in its tracks: who would dare of himself to approach me? Nobody. That is the honest answer, and Israel's whole system of temple curtains and courts, with one entrance a year by the high priest alone, existed to say so. A prince who is both from among the people and able to approach God is a figure the Old Testament keeps sketching and never produces.

He dared, and takes us in with him. Hebrews does not quote this verse, but it names the figure. Since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near (Heb 10:19-22). One of ourselves, brought near by God, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (Heb 7:25). Nobody would dare of himself. He dared, and takes us in with him.

You shall be my people, and I will be your God. Then comes the covenant sentence, the thing all of it was for. It is not real estate or independence but belonging, and it is the sentence still being spoken at the end of the Bible: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God (Rev 21:3).

Why we no longer tremble. Most people today who believe in God at all assume he can be approached on any terms: warm, informal and above all safe. The question who would dare? sounds like a relic of a more fearful age. Yet the age that lost the fear of God has hardly lost fear; it has moved it onto the economy, the climate and the opinions of strangers. Annie Dillard once wrote that if churchgoers grasped the power they so casually invoke, they would come in crash helmets and the ushers would hand out life preservers. The Bible will not let us have it either way. The moralist approaches God on the strength of his own record, and the casual modern on the strength of God’s niceness, and both assume they have a right to walk in. Nobody has. But the answer is not to stay outside trembling. It is the Prince who dared, and who went in by way of a cross, so that we may now with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16): with confidence, because of him, and still with awe, because our God is a consuming fire (Heb 12:29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–24 — The Storm of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with the storm of the LORD on the wicked, an anger that will not turn back until his purpose is done, understood only in the latter days (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Comfort that has a storm at the end of it is the only kind worth having.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. In the latter days you will understand this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold the storm of the LORD! And after all that comfort, a storm. It reads like an intrusion until you notice what it protects.

Why the storm belongs here. A promise of restoration that quietly dropped the subject of judgment would be a promise that evil simply stops mattering. Instead the chapter that healed an incurable wound insists in its last breath that wrath has gone forth and will burst upon the head of the wicked. The comfort is for people who needed rescuing from something real. The words are almost exactly those of 23:19-20, where the storm was aimed at the prophets who promised peace; repeated here, at the close of a chapter of promises, they mark the difference between God’s comfort and the cheap peace those prophets sold.

Will not turn back. God's anger is not a temper that flares and cools; it is a purpose he carries through: it will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. That is a fearful sentence about the wicked and a steadying one about everything else God intends, since the same resolve stands behind the promises in this chapter.

In the latter days you will understand this. And the last line is a hand on the shoulder of anyone reading too early: In the latter days you will understand this. Not now. The generation holding this book in Babylon would not see how a wound God inflicted could be a wound God heals, or how a prince could walk in where nobody dares. Later, they would. We read it on the far side of a cross, and the storm and the healing turn out to have met in one place.

30.title: Write It in a Book: The Healing of an Incurable Wound
30.overview:
Chapters 30 to 33 are often called the Book of Consolation. God tells Jeremiah to write his words in a book, because days are coming when he will restore Israel and Judah to their land (vv. 1-3).

First the terror is named honestly: a day of distress for Jacob, and yet he will be saved out of it. God will break the yoke, and his people will serve him and David their king; he will discipline them in just measure but never make a full end of them (vv. 4-11).

God calls their wound incurable and the blow his own, and then, with nothing changed in the patient, promises to heal it (vv. 12-17). The city will be rebuilt, a prince from among them will be brought near to God, and they shall be his people (vv. 18-22). The chapter ends with the storm of his wrath on the wicked (vv. 23-24).
30.theology:
God does not promise his people an easier day than the one coming, but that the day will not have the last word (v. 7). Because of his covenant they are exempt from destruction, never from discipline, and the discipline is measured out as a father measures it (v. 11).

He himself declares the wound incurable and then heals it, for the sake of his own honour and not for anything in the patient (vv. 12-17); and the one who will draw near to God for his people is one of themselves, brought near by God (v. 21). The storm at the end guards the healing at the centre: comfort that dropped the subject of wrath would mean evil no longer mattered (vv. 23-24).
30.examples:
The Book of Consolation opens with screaming, and that is a lesson for anyone who comforts the suffering: real comfort never begins by understating the trouble.

For frightened people the promise is small and domestic: not empire or revenge, but quiet, ease and sleep without fear, grounded in a person: I am with you to save you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Loved with an Everlasting Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God grounds the whole chapter in an everlasting love older than Israel's failure (vv. 1-3). So the ruined nation will be built again, with dancing and vineyards, and gathered from the ends of the earth, the weakest among them, by a father and shepherd, until their mourning turns to joy (vv. 4-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything promised here rests on a love that started before the ruin and did not depend on it ending.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, I will be the God of all the clans of Israel, and they shall be my people." Thus says the LORD: "The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness; when Israel sought for rest, the LORD appeared to him from far away. I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the clans of Israel. The chapter opens with the promise the whole Bible is driving at, that God will be their God and they will be his people, and it is made to all the clans: the ten tribes lost to Assyria more than a century before, written off by everyone as gone, included by name.

Found grace in the wilderness. The picture reaches back to the exodus: survivors of the sword, out in the desert, finding grace there. That was the pattern once and it will be the pattern again. God meets his people in the wilderness, not after they have got themselves home.

The LORD appeared to him from far away. The ESV notes that where the main text reads that the LORD appeared to him from far away, following the Septuagint, the Hebrew reads "me". Either way the striking thing stands: God appears, and the distance is crossed from his side.

I have loved you with an everlasting love. Here is the ground of everything that follows in this chapter, and it is not anything in them.

Everlasting. Weigh the word everlasting. A love with no beginning cannot have been started by anything Israel did, and a love with no end cannot be stopped by anything Israel did either. It was not switched on by her obedience in the wilderness and it was not switched off by her adultery in Canaan.

Therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you. And then therefore. His love is the cause and his faithfulness is the result. He keeps on with this people because he loved them first, which is the only explanation the Bible ever gives for why any of us are still here.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin Israel! Again you shall adorn yourself with tambourines and shall go forth in the dance of the merrymakers. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; the planters shall plant and shall enjoy the fruit. For there shall be a day when watchmen will call in the hill country of Ephraim: 'Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again I will build you. Three times in two verses comes the word again: built again, dancing again, planting again. The word is chosen to comfort, because the fear of a ruined people is not that God is unable but that the good days are simply over.

O virgin Israel! And consider what he calls her: O virgin Israel, spoken to the nation this book has called a prostitute, a faithless wife, a camel in heat. The name is not a polite fiction; it is what God intends to make her, and he uses the future name now.

In the dance of the merrymakers. The restoration is not solemn. It is tambourines and dancing, the noise of a village wedding.

Plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. Samaria is the old northern capital, the heartland of the tribes everyone had given up on, and the promise is of vineyards there: a crop that takes years to bear, planted by people who expect to be around to drink the wine. The covenant curse, that they would plant vineyards and others would enjoy the fruit (Deut 28:30), is lifted.

Let us go up to Zion. And then the most unlikely sentence yet. Ephraim was northern territory, where the rival shrines had stood for two centuries specifically so nobody would go up to Zion; now its watchmen shout to their own people to go and worship in Jerusalem. The division that split the kingdom is healed from the northern side.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob, and raise shouts for the chief of the nations; proclaim, give praise, and say, 'O LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel.' Behold, I will bring them from the north country and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor, together; a great company, they shall return here. With weeping they shall come, and with pleas for mercy I will lead them back, I will make them walk by brooks of water, in a straight path in which they shall not stumble, for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob. They are told to sing the rescue before it happens, and to pray for it in the same breath. Praise and asking are not two separate steps here; the certainty of the promise is exactly what makes the asking confident.

The blind and the lame. Consider who is on this march. Not the fit and the useful, but the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor, the four categories any commander would leave behind, because a column moves at the pace of its slowest member.

Nobody left behind. God lists them deliberately. A rescue that quietly loses the weak on the road is not the rescue he is describing; nobody here is expendable, and the party travels at the speed of the woman in labour.

With weeping they shall come. They come home crying. The tears are not a failure of faith but the sound of repentance, and God leads a weeping people gently, by brooks of water, on level ground, along a road chosen so the lame will not stumble on it.

I am a father to Israel. And the reason is family: I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn. Ephraim, of all names, the tribe that led the rebellion and the shorthand for everything that went wrong in the north, is called the firstborn son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear the word of the LORD, O nations, and declare it in the coastlands far away; say, 'He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock.' For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and has redeemed him from hands too strong for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear the word of the LORD, O nations. The nations are called as witnesses. They had watched the scattering and drawn the obvious conclusion, that Israel's God was weak or finished, and now they are told to publish the correction as far as the coastlands reach.

He who scattered Israel will gather him. The sentence they must carry holds the two halves together without flinching: He who scattered Israel will gather him. No rival power scattered them. The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the hand that drove the flock apart is the hand that keeps it.

The LORD has ransomed Jacob. Then come two words, ransomed, the price paid to set a slave free, and redeemed, a kinsman buying back a relative or his land, and a phrase that explains why any of this had to be God's work: from hands too strong for him.

From hands too strong for him. That is the honest assessment. Jacob was not held by something he could have shaken off with more effort. Babylon was stronger than him, and so was the sin that put him there. He could never have rescued himself, which is why throughout this chapter it is always God who acts: I will build, I will gather, I will lead, I have ransomed.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall come and sing aloud on the height of Zion, and they shall be radiant over the goodness of the LORD, over the grain, the wine, and the oil, and over the young of the flock and the herd; their life shall be like a watered garden, and they shall languish no more. Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy; I will comfort them, and give them gladness for sorrow. I will feast the soul of the priests with abundance, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Radiant over the goodness of the LORD. They will be radiant over the goodness of the LORD. Their faces shine, and the thing they are shining about is named: grain, wine, oil, lambs, calves. It is ordinary provision, received as goodness from a person.

Like a watered garden. The image of the watered garden would land hard on people who knew what a dry season did to a field. Everything in this book about drought, cracked cisterns and withered pasture is reversed in four words.

The young women rejoice in the dance. Three generations dance in the same sentence: girls, young men and the old. The community that lost its future is given one with children in it.

I will turn their mourning into joy. And the verb is turn: I will turn their mourning into joy. God does not replace the mourning with joy once it has run its course; he turns the thing itself. The grief is not deleted from their history; it is itself changed into gladness, which is a harder and better promise.

My people shall be satisfied with my goodness. The word to end on is satisfied. This book opened with people digging broken cisterns that could hold no water, forsaking the fountain; it promises here that the thirst will finally be met, and met with God's own goodness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — Rachel's Tears and Ephraim's Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rachel weeps for her children, and God answers her tears with the promise that they will come back (vv. 15-17). He has overheard Ephraim praying to be brought back, and answers with a father's yearning and mercy (vv. 18-20); Israel is to mark the road home (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: God overhears a prayer for the very turning he commands, and answers it with yearning.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more." Thus says the LORD: "Keep your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, declares the LORD, and they shall come back from the land of the enemy. There is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back to their own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice is heard in Ramah. In the middle of the singing, someone is crying, and God stops the chapter to listen.

Rachel is weeping for her children. Rachel is Jacob's beloved wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and tradition placed her tomb in Benjamin's territory near Ramah (1 Sam 10:2). Ramah is where the deportees were mustered in chains before the walk to Babylon. So the poem pictures the long-dead mother of the northern tribes waking to watch her descendants marched past her grave, and weeping. She refuses to be comforted, and she is not rebuked for it. Some griefs should not be hurried into comfort. Parents who have buried a child may take that as permission: God does not hurry their tears, and he answers them, as he does here, with a promise rather than a lecture.

Matthew hears it again. Matthew heard this verse again on a night in Bethlehem when soldiers came for the children: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more (Matt 2:18). The mothers of Bethlehem wept while the child who would one day wipe away every tear was carried to safety in Egypt.

They shall come back from the land of the enemy. God does not answer the tears with an explanation. He answers them with a fact: they shall come back. When he does tell her to keep her voice from weeping, it is because he has news for her, not because her grief was wrong.

There is a reward for your work. And he calls her grief your work, with a reward attached: the years of weeping over lost children are counted as labour that will be paid. There is hope for your future is said to a woman in a graveyard, which is where that sentence is needed most.

How does Herod’s slaughter “fulfil” this? Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping at Ramah for her children going into exile, with God’s promise that they will return (vv. 16–17). Matthew sees the same grief at Bethlehem, near Rachel’s tomb, and the same hope: the Child who escaped would bring the true return from exile (Matt 2:17–18). Scripture links Rachel’s tomb both with the road to Bethlehem (Gen 35:19) and with Benjamin’s territory (1 Sam 10:2); Ramah and Bethlehem both lie a few miles from Jerusalem, and Matthew’s point is the pattern, not the map. “Fulfil” here means that the exile’s grief, and its promised end, reach their full meaning in Jesus’ story.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah himself was later released from his chains at Ramah, where the captives were gathered for Babylon (40:1).

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard Ephraim grieving, 'You have disciplined me, and I was disciplined, like an untrained calf; bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God. For after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth.' Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard Ephraim grieving. God has been listening to his son talk to himself.

Like an untrained calf. The image Ephraim reaches for is honest: like an untrained calf, a young animal that fights the yoke, bucks, and has to be broken to be any use. He does not dispute the discipline or ask for it to stop.

Bring me back that I may be restored. And then the prayer that lies at the heart of all true conversion: bring me back that I may be restored. He asks God to do the turning. He knows he cannot return by his own strength, and this is the answer to the question the book has pressed since it asked whether a leopard can change its spots (13:23): the return God commands is the return God must give.

I struck my thigh. Striking the thigh is a gesture of grief at oneself. The order in the sentence matters: the turning came first, then the instruction, then the shame. Deep sorrow over sin often comes last, not first; the shame here is the fruit of being brought back, not the price paid for it.

Is Ephraim my dear son? God answers with two questions, and answers them by the way he asks them. Even while pronouncing judgment, as often as I speak against him, he never stopped remembering him.

My heart yearns for him. Where the ESV has my heart yearns for him, the note records that the Hebrew word is "bowels": the physical seat of feeling, the churn you feel in your stomach over someone you love. This is not a mild, distant goodwill. It is a father who cannot get his son out of his mind.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea heard the same struggle in God's heart over Ephraim: My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hos 11:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up road markers for yourself; make yourself guideposts; consider well the highway, the road by which you went. Return, O virgin Israel, return to these your cities. How long will you waver, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing on the earth: a woman encircles a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set up road markers for yourself. Here is a practical instruction for people about to be marched away: mark the route. Pile the stones, note the landmarks, pay attention to the road you are being taken along, because you are coming back down it.

Planning the way home. It is a strange kind of comfort, to plan your return journey while you are still going out, and it treats the promise as solid enough to plan a route by.

How long will you waver? The rebuke is gentle and impatient at once: How long will you waver? The wavering is the old habit of trying to keep both God and the other things they trusted.

A woman encircles a man. Then comes a line that has long puzzled readers, and it is better to say so. The words are plain, a woman encircles a man, and the sense is not. What the verse does make clear is its setting: this is a new thing that the LORD has created, and created is the verb Genesis uses when God makes the heavens and the earth.

A new thing on the earth. Something is coming that reverses the expected order, and it will be God's own creation rather than Israel's achievement. That is the same direction the rest of the chapter runs: the faithless daughter will be made new by an act of creation, not by finally pulling herself together.

The likeliest sense. Israel, the faithless daughter (v. 22), will at last embrace and cling to her LORD. Some early Christians saw the virgin conceiving a son, but that reads more into the words than they say.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–30 — Watching to Build and to Plant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah's towns will bless Jerusalem again, the weary will be satisfied, and the prophet wakes from a sweet sleep (vv. 23-26). The God who watched over the tearing down will watch over the building and planting, and the sour-grapes proverb is retired (vv. 27-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The same watchfulness that pulled the nation down is now set to building it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Once more they shall use these words in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their fortunes: "'The LORD bless you, O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill!' And Judah and all its cities shall dwell there together, and the farmers and those who wander with their flocks. For I will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish." At this I awoke and looked, and my sleep was pleasant to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O habitation of righteousness. An old blessing comes back into everyday use, the sort of thing neighbours say to each other in the street. And the name it uses for Jerusalem is habitation of righteousness, which is precisely what the city had stopped being.

The farmers and those who wander with their flocks. The picture in the next line is of ordinary society knitted back together: settled farmers and wandering herdsmen living in the same land without preying on each other.

I will satisfy the weary soul. The promise uses two words for exhaustion, weary and languishing, and makes two promises, to satisfy and to replenish. This is the pastoral centre of the chapter for anyone reading it tired.

At this I awoke and looked. And here the prophet himself appears, waking up.

My sleep was pleasant to me. Think of what this man's nights had been like: the boiling pot, the drought, the broken flask, the trial for his life, the stocks, the day he cursed his own birth. Now, after being shown all this, he wakes and records that his sleep had been sweet. It is the only moment of personal comfort he is given in the entire book, and it comes from having seen what God intends to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of beast. And it shall come to pass that as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, to overthrow, destroy, and bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will sow the house of Israel. The land that was emptied gets resown, and the metaphor is agricultural: God scatters people across it as a farmer scatters grain. Both houses come back, and livestock with them, a country coming back to life down to its herds.

To pluck up and break down. These are the words of Jeremiah's calling forty years earlier: to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10). For four decades he has been announcing the tearing down, and here the building and planting finally get their turn, with the same watchful care of God behind them.

So I will watch over them to build and to plant. The repeated word is watched over. God was not careless in the demolition and he will not be casual in the rebuilding. The same vigilance that saw every stage of the tearing down is now fixed on the building and planting, which means the ruin was never a loss of control, and the restoration will not be left to chance.

For Jeremiah himself. For a man who had spent his life announcing the tearing down, it must have been something to be told that he had always been serving the building and the planting.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days they shall no longer say: "'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' But everyone shall die for his own iniquity. Each man who eats sour grapes, his teeth shall be set on edge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fathers have eaten sour grapes. The proverb was the popular theology of a defeated generation, and it was a complaint: our grandfathers sinned and we are the ones with our teeth on edge. There was something true in it, because consequences do run downhill through families and nations, but as they used it, it was a way of saying that nothing they did mattered either way.

Ezekiel heard it too. Ezekiel was told to stop the same saying among the exiles: this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel (Ezek 18:3).

Everyone shall die for his own iniquity. The answer is not that inherited consequence is a myth. It is that no one will be able to hide behind it. Everyone shall die for his own iniquity: each person is dealt with by God directly, for what he himself has done.

Just before the new covenant. That sounds severe until you see where it sits. It comes immediately before the new covenant, where God deals with each person individually in mercy, writing on this heart, knowing this man, forgetting these sins. The end of hiding behind your ancestors is also the end of being trapped by them.

Isn’t everyone simply a product of their past? The sour-grapes proverb has a modern edition. The biologist Robert Sapolsky argued in Determined (2023) that free will is an illusion: every choice is the sum of genes, hormones, childhood and culture, so nobody truly deserves praise or blame. Everyday speech says something gentler and similar: I am like this because of how I was raised. There is real truth in it, and Scripture itself traces how sin runs down the generations. But notice the cost. If no one is answerable, no one can be forgiven either, because there is nothing to forgive, and change becomes only a change of causes. The fatalist explains the prisoner and then leaves him in the cell. God is more radical than either the moralist, who says try harder, or the fatalist, who says you cannot help it. He holds each person answerable, and then offers each person a new beginning that no family history can block. Peter tells believers that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises a new covenant, unlike the one Israel broke after the exodus (vv. 31-32): the law written on their hearts, every member knowing him, and their sin forgiven and remembered no more (vv. 33-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The law moves from tablets to hearts, and the sins move out of God's memory.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new covenant. This is the sentence the rest of the Bible is built on, and the phrase new covenant appears nowhere else in the Old Testament: this is where it is given.

Not a repair. Consider who says it and when. A prophet standing in a doomed city, watching the old arrangement collapse around him, announces that God's answer is not a repair. It is a new covenant, and the promise is made to the same two houses that had just finished breaking the old one.

The day when I took them by the hand. The tenderness of the memory is startling: the day when I took them by the hand, like a father teaching a child to walk, out of Egypt. That is how God remembers the exodus.

My covenant that they broke. And then the failure, stated without excuse, my covenant that they broke, followed by five words that carry the ache of the whole book: though I was their husband. The problem with the old covenant was never its terms, which were holy, or its giver. It was that one party to a marriage kept the vows and the other did not.

What Hebrews concludes. Hebrews quotes this passage at length and draws the conclusion: God finds fault with them (Heb 8:8), not with the covenant. A law written on stone can tell you what to do and cannot make you want to do it.

Is the new covenant with Israel or with the church? It is promised to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Dispensationalists hold that it awaits fulfilment with national Israel.
