But Jesus established it in his blood at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes this passage of the church (Heb 8:6–13). It is made with the true Israel, Jews and Gentiles who believe in Christ (Gal 6:16; Rom 11:17). Many dispensationalists today agree that the church already shares in its blessings through Christ, while still expecting a future fulfilment for national Israel; faithful Christians differ on that second part. This commentary’s reason for its reading is that the New Testament applies the whole promise, forgiveness and the law on the heart, to every believer now (Heb 10:15–18).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers hear this as God's promise to renew, not replace, the covenant of Sinai: the same Torah, written no longer only on stone but on Israel's heart, so that the people at last keep it. Many place its fulfilment in the days of the Messiah, and note that it is made with Israel and Judah. This commentary agrees that the law is not changed but written within, and that the promise belongs to Israel. It reads it as begun in Jesus, who called the cup the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20), and as opened to Gentiles grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17).
verseByVerse.note: Hebrews quotes verses 31-34 in full (Heb 8:8-12), the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and returns to them in 10:16-17.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will put my law within them. The law does not change. The place where it is written does.

I will write it on their hearts. The old covenant put God's commands on tablets outside the man, where they instructed him and condemned him and could not help him. The new one puts the same law within them and writes it on their hearts, which answers precisely the diagnosis this book has been making for thirty chapters: sin engraved on the tablet of the heart (17:1), a heart deceitful above all things (17:9), a people who could no more change than a leopard could change its spots (13:23). If the problem is the heart, only a new heart is a solution.

Paul saw it happen. Paul saw it happen in his converts: a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor 3:3).

Duty or desire? Our culture is torn between two ways of being good. One says morality is duty: rules you keep whether you feel like it or not. The other says the only authentic life flows from your own desires, and any rule imposed from outside is a kind of violence against the self. The first produces people who are upright and joyless; the second, people who are free and adrift. The new covenant overturns both. It does not abolish the law to liberate the heart, and it does not set the law against the heart to tame it. It writes the law on the heart, so that what God commands and what we want begin to be the same thing. Augustine put the result in a famous sentence: “Love, and do what you will.” He did not mean that love excuses anything, but that a remade heart wants what God wants. Only one person has ever lived like that completely, and the psalm puts it on his lips: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart (Ps 40:8; Heb 10:5-7). The new covenant is his Spirit, writing that same delight in us.

They shall all know me. Under the old arrangement the covenant community was a mixed body, including circumcised men who did not know God at all, which is why they had to be told to know him. In the new one, membership and knowing God are the same thing. Teaching does not end, but nobody inside this covenant needs to be introduced to its God. They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest: the child and the scholar on the same footing.

What it means to know the LORD. We use the word know in two very different ways. I know who the prime minister is; I know my wife. The first is information; the second is a relationship. The new covenant promises the second kind. To know the LORD is not merely to hold correct opinions about him; it is to be on speaking terms with him, trusting and trusted, and the Hebrew uses the same word for the closeness of husband and wife. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a real relationship needs a God who can contradict you: a God who only ever agrees with you is not a person you know but an idea you are managing. So knowing him starts where this verse starts, with God speaking and God forgiving. Jesus said, “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), and Paul corrects himself in mid-sentence: “now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God” (Galatians 4:9). He knew us first. So when a passage of his word cuts across what you wanted, do not explain it away. Take it as the sign that you are dealing with someone real, and answer him.

For I will forgive their iniquity. And then the foundation, introduced with For, because it is the reason the rest is possible: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Not overlook, not suspend. God puts his people's sin out of his own memory.

The new covenant in his blood. It cost him everything to be able to say it. On the last night, holding a cup, the Lord told his friends what would make this covenant new in fact and not only in promise: This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). Hebrews, having quoted these verses twice, rests the whole assurance of a Christian on the final clause: I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more (Heb 10:17).

If all in the new covenant shall know the LORD, what of a church with unbelievers in it? Paedobaptists hold that the covenant community, like Israel, includes the children of believers, and some who do not truly know God. Baptists answer that this verse marks the difference between the covenants: in the new, every member knows the Lord, so the church should receive by baptism those who profess faith. The second reading fits the verse best, though no church can see hearts perfectly. That is the view of the 1689 London Baptist Confession, which this commentary follows; Presbyterian and other paedobaptist brothers, with the Westminster Confession, read the covenants as more continuous, and they hold their view from Scripture with equal seriousness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 35–40 — As Fixed as the Sunrise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes Israel's future on the fixed order of sun, moon and stars (vv. 35-37). The city is surveyed for rebuilding, and even the valley of the dead bodies and the ashes is declared sacred to the LORD forever (vv. 38-40).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where they burned their children is the last plot of land God claims as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day and the fixed order of the moon and the stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name: "If this fixed order departs from before me, declares the LORD, then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation before me forever." Thus says the LORD: "If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who gives the sun for light by day. Before the guarantee come the credentials. The God about to make a promise is the one who runs the solar system and the tides.

If this fixed order departs from before me. The logic is simple: only if sun, moon and stars leave their fixed order will Israel cease to be a nation. Her future is as secure as sunrise. Anyone doubting the promise is invited to test it against the evidence available every morning.

Said of a nation being dismantled. And this is said about a nation that was, at that moment, being dismantled. Nothing in its circumstances suggested it would survive. It was staked on the constancy of the God who keeps the moon in its course.

If the heavens above can be measured. The second guarantee is built on immensity rather than regularity: only if someone could measure the sky and explore the foundations of the earth would God cast Israel off. No one can.

For all that they have done. The last clause is honest: for all that they have done. God does not minimise the record. The guilt is real and it is not the deciding factor, because the question was never whether they deserved to be cast off.

Does this guarantee ethnic Israel’s future as a nation? It promises that God will never cast off the offspring of Israel. Paul says the same: God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:1–2), and, on the most natural reading, he looks for a great turning of Jews to Christ (Rom 11:26). That is a promise of salvation, not of a modern state or territory. Faithful Christians differ on whether the modern State of Israel has a place in prophecy; this commentary holds that the promise here is God’s faithfulness to save, while gladly affirming that Jewish people remain beloved for the sake of their forefathers (Rom 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line shall go out farther, straight to the hill Gareb, and shall then turn to Goah. The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes, and all the fields as far as the brook Kidron, to the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. The chapter ends with a survey. Named towers, named gates and a measuring line pulled across specific hills give the promise as a plan an engineer could work from. The Tower of Hananel stood at the north-east of the city wall (Neh 3:1; 12:39) and the Corner Gate probably at the north-west (2 Kgs 14:13), so the survey begins along the northern wall; and that tower was among the first stretches of wall rebuilt after the return (Neh 3:1).

The measuring line shall go out farther. And the line goes farther. Gareb and Goah can no longer be located, but the picture seems to be of a city larger than the one about to be destroyed.

The worst ground of all. Of every acre God could have chosen for the last word of this chapter, he takes the worst one.

The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes. The valley of the dead bodies and the ashes is most likely the ravine below the city, the Valley of Hinnom, the place Jeremiah had stood with a clay flask and called the Valley of Slaughter, where they had burned their own children to Baal (19:5-6). It was the most defiled ground in Israel, and its name became the New Testament's word for hell.

Shall be sacred to the LORD. That valley, God says, shall be sacred to the LORD.

What the new covenant does. The book that began by measuring a nation's guilt ends this chapter by measuring a city that includes its own worst place inside the holy ground. This is what the new covenant does. It does not quarantine the shameful part of the record and build around it; it takes the ash heap into the city and calls it holy, and it fixes the boundary with a promise that has no expiry: It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever. The words of tearing down from Jeremiah’s calling are used one last time, now to say what will never happen again.

31.title: The New Covenant
31.overview:
God promises to be the God of all the clans of Israel, and grounds everything in an everlasting love. The ruined nation will be built again with dancing and vineyards, and gathered from the ends of the earth, the weakest among them, by a father who turns their mourning into joy (vv. 1-14).

Rachel weeps for her lost children, and God answers with the promise that they will come back. He has heard Ephraim praying to be brought back and answers with a father's yearning; Israel is told to mark the road home (vv. 15-22).

The weary will be satisfied, and the God who watched over the tearing down will watch over the building and planting (vv. 23-30). Then comes the new covenant: the law written on the heart, every member knowing God, and sin remembered no more (vv. 31-34). Israel's future is staked on the fixed order of the heavens, and the rebuilt city takes in even the valley of the dead as holy ground (vv. 35-40).
31.theology:
Everything here rests on an everlasting love. Israel's obedience did not start it and her sin cannot end it, and God keeps faith with her because he loved her first (v. 3). The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the rescue had to be his because Jacob was held by hands too strong for him (vv. 10-11).

Even repentance is asked for as a gift (v. 18). The new covenant differs from the old not in its law but in where the law is written, and its foundation is forgiveness: God puts his people's sin out of his own memory (vv. 33-34). And grace claims the worst ground, taking the valley of the dead inside the holy city for ever (v. 40).
31.examples:
To people who think the good days are over, God says again, three times. To a nation he had called faithless he gives her future name, virgin Israel. And he sets the pace of the journey home by the woman in labour, so that nobody is left on the road.

To a weeping mother he speaks of hope; to a son ashamed of himself he shows a father who cannot get him out of his mind; and to all of us he promises a law written inside us and sins put out of his memory.

32.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.<sup>2</sup>At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah.<sup>3</sup>For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it;<sup>4</sup>Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye.<sup>5</sup>And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"<sup>6</sup>Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>7</sup>Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.'<sup>8</sup>Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver.<sup>10</sup>I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales.<sup>11</sup>Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.<sup>12</sup>And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard.<sup>13</sup>I charged Baruch in their presence, saying,<sup>14</sup>'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time.<sup>15</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'<sup>16</sup>"After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying:<sup>17</sup>'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.<sup>18</sup>You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts,<sup>19</sup>great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.<sup>20</sup>You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day.<sup>21</sup>You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror.<sup>22</sup>And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>23</sup>And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them.<sup>24</sup>Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it.<sup>25</sup>Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"<sup>26</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>27</sup>"Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?<sup>28</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it.<sup>29</sup>The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger.<sup>30</sup>For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.<sup>31</sup>This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight<sup>32</sup>because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>33</sup>They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction.<sup>34</sup>They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.<sup>35</sup>They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.<sup>36</sup>"Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence':<sup>37</sup>Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety.<sup>38</sup>And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.<sup>39</sup>I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them.<sup>40</sup>I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me.<sup>41</sup>I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.<sup>42</sup>"For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them.<sup>43</sup>Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.'<sup>44</sup>Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — A Field Bought in a Besieged City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the Babylonian army round Jerusalem and Jeremiah shut up in the court of the guard (vv. 1-5), his cousin Hanamel comes, as God had said, offering him the family field at Anathoth (vv. 6-8). Jeremiah buys it with full legal formality and has the deeds stored in a jar, because houses and fields will again be bought in this land (vv. 9-15).
verseByVerse.theology: A prisoner buys real estate in a country that is about to be confiscated, and has the paperwork witnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah. For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it; Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye. And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the tenth year of Zedekiah. Fix the situation before reading the story, because everything in this chapter depends on it. It is 588 or 587 BC. The Babylonian army is camped around the walls. Food is running out. And the prophet is under arrest in the palace compound. Chapters 37 and 38 tell how he came to be there: arrested at the city gate as a supposed deserter during a lull in the siege, beaten, kept in a cellar, and then moved to this courtyard by the king (37:11-21).

It is an unpromising moment for a property transaction.

The king’s question. The king's question is almost plaintive. He does not ask whether it is true, but why Jeremiah keeps saying it. Zedekiah spends this whole book half-believing Jeremiah and never acting on it, and here he jails the man rather than answer him.

See him eye to eye. The detail about seeing Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye would be fulfilled with terrible precision: Zedekiah was brought before him at Riblah, watched his sons killed, and was then blinded. He saw the king of Babylon eye to eye, and the last thing those eyes saw was his own sons dying.

Until I visit him. And even here the wording is open: until I visit him. In this book God's visiting can mean coming in judgment or in mercy; it is the same verb that carried the promise to the exiles (29:10). Scripture does not tell us which Zedekiah met; it records only that he died a prisoner in Babylon (52:11).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 37 and 38 tell how Jeremiah came to be confined in the court of the guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.' Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you. God tells him what is about to happen before it happens, and it is nothing spectacular: a relative is going to turn up with a business proposition.

The right of redemption by purchase is yours. The legal background is the law of redemption. When an Israelite fell into poverty and had to sell family land, the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy it, keeping the inheritance inside the family: his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold (Lev 25:25). It is the transaction Boaz performed at the gate, calling the town to witness that he had bought the inheritance of a dead man to keep his name alive (Ruth 4:9-10).

A picture of Christ. Christians have long heard in this law a picture of Christ, though Jeremiah does not draw it. The redeemer had to be a near kinsman, and the Son of God became our brother, sharing our flesh and blood that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb 2:14), and buying back an inheritance we had lost and could not recover.

Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD. The confirmation did not come by a vision or a voice. It came when a cousin walked into the guardhouse and said what God had said he would say.

Buy my field that is at Anathoth. Hanamel's motive is easy to guess and not held against him. Anathoth was three miles north of Jerusalem, in territory the Babylonians already controlled. The field was worthless and he wanted out. In business terms he was selling a loss, and God had told his prophet to be the buyer.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver. I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales. Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seventeen shekels of silver. He paid. That is the whole force of the sign, and it cost him real silver, seventeen shekels, recorded exactly, as a man records a sum he has genuinely parted with.

What faith looks like here. Faith here is not a feeling about the future. It is money leaving a purse for land the buyer will never walk on, in a district already under enemy control, paid by a man who had just been told the country was finished.

I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses. Every one of the four verbs, signed, sealed, witnessed, weighed, is the ordinary legal procedure for selling land. God's prophet does not make a gesture; he completes a legally binding sale with the correct formalities in front of observers.

Hope with paperwork. There is something bracing in that. An extravagant act of hope is carried out with paperwork. Faith that expects God to keep his word will generally look like something concrete and slightly inconvenient rather than like an inspiring mood.

The sealed deed of purchase. Two documents were made, as was standard practice: a sealed copy that could not be tampered with, and an open copy for consultation. Both are kept, because the sale is meant to be verifiable generations later by people who will need to know exactly where the boundary ran.
verseByVerse.note: Seventeen shekels was about 7 ounces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard. I charged Baruch in their presence, saying, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baruch the son of Neriah. Baruch appears, the scribe who will write this book down at Jeremiah’s dictation (36:4). And note the audience: the cousin, the official witnesses, and all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard, a yard full of prisoners and hangers-on, watching a man buy a field he could not reach.

In their presence. The sign was performed publicly on purpose. In a city where everyone was calculating how long the food would last, here was a man behaving as though there would be a Judah in which to own land.

Put them in an earthenware vessel. The deeds go into an earthenware jar, that they may last for a long time. The instruction quietly admits how long this will take: decades. Jeremiah will never use the field himself; the jar is for somebody's grandchildren.

How documents were kept. Storing documents in sealed pottery is how the ancient world preserved what mattered, and how the Dead Sea Scrolls survived two thousand years in the same region. Hope with a long timescale needs a container.

Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought. And here is the interpretation, given after the act rather than before it. The point of the purchase was never the field. It was the sentence: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land. Normal life, with markets functioning and families buying property, would return to the country whose destruction had just been guaranteed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — Nothing Is Too Hard for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the deed filed, Jeremiah prays. He begins with the Creator for whom Nothing is too hard, rehearses the exodus and the gift of the land, agrees that the disaster is deserved, and lays his bewilderment down: yet you told me to buy a field (vv. 16-25).
verseByVerse.theology: He obeyed first and asked his question afterwards, which is the right order.

verseByVerse.quote: "After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying: 'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After I had given the deed of purchase. The sequence matters. He obeyed, completed the transaction, filed the deeds, and then prayed about it. The obedience was not waiting on the explanation.

Ah, Lord GOD! The prayer opens with a sigh, Ah, Lord GOD!, the sound of a man who has done something he does not understand and has come to talk about it.

Nothing is too hard for you. And then, before any question, he states what he knows: God made the heavens and the earth, and Nothing is too hard for you. That is the right foundation for a confused prayer. He does not begin with the problem; he begins with the Creator, and the problem gets measured against him rather than the other way round.

Borrowed words. The words are borrowed. When Sarah laughed behind a tent flap at the idea of a baby, the LORD said to Abraham, Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14). The same truth would be told to a girl in Nazareth in the plainest form: For nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). A barren womb, a doomed city, a virgin: the question turns up at every point where God's promise looks physically ridiculous.

verseByVerse.quote: You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts, great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You show steadfast love to thousands. Jeremiah holds two things together that we find easier to separate: steadfast love to thousands, and guilt repaid into the next generation. He is quoting God’s own words about himself, and he does not edit them to make the prayer more comfortable.

Praying honestly. Praying honestly means praying to the God who is actually there, including the justice that is at this moment battering your city.

Words from Sinai. The words come from the moment God proclaimed his own name to Moses: keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children (Exod 34:7). And the proportion inside that sentence is telling. Love reaches thousands; the visiting of guilt reaches three or four generations. Even in the verse that warns, mercy is the larger number.

Great in counsel and mighty in deed. Then come two pairs of qualities that a man in a besieged city most needs to believe. Great in counsel and mighty in deed: God both knows what he is doing and is able to do it. Wisdom without power would be tragic, and power without wisdom would be terrifying.

Whose eyes are open. Then whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man. Nothing in the siege, or in the guardhouse, or in the conduct of the men who put him there, is unobserved.

According to the fruit of his deeds. And the last clause is one God had already spoken about himself in this book: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds (17:10). Jeremiah prays God's own words back to him. That is often the safest way to pray when a situation makes no sense: not with a theory, but with what God has said.

Does God punish children for their fathers’ guilt, when 31:30 says each dies for his own sin? Each is judged for his own guilt; but sin’s consequences fall on families, and children who continue in their fathers’ sin share their judgment (Exod 20:5, of those who hate me).

verseByVerse.quote: You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day. You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror. And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reasoning from history. The prayer turns to history, which is where Israel always went for confidence. He does not reason from his circumstances to God's character; he reasons from what God has already done.

With a strong hand and outstretched arm. So a prisoner recites the exodus during a siege. And the phrase outstretched arm is the one he had already used of creation in verse 17: the arm that made the world is the arm that emptied Egypt, and it has not grown weaker.

Not nostalgia. Praying through the record like this is not nostalgia. It is how a believer talks himself into hope: God has done the impossible before, with witnesses, and the account is public.

Which you swore to their fathers. The land was a gift and an oath, which you swore to their fathers. That is precisely what makes the present moment so painful to pray about. The property Jeremiah has just bought is part of a gift God swore to give, and it is about to be taken away. He lays that contradiction in front of God rather than resolving it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them. Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it. Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. The prophet's prayer contains no defence of his people. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do, and the disaster is traced to its author without complaint: you have made all this disaster come upon them.

Agreeing with the verdict. He is not asking God to be fair. He agrees with the verdict, which is the only honest place to pray from.

Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city. He describes what is out of the window: earth ramps rising against the wall, sword, famine and pestilence arriving as the whole book had warned, and a flat acknowledgement, What you spoke has come to pass. He had been called a traitor for forty years for saying this, and there is no note of triumph in his tone at all.

Buy the field for money and get witnesses. And there is the question, finally, and it is left unfinished. Everything you said would happen is happening, yet you told me to buy a field.

Faithful bewilderment. He does not accuse God of anything and he does not pretend to understand. He simply sets the command beside the circumstances and leaves them both in God's hands. That is what faithful bewilderment sounds like, and it is available to anyone who has obeyed something they could not explain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — Is Anything Too Hard for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hands the confession back as a question, Is anything too hard for me? (vv. 26-27). Then he confirms the city's burning, with an indictment running from the day Jerusalem was built through every class of its people to the valley where they offered their children (vv. 28-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The same question stands over both the judgment and the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anything too hard for me? God answers the prayer by quoting it.

A gentle correction. Jeremiah had said Nothing is too hard for you; God replies Is anything too hard for me? It is the gentlest possible correction, and it is a real one. The prophet had stated the doctrine and then laid a difficulty beside it as though the two might not fit. God takes the man's own confession and turns it into the answer to his problem.

What we need in bewilderment. There is a great deal of pastoral help in that. What we mostly need in bewilderment is not new information but the application of what we already say we believe.

The God of all flesh. And the title God chooses is exact for the occasion: the God of all flesh. He is not the God of Judah only, whose reach ends at a besieged wall, but of every living thing, including the Babylonian army, the cousin selling a field, and the generations who will one day open a clay jar.

Zechariah heard it too. Zechariah heard the same question asked after the exile, when the few who had returned thought the promised restoration too great to believe: If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight? (Zech 8:6). What looks impossible to people standing in rubble does not look impossible from where God stands.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it. The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger. For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans. Before the comfort, God confirms the catastrophe. He does not answer the hard question by softening the facts, and the first thing he says after Is anything too hard for me? is that the city will fall.

The houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal. The detail about the roofs is precise and damning. Flat roofs were where families sat in the evening, and they had been using them as private altars. Those same houses are named as fuel.

Nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The verdict has nothing good to say, and it matters that it comes here rather than in a chapter of pure judgment. The restoration promised in a few verses is not going to rest on finding the nation better than it seemed. That record is being read out at full severity first.

verseByVerse.quote: This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the day it was built. The city has done evil from the day it was built: not since Manasseh, not since the monarchy went bad, but from the beginning. God's review of Jerusalem's history finds no golden age to appeal to.

No golden age. That is a sobering word about institutions and cities we are tempted to idealise, and it clears away any idea that the coming restoration is a return to an earlier, purer Jerusalem. There was never one.

Ezekiel says it more bluntly. Ezekiel said the same thing even more bluntly about the city's origins: Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite (Ezek 16:3). Jerusalem had been a pagan city before David took it, and it never fully stopped being one. Whatever God does with it will be grace from the ground up, not a restoration of past merit.

The golden age that never was. Almost every movement runs on a story about a golden age. For some it lies behind us: the country before it was spoiled, the church before it lost its way, the family as it used to be. For others it lies ahead, in the just society we will build once the old one is cleared away. Both stories are powerful because they name the villains and promise that, with the right people in charge, paradise can be recovered or constructed (on politics as a substitute religion, see the note on Acts 17:6–7). God’s review of Jerusalem pulls the ground from under both. There was never a pure city to go back to. That is not cynicism; it is the lifting of a burden. If no generation is the golden one, then no generation, ours included, has to be idolised or demonised, and no programme has to carry the weight of salvation. The hope of Scripture is a city God builds himself. The patriarchs, Hebrews says, desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb 11:16), and its gate was opened by a King who was led out of the old city to die.

Their kings and their officials. The list of the guilty runs from the palace to the street: kings, officials, priests, prophets, the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Leaders and ordinary people stand together, with no class exempted and nobody left to blame the others.

verseByVerse.quote: They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction. They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their back and not their face. The image is domestic and wounding: a person who will not turn round. It is not argument or rival theology but the posture of someone who has decided not to look at you.

Though I have taught them persistently. And though I have taught them persistently uses the adverb of this whole book. God is the long-suffering teacher, sending prophet after prophet into a classroom whose pupils face the wall.

Their abominations in the house that is called by my name. They even set up idols inside the temple. The building existed to display his name and was used to insult it.

To offer up their sons and daughters to Molech. The charges end with the worst of all: the valley below the city where they burned their children.

Nor did it enter into my mind. And God adds a clause about himself that is almost unbearable to read: nor did it enter into my mind. Whatever the worshippers told themselves about devotion and cost, God disowns the whole idea as something he never willed or wanted.

The same valley made holy. This valley is very likely the same ground God promised in 31:40 would be sacred to the LORD. The place named here as the lowest point of Judah's guilt is the place named there as holy, and between the two statements stands everything the gospel has to do.

Does “nor did it come into my mind” mean God did not foresee child sacrifice? No; he knows all things (Ps 139:4). It means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — One Heart and One Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now therefore (v. 36) turns the whole chapter. God will gather his people from every country he drove them to, and they shall be his people (vv. 37-38). He will give them one heart and one way, make an everlasting covenant, and rejoice in doing them good with all his heart and soul (vv. 39-41).
verseByVerse.theology: God himself keeps his people faithful, as he requires, and says he will enjoy doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence': Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now therefore. Two words carry the weight of the chapter: Now therefore.

A promise, not a punishment. Read what precedes them: evil from the beginning, every class guilty, children burned in the valley, the city to be removed from God's sight. A therefore after that should introduce the punishment. Instead it introduces the promise. There is no logic in the world by which verse 37 follows verse 35, except the logic of grace.

I will gather them. The same hand appears on both ends of the action: he drove them, and he will gather them. The anger was real (God does not now describe the exile as a misunderstanding), and it is the same God who ends it.

They shall be my people. Then the covenant sentence comes again, and in this setting it is the answer to everything in the indictment. These are not a people who deserve him, but a people who are his.

Hosea and Peter. Hosea gave the same promise to a people who had been named for their rejection: I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God' (Hos 2:23). And Peter applies it to Gentile believers who had never belonged to Israel at all: Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy (1 Pet 2:10). The covenant sentence spoken to exiles in a doomed city is the sentence spoken over every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them. I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me. I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One heart and one way. The gift is a heart, as it has been throughout this book: the heart to know him (24:7), the law written inside (31:33), and here one heart and one way. Ezekiel was given the same promise in almost the same words: I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them (Ezek 11:19).

An undivided heart. The word one matters. A divided heart was Judah's disease, wavering between the LORD and Baal, the temple and the roof altar. The cure is not more willpower but an undivided heart, given.

That they may not turn from me. There are two guarantees, one on each side of the relationship. God will not turn away from doing them good, and, this is the astonishing half, he will see to it that they do not turn away from him either. The covenant is secured at both ends by the same person. Hebrews calls it the eternal covenant and names the price: the blood of the great shepherd of the sheep (Heb 13:20).

I will rejoice in doing them good. And then God says something about his own feelings. He will rejoice in doing them good, and he will do it with all my heart and all my soul: the phrase Israel was commanded to use about loving him, turned round and spoken by God about blessing them.

Not a reluctant God. This is not a God who forgives reluctantly and blesses grudgingly. Zephaniah saw the same thing: he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing (Zeph 3:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–44 — Deeds Signed and Sealed Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Just as God brought the disaster, so he will bring all the good he promises (v. 42). In the land everyone calls a desolation, fields will again be bought and deeds signed, sealed and witnessed, district by district (vv. 43-44).
verseByVerse.theology: The land registry will reopen, district by district, and that is the shape the hope takes.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them. Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.' Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as I have brought all this great disaster. The argument is simple: as surely as the disaster came, the good will come. It is a practical sentence for anyone who has watched God keep a hard word.

Judgment as evidence. They had just seen every threat land: siege mounds, famine, the city given over. Very well, says God: that same reliability is now working for you. The accuracy of the judgment is the evidence for the promise. A God whose warnings come true is a God whose assurances can be relied on, and the logic runs the way Paul's does when he argues from the greater gift to the lesser (Rom 8:32).

A desolation, without man or beast. God quotes the pessimism of the moment accurately, a desolation, without man or beast, and does not dispute it. That is exactly what the land is about to become. And in that land, fields will be bought.

Signed and sealed and witnessed. The chapter ends in a solicitor's office, and the vocabulary is the vocabulary of verse 10: bought for money, signed, sealed, witnessed. Jeremiah's private transaction in a prison yard turns out to be the first entry in a register that will reopen across six named districts: Benjamin, the area round Jerusalem, the cities of Judah, the hill country, the Shephelah (the western foothills) and the Negeb (the dry south).

What this hope looks like. That is how this hope is described: not as a vision or a feeling, but as ordinary people doing ordinary business in a country God had promised to empty and then promised to fill. And the man who bought the first field never saw it. He paid seventeen shekels, filed the deeds in a jar, and died elsewhere, which is the pattern for every believer who has ever acted on a promise whose fulfilment lay past his own lifetime.

32.title: The Field at Anathoth
32.overview:
In Zedekiah's tenth year, with Babylon besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah imprisoned in the court of the guard, his cousin Hanamel offers him the family field at Anathoth, just as God said he would. Jeremiah buys it before witnesses and has the deeds sealed in a jar, because houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (vv. 1-15).

Then he prays, confessing that nothing is too hard for God and laying down his bewilderment: yet you told me to buy a field (vv. 16-25). God answers with his own question, is anything too hard for me?, and confirms that the city will burn for its long record of evil (vv. 26-35).

Now therefore God will gather his people, give them one heart and an everlasting covenant, and rejoice in doing them good. Just as he brought the disaster, he will bring the good, and fields will be bought again across the land (vv. 36-44).
32.theology:
Faith acts before it understands: Jeremiah completed a binding purchase and asked his question afterwards (vv. 9-10, 25). And God answers bewilderment not with new information but by applying what the believer already confesses (vv. 17, 27).

Grace does not depend on finding the record better than it looked. The charges are read out in full, and then comes the therefore that introduces the promise (vv. 30-37). The covenant is secured at both ends by God, who will not turn from doing his people good and will keep them from turning from him; and he does it gladly, with all his heart and soul (vv. 39-41).
32.examples:
A prisoner buys farmland in a country under sentence, weighs out seventeen shekels in front of witnesses, and seals the deeds in a clay jar for somebody's grandchildren. Hope that trusts God's word usually looks like something concrete and slightly inconvenient.

When a command makes no sense, Jeremiah's prayer is a pattern: begin with who God is, recite what he has done, agree with his verdict, and then lay the question honestly before him.

33.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it— the LORD is his name:<sup>3</sup>Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.<sup>4</sup>For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword:<sup>5</sup>They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security.<sup>7</sup>I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first.<sup>8</sup>I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.<sup>9</sup>And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it.<sup>10</sup>"Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again<sup>11</sup>the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks.<sup>13</sup>In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.<sup>15</sup>In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>16</sup>In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>17</sup>"For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,<sup>18</sup>and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever."<sup>19</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>20</sup>"Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time,<sup>21</sup>then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers.<sup>22</sup>As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."<sup>23</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>24</sup>"Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight.<sup>25</sup>Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth,<sup>26</sup>then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second word to the imprisoned prophet, with an invitation to call and be told hidden things (vv. 1–3). The city is tearing down its houses for a defence that cannot hold, because God has hidden his face (vv. 4–5). Then the turn to healing, resting on the forgiveness of all their guilt (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers a man in prison by offering to tell him things he could not have worked out.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard: "Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it— the LORD is his name: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second time. Two details, and both matter. A second time: God had not finished speaking after the field was bought. And still shut up in the court of the guard, with the siege tightening outside and the prophet no closer to release.

More revelation, not release. The circumstances have not improved by one degree between chapter 32 and chapter 33. What arrives instead is more revelation. God's answer to a faithful man in a bad situation is often not a change of situation but a further word about himself.

The LORD who made the earth. Before the promise, the credentials again: the God who made the earth and formed it to establish it. He built it to stand. The ESV notes that its wording here follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew simply has "it"; but the sense of a Creator who makes things in order to make them last is what the verse is for, and it is the ground of everything promised in the chapter.

To a prisoner. Here is the invitation, and consider its recipient. A prisoner. A man whose preaching has failed by every visible measure, who has just spent silver on a field he will never see, and who prayed a bewildered prayer in the previous chapter.

Call to me and I will answer you. God's reply to that prayer is to invite more of them. Call to me and I will answer you: not a rebuke for asking, but an offer of more. And what is promised is not a change of plan but knowledge: great and hidden things that you have not known. There are things about God's purposes that will not be worked out by looking at the siege ramps. They have to be told, and they are told to people who ask.

How do I call to him? Jeremiah is the pattern, because this invitation answers a prayer that was honest and confused. Bring the bewilderment as it is. He began Ah, Lord GOD! and then said plainly that buying the field made no sense to him (32:17, 24–25). You may tell God that the diagnosis, the stalled career or the wandering child makes no sense to you. Ask to know him, not only to escape. The promise is great and hidden things, so pray, “Show me what you are doing, and who you are in this,” and then open the Scriptures, where he has told them. Keep calling from the same cell. The answer came while Jeremiah was still shut up; do not wait for things to change before you pray again. Come through the Son. We call with more confidence than Jeremiah could, because Christ has opened the way: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16). The Father is not irritated by the asking: he gives generously to all without reproach (Jas 1:5).

Is this a promise of private revelation? It was God’s word to Jeremiah, then promising the restoration that follows. Believers today are given God’s great and hidden things in the gospel, revealed in Scripture (1 Cor 2:9–10; Col 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword: They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds. A picture of a city in its last weeks. They are pulling down their own homes, royal buildings included, for stone and timber to block the breaches where the Babylonian ramps are coming over the wall.

What the end looks like. That is what the end looks like in practice: dismantling your own house to slow the enemy down for another day. Every resource turned to a defence that cannot hold.

To fill them with the dead bodies of men. The ESV's note explains what gets filled with the dead: "That is, the torn-down houses". The improvised barricades become the morgue. The stones pulled from bedrooms end up packed with the bodies of the men who stacked them.

I have hidden my face from this city. And underneath the military facts is the theological one: I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil. That is the real cause of the collapse. Not siege engineering, not the balance of power, but the averted face of God. The worst thing that can happen to a people is not that their walls fail but that God looks away, and this verse names it as the reason the walls fail at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security. I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first. I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will bring to it health and healing. The same Behold that introduced the barricades full of corpses now introduces healing, in the same breath and about the same city. This is the wound of chapter 30, the hurt God called incurable, with no medicine and no healing, and here is the physician arriving. Nothing has changed in the patient. What changes is that God announces he will do it himself.

As they were at first. Both houses again, the northern kingdom included well over a century after it vanished, and as they were at first, with the damage of the centuries undone.

I will cleanse them from all the guilt. Under the health, the prosperity and the security lies this foundation: the guilt has to go, and the sentence says it twice, with all both times.

Cleansing and forgiveness. Cleansing and forgiveness are not quite the same thing, and both are needed. Forgiveness deals with the record; cleansing deals with the stain. A pardoned man who still feels filthy has only half of what God is promising here.

Their sin and rebellion against me. And the offence is named for what it is: sin against me, twice. Judah's problem was never merely social collapse or bad policy. It was personal, and so is the remedy: God himself takes the guilt away, which is why a believer who has failed can come back by confession rather than by first making himself clean (Ps 32:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — The Voice of the Bridegroom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The place everyone calls a waste will hear weddings and thanksgiving again (vv. 10–11), and shepherds will count their flocks in every district (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Weddings, singing and a shepherd counting sheep: the restoration measured in ordinary noise.

verseByVerse.quote: And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it. "Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A name of joy, a praise and a glory. The city that had become a curse and a byword among the nations becomes a name of joy, a praise and a glory, and what changes her name is no strength of her own but what God does for her.

They shall fear and tremble. The odd phrase is the last one. The nations shall fear and tremble, not at judgment but because of all the good. God's generosity is itself awe-inducing. Grace on that scale is not a comfortable thing to watch.

It is a waste without man or beast. God quotes the pessimism verbatim, as he did in the previous chapter, and grants every word of it. The place is a waste. Then: there shall be heard again.

The voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride. Earlier in this book God had silenced exactly these sounds, promising to take away the voice of mirth and the voice of the bridegroom and bride (7:34; 16:9). Now he gives them back, item by item, in the same words: weddings in the streets, singing, people walking up to the temple with thank offerings.

Give thanks to the LORD of hosts. And the song they sing is the one Israel had always sung, the refrain of Psalm 136: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever (Ps 136:1). It is sung by people who have watched the worst happen. They are not singing that nothing bad occurred; they are singing that his steadfast love outlasted it.

What steadfast love means. The refrain’s last words, steadfast love, translate the Hebrew hesed, and English needs two words for it because one will not do. It is love that has bound itself by promise: not a feeling that rises and falls with how lovable we are, but loyalty that keeps going when the other side has given it every reason to stop. The people singing are the ones who broke the covenant; the love bringing them home is the love that would not break it from his side. When God passed before Moses he named himself “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6), and John, describing the Son, seems to echo that pair: “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). So on the day your own record makes you doubt your welcome, do not look for the answer in yourself. Say the refrain out loud anyway. It was written for people who had failed. See Steadfast Love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks. In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Habitations of shepherds resting their flocks. After the weddings, the sheep. The promise keeps getting more ordinary, which is how you can tell it is meant literally: shepherds with somewhere to settle, flocks lying down in country that had been emptied.

In the cities of the hill country. The same six districts as the land-registry promise at the end of chapter 32, listed again. God maps his promises.

Under the hands of the one who counts them. And the closing image is a man counting sheep as they file past him under his hand. It is the smallest detail in the chapter and one of the most reassuring: flocks numerous enough to need counting, a shepherd unhurried enough to count them, and peace enough in the countryside for both. Nothing dramatic. Just a working farm in a land God had promised to empty and then promised to fill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — A Righteous Branch, and a Name for the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous Branch of chapter 23 returns (vv. 14–15), but the name has moved: where chapter 23 gave it to the king, here the city wears it (v. 16). Throne and priesthood are guaranteed in perpetuity (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's own name is handed to the people who live under him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will fulfill the promise. The verb is fulfill, and the object is a promise already made. God is not improvising a new plan to cope with the disaster; he is keeping an old word, and the disaster has not altered it. Ten chapters earlier, amid an indictment of worthless shepherds, God had said Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land (23:5). Now the same promise is repeated to a man in prison in a city about to fall.

A righteous Branch to spring up for David. The image is agricultural and deliberately humble. A branch is what sprouts from a stump, which is what the house of David was about to become, with Zedekiah blinded and his sons dead. Out of that stump, a shoot. And spring up is the language of something growing quietly rather than being installed by force. What he does when he comes is named in the plainest terms: justice and righteousness in the land. Not ceremony, not conquest. The two things chapter 22 said a king was for, and that the actual kings never delivered.

The Branch has a name. The righteous Branch is Jesus, the Son of David (23:5–6); he is The LORD is our righteousness, for Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

A note on the text. Verses 14 to 26 are absent from the ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah, which is shorter than the Hebrew in many places. They are part of the Hebrew text our Bibles follow, and they echo 23:5–6 closely.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.' "For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is our righteousness. Read this beside chapter 23 and you find one word changed, and it is a glorious change. There, the name belonged to the king: this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness' (23:6). Here it is given to the city.

A picture of justification. The king's name has passed to his people. That is a picture of justification, in which God counts the king's righteousness as theirs. His righteousness is not admired from a distance; the city carries it as its own name. Jerusalem is not renamed The City That Finally Got Its Act Together. It is called by his name, because the righteousness it lives on is his. That is the gospel for every reader who has not kept God's law: Christ's obedience is counted as ours (2 Cor 5:21).

Everyone is building a case. We tend to think the language of righteousness belongs to religious people. But watch any modern life and you will find someone assembling a defence. The CV, the curated feed, the causes we are seen to support, the reminders of how hard we work and how much we have given up: all of it is evidence for a verdict we badly want, that we are good, worthy, on the right side. The devout build the case out of prayers and attendance; the secular build it out of achievement and moral seriousness about the issues of the day. It is the same project, and it is exhausting, because the court never rises and the case is never closed. Jeremiah’s name for the city ends the trial from outside. The people do not earn righteousness; they are given a name, The LORD is our righteousness, and carry it as their own. Paul describes the relief of a man who stopped building: not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ (Phil 3:9). Only someone whose case is already settled can afford to admit he was wrong.

David shall never lack a man. This is the promise of 2 Samuel 7, restated at the moment of its apparent collapse: your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam 7:16).

How the promise held. Within months there would be no king in Jerusalem at all, and no son of David would sit on that throne again. The promise held anyway, and an angel told a girl in Nazareth how: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33).

Will the Levitical priests and sacrifices be restored literally? Some dispensationalists expect them in a millennial temple. But the promise is kept in Christ, who is both King of David’s line and the high priest who offered one sacrifice for ever (Heb 7:24–27; 10:12), and in his people, a royal priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Pet 2:5, 9). Faithful Christians differ on this; this commentary reads it through Hebrews, which says Christ’s one offering has made the old sacrifices obsolete (Heb 8:13; 10:18), so that a return to animal sacrifice would look backward rather than forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Covenant with the Day and the Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes the throne and the altar on the sunrise (vv. 20–21), and promises not mere survival but increase, in the terms sworn to Abraham (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Anyone who wants the promise cancelled must first stop the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever." The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levitical priests shall never lack a man. Alongside the endless throne, an endless altar. The temple was not much more than a year from being burned and its priesthood scattered, and God promises that there will never be a moment without a priest in my presence making offerings.

Taken literally. Taken literally that promise failed twice over: the sacrifices stopped in 586, resumed, and stopped again in AD 70, this time for good. So either the word was broken, or it was pointing at a priesthood that does not depend on mortal men.

Hebrews explains. Hebrews takes the second view and explains what was always wrong with the Levitical arrangement: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb 7:23-24). The reason Israel needed a succession of priests was that each one kept dying. A priest who does not die needs no successor, and there has not been an hour since the cross when God has lacked a man in his presence offering, because he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25).

The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah. A new word begins in verse 19, and even its opening, that the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, says something in a chapter about permanence. God keeps speaking to this prisoner, paragraph after paragraph, while the city burns down around him.
