verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time, then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers. As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you can break my covenant with the day. God offers a test anybody can attempt. Stop tomorrow morning from arriving.

My covenant with the night. Calling the sunrise a covenant is a striking way to describe creation's regularity. Day and night are not mere physics; they are God keeping an appointment he made, every evening and every morning, without fail, in front of everyone.

A simple argument. The logic is simple. Only if someone could stop day and night coming would God’s covenant with David be broken; until then, the matter is closed.

Better evidence than his eyes. And the man hearing this could see the Babylonian army from the courtyard. His own eyes told him the Davidic line was finished. God does not dispute the evidence of his eyes; he gives him a better one, available every morning.

So I will multiply the offspring of David my servant. Not merely preserved but multiplied, and in the exact terms of the oath to Abraham: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen 22:17).

Beyond counting. That is a promise of a royal family and a priesthood beyond counting, spoken over a dynasty about to lose its last king. It is hard to read it, on this side of the cross, without thinking of a kingdom of priests too many to number from every tribe and tongue (Rev 5:9–10; 7:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Two Clans He Chose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the rumour that he has rejected the two clans he chose (v. 24) with the same covenant of day and night (v. 25), and the Book of Consolation ends in mercy (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The rumour was that God had finished with them; the reply ends in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight. Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose. God has been listening to the talk, and he repeats it back. The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose: Israel and Judah, both apparently finished, and the conclusion drawn everywhere that God had changed his mind about the people he chose.

No longer a nation in their sight. The consequence is public: his people are despised and no longer a nation in their sight. When God's people are visibly defeated, the watching world does not usually conclude that God is disciplining them. It concludes that he has dropped them, or was never there.

If I have not established my covenant with day and night. The same argument as before, now aimed at the rumour rather than at the prophet's doubt. God answers gossip about his faithfulness the way he answered his servant's confusion, by pointing at the sky.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And the name-stacking at the end is deliberate: Jacob, David, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob again. Every layer of the promise is named, so that rejecting this people would mean breaking all of it at once.

And will have mercy on them. And so the Book of Consolation ends, not with an argument won but with mercy.

Where these chapters came from. Weigh where these four chapters have come from. They were written by a man in custody, in a city eating itself, under a king who would be blinded, about a temple that would be ash within months. And they contain the new covenant, the everlasting love, the sins remembered no more, the healed wound, the field bought in faith, the Branch, and this last word of mercy. The circumstances never improved while he wrote. The revelation simply got better.

The answer to the invitation. That is the answer to the invitation at the head of the chapter. He called, and God told him great and hidden things he had not known, and the greatest of them was a name he would not live to hear anyone use, given first to a king and then handed to his people: The LORD is our righteousness.

33.title: Call to Me and I Will Answer You
33.overview: Jeremiah is still a prisoner in the court of the guard, and the siege is closing in, when a second word comes with an invitation: call to me, and I will tell you great and hidden things (vv. 1-3). The chapter then sets the city's last weeks, with houses torn down for barricades that will fill with the dead, beside the healing, forgiveness and joy God promises afterwards (vv. 4-13). It returns to the righteous Branch of chapter 23, now giving his name to the city, and stakes the throne of David and the priesthood on the sunrise, God's covenant with day and night (vv. 14-22). It answers the rumour that God has rejected his people, and the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33) closes in mercy (vv. 23-26).
33.theology: The chapter turns on two things God gives a prisoner in place of release: a further word about himself, and an invitation to ask for more. Its promises rest on forgiveness that deals with both the record and the stain of sin (v. 8), and they reach their height when the name of the king, The LORD is our righteousness, is given to his people (v. 16; 23:6). That pictures justification, the king’s righteousness counted as his people’s, and it is fulfilled in the Son of David whose kingdom has no end and the priest who always lives to intercede (Luke 1:32-33; Heb 7:23-25). God answers both private doubt and public rumour the same way, by pointing at the sunrise he keeps as a covenant (vv. 20, 25).
33.examples: A family dismantling its own bedroom to plug a breach in the wall for one more day is what verse 4 describes, and it is a picture of every defence that cannot hold once God has hidden his face. Against it stand the smallest images of hope in the chapter: wedding songs back in streets God had silenced, and a shepherd unhurried enough to count his sheep. And when doubt says God has finished with his people, the chapter's own answer is still available to anyone: stop tomorrow morning from arriving, and then we will talk.

34.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion and all the peoples were fighting against Jerusalem and all of its cities:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.<sup>3</sup>You shall not escape from his hand but shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face. And you shall go to Babylon.'<sup>4</sup>Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! Thus says the LORD concerning you: 'You shall not die by the sword.<sup>5</sup>You shall die in peace. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so people shall burn spices for you and lament for you, saying, "Alas, lord!"' For I have spoken the word, declares the LORD."<sup>6</sup>Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem,<sup>7</sup>when the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, Lachish and Azekah, for these were the only fortified cities of Judah that remained.<sup>8</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them,<sup>9</sup>that everyone should set free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother.<sup>10</sup>And they obeyed, all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant that everyone would set free his slave, male or female, so that they would not be enslaved again. They obeyed and set them free.<sup>11</sup>But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free, and brought them into subjection as slaves.<sup>12</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD:<sup>13</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I myself made a covenant with your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying,<sup>14</sup>'At the end of seven years each of you must set free the fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you six years; you must set him free from your service.' But your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me.<sup>15</sup>You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name,<sup>16</sup>but then you turned around and profaned my name when each of you took back his male and female slaves, whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your slaves.<sup>17</sup>"Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.<sup>18</sup>And the men who transgressed my covenant and did not keep the terms of the covenant that they made before me, I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts—<sup>19</sup>the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.<sup>20</sup>And I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives. Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.<sup>21</sup>And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the empire's armies at the walls, Jeremiah brings Zedekiah a message that gives and takes in the same breath: capture, and yet a death in peace (vv. 1–5), delivered while Lachish and Azekah still hold (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise of an honourable funeral, offered to a king who will be blinded first.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion and all the peoples were fighting against Jerusalem and all of its cities: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire. You shall not escape from his hand but shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face. And you shall go to Babylon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion. The scale is spelled out to make the odds plain: not merely Babylon but every vassal nation in the empire, conscripted into the siege lines. Jerusalem is facing the known world.

Go and speak to Zedekiah. And the prophet is sent to the palace with it. Not a written note: Go and speak to Zedekiah, face to face, the man who had already imprisoned him for saying this.

You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye. The phrase eye to eye had been used of this king before (32:4), and its fulfilment was exact in a way nobody would have wanted. Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, made to watch his sons executed, and then blinded. He did meet him eye to eye, and it was the last thing he ever saw.

God's words come true in their detail, and the detail is not always the comfort we imagined when we heard them.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! Thus says the LORD concerning you: 'You shall not die by the sword. You shall die in peace. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so people shall burn spices for you and lament for you, saying, "Alas, lord!"' For I have spoken the word, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! After the sentence, a concession, and it is addressed to him personally, by name and title, with an urgency that reads almost like pleading.

As spices were burned for your fathers. What is offered is a decent death and a proper funeral: the royal spices, the formal lament, the cry Alas, lord! that had been denied to Jehoiakim, who was promised the burial of a donkey (22:18-19).

You shall die in peace. It is a strange mercy. Zedekiah will lose his city, his sons and his sight, and yet he is told he will die in peace, with mourners to lament him. But weigh it against the alternative he was courting, and against the treatment his brother received, and it is real. God keeps a kindness back even for a weak and faithless king.

For I have spoken the word. And the guarantee is the same one attached to every threat in this book: For I have spoken the word. The promise of the funeral rests on exactly the same authority as the promise of the fire.

Did this promise fail? Zedekiah was promised to die “in peace”, yet he was blinded and died in prison (52:11). Some take the promise as conditional on his obeying (vv. 2–5; 38:17–18): he refused, and so lost it. Others read “in peace” as meaning not by the sword, with mourning rites, which he may have received in Babylon. This commentary prefers the second reading, since verse 5 contrasts his death with the sword and speaks of the mourning itself; but the appeal in Yet hear the word of the LORD also shows how much more he could have had if he had listened.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem, when the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, Lachish and Azekah, for these were the only fortified cities of Judah that remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words. He delivered the funeral and the fire, the concession and the sentence, without editing either half to suit the audience. It is the same obedience as chapter 26: do not hold back a word.

Lachish and Azekah. Two names, and they date the scene precisely. Lachish and Azekah were the last strongpoints in the Judean lowlands, and archaeologists digging at Lachish found in a guardroom a group of ostraca, letters written on pottery by officers in these final months. One of them reports that the writer could no longer see the signals of Azekah, which many take to mean that Azekah had already fallen.

A kingdom reduced. The kingdom has been reduced to a capital and two garrisons, the beacons are going out one by one, and in that atmosphere the king of Judah decides to do something religious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — The Proclamation and the Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah covenants to free every Hebrew slave, the people obey, and then they take them back (vv. 8–11). God answers from the exodus and the law of release (vv. 12–14): they had repented, and then profaned his name (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform lasted exactly as long as the siege did.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them, that everyone should set free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. And they obeyed, all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant that everyone would set free his slave, male or female, so that they would not be enslaved again. They obeyed and set them free. But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free, and brought them into subjection as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. For one moment, Judah does the right thing. This is a genuine reform, formally covenanted, and its wording is beautiful: no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. The word brother is the argument. A fellow Israelite is not labour to be owned; he is family.

Why they did it. The motive was very probably the siege. With the enemy at the wall, freeing slaves put more men on the ramparts and fewer mouths in private households, and a public act of obedience might move God to relent. Repentance under pressure is still repentance, and God takes it at face value in verse 15.

They obeyed and set them free. They obeyed, says the narrator, twice, in a book where nobody obeys anything. For a short while in the last months of Judah, the law of Moses was actually kept in Jerusalem. Then they took them back. Men and women who had walked out of their owners' houses, perhaps found family and started to plan a life, were rounded up and put back. Somebody had to go and fetch them. It is one thing never to free a slave; it is another to free him, watch him taste it, and then take it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I myself made a covenant with your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying, 'At the end of seven years each of you must set free the fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you six years; you must set him free from your service.' But your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the house of slavery. God's answer begins with the exodus, and the phrase he chooses cuts deepest: out of the house of slavery. He is talking to slave-owners who have just re-enslaved their brothers, and he identifies himself as the God who empties houses of slavery.

The shape of a freed life. Everything Israel possessed came out of that rescue; the law of release was the shape of life for people God had already freed. To hold a fellow Hebrew in bondage was to contradict the event that made them a people at all.

At the end of seven years. The law being quoted is Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12: six years of service, release in the seventh, he shall go out free, for nothing (Exod 21:2). It was not an obscure statute. It was one of the first ordinances given after Sinai, designed precisely so that poverty could never become a permanent status in Israel. So At the end of seven years means in the seventh year, after six of service; the two counts agree.

Why did God’s law allow Hebrews to be held as slaves at all? What it regulated was mostly debt-service: a man too poor to pay what he owed sold his labour for a limited term, and the law hedged it round with protections (release in the seventh year, gifts to start again (Deut 15:13–14), no ruling with harshness (Lev 25:43), and death for kidnapping a man to sell him (Exod 21:16)). That is far from the race-based slavery of later centuries. The law did allow foreigners to be held longer (Lev 25:44–46), a concession to a hard world which the gospel undoes by making slave and free one family in Christ (Gal 3:28; Philem 16).

But your fathers did not listen to me. And it had been ignored for centuries: your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me. Zedekiah's proclamation was not an innovation but the overdue obedience of generations, which makes its reversal worse. They restored a law their ancestors had let lapse, and then let it lapse again almost at once.

verseByVerse.quote: You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name, but then you turned around and profaned my name when each of you took back his male and female slaves, whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You recently repented. God gives them full credit for it. You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes. He does not dismiss the reform as insincere theatre, even though the timing was self-interested. It was right, and he says so.

In the house that is called by my name. And the setting is noted: the covenant was made in the house that is called by my name, in the temple, with God as witness to a promise about other people's freedom.

You turned around and profaned my name. The charge is profaned my name. Not merely broke a promise, not merely wronged the poor, but dragged God's reputation through it, because his name had been invoked over the transaction.

Why a broken vow is worse. That is what makes a broken religious commitment different in kind from a broken private one. When a vow is made before God and then reversed, the watching world learns something false about God.

According to their desire. The small phrase according to their desire says much. The freed slaves wanted their freedom. The masters knew it, and took it away anyway.

The freedom we keep for ourselves. It is easy to look down on the slave-owners of Jerusalem. Ours is a culture that prizes freedom above almost everything, and slavery appals us. Yet the 2022 global estimates published by the International Labour Organization and its partners put the number of people in forced labour or forced marriage today at about fifty million, and some of what forced labour makes ends up in our shops at prices we enjoy. The masters in this chapter were not monsters. They had grown used to an arrangement that kept their households comfortable, and when the emergency passed, comfort won. That is the idol beneath the scene: not cruelty but convenience, which will quietly accept someone else’s chains rather than suffer its own inconvenience. The moralist answers with outrage at other people’s sins; the cynic shrugs that this is how the world works. The gospel goes deeper than either, because it shows us a Lord who gave up his own freedom for ours: he emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:7). People set free at that cost cannot be indifferent to who else is still bound.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence is built from their own word, liberty (v. 17), and from the ceremony they used to ratify the covenant (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: They walked between the halves of a dead animal to seal their promise, and became the animal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. And the men who transgressed my covenant and did not keep the terms of the covenant that they made before me, I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts— the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I proclaim to you liberty to the sword. God takes their own word and turns it round, and the result is one of the grimmest lines in Scripture. You would not proclaim liberty, so I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine.

Judgments set free. The sword, plague and famine are given their freedom. The three judgments that have stalked this book are released into the city like slaves let out of a house: the only emancipation Jerusalem will get, because it refused the one it had promised.

Measure for measure. The punishment matches the sin here. Refuse to release, and something else gets released.

The calf that they cut in two. Now we learn how the ceremony had been conducted. They had cut a calf in half, laid the two halves apart, and walked between them, in the oldest and most graphic form of covenant-making, whose meaning is unmistakable: may this be done to me if I break my word. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the words “them like”: it says more bluntly that God will make the men the calf.

The ceremony of Genesis 15. It is the ceremony of Genesis 15. Abram cut the animals and laid the halves against each other (Gen 15:10), and then, in the dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces (Gen 15:17). God walked the path alone, as many read it, taking the curse of the covenant on himself while Abram slept.

All the people of the land who passed between the parts. The list names everyone who took that walk, and the sentence is simply that what they swore should happen to them will happen.

Toward the gospel. And this is where the chapter turns toward the gospel, because there are only two ways the curse of a broken covenant can fall. It can fall on the one who broke it, as here. Or it can fall on someone who walks the bloody path alone in the dark on his behalf, which is what God did for Abram, and what he did at the cross for covenant-breakers who have taken back every freedom they ever promised: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: The rite lies behind the Hebrew idiom for making a covenant, which is literally to “cut” one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Army That Withdrew Will Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unburied bodies (v. 20), and a king handed to the army which has withdrawn (v. 21), the detail that explains the whole chapter. God will command it back (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The relief that made them confident enough to re-enslave their brothers was temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives. Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth. And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you. Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Food for the birds of the air. No burial. The men who had denied their brothers a life will be denied a grave, left in the open for scavengers, the ancient world's picture of total disgrace.

Not according to rank. Set it beside verse 5, where the king is promised spices and mourners. God treats people differently, and not according to rank: the officials of verse 19 are among the unburied.

Which has withdrawn from you. The siege had lifted. Egypt had marched north, and Nebuchadnezzar pulled back to deal with it (37:5), and suddenly the pressure was off. That is when the slaves were taken back. The covenant had been made when the ramps were rising; it was revoked when the dust cleared and the fields were safe to work again.

Religion while frightened. It is a devastating diagnosis of a certain kind of religion: sincere while frightened, and no longer required once the danger passes. The vow made in the hospital corridor, forgotten in the car park. Peter described the pattern bluntly: the last state has become worse for them than the first (2 Pet 2:20).

In practice. Most believers have made a promise to God in a hard week: to give, to forgive, to pray, to stop something. When the pressure lifts, take that promise out and look at it again. When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it (Eccl 5:4). If it was rash, say so to him honestly rather than letting it quietly lapse; if it was right, keep it now that keeping it costs more, especially when it concerns other people, as Judah’s promise concerned real men and women. The point is not to earn favour with kept vows but to honour the name spoken over them, the name of the God who freed you.

Behold, I will command. God recalls the army. I will command: Nebuchadnezzar will think he is choosing his moment, and he will be answering an order he never heard.

Liberty, lost and fulfilled. And the chapter ends by leaving the word liberty ringing. Judah proclaimed it, took it back, and lost everything. The Hebrew word for liberty here is the word for the release of the Jubilee year (Lev 25:10), and Isaiah used it of the anointed one’s mission (Isa 61:1). Centuries later a man stood up in a synagogue in Nazareth, read that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to proclaim liberty to the captives, and told the room it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18). He proclaimed it and did not take it back. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery (Gal 5:1), which is the one warning this chapter exists to give. Christ gives the freedom, and his Spirit, not our nerve under pressure, is what keeps us in it (Gal 5:16).

34.title: Liberty Proclaimed and Taken Back
34.overview: The armies of the whole empire are at the walls, and Jeremiah brings King Zedekiah a word that gives and takes at once: capture, and yet a death in peace (vv. 1-7). Then comes the story the chapter is really about. Under pressure of the siege, king and people covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew slaves, they obey, and as soon as the Babylonian army withdraws they take them back (vv. 8-11). God answers from the exodus and the law of release, and turns their own word, liberty, and their own covenant ceremony against them (vv. 12-22).
34.theology: God credits repentance honestly, even when it comes under pressure (v. 15), but a vow made in his name and then reversed profanes that name (v. 16), and a religion that lasts only while the danger lasts is exposed the moment the siege lifts (v. 21). The punishment matches the sin: refuse to release, and God releases sword, famine and pestilence instead. Above all, the chapter shows that the curse of a broken covenant falls either on the breaker or on a substitute. The covenant-breakers are made like the calf they cut in two and walked between (v. 18); God walked that path alone for Abram in the dark (Gen 15:17), and Christ bore the curse at the cross (Gal 3:13). Liberty proclaimed and withdrawn by Judah is proclaimed and never withdrawn by him (Luke 4:18; Gal 5:1).
34.examples: Somebody had to go and fetch the freed slaves back, and that small detail is the measure of the chapter: freedom given, tasted, and taken from people who plainly wanted it. The same pattern shows in the promise made to God in a hospital corridor and forgotten in the car park, and in any kindness that lasts only as long as we feel we need God's help.

35.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."<sup>3</sup>So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites.<sup>4</sup>I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold.<sup>5</sup>Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."<sup>6</sup>But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever.<sup>7</sup>You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'<sup>8</sup>We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters,<sup>9</sup>and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed,<sup>10</sup>but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us.<sup>11</sup>But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."<sup>12</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD.<sup>14</sup>The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.<sup>15</sup>I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."<sup>18</sup>But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you,<sup>19</sup>therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Wine Set Before the Rechabites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jehoiakim's reign God tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabite clan into a temple chamber and set wine before them (vv. 1–5).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet sets out drinks in the temple and presses them on men he knows will refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the days of Jehoiakim. The date takes us back. Jehoiakim died in about 598 BC, and the raiders named in verse 11 (compare 2 Kgs 24:2) probably place this episode in his last years, so it belongs some ten years before the siege chapters on either side of it. The book is arranged by theme here rather than by calendar, and this chapter has been placed next to the broken covenant of chapter 34 for a reason: there, men who promised obedience to God went back on it almost at once; here, men who never promised God anything have kept their word for generations.

Then offer them wine to drink. It is one of the strangest commands given to any prophet. Fetch a particular family, take them into the temple, and put wine in front of them.

Theatre for Judah. God knows exactly what will happen. This is not a test of the Rechabites, who are in no danger of failing it; it is a piece of theatre with an audience in mind, and the audience is Judah. Jeremiah has smashed a flask and worn a yoke; now the visual aid is a group of tent-dwellers who never touch wine, and a tray of drinks.
verseByVerse.note: Jonadab appears in 2 Kings 10:15-16; the clan's tents and abstinence are explained in verses 6 to 10 below.

verseByVerse.quote: So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites. I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold. Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah. Names, and a whole household: brothers, sons, the entire clan. Their head's father happens to share the prophet's name, which is a coincidence the narrator lets stand.

Who were they? Descendants of Jonadab son of Rechab, and that man appears once elsewhere in Scripture, riding in Jehu's chariot during the purge of Baal worship. Jehu asked him, Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?, and then said Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD (2 Kgs 10:15-16). So the family's founder was a man known for his allegiance, two and a half centuries before this scene.

The chamber of the sons of Hanan. The address is given with a surveyor's precision: whose room, next to which, above which. The point of the detail is that this happened somewhere real, with officials in the adjoining rooms who could look in.

Pitchers full of wine, and cups. Not a token glass. Pitchers full of wine, and cups, laid out properly, with a prophet of the LORD in the temple of the LORD telling them to help themselves.

Drink wine. Every pressure in the scene runs one way. The setting is sacred, the host is a man of God, the invitation is direct, and refusing would look rude and possibly impious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — We Will Drink No Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They decline, citing their father Jonadab's rule: no wine, no houses, no fields, tents only (vv. 6–10), with one honest exception, the flight into Jerusalem from the Chaldean army (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Two and a half centuries of obedience to a man none of them had ever met.

verseByVerse.quote: But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever. You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
We will drink no wine. They do not hesitate and they do not argue. They simply cite their father.

For Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us. What they do not say matters. They do not claim wine is evil, or that God forbade it, or that they are holier for abstaining. Their whole reason is that Jonadab told them not to. Their obedience does not need a justification beyond the person who gave the command.

You shall live in tents all your days. The rule is wider than drink. No houses, no crops, no vineyards, tents only. It is a deliberate refusal of settled life, and the likeliest reason is spiritual: Canaanite religion was bound up with agriculture, with Baal as the god of rain and harvest, and a family that owned no fields had less to be tempted by. The tents kept them strangers.

That you may live many days in the land where you sojourn. And a purpose is attached: that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn. Even the word sojourn concedes that the land was not theirs. The Rechabites were resident aliens who had made peace with never settling down.

A family rule, not God’s law. It must be said plainly that God nowhere commanded this. It is a family rule, not a law of Moses. Scripture does record a God-given abstinence, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, in which a man shall separate himself from wine and strong drink (Num 6:2-3), but that was voluntary, usually temporary, and instituted by God. Nothing here is being held up as a standard for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters, and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed, but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us. But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters. The report is in the plural and covers everybody: wives, sons, daughters. This was not one impressive individual but a culture, handed down until it was simply how the family lived.

We have no vineyard or field or seed. And it cost them. We have no vineyard or field or seed is a statement of poverty. Generation after generation watched their neighbours plant, harvest, build and inherit, and stayed in tents.

We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab. The verb obeyed appears again, and it is the word the whole chapter turns on. In a book where Judah has not obeyed anything, here is a family whose summary of two and a half centuries is: we did what we were told.

So we are living in Jerusalem. And here they volunteer the exception, which is the most attractive thing about them. They are not in a tent as they speak; they are inside city walls, in a room in the temple, because an army was in the countryside.

Intelligent obedience. They do not pretend otherwise and God does not reproach them for it. Their obedience was intelligent rather than wooden: the rule existed to keep them separate from Canaan's settled religion, not to get them killed by Babylonian cavalry. That distinction, between the purpose of a command and its letter, is one that Judah’s own worshippers in the temple had never learned to make.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Will You Not Receive Instruction?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the sermon the scene was arranged for (v. 13): Jonadab's command has been kept, but God has spoken persistently and Judah has not listened (vv. 14–15), so the disaster comes (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: A dead man's house rule was kept for centuries; the living God's word was not kept for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD. The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? The sermon begins, and the Rechabites were never the subject; they were the exhibit. The question is put to Judah with the tray of untouched wine still in the room.

They drink none to this day. On one side: a command from a man long dead, about a matter of no moral weight, with no penalty attached, kept for eight or nine generations. On the other: the word of the living God, on matters of life and death, backed by every warning and every mercy, delivered persistently by prophet after prophet, and ignored.

No excuse of difficulty. The argument is not that the Rechabites were righteous. It is that Judah cannot plead difficulty. Obedience across centuries is evidently possible, because a family of nomads managed it over wine. What Judah lacked was not capacity but willingness, and the untouched pitchers proved it in front of witnesses.

The obedient Son. The scene leaves a question over the whole Old Testament: will anyone ever answer God's voice with a whole heart? The New Testament's answer is the Son. Jesus could say, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), and he learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8), all the way to the cross. The Rechabites kept a father's rule about wine; Christ kept his Father's whole will, and by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19).

How do I listen to his words? Judah heard the prophets for years and listened to none of them. Listening, in this chapter, means letting the word decide what you do. Give it a fixed place. The Rechabites kept their rule every day; give Scripture a regular time, before the phone and the news, not whenever there is room. Read for a reply. Ask of each passage what God is saying about himself, and what one thing he is telling you to stop, start or trust today. Answer the first time. When a verse touches the sharp remark you made at work or the money you have been holding back, act that day; the danger here is the habit of hearing without moving (Jas 1:22). Listen with others. Sit under preaching, and let a friend ask what you are doing about it (Heb 3:13). And listen as a child, not a slave. Christ has already given the Father the whole obedience Judah withheld, and his voice now comes to us as a shepherd’s: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (John 10:27).

verseByVerse.quote: I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me. The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me. Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn now every one of you from his evil way. The message had been reasonable. Not a demand for tents or abstinence, but Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, with the promise of keeping the land attached. God asked less of Judah than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more for compliance.

Sending them persistently. And the word persistently appears a second time in three verses. This is the sorrow of the whole book: God as the sender who will not stop sending.

This people has not obeyed me. The charge is not that they failed to keep a code, but that this people has not obeyed me. Disobedience in this book is always personal. God does not list idols or injustices here, though the book has catalogued both. The charge is simply that he kept speaking and calling, and they never replied: two attempts, two silences. Behind it stands a God who, after centuries of being ignored, is still the one doing the talking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–19 — Never Lack a Man to Stand Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last word is a blessing on the visual aid. Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you (v. 18), God promises: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The same promise given to David's throne and Levi's altar, handed to a clan from outside the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you, therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But to the house of the Rechabites. Before the chapter closes God speaks to the Rechabites themselves, who until now have served only as an illustration, beginning with a full recital of what they did right.

Shall never lack a man. Weigh that promise against the one given two chapters earlier. David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne, and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence (33:17-18). The formula is identical, and here it is given to a clan that was not one of the twelve tribes at all, most likely a family of Kenite outsiders (1 Chr 2:55), attached to Israel but not descended from Jacob.

To stand before me. And to stand before me is priestly language, the posture of a servant in the sanctuary. Outsiders are promised a permanent place in God's presence in the same breath that insiders are told their city will burn. The book has been moving this way for a while, and it is where the gospel goes: a household with no tribal claim, blessed for faithfulness, given standing before God. In Christ, people who were once strangers to the covenants of promise become fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph 2:12, 19).

What the tents preached. Their tents turn out to have been preaching all along. Abraham had lived the same way, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, because he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Heb 11:9-10). Men who refused to build houses were saying, for two hundred and fifty years, that they were not home yet.

What this chapter does not teach. And a last word so nobody mistakes the lesson. This chapter is not a call to give up wine or to live in tents. God never issued the Rechabite rule, and the Lord himself warned about the trick of treating human tradition as divine command: So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God (Matt 15:6). He came eating and drinking and was slandered for it, while John came eating no bread and drinking no wine and was called demon-possessed (Luke 7:33-34): the same crowd finding fault either way. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17). The pitchers were only ever a mirror, and the question they asked was never about wine: he has spoken to you persistently. Have you answered? The same God who kept calling Judah still calls the one who has not answered, not to be scolded but to come home, and the Spirit he gives is what turns a deaf ear into a listening one (Ezek 36:27).

35.title: The Rechabites
35.overview: This chapter steps back about ten years, to the reign of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah sets wine before the Rechabites, a clan who for generations have kept their ancestor's rule of no wine, no houses and no fields (vv. 1-11). Their refusal becomes a living sermon to Judah: a dead man's house rule has been kept for centuries, while the living God's word has been ignored (vv. 12-17). The chapter ends with a blessing on the Rechabites themselves (vv. 18-19).
35.theology: The chapter makes a comparison; it does not lay down a rule. God never gave the Rechabite rule, and it is held up as an example of constancy, not as a standard of holiness (Matt 15:6; Rom 14:17). Its point is that Judah cannot plead difficulty: God asked less of them than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more. Disobedience is personal; God spoke and called, and they neither listened nor answered. And the outsiders are given the promise made to David's throne and Levi's altar, never to lack a man to stand before God, while the insiders are told their city will burn, which is the direction the gospel takes (Eph 2:12, 19).
35.examples: The scene is a mirror held up to anyone who keeps a family custom, a sports routine or a work habit with perfect discipline while leaving God's plain word unanswered. The Rechabites' tents also have something to say: like Abraham's, they told the neighbours for two hundred and fifty years that this family was not home yet (Heb 11:9-10).
