You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities.<sup>7</sup>It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people."<sup>8</sup>And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.<sup>9</sup>In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD.<sup>10</sup>Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house.<sup>11</sup>When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,<sup>12</sup>he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials.<sup>13</sup>And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people.<sup>14</sup>Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.<sup>15</sup>And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them.<sup>16</sup>When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king."<sup>17</sup>Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"<sup>18</sup>Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll."<sup>19</sup>Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."<sup>20</sup>So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king.<sup>21</sup>Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king.<sup>22</sup>It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.<sup>23</sup>As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot.<sup>24</sup>Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.<sup>25</sup>Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them.<sup>26</sup>And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.<sup>27</sup>Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>28</sup>"Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.<sup>29</sup>And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"<sup>30</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night.<sup>31</sup>And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'"<sup>32</sup>Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Write It on a Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jehoiakim's fourth year God tells Jeremiah to write twenty-three years of preaching on a scroll (v. 2), in the hope that Judah may turn and be forgiven (v. 3). Baruch writes it, and since the prophet is banned from the temple, Baruch must read it there (vv. 4–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of sermons copied out, on the chance that somebody might still repent.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today. It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The fourth year of Jehoiakim is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the power every nation in the region had to reckon with. And Jeremiah is told to make a book.

From the days of Josiah until today. Count the span: from the days of Josiah until today. He had begun in Josiah's thirteenth year, so this is twenty-three years of preaching to be collected into one document: the sermons nobody acted on, gathered up and written down.

It may be. And here is why God wanted it written, in words that should govern how the whole book is read: It may be.

That I may forgive their iniquity and their sin. The scroll is not an archive for the record, or evidence for the prosecution. It is an attempt. The aim is that they might turn, and the goal beyond that is forgiveness: that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin. Every threat in the collection exists to make the pardon possible.

A sincere offer. “It may be that they will turn” (v. 3): God knows the end, but he speaks to people as responsible beings, and his call to repent is real. His foreknowledge never makes the offer insincere.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah's call had come in Josiah's thirteenth year, 627 BC (1:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him. And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the dictation of Jeremiah. Jeremiah spoke, Baruch wrote, and the prophetic word is moving from air into text, where it can be carried, copied, read in rooms the prophet cannot enter, and survive him. This chapter is the Bible describing its own production.

I am banned from going to the house of the LORD. Baruch must do the reading because Jeremiah is banned. The prophet is barred from the temple, presumably since the trial of chapter 26, or the confrontation of chapter 20.

Routing around the ban. So the man with the message cannot reach the place where the crowds are. And God's response to that obstacle is not to remove it but to route around it: if the preacher is banned, send the book.
verseByVerse.note: Baruch was Jeremiah’s scribe and friend.

verseByVerse.quote: so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities. It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people." And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a day of fasting. The instructions are strategic. A fast day, when the temple is full and the mood is already serious, and an audience including country people up from the towns. One reading will reach as many people as possible.

What is asked of Baruch. Consider what is asked of Baruch. He is to stand in the temple and read aloud a document predicting national ruin, in the name of a man the king has banned, to a crowd that has beaten and imprisoned that man before. The scribe is taking the prophet’s risk, though God had called Jeremiah to this work and not him.

It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD. It may be, a second time, now on Jeremiah's own lips. He had no illusions left about his audience and he still would not close the door.

Great is the anger and wrath. He holds out that hope and announces the sentence in the same breath: great is the anger and wrath. Faithful preaching does both, because the severity is exactly what makes the appeal urgent.

Baruch did all of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — Read It to the Officials
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On a fast day Baruch reads the scroll in the temple (vv. 9–10); word reaches the officials, who hear it read, turn to one another in fear and resolve to tell the king (vv. 11–18). First they tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The civil servants were frightened by the book, and warned the men who wrote it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD. Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house. When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the ninth month. A year has passed between the command and the reading: the scroll took time to write, and the right day had to come. The fast in the ninth month was probably called because of Babylon; fear makes people religious, as chapter 34 showed.

The chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan. The location is given exactly, and two details in it carry weight. The chamber belongs to a son of Shaphan, that family again, whose members keep turning up on the right side of this story, as Ahikam did when he saved Jeremiah's life (26:24). Somebody sympathetic lent Baruch a room.

A seal from the City of David. A clay seal impression reading “Gemaryahu son of Shaphan” was found in excavations in the City of David in the 1980s. Many think it belonged to this very man, though that cannot be proved.

At the entry of the New Gate. And it stands at the entry of the New Gate, which is where the officials had convened the court that acquitted Jeremiah (26:10). The book is being read at the spot where its author was once tried.

Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan. Three generations of the same family are named across these verses (Shaphan, Gemariah, Micaiah), and the young man who hears the reading does not shrug it off. He goes to tell the government.

verseByVerse.quote: he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials. And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people. Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the officials were sitting there. A cabinet meeting, with the members listed by name. These lists are not padding; they are the marks of eyewitness testimony.

Elnathan the son of Achbor. One name should stop us: Elnathan the son of Achbor. He is the man Jehoiakim sent to Egypt to extradite the prophet Uriah, who was brought back and executed (26:22-23). In a few verses he will be one of three men urging the king not to burn this scroll. People are not always consistent, and God uses them at the point where they are willing.

Took the scroll in his hand and came to them. A summons from the government, and Baruch goes, carrying the evidence against himself in his own hand. He could have hidden it or left it behind. He takes it to the palace because he was asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them. When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king." Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sit down and read it. They want to hear the whole thing, not a summary, and they give the scribe a chair. It is the second public reading of the day.

They turned one to another in fear. And this is the reaction the book has been waiting twenty-three years to record. They turned one to another in fear. Not agreement necessarily, not repentance yet, but men visibly shaken by what they have heard, looking at each other because it is too much to absorb alone.

We must report all these words to the king. Their instinct is that the king must hear it. They are not trying to suppress the document; they are ordinary officials doing their job well, and God's word is making its way up through a bureaucracy.

How did you write all these words? The question is the mark of serious men. How did you write all these words? They want to know where it came from: is this really Jeremiah's, and how did it get onto the page?

verseByVerse.quote: Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll." Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dictated all these words to me. The answer is unglamorous and precise: he spoke, I wrote, with ink.

A doctrine of Scripture. There is a doctrine sitting in that sentence. The words are God's, given to a prophet, spoken to a scribe, and fixed in ink by an ordinary man doing careful work, and the humanity of the process takes nothing away from the divinity of the words. All Scripture is breathed out by God (2 Tim 3:16), and this chapter shows what that looked like from the inside: a voice, a pen, a bottle of ink, a long labour.

Go and hide, you and Jeremiah. They know their king. Before they walk into his presence with this, they tell the two men to disappear, and they tell them properly: hide, and let no one know where you are, so that no official, under pressure, can give them away.

Courage with careers at stake. It is a small act of courage from men with careers to protect. God's care for his servants keeps arriving in this book through people who decide to act decently at some cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Knife and a Fire Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiakim has the scroll read to him by the winter fire and cuts it up column by column into the flames, unafraid (vv. 20–24). Three men urge him not to; he orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hid them (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: He listened to three or four columns at a time, and only long enough to know what to cut off.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king. Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king. It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama. They leave the scroll behind in a side room, perhaps hoping a verbal report would be enough, and the document itself might survive.

The king sent Jehudi to get the scroll. Jehoiakim will not have it second-hand. He sends for the scroll and has it read aloud, and the detail that the officials stood beside the king while he sat shows how a royal court worked: everyone else on their feet, the king in his chair by the fire.

A fire burning in the fire pot before him. The scene is set with a novelist's economy. The ninth month, around December, the winter palace, a brazier of coals at the king's feet, and a man standing in front of him unrolling the word of God. The narrator lets us see the fire before the king uses it.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot. Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king would cut them off with a knife. Notice the wording: would cut them off describes something done again and again. This was not one hot-blooded gesture. It was repeated the whole length of a long document: listen to three or four columns, slice them off with a knife, feed them to the coals, listen again.

Attention worse than neglect. He heard every word. He simply destroyed each section as soon as he had heard it. There is a kind of attention paid here that is worse than not listening at all: the deliberate, unhurried, methodical disposal of God's word by a man warm and comfortable in his winter room.

Yet neither the king nor any of his servants. Now set this against the officials in Elishama's chamber, who turned one to another in fear. Same words, opposite response.

Nor did they tear their garments. And set it against his father. Some eighteen years earlier a scroll had been found in this same temple and read to King Josiah, and When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes (2 Kgs 22:11). That tearing began the last reformation Judah ever had.

Father and son. Josiah tore his robe at the word of God. His son took a knife to the word of God and kept his robe intact. The two men are father and son, the two scrolls were read in the same city, and everything that follows in the history of Judah runs out of that difference.

In practice. Few readers take a knife to a Bible, but the same thing can be done quietly: skipping the passages that unsettle us, reading with our conclusions already fixed, or hearing a sermon only to decide which parts to discard. Josiah’s way is open to anyone. When a passage finds you out, stop there, admit to God that it is true, and ask what he wants changed, without dread, because the word that exposes was given that I may forgive (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them. And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king. Three men speak up, and they are named so that we know somebody in that room tried. Elnathan, who had once been the instrument of a prophet's death; Delaiah; Gemariah, in whose son's hearing the scroll had first been read.

He would not listen to them. It is the verdict of the whole book, applied here to a man refusing not a prophet but his own advisers. By this point Jehoiakim will not hear God, will not hear Jeremiah, and will not hear the officials he appointed.

To seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet. Burning the book is not enough; he wants the men. A royal prince and two officers are detailed to find them, with the same energy that once sent an extradition party to Egypt after Uriah.

But the LORD hid them. And then five words end the paragraph: but the LORD hid them. No angel, no miracle described, no method given. The officials had said go and hide; the narrator says God hid them. Both are true, and that is usually how providence looks: sensible advice taken, a friend's back room, and behind it all a hand the searchers never see.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's answer is immediate: write it again (v. 28). The king is sentenced for the burning (vv. 29–31), and the scroll is rewritten with many words added (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The book came back longer than the one he burned.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned. And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after the king had burned the scroll. The king destroys the words, and the word comes again. That sequence is the point of the chapter, and the narrator does not even pause over it.

Take another scroll. The instruction is almost dismissive in its simplicity. Write it again.

The word cannot be burned. A book can be burned; the word it carries cannot. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8), and the Lord Jesus said the same of his own words: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matt 24:35). Peter quotes Isaiah's line and then says what that enduring word is: And this word is the good news that was preached to you (1 Pet 1:25). Every regime that has since burned Bibles has been doing what Jehoiakim did in a warm room in winter, with the same result.

So he came back from the grave. The pattern reached its end in Jesus. The God who spoke at many times and in many ways by the prophets has in these last days spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:1-2), and Jesus told the parable of the vineyard owner who sent servant after servant and at last his beloved son, whom the tenants killed (Mark 12:1-8). The rulers of his day dealt with God's final word as Jehoiakim dealt with the scroll: they heard him out, and then got rid of him. And as the scroll came back, so he came back from the grave, and the message they tried to silence went out to the nations.

You have burned this scroll. God quotes the king's objection back at him, and the offence, it turns out, was specific. Not the moral demands, not the accusations of injustice, but the prediction about Babylon. He burned the scroll because of its politics.

Burning a forecast does not alter the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night. And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'" Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heat by day and the frost by night. The sentence answers the crime in kind. He fed the scroll to the fire in his warm room; his own body will lie out in the open, in the heat by day and the frost by night.

He shall have none to sit on the throne of David. Both parts of the sentence, the unburied body and the empty throne, had been announced before. Jeremiah had already said of this king that With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem (22:19), and of his son Coniah that none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David (22:30). His son Jehoiachin reigned three months and was deported, and no son of his ever sat on that throne.

How then is Jesus David’s heir? Readers ask how Jesus can then be David's heir, when Matthew's genealogy runs through Jeconiah, that is Jehoiachin (Matt 1:11-12). The sentence meant that no son of this line would reign on David's throne in Jerusalem, and none ever did. But God had not abandoned David: he had already promised a righteous Branch who would reign (23:5-6; 33:15), and Jesus, David's son through Joseph as his legal father, reigns not from Jehoiakim's palace but from the right hand of God (Acts 2:30-36).

But they would not hear. The last clause is the epitaph of the whole reign: but they would not hear. Everything else in the verse is consequence; this is the cause.

Then Jeremiah took another scroll. So they sat down and did it all over again: the same long labour, voice and pen and ink, with a price now on both their heads.

And many similar words were added to them. And the final clause is the quiet triumph of the chapter: And many similar words were added to them. The second edition was longer. Everything Jehoiakim had cut off came back, and more with it, including the paragraph about his own corpse that only exists because he burned the first one. He could not even succeed in making the book shorter.

The book we are reading. What he held in his hands that December was the book we are reading. It survived him, outlasted his dynasty, outlasted Babylon, and is still being read aloud in rooms full of people, which is what it was written for in the first place: It may be that someone will hear, and turn, and be forgiven.

Did he have a donkey’s burial? Jehoiakim was to have the burial of a donkey, yet Kings says he slept with his fathers (2 Kgs 24:6). That phrase means simply that he died; it says nothing of honourable burial. He probably died in late 598 BC, as the Babylonian army closed in. Chronicles adds that Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chr 36:6), which may never have been carried out. Scripture does not describe what was done with his body, but this commentary takes Jeremiah's word as fulfilled.

36.title: The Scroll Burned and Rewritten
36.overview: In 605 BC, the year Babylon became master of the region, God has Jeremiah dictate twenty-three years of preaching to Baruch, in the hope that Judah may yet turn and be forgiven (vv. 1-8). Baruch reads the scroll in the temple and then to the shaken royal officials, who send him and Jeremiah into hiding (vv. 9-19). King Jehoiakim hears it by his winter fire and burns it column by column, but the LORD hides his servants (vv. 20-26), and the scroll is written again, with more added (vv. 27-32).
36.theology: God's purpose in writing down the threats is repentance and pardon, not record-keeping: it may be that they will turn. When the preacher is barred, God sends the book, and the word moves from air into ink so that it can enter rooms the prophet cannot and outlive the men who carry it (2 Tim 3:16). Attention is not obedience: Jehoiakim heard every column and destroyed each one, while his father Josiah had torn his clothes at a scroll. And a book can be burned, but the word cannot; it came back longer, as Jesus, God’s final Word, came back from the grave (Matt 24:35; Mark 12:1-8).
36.examples: The officials who warned Baruch and Jeremiah to hide had careers to protect, and still did what was decent; much of God's care for his servants in this book arrives that way. Jehoiakim's knife is the opposite: the reader who hears the Bible out, column by column, only to know which parts to cut away.

And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah, Babylon's appointee, does not listen (vv. 1–2), yet he asks the still-free prophet to pray for them (vv. 3–4), just as an Egyptian army draws the Chaldeans away from Jerusalem (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: They will not hear a word he says, and they would like him to pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim. But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king. Verse 1 tells you everything about his position. He is Josiah’s son, so he is of David’s royal line, but he sits on the throne because a foreign emperor put him there, in place of a nephew who was deported. He reigns only by another king’s permission.

A king without authority. That is the man the rest of this chapter shows us: a king with a title and no authority, frightened of his own officials, frightened of Babylon, and half-persuaded that Jeremiah is right.

Neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened. Before a single event is narrated, the narrator gives the verdict, and it covers the whole society: the king, the civil service, and the ordinary population. Nobody listened.

The chapter’s real subject. Put that verdict beside what happens next and the chapter's real subject appears. This is a study of what religion looks like in people who have already decided not to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God." Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison. The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Please pray for us to the LORD our God. A polite request for intercession, one verse after we are told this king listens to nothing the prophet says. Weigh the phrase the LORD our God. They claim him as theirs while ignoring his word, and they want his power without his instruction, as if prayer were a service the prophet provides, detached from the message the prophet brings.

Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest. Both messengers have histories. Zephaniah son of Maaseiah had come on this same errand once before, when Zedekiah sent to say Inquire of the LORD for us (21:2), and he was the priest who read Shemaiah's hostile letter aloud to Jeremiah rather than acting on it (29:29). Jehucal will shortly stand in front of the king demanding this prophet's death, on the ground that he is weakening the hands of the soldiers (38:4). The man who carries the prayer request is the man who will call for the execution.

He had not yet been put in prison. The words not yet been put in prison (v. 4) quietly warn us of what is coming. And here is why the palace suddenly wants prayer, and why it is about to stop wanting it. Pharaoh Hophra (almost certainly the king of 44:30) has marched north, Nebuchadnezzar has broken off the siege to deal with him, and the pressure is off.

They withdrew from Jerusalem. This is the same withdrawal named three chapters earlier, the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you (34:21): the breathing space in which the slave-owners of Jerusalem went and fetched back the people they had just freed. The same lifted siege that produced the broken covenant produced this request for prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Hophra reigned in Egypt from 589 to 570 BC; his name appears in Scripture only at 44:30.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer is unwelcome: Egypt will go home and the Chaldeans will come back and burn the city (vv. 7–8). Do not deceive yourselves (v. 9): even wounded Babylonians would rise and burn it (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The outcome was never a military calculation, so a lifted siege proves nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet: "Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land. And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is about to return to Egypt. They asked for prayer; they get a word. God answers the request, and the answer is not the one they wanted. It begins by dismantling the very thing that had raised their spirits: the relieving army is going home. Not defeated in a great battle, just about to return: the help everyone was counting on will simply turn around and leave.

An old sickness. Judah's reliance on Egypt was an old sickness. Isaiah had named it a century before: men who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt (Isa 30:2), and who would find that the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame (Isa 30:3).

They shall capture it and burn it with fire. Come back, capture, burn: the empty siege lines are a pause, not a deliverance, and God says so before anyone can conclude from the good news that he has rescued them.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away. For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not deceive yourselves. The command is about the inside of their heads: Do not deceive yourselves.

The Chaldeans will surely go away from us. Nobody was lying to them here. They were doing it themselves, and they were doing it with evidence: the army really had gone, the fields really were passable again, the relief was real. Self-deception rarely needs false facts; it only needs true facts read the way we want them read. God even supplies the sentence they were saying to each other, in quotation marks, and answers it directly: for they will not go away. The cure is not sharper willpower but letting God's word, which knows the exact form our wish has taken, tell us the truth; he says hard things to people he means to save.

Shouldn’t I live by my own truth? We now speak easily of “my truth”, and there is something right in it: each of us has a story only we can tell. But the phrase slides from my experience to my reality, as if believing something hard enough could make it so. Jerusalem had its own truth: the Babylonians had gone, the fields were open, the worst was over. They had evidence, and they had each other, and none of it moved the army one mile. In The Brothers Karamazov Dostoevsky gives the old monk Zosima a warning about exactly this: above all, do not lie to yourself, because the one who listens to his own lie ends up unable to see any truth, in himself or around him. And the deepest reason we lie to ourselves is that the truth about us is more than we can bear. That is why the gospel is the one safe place to stop pretending. It tells us the truth about ourselves at its worst, and then shows us a Saviour who knew all of it and came for us anyway. You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free (John 8:32).

How do I stop deceiving myself? The New Testament repeats the warning, because the heart has not changed: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8). Notice the sentence you keep repeating. “It will blow over.” “Everyone does this.” “I can stop whenever I like.” Judah’s was The Chaldeans will surely go away from us; write yours down and hold it up against Scripture. Ask God to search you. Pray Search me, O God, and know my heart! (Ps 139:23), especially about the thing you least want to look at: the overdraft, the drinking, the friendship that has gone wrong. Let someone tell you the truth. Give one honest friend permission to say what they see, and do not argue the first time they do. Remember why you can afford to look. We deceive ourselves to escape a verdict. For those in Christ the verdict has already fallen, on him, so you can face the worst about yourself without being destroyed by it. The truth that exposes you is the same truth that forgives you.

Only wounded men, every man in his tent. The picture is deliberately extreme. Suppose you won. Suppose the entire Babylonian army lay wounded in their tents. Those men would get up and burn Jerusalem anyway.

God’s decision, not military strength. That is not a comment on Babylonian toughness. It is a statement that the fall of this city is God's decision, and therefore no army can overturn it. This war was never going to be decided by military strength.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaving for Benjamin during the lull, Jeremiah is arrested at the gate as a deserter (vv. 11–14), beaten, and held many days in the dungeon cells (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Forty years of being called a traitor, and when the charge is finally laid it is false.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army, Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people. When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans." And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To receive his portion there among the people. With the roads briefly open, the prophet goes home to Anathoth on family business, to receive his portion there among the people: some matter of inherited land. Scripture does not say what, though it may have been the same family property his cousin Hanamel would later offer him (32:6-9).

It is an ordinary errand, and that is what makes what follows so bitter.

A sentry there named Irijah. A sentry with a name and a grandfather, doing what sentries do in a war. And the charge was not absurd on its face: Jeremiah had publicly advised the city to surrender, telling them that whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live (21:9). A man with those views, walking out of the north gate during a lull, looked exactly like a defector.

It is a lie. The denial is blunt and it is true. It is a lie. For nearly forty years he had been called a traitor for telling Judah what God said, and when an actual charge of treason was finally laid against him it was false. He had urged surrender because God had spoken, and he was not slipping away himself.

But Irijah would not listen to him. And then the phrase that has echoed through the whole book, now from a soldier at a gate: Irijah would not listen to him. Nobody in this chapter listens to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison. When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials were enraged at Jeremiah. These are not the officials of chapter 26 who convened a fair court, nor those of chapter 36 who trembled at the scroll and told Baruch to hide. A different generation is in office now, and they are enraged.

They beat him and imprisoned him. He is beaten and locked in a private house converted into a jail. There is no trial mentioned, no hearing, no examination of the sentry's claim. The man who had just been asked to pray for the king is flogged by the king's officials.

The dungeon cells. Two details, and they are the whole cost of his obedience in this chapter: dungeon cells, and many days.

What speaking cost him. The narrator does not dwell on it and gives us no lament from the prophet. But this is the same man who had written that God's word was a fire in his bones he could not hold in, and this is what speaking it out cost him: a cellar, for weeks, with no prospect of release and a fair expectation of dying there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Is There Any Word from the LORD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king questions him secretly and gets the same word (v. 17). Only then does Jeremiah plead his own case (vv. 18–20), and he is moved to the court of the guard with a daily loaf until all the bread of the city was gone (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers honestly first and asks for mercy second, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king questioned him secretly in his house. Everything about this interview is furtive. The king has the prophet brought up from the cells and questions him secretly in his house, because he dare not be seen consulting the man his officials have just beaten.

Is there any word from the LORD? His question is one of the saddest in Scripture: Is there any word from the LORD? He has heard the word for years, refused it, imprisoned the man who brought it, and now asks in a private room whether there is any more of it. He wants a different answer, and he asks the one person guaranteed not to give him one.

Jeremiah’s position. And consider Jeremiah's position as he replies. He is standing in front of the only man who can release him, bruised from a beating, expecting to die in a cellar. One softened sentence would have helped his case enormously.

There is. What he says is There is, and then the same sentence that put him where he is: You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. No hedging, no trading. The message did not change because the prophet's circumstances had.

Another prisoner, another ruler. Six hundred years later another prisoner stood in front of another frightened ruler who kept asking questions in private, and there the answer was different: he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed (Matt 27:14). Jeremiah spoke the word and was spared; Jesus, the Word himself, was silent before his judge and was not spared, and it was for us.

Two fair questions. Only after delivering the word does he speak for himself, and both questions are fair.

Where are your prophets who prophesied to you. The first is the protest of an innocent man: What wrong have I done? The second is unanswerable: Where are your prophets, the ones who promised Babylon would never come? They had been believed and he had been beaten, and now the Babylonians were camped in the fields and the optimists had nothing to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there." So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let my humble plea come before you. And here the iron prophet asks for something, courteously and without pretence. Let my humble plea come before you.

Lest I die there. He does not ask for vindication, or for his accusers to be punished, or even for freedom. He asks not to be sent back to that particular cellar, and he says plainly why: lest I die there. There is no false bravery in this. He was afraid of dying in a hole, he said so, and asking a weak king for a small mercy was not beneath him.

They committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. The king does the one decent thing within his power. Not release, for he has not the courage for that, but a transfer to the court of the guard, and a daily loaf.

A loaf of bread was given him daily. Compare the rations another prophet was promised for telling a king the truth: Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water (1 Kgs 22:27). Jeremiah gets a loaf a day from the bakers' street, and it comes through the frightened man who had him beaten.

Until all the bread of the city was gone. Then the clause that quietly measures the whole siege: until all the bread of the city was gone. His provision lasted exactly as long as there was any bread in Jerusalem to be had. God kept him alive on the last supplies of a starving city, one loaf at a time, in a courtyard. And it was in that courtyard, on that daily bread, that he bought the field at Anathoth and was given the promises of chapters 32 and 33.

The answer to his question. Which is the answer to Zedekiah's question, though he never grasped it. Is there any word from the LORD? There was, and the chapters we have just read are it, given to a beaten man on a bread ration, about fields bought again and a righteous Branch for David.

37.title: Arrested at the Benjamin Gate
37.overview: The Babylonian siege has lifted for a time, because an Egyptian army has marched north, and King Zedekiah, who will not listen to Jeremiah, asks him to pray (vv. 1-5). The answer is that Babylon will return and burn the city (vv. 6-10). During the lull Jeremiah is arrested at the city gate as a deserter, beaten and thrown into a cellar (vv. 11-16), until the king secretly sends for him, hears the same word again, and moves him to the court of the guard with a daily loaf of bread (vv. 17-21).
37.theology: People who have already decided not to obey still want the benefits of prayer, claiming the LORD as our God while ignoring his word. Self-deception rarely needs false facts, only true facts read as we wish: the siege really had lifted, and the conclusion drawn from it was still a lie. Against this stands a prophet who will not trade the message for better treatment, yet is honest enough to ask for mercy and admit his fear. And God's provision can come through the hand of a frightened man who wronged you, and be exactly enough: a loaf a day, as long as the city had bread.
37.examples: Most of us know the pull of Zedekiah's position: asking God for help in a crisis while having decided in advance not to do what he says. And most of us know the relief that makes us read a lull as a deliverance. Jeremiah's plea not to be sent back to the cellar is a gift to anyone who has been ashamed of being afraid: the bravest prophet in the book asked a weak king for a small mercy, and God gave it through him.

38.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."<sup>4</sup>Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm."<sup>5</sup>King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."<sup>6</sup>So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud.<sup>7</sup>When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate—<sup>8</sup>Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,<sup>9</sup>"My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city."<sup>10</sup>Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."<sup>11</sup>So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes.<sup>12</sup>Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so.<sup>13</sup>Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.<sup>14</sup>King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me."<sup>15</sup>Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me."<sup>16</sup>Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."<sup>17</sup>Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live.<sup>18</sup>But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand."<sup>19</sup>King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."<sup>20</sup>Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared.<sup>21</sup>But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me:<sup>22</sup>Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.'<sup>23</sup>All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."<sup>24</sup>Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die.<sup>25</sup>If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,'<sup>26</sup>then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'"<sup>27</sup>Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard.<sup>28</sup>And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Is in Your Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four officials hear Jeremiah urging surrender (vv. 1–3) and demand his death (v. 4). Zedekiah's reply gives away his whole reign (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A king who cannot say no, and hands over a man he believes to be a prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people: "Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live. Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jucal the son of Shelemiah. Four men, each named with his father, and one of them we have met. Jucal son of Shelemiah is the Jehucal who carried the king's request for prayer to this same prophet one chapter ago (37:3). The man sent to ask for intercession now appears at the head of the party demanding an execution.

Saying to all the people. See also where Jeremiah is and what he is doing. He is confined to the court of the guard, and he is still preaching to all the people. A prison in the middle of a palace compound turned out to be a pulpit.

He who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. This is the word that made him hated, and it pays to be clear about what it actually offered. It was not propaganda for Babylon. It was an escape route: stay and die, go out and live, and live, repeated as if to make sure nobody missed the offer inside the threat.

This city shall surely be given. The offer rests on the fact that the city will certainly fall: that is why leaving it means life. Everything depends on whether what God has announced is true, which is precisely what his hearers would not believe.

His life as a prize of war. This means that he will come out of the disaster alive, and that his life is all he will carry off.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm." King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is weakening the hands of the soldiers. The charge is that he is damaging the soldiers’ will to fight, and on its own terms it is not stupid. A man telling the garrison that the city will fall and they should surrender is, militarily, a liability. Any war cabinet in history would have said the same.

Not seeking the welfare of this people. But listen to the last clause, because it is the exact opposite of the truth: this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm. This is the prophet who had written to the exiles telling them to seek the welfare of the city and pray for it (29:7), who had pleaded with Judah for forty years to turn and live, and who was at that moment offering the only survivable course available. The men who were marching the city into a furnace accused him of wanting its harm.

An accusation with a long life. That accusation has a long life. The person who tells an uncomfortable truth is charged with wishing the harm his warning is trying to prevent.

The king can do nothing against you. The king's plea of powerlessness is one of the most pitiful sentences in the book, and it is not true: he will overrule these same men almost at once when someone asks him to. What he lacks is not authority but nerve. He hands over a man he believes to be a prophet, to men he is afraid of, and consoles himself with the fiction that he had no choice. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov 29:25).

Pilate did the same. Pilate would one day say the same thing by washing his hands before the crowd. He knew the prisoner was innocent, and gave him up because the crowd was louder than his conscience (Matt 27:24; John 19:12-16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Cast Into the Mud, and Lifted Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet is lowered into a muddy cistern (v. 6). Ebed-melech the Ethiopian goes to the king, wins permission (vv. 7–10), and draws Jeremiah up with ropes padded with old rags (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A foreigner and a eunuch, thinking about how the ropes would cut.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud. When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate— Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cistern of Malchiah. A cistern is a bottle-shaped pit cut into rock, narrow at the neck and wide below, designed to hold rainwater. This one held no water, only mud.

Jeremiah sank in the mud. So they lowered him into a stone jar in the ground, in the dark, and he sank in the mud. There is no way out of such a hole without help from above: the walls curve inward and the floor gives way beneath you. They did not need to kill him; they only needed to leave him.

A psalm’s picture of salvation. Hold the image, because a psalm turns it into the picture of salvation itself: He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure (Ps 40:2). That is exactly what is about to happen to Jeremiah, and it is what God does for sinners: not advice shouted down the shaft, but someone coming to haul us out.

Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch. And the rescuer is introduced with three details that in that society were all disqualifications: a foreigner, from Ethiopia, and a eunuch.

The one man who moves. Every Judean official in this chapter behaves badly. The one man who moves is an African court servant who, under the law of Deuteronomy 23:1, could not enter the assembly of the LORD, and he moves immediately: he heard, and then he went. No committee, no delay.
verseByVerse.note: Ebed-melech means “servant of the king”; he was a Cushite, from south of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: "My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city." Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These men have done evil. He says it to the king's face, in public at the Benjamin Gate, with the officials' faction in power and his own position entirely dependent on royal favour: these men have done evil.

There is no bread left in the city. He calls Jeremiah what the officials would not, the prophet, and his argument is practical and humane: the man will starve down there, because there is no bread left in the city. The daily loaf of the previous chapter has run out, which probably places this scene in the last weeks of the siege.

Take thirty men with you. And Zedekiah, who had just said that the king can do nothing, immediately orders thirty men to the rescue. The king could act all along; the difference between a prophet dying in mud and a prophet drawn out of it was one man willing to speak up.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes. Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so. Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rags before ropes. He had his authorisation and thirty men, and before he pulled, he went looking for rags.

Old rags and worn-out clothes. Think about what that means. He detoured to a palace storeroom, found old rags and worn-out clothes, and lowered them down the shaft first, because a man hauled out of a pit on bare ropes, by thirty men pulling hard, would have the rope cut into his armpits.

Put the rags and clothes between your armpits. He even explains the padding to the exhausted man below, telling him exactly where to place it.

Kindness over details. Scripture spends three verses on this. It could have said they pulled him out. Instead it records the wardrobe, the old clothes, the instruction about the armpits, because God takes notice of kindness that troubles itself over details. Anyone can want a man rescued. This is what it looks like to actually care whether the rescue hurts.

Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard. Out of the mud and back to the courtyard: still a prisoner, but alive and above ground.

Ebed-melech’s reward. Ebed-melech is not finished in this book. When the city falls, God sends a private word to him: I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me (39:18). The same phrase offered to anyone who would leave the city is given personally to the man who pulled the prophet out, and the reason given is not his courage but his trust.

A promise for eunuchs. And there is a promise made for men in exactly his position. Isaiah had said: let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree", for God would give such men a monument and a name better than sons and daughters... an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isa 56:3-5). A childless foreign servant has his name written in Scripture, remembered for one day's decency, long after the officials who outranked him are recalled only as the men who did evil.

The promise comes true. The New Testament shows that promise coming true. On a desert road an Ethiopian eunuch, another court official from the same far country, was reading Isaiah's servant song, heard that it spoke of Jesus, and was baptised (Acts 8:26-39). The outsider who pulled a prophet from a pit was a forerunner of a great company of outsiders welcomed into God's household by Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a secret meeting (vv. 14–16) the offer is set out twice: surrender and live with the city spared, or refuse and see it burn (vv. 17–18). The king fears the deserters (v. 19), and a vision answers him (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience was offered to the end, and refused for fear of the wrong people.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me." Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me." Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the third entrance of the temple. Another secret meeting, in a discreet corner of the temple. The king who let him be thrown in a pit wants a private consultation, and he opens with a demand for total honesty from a man he has failed to protect.

If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? The prophet's reply is two accusations, and both are accurate.

If I give you counsel, you will not listen to me. The first is about his own safety; he had just been left to die and had every reason to expect it again. The second is sadder and sharper: if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me. He has read the man. There is no point in advising someone who has already decided that advice will not move him, and Jeremiah says so before he speaks.

As the LORD lives, who made our souls. The oath is solemn and beautifully phrased, As the LORD lives, who made our souls, and it is sworn secretly. A king who dares not be seen keeping faith with a prophet swears by the God who made them both, in a side entrance, where nobody will hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live. But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand." King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Still an offer. And here, in the final weeks, with the walls about to break, God is still making an offer.

This city shall not be burned with fire. Read what is on the table: the king's life, his household, and this city shall not be burned with fire. Jerusalem could still have been spared. The temple need not have burned. Everything depended on one man walking out of a gate.

Two roads. Two roads, stated plainly, with nothing hidden: exactly what the king had asked for. This is the same structure as the whole book: repent and live, refuse and perish, and the choice genuinely open until the last hour.

I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted. And this is his answer to the offer of his city's survival: he is worried about being mocked.

The calculation. The men who had already defected, following Jeremiah's advice, would jeer at the king who arrived last. That is the calculation. Weigh it: Jerusalem burned, the temple destroyed, his sons killed, his own eyes put out, thousands dead of famine, because a frightened man could not bear the humiliation of walking out to people who had gone before him.

What fear of man does. Fear of man does this. It will accept enormous real disaster to avoid a small loss of face, and it always presents itself as prudence. Its cure is not a stronger nerve but a greater fear, of the LORD, who made our souls and still holds out life; and the Spirit given to believers is a Spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control (2 Tim 1:7).

Was the fall certain? The city would certainly fall (v. 3), yet Zedekiah is told it need not burn if he surrenders. The fall was certain, but its manner depended on him: surrender, and the city and his household would be spared the fire. God’s warnings are real, and they call for a response.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared. But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me: Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.' All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not be given to them. The prophet answers the actual fear directly, You shall not be given to them, and then presses the one thing needed: Obey now the voice of the LORD.

It shall be well with you. Note the pastoral patience of it. He does not lecture the king on cowardice. He removes the objection, promises that it shall be well with you, and asks for obedience today.

Now that your feet are sunk in the mud. The vision is of the royal harem marched out of the palace, and the words God gives them are a taunt in verse, the sort of thing that would be sung about him afterwards. Now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you. The king who left a prophet to sink in mud will himself be stuck in it, abandoned by the officials he was too frightened to cross. Jeremiah was pulled out by a foreigner with rags; nobody will come down for Zedekiah.

Your trusted friends have deceived you. His trusted friends, the men whose approval cost him his city, will be the ones who prevailed against you and then walked away. The approval of men had been his idol, and this is what every idol does: it demands everything, and abandons you when you need it.

The cost of refusal. The last word of the appeal is the list of what refusal will cost: wives, sons, his own capture, the city burned. Every item arrived exactly as stated.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah's last concern is secrecy (vv. 24–26); Jeremiah answers the officials as instructed, and stays in the court of the guard until the city falls (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The king protected the secret of the conversation and not the city it was about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die. If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,' then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'" Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one know of these words. The offer of life for his city has just been laid before him, along with the vision of his wives led away. His response is to worry about who might find out that they had spoken.

I made a humble plea to the king. He scripts the answer, and the line he supplies is a real one, the same plea Jeremiah had made to him at their last meeting: do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there (37:20). The king is telling him to give a true statement about an earlier conversation instead of the subject of this one.

Hide nothing from us. The officials, too, will offer Jeremiah the same bargain the king just did: tell us everything and we will not kill you. Everyone in this palace bargains by threatening a man’s life.

He answered them as the king had instructed him. They came, exactly as the king predicted, and Jeremiah answered as instructed. The interrogation stopped because nobody could contradict him.

Until the day that Jerusalem was taken. He stayed in the courtyard while the food ran out, and the city fell around a man nobody would listen to.

Two figures side by side. Set the two figures of this chapter side by side. A king of David's line, with armies, officials and the word of God delivered privately into his hand, who could do nothing; and an African eunuch with no rights at all, who heard about an injustice, walked to the gate, said so, fetched rags, and saved a prophet's life. God’s verdict on them is recorded in the next chapter: one lost his sons, his sight and his city; the other was told, because you have put your trust in me (39:18).

The gospel in a cistern. And the mud is the picture to keep: a man who could not climb out, and the ropes, padding and hands that came down for him (Ps 40:2). That is the gospel in a cistern, and Christ, who came down for us, was not ashamed to be seen doing it.

Was Jeremiah lying? He told the officials only what the king instructed, a true part of the conversation (cf. 37:20), and withheld the rest. Withholding the truth from those who have no right to it, to protect life, is not the same as bearing false witness.

38.title: The Cistern and the Ethiopian
38.overview: In the last weeks of the siege, officials who hate Jeremiah's call to surrender have him lowered into a muddy cistern to die, with the king's weak consent (vv. 1-6). An Ethiopian palace servant, Ebed-melech, pleads for him and draws him out with ropes padded with old rags (vv. 7-13). In a final secret meeting Zedekiah is offered his life and the city's survival if he will surrender, and refuses for fear of mockery (vv. 14-23); Jeremiah stays in the court of the guard until Jerusalem is taken (vv. 24-28).
38.theology: Jeremiah was hated for telling the city to surrender, yet that message was a way of escape, and it stayed open until the final weeks. Fear of man is a snare that disguises itself as helplessness: the king who said he could do nothing ordered thirty men to the rescue the moment somebody asked him (Prov 29:25; John 19:12-16). God notices kindness that troubles itself over details, and he commends the outsider with no standing: a foreign eunuch is given a name in Scripture for his trust (Isa 56:3-5). And the mud is a picture of salvation, a pit with no way out but hands from above.
38.examples: A rescuer who stops to fetch rags so that the ropes will not cut is a model for every kind of practical care: the hospital visit, the meal left on a doorstep, the hard conversation with someone in power. And Zedekiah's choice, a city lost rather than face being laughed at, is a warning to anyone who knows what is right and fears the opinion of friends more than God.

39.text: <sup>1</sup>In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it.<sup>2</sup>In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city.<sup>3</sup>Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.<sup>4</sup>When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah.<sup>5</sup>But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.<sup>6</sup>The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.<sup>7</sup>He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.<sup>8</sup>The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained.<sup>10</sup>Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.<sup>11</sup>Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you."<sup>13</sup>So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon<sup>14</sup>sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.<sup>15</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:<sup>16</sup>"Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day.<sup>17</sup>But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.<sup>18</sup>For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Breach Was Made in the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A long siege ends in one line, a breach was made in the city (vv. 1–3). Zedekiah flees by night, is caught near Jericho and judged at Riblah (vv. 4–5), where he sees his sons killed and is then blinded (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing he ever saw was what his refusal cost his own children.

verseByVerse.quote: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city. Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the ninth year of Zedekiah. Two dates, roughly January 588 BC and July 586 BC (some reckon a year earlier), and about a year and a half of siege between them.

Came against Jerusalem and besieged it. The narrator gives the siege no adjectives. Everything that happened inside those walls, the bread running out, the cistern, the last loaf from the bakers' street, the horrors Lamentations records of starving families, sits compressed into the gap between one month and another. Then seven words: a breach was made in the city.
