A breach was made in the city. This is the sentence the whole book has been walking toward. Forty years of warning, and when it arrives it is reported like a line in a chronicle.

Sat in the middle gate. Foreign officers sit down in the gate, and the detail is precise: these are Babylonian names and Babylonian titles. A clay tablet from Nebuchadnezzar’s court names a chief officer (the title Rab-saris) whose name is very like Nebu-sar-sekim’s. Rab-saris and Rab-mag are titles, not names: the first means something like “chief official”, and the second is a high court office whose exact sense is uncertain. The first Nergal-sar-ezer is probably Neriglissar, Nebuchadnezzar’s son-in-law, who later seized the throne of Babylon.

The seat of justice. And the gate is the point. The gate was where Israel's elders sat to judge, where Boaz called witnesses, where the officials had once acquitted Jeremiah. Now other men sit there, and their language is not Hebrew. The seat of justice in Jerusalem has changed occupants.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 52 and 2 Kings 25 give fuller accounts of the same events.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offer he refused. He had been told, twice and plainly, that if he walked out to the Babylonians his life would be spared and the city would not burn (38:17). He would not do it in daylight as an act of obedience.

Going out of the city at night. So here he goes out anyway: at night, by a garden gate, through a gap in the walls, running for the Jordan valley. The same feet that would not carry him out in surrender carry him out in flight. What obedience would have cost him was his dignity; what disobedience cost him is in the next three verses.

In the plains of Jericho. They catch him on the flat ground near Jericho, where Israel had first entered the land. The story of the possession of Canaan ends where it began, with the last king of Judah taken prisoner.

They brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar. And he is brought to Riblah, some two hundred miles north, to have sentence passed on him. He is tried as a vassal, a subject king, who has rebelled, because that is what he was: Nebuchadnezzar had put him on the throne and he had broken his oath.

verseByVerse.quote: The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before his eyes. The order of events is deliberate: his sons are killed while he watches, as the parallel accounts record identically (52:10; 2 Kgs 25:7), and then they blind him.

He put out the eyes of Zedekiah. God had told him, through the man he left in a cistern, that he would see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face (32:4), and that he would go to Babylon. Every clause came true, and not one the way he would have imagined. The last image his eyes ever held was his own children dying. They had done nothing; his fear of being laughed at had cost them everything, and the narrator records it without a word of comment, as if it were too heavy for one.

No bargaining with God’s word. God’s words are not riddles, and they cannot be negotiated. Zedekiah had heard this sentence for years and treated it as an opening offer that could be bargained down. It was a plain statement of what would happen.

The promise of peace. Is anything left of the promise of chapter 34, that he would not die by the sword but in peace, with mourners and spices (34:4-5)? It is a thin mercy beside what he lost, but as far as we are told he died in prison in Babylon, not by the sword (52:11), and this commentary reads that as the promise kept, even to a king who had earned nothing.

To take him to Babylon. Ezekiel said Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon yet he shall not see it (Ezek 12:13). Here is the answer: he was blinded at Riblah, then taken to Babylon, where he died.

Why would God allow children to be killed for their father’s sin? It is a terrible question, and the text does not soften the scene; Jeremiah himself would weep over the children of this city (Lam 2:11). The cruelty was Nebuchadnezzar's, and Scripture never calls it good. God foretold it and used it as judgment on a king who had broken a sworn oath (Ezek 17:15-19), and Babylon's own cruelties would in turn be judged (25:12; 51:24).

The promise to David. And what became of the promise that David would never lack a man on the throne (33:17)? On this day the throne is empty and the king's sons lie dead at Riblah. But David's line survived in the exiled Jehoiachin (52:31-34), and the promise waited for the Branch. Six centuries later a son of David was crowned with thorns outside this same city, hailed in mockery as King of the Jews, and raised to the throne of his father David that has no end (Luke 1:32-33).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The city is burned and its people deported (vv. 8–9), and then the poor who owned nothing are given vineyards and fields (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The people with nothing to lose ended the day owning land.

verseByVerse.quote: The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem. Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Broke down the walls of Jerusalem. The palace, the houses, the walls. Everything Judah had trusted in, dynasty, city and defences, dismantled in one verse, exactly as the scroll Jehoiakim burned had said: the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land (36:29).

No word of the temple. The temple is not mentioned here. Chapter 52 will supply that detail, and perhaps this account cannot bring itself to say it yet.

Carried into exile to Babylon. Three groups, all deported: those who held out, those who defected, and the remainder. Even the deserters go, which shows that surrendering was never a trick to avoid exile; it was how to stay alive. Jeremiah had promised life as a prize of war, not a comfortable outcome.

And then this, in a chapter about catastrophe.

The poor people who owned nothing. The people left in the land are the poor people who owned nothing, and a pagan general hands them vineyards and fields. The landless get land on the day the landowners lose everything. Men who had been at the bottom of every list in Judah, cheated by the officials of chapter 34, sold and re-enslaved, denied their wages by the house-builders of chapter 22, wake up as freeholders.

An exact reversal. Nobody planned this as justice. Nebuzaradan was solving an administrative problem: keep the countryside producing, deport anyone who could organise a revolt. But the effect is a reversal so exact that it reads like a verdict, and the New Testament states as a principle what this verse only shows happening: has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (Jas 2:5). Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matt 5:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Deal With Him As He Tells You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar orders that the prophet be treated well (vv. 11–12), and the Babylonian officers entrust him to Gedaliah (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The emperor's standing order for one prisoner: do whatever he asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying, "Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you." So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deal with him as he tells you. The emperor of the world has one named prisoner on his mind, with the extraordinary instruction deal with him as he tells you. Weigh the irony without missing the providence. For forty years the rulers and priests of Judah imprisoned this man, beat him, banned him from the temple, burned his book and dropped him in a pit. The pagan king who destroyed the city gave orders that he was to be treated well and have his own way.

Why Babylon cared. Presumably the Babylonians knew he had urged surrender and counted him useful. God's protection of his servants routinely arrives through people acting for their own reasons.

Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. The whole senior staff of the occupying army is involved in fetching one old man out of a courtyard, and the man they entrust him to, Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, is a gift. Ahikam protected him at a trial decades earlier (26:24); Ahikam's son takes him home after the city falls. Shaphan's family has turned up at every turning point of this book: reading the law to Josiah, lending Baruch a room, carrying the letter to Babylon, and now this. Faithfulness across generations does not make headlines, and it keeps quietly holding things up.

So he lived among the people. After the stocks, the cistern, the dungeon cells and the court of the guard, the prophet ends the chapter a free man living among ordinary Judeans.

Chains at Ramah. Jeremiah was released into Gedaliah’s care here, but 40:1 finds him in chains at Ramah. He was most likely rounded up with the captives by mistake, then released again at Ramah when the commander recognised him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Because You Have Put Your Trust in Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter reaches back into the siege for a word to Ebed-melech: he will see the city fall (vv. 15–16), but God will deliver him, because you have put your trust in me (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who fetched the rags is told why he will live, and it is not because of the rags.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard: "Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day. But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid. For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For harm and not for good. This word, given before the walls broke, is placed out of order so that we read it after the catastrophe it spoke of. It begins with the truth: Ebed-melech will see the palace he worked in burn. There is no promise that he will be spared the sight; only that he will come through it.

The men of whom you are afraid. God names the fear without rebuking it. Ebed-melech had walked up to the king at a public gate and accused four powerful officials of evil, and he had been frightened of them ever since, as well he might be.

Courage while afraid. Courage, in this book, is not the absence of fear. It is what Ebed-melech did while afraid, and God's answer is not that his fear was foolish but that those men will never have him.

Your life as a prize of war. This phrase is the one Jeremiah had shouted to the whole city: whoever goes out to the Chaldeans shall have his life as a prize of war, and live (38:2). What was offered publicly to everyone is now guaranteed personally to one man.

Because you have put your trust in me. And mark the reason God gives. Not because you rescued my prophet. Not because you were brave, or kind, or fetched padding for the ropes, but because you have put your trust in me.

A king and a eunuch. That is the verdict of the chapter, and it sorts everyone in it. A king of David's line, who had the promises, the temple and the prophet's private counsel, lost his sons and his sight because he trusted the opinion of men he was afraid of. A foreign eunuch with no tribe, no children and no rights was saved because he trusted God, and his trusting showed itself, as it always does, in what he did about a man sinking in mud. It is the same ground on which any sinner is rescued: by grace you have been saved through faith (Eph 2:8), trusting the God who keeps his word, a faith that then shows itself in love.

Known by name. The city fell, and the promise held: God knew the name of the one servant in Jerusalem who believed him, and had a word addressed to him by name before the first stone came down.

Doesn’t it matter more how you live than what you believe? It is one of the most widely shared convictions of our time, and there is a fine instinct behind it. People have seen cruelty done by the doctrinally correct and kindness done by people with no creed at all, and they conclude that deeds are what count. This chapter seems to agree, until you look closely. The eunuch is the one who acted; the king is the one who talked. But God does not say “because you were brave”. He says because you have put your trust in me. Ebed-melech’s courage did not come from nowhere. He believed that the God of the prophet in the mud was real and would keep his word, and that belief sent him to the king at the gate. Zedekiah believed something too: that the officials and the crowd were more real than God, and his belief also showed itself in what he did. Everyone lives by a creed; the only question is whether it is true. The gospel does not make us choose between believing and doing. It gives us a God so trustworthy that trusting him at last makes cowards brave.

39.title: The City Falls
39.overview: After a siege of a year and a half, the wall of Jerusalem is breached. Zedekiah flees by night, is caught near Jericho, sees his sons killed at Riblah and is blinded (vv. 1-7). The city is burned and its people deported, while the poorest are given vineyards and fields (vv. 8-10). Nebuchadnezzar orders that Jeremiah be treated well, and he is entrusted to Gedaliah (vv. 11-14). The chapter closes by reaching back into the siege for God's promise to Ebed-melech, the man who pulled Jeremiah from the cistern (vv. 15-18).
39.theology: God’s warnings state what will happen; they are not opening offers to be bargained down. Zedekiah treated the sentence as one, and every clause of it came true. Yet even here God's care shows. The landless are given land on the day the landowners lose everything, and the prophet whom Judah's rulers imprisoned is protected by a pagan emperor and taken home by a faithful family (Jas 2:5; Matt 5:5). And in the ruins, the one man promised his life is saved not for his bravery but for his trust, as every sinner is (Eph 2:8).
39.examples: Zedekiah walked out of the city in the end, by night and in flight, having refused to walk out by day in obedience. It is a picture worth keeping for anyone putting off a costly step God has made plain: delay does not usually spare us the step, only the blessing that went with it. Ebed-melech, frightened and faithful, is the other picture, and the more hopeful one.

40.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon.<sup>2</sup>The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place.<sup>3</sup>The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.<sup>4</sup>Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go.<sup>5</sup>If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go.<sup>6</sup>Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.<sup>7</sup>When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon,<sup>8</sup>they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.<sup>9</sup>Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.<sup>10</sup>As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."<sup>11</sup>Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them,<sup>12</sup>then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.<sup>13</sup>Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah<sup>14</sup>and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.<sup>15</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?"<sup>16</sup>But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Whole Land Is Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Found in chains among the captives at Ramah, Jeremiah hears the Babylonian captain state Jeremiah’s own message back to him (vv. 1–3). Freed and given the choice, he goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and stays among the people left in the land (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: A pagan officer with better theology than Judah's kings, handing a prophet his freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon. The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place. The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bound in chains. Something has gone wrong between chapters, and the narrator does not hide it. The emperor had ordered that this man be looked after and given his own way (39:12), and here he is bound in chains in a column of deportees at Ramah, the staging camp where the prisoners were mustered. The verse promises the word that came to Jeremiah, yet no oracle follows at once; the heading probably introduces the whole story of the remnant that follows, in which the word of the LORD comes at last in 42:7.

Had let him go from Ramah. Ramah is where Rachel was heard weeping for her children (31:15). The prophet who wrote that verse is now standing in the very place, chained, among the people it was about. Matthew would hear that weeping again when Herod killed the children of Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18), while the child Jesus, through whom the comfort promised to Rachel would come, was carried to safety.

Lost orders. Orders get lost, and God's promises to his servants are not always administered smoothly by the people carrying them.

The LORD your God pronounced this disaster. A Babylonian general, an idolater, summarises Jeremiah's entire ministry in three sentences and gets it right. He says who did it: The LORD has brought it about. He says that God kept his word: has done as he said. He says why: Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice.

Truth from an outsider. Forty years of preaching that to Judah had produced a beating, a cistern and a burned scroll. The occupying officer worked it out from the outside, and said it to the one man in the country who had been saying it all along.

A warning for the church. It is a strange, bleak vindication. The nations understood what Judah would not, and there is a warning in that for anyone who has grown deaf inside the church while outsiders can see plainly what God is doing. Yet God still speaks, and those who have been deaf and turn to him are heard.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay about five miles north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go. If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go. Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I release you today. The chains come off, and the old man is handed something he has not had in decades: a choice.

Come with me to Babylon. Babylon means comfort, safety and status: the deportees included the skilled and the well-connected, and a prophet with a record of urging surrender would have been honoured there. Judah means rubble, poverty and a wrecked community.

See, the whole land is before you. The phrase would echo for any Israelite; it is the language of Abraham and Lot looking over Canaan. Except that the land before him now is ash.

Rations and a gift. The ESV notes that the opening of verse 5 follows the Syriac, the Hebrew being uncertain; what is clear is the kindness: rations and a gift, from the man who burned the temple, to the prophet who said it would burn.

Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah. He stays. Offered Babylon, with a pension and a hearing, he chooses the ruined country and the poor people in it. Mizpah, a Benjamite town a few miles north of the ruined capital, had become the seat of government; it was where Samuel had once gathered Israel to repent and judged the people (1 Sam 7:5-6).

Staying with the broken. It is one of the last great acts of his ministry. He had wept for this people for forty years while they hated him; now that they are broken and leaderless he will not leave them. A man who had every reason to shake the dust off his feet went and lived among them instead.

Christ became poor himself. It is a small picture of a far greater choice. The Son of God, who had every right to the glory of heaven, emptied himself and came to live among a ruined people (Phil 2:7), and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb 2:11). Jeremiah stayed with the poor of Judah; Christ became poor himself, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9).

The career move nobody makes. Every modern life is expected to go up. We talk of career ladders, of trading up, of moving on to bigger things, and an offer like Nebuzaradan’s, a place in the capital with provisions and a hearing, is exactly what we are trained to accept. Turning it down to stay among the poor looks like a failure of ambition. Henri Nouwen, the Dutch priest and writer, gave up a teaching post at Harvard in the 1980s to live in a L’Arche community among people with severe learning disabilities, and he described the way of Jesus as downward mobility. He did not mean that poverty is holy or that every ambition is wrong. He meant that the love of God moves toward need rather than away from it, and that those who most resemble Christ are often walking the other way from the crowd. Jeremiah took the road to Mizpah. The Son of God came all the way down, and the surprise is that those who follow him find they have lost nothing: whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matt 16:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Gather Wine and Summer Fruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The captains still at large come in to Gedaliah (vv. 7–8), who swears that serving Babylon will be well with them and sends them to the harvest (vv. 9–10). The scattered Judeans come home and gather in abundance (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: A harvest in the year the city burned.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon, they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those of the poorest of the land. Judah is now a province run by a Judean governor, and its population is described without flattery: the poorest of the land. The people Nebuzaradan gave vineyards to (39:10) are the nation now.

All the captains of the forces in the open country. Out in the countryside are armed bands, officers whose units survived by staying out of the city. They come in when they hear there is a government again.

Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. Five commanders, named. The first of them, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, will murder the governor within months; the second, Johanan the son of Kareah, will try to prevent it and then lead the survivors down to Egypt against God’s word (chapters 42–43).

Listed without comment. The narrator lists them without comment, the future assassin first, because at the time they looked like five loyal officers.
verseByVerse.note: Gedaliah ruled from Mizpah, north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you. As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Gedaliah’s first act as governor is to make Jeremiah’s preaching his policy.

Jeremiah’s own words. Compare what the prophet had been saying for years: bring your neck under the yoke of Babylon and serve him and his people and live (27:12), and it shall be well with you. Gedaliah says the same three things (do not be afraid, serve Babylon, dwell in the land) and adds an oath to guarantee it.

Believing the prophet. This is what it looks like when someone finally believes the prophet. And it is no accident that the man doing it is Ahikam's son. He grew up in a house where Jeremiah was taken seriously.

To represent you before the Chaldeans. He takes the unpleasant job himself, to represent you before the Chaldeans, standing between his people and the occupiers, and gives everyone else the ordinary work: pick the grapes, gather the summer fruit, press the oil, fill the jars, live in your towns.

The way back. It is the same instruction God had sent to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, live (29:5). After catastrophe, the path back is not a grand project but harvest, storage and settled homes. Leaders who take the hard conversations on themselves and leave their people free to get on with ordinary faithful life are doing something very close to pastoral work.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them, then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant. The refugees hear. Judeans had scattered into Moab, Ammon, Edom and further during the invasion, and news reaches them that there is a remnant, a surviving group left in Judah, and a governor.

In great abundance. They come home, and the year produces a harvest in great abundance.

A harvest in the year of ruin. It is a real mercy, and the book does not oversell it. In the year Jerusalem burned, with the temple gone and the king blinded, the vines and the fruit trees of Judah bore heavily, and scattered people came back from Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands to pick them. God had said he would gather them from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you (29:14), and here is a first small instalment, small enough to miss and real enough to eat.

What mercy looks like. Mercies after judgment often look like this: not a restored temple, but a good grape harvest and somewhere to put it. The God who had every right to leave the land empty sent fruit on the vines for people who had nothing, in the very year they had least reason to expect it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — He Would Not Believe Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Johanan and the commanders warn Gedaliah of an Ammonite plot, and he will not believe them (vv. 13–14). Johanan offers privately to kill Ishmael, and Gedaliah calls the warning false (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: A good man's refusal to think ill of anyone, and the remnant paid for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baalis the king of the Ammonites. The intelligence is specific: a named foreign king, a named agent, a named target. Baalis of Ammon wants the order Babylon has set up in Judah to collapse, and Ishmael, who (chapter 41 tells us) was of the royal family, has his own reason to resent a commoner governing Judah.

A true report. It is brought by several commanders together, not by one grudge-bearer, and it was true.

Would not believe them. Then comes one sentence on which the future of the remnant turns: But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.

Why would he not believe it? Everything we know of him suggests a generous man: he had sheltered Jeremiah, he had sworn oaths of safety to these very officers, his policy was trust and ordinary life. A man like that finds it hard to credit that someone who eats at his table is planning to kill him.

Charity without discernment. And that is the uncomfortable point of the paragraph. This is not the failure of a fool or a cynic. It is a good man's charity applied where discernment was needed, and Scripture does not praise it; it simply records what it cost. Refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and leaders who will not hear a warning about a colleague can be as destructive as leaders who trust nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one will know it. Johanan tries again in private, and his proposal is ugly: let me kill him quietly, and no one will know it. A secret assassination to prevent an assassination.

Rightly refused. Gedaliah was right to refuse that. Nothing justifies murdering a man on the strength of a report, however good, and the governor who had just sworn oaths of safety could hardly begin with a private killing.

The remnant of Judah would perish. But look at the reasoning Johanan attaches, because he had seen further than anyone: Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish? He understood that everything now rested on one man's survival. Kill Gedaliah and the harvest, the returning refugees, the whole fragile settlement come apart.

Right danger, wrong remedy. He was exactly right, and he was proposing the wrong remedy. People often see a danger correctly and reach for a sinful way to stop it.

You are speaking falsely of Ishmael. And there is the sentence that ends the chapter, and very nearly ends the remnant. He does not merely decline the murder; he calls the warning a lie. You are speaking falsely of Ishmael.

Precautions not taken. He could have refused the assassination and still taken precautions: kept Ishmael at a distance, declined to dine with him, posted a guard. Instead he accused the men telling him the truth of slander, and took no measures at all. Soon afterwards, in the seventh month and probably the same year, Ishmael came to Mizpah with ten men, and as they ate bread together there they rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword (41:1-2).

No rebuke, no eulogy. So the last good governor of Judah, from the family that had protected the prophet for three generations, was murdered at his own table by a man he refused to suspect, and the remnant scattered exactly as Johanan had said. The book gives him no rebuke and no eulogy. It simply records that he would not believe them, and lets the next chapter say what it cost.

How communities are lost. Judah's story does not end with a Babylonian army but with a dinner party and a knife, which is a sober word about how communities that have survived catastrophe are usually lost. Not to the great enemy outside, but to one of their own, welcomed at the table, while a warning went unheeded.

40.title: Released at Ramah
40.overview: The fall of Jerusalem is over, and this chapter begins the story of those left behind. Jeremiah, found in chains among the deportees at Ramah, is freed by the Babylonian commander and chooses to stay with the poor of the land under the new governor, Gedaliah (vv. 1-6). Gedaliah gathers the scattered soldiers and refugees, and the year yields an abundant harvest (vv. 7-12). But he refuses to believe a warning that Ishmael has been sent to murder him (vv. 13-16).
40.theology: An outsider can state plainly what those inside the covenant refuse to hear: a Babylonian officer summarised Jeremiah's whole message and got it right. Offered comfort in Babylon or ruin in Judah, the prophet chose his broken people, a small picture of the Son of God who became poor for us (2 Cor 8:9). After catastrophe, God's mercy often looks like a harvest and settled homes rather than a grand restoration. And the chapter ends with two warnings for leaders: refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and a man can see a danger correctly and still propose a sinful way to stop it.
40.examples: Communities that survive a catastrophe are often lost not to the enemy outside but to trouble within, welcomed at the table while a warning goes unheeded. A church, a family or a business can learn from Gedaliah to take a sober warning seriously without slandering anyone, and from Johanan that seeing the danger clearly does not justify doing wrong to stop it.

41.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah,<sup>2</sup>Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land.<sup>3</sup>Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.<sup>4</sup>On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it,<sup>5</sup>eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam."<sup>7</sup>When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.<sup>8</sup>But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions.<sup>9</sup>Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.<sup>10</sup>Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,<sup>12</sup>they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.<sup>14</sup>So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.<sup>15</sup>But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.<sup>16</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt<sup>18</sup>because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — As They Ate Bread Together
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael, a prince of the royal family, comes to Mizpah with ten men and kills Gedaliah at his own table (vv. 1–2), and the Judeans and Chaldean soldiers with him (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A guest at the governor's table, with a sword under the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land. Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of the royal family. Probably barely two months after the city fell (the year is not given), the assassin arrives, and now we learn who he was. Of the royal family, and one of the chief officers of the king. A prince of David's line, and Gedaliah was a commoner appointed by Babylon.

As they ate bread together. That is motive enough without Ammonite money. What makes it more than politics is As they ate bread together: received as a guest, he drew his sword across the table.

The bond of a meal. In the ancient world a shared meal was a bond. To eat a man's bread was to place yourself under obligation to him, which is why a psalm reaches for exactly this image to describe the deepest wound available: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps 41:9).

He passed him the bread anyway. The Lord took that verse onto his own lips in an upper room, of Judas, who sat at his table having already been paid to betray him: He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18). And there is a difference between the two tables that is the whole gospel. Gedaliah did not know, and had refused to be told. Jesus knew exactly who was reaching for the dish, and passed him the bread anyway.

An epitaph. The full genealogy is given as an epitaph: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. Shaphan read the law to Josiah; Ahikam's hand saved Jeremiah's life at his trial; Gedaliah took the prophet home when the city fell. Three generations of quiet faithfulness, and the line ends at a dinner table.

A reprisal guaranteed. The Chaldean garrison dies too, and with them any hope that Babylon will treat this as an internal matter. Ishmael has not merely killed a governor; he has guaranteed a reprisal, and fear of it drives the next three chapters.

In the seventh month. The fast of the seventh month that the Jews later kept (Zech 7:5; 8:19) is usually taken to remember the murder of Gedaliah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Eighty Pilgrims and a Cistern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next day eighty mourning pilgrims from the north arrive with offerings (vv. 4–5). Ishmael weeps his way into their confidence and slaughters them (vv. 6–7), sparing ten who know where food is hidden, and fills Asa's great cistern with the dead (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief counterfeited at the gate, and a reservoir built to save life packed with the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it, eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria. For one day nobody outside knows of the murder, and Mizpah still looks like a working capital with a governor in it. These eighty men are among the saddest details in the book. They come from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, the old northern kingdom, whose people had been deported by Assyria well over a century before. These are the descendants of those left behind, and they are still walking south with offerings for the God of Israel. They were probably heirs of Josiah’s reform, which had reached into the old northern territory and turned its worshippers toward Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:15-20; 2 Chr 34:9). It was also the seventh month, the month of the Feast of Booths (Lev 23:34), which may explain the journey.

Their bodies gashed. They are in mourning for Jerusalem: beards shaved, clothes torn, bodies cut. And two of those three were expressly forbidden. You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead (Lev 19:28); You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). Their grief was genuine and their practice borrowed what the law forbade, learned from neighbours over generations without the law to correct it.

Grain offerings and incense. And they are carrying grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD, to a temple that had been ash for perhaps two months. Either they had not heard, or they were going to the site anyway to lay offerings in the ruins.

Sincere but muddled. It would be easy to be superior about them, and it would be wrong. Eighty men walked thirty miles or more through occupied country, disfigured with grief, to bring flour and incense to a God whose house was rubble. Their theology was muddled and their hearts were not. God's people are often more sincere than they are well-taught, and the answer to that is teaching, not contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam." When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weeping as he came. It was the day after the murder. The tears were the trap: the one sure way into mourners' confidence was shared grief. Then he invited them in the name of the man he had just killed: Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.

Hypocrisy as a tool. This is what hypocrisy is for. Not self-deception, but a tool: the borrowing of the forms of godliness and sorrow in order to get close enough to do harm. Wolves come in sheep's clothing because the clothing works.

Slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern. Eleven men killed seventy of the eighty pilgrims inside the walls, and the bodies went into a water pit. Each of them had a name and a home in the north, and had come to mourn; Scripture does not let them become a statistic, and neither should we.

Two cisterns. Hold the cistern beside the one three chapters ago. Jeremiah had been lowered into a cistern with no water in the cistern, but only mud (38:6), and a foreigner came with ropes and old rags and drew him out. Here the same kind of pit is used to hide a massacre. It is the same kind of pit in the same country: in one, a man is hauled up to live; in the other, seventy worshippers are thrown down. What differs is not the hole but the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions. Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hidden in the fields. Ten men live because they knew where food was buried, hidden in the open country because anything kept in a house was taken. And it shows what Ishmael valued: seventy murders were nothing to him, and a cache of grain was enough to stay his hand.

Bargains famine forces. There is no comment on the ten. They bought their lives with the location of their food, which is the kind of bargain famine forces on people, and Scripture records it without either praise or blame.

That King Asa had made. The narrator stops to tell us who dug the hole, and the ESV notes that where the English reads that these men were struck down along with Gedaliah, the Hebrew has "by the hand of": the bodies of the men killed by Gedaliah's side, in his company.

For defense against Baasha king of Israel. Three hundred years earlier King Asa had fortified Mizpah against the northern kingdom, carrying away the stones of Ramah to build it (1 Kgs 15:22). The cistern was part of that work: a reservoir to keep a garrison alive through a siege. It was engineering in the service of survival.

Filled it with the slain. And a prince of Asa's own line filled it with the slain. Things built by good men to preserve life get used by later men for atrocity, the thing itself still standing, but now serving the opposite purpose. Judah's story is full of it: a temple built for God's name used to house idols, a covenant ceremony used to seal a lie, and now a waterworks made into a grave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — Recovered at the Pool of Gibeon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael drives the remnant toward Ammon (v. 10); Johanan pursues and overtakes him at Gibeon, and the captives rejoice and come over to him (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The one glad moment in the chapter: prisoners seeing who has come for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s daughters. The whole remnant of Judah walks east in ropes, and it is a small shock to find the king's daughters here. Zedekiah's sons were killed at Riblah; his daughters survived the fall of the city, were left behind as no threat to anybody, and are now being driven toward Ammon as spoil by a man of their own royal house.

Had committed to Gedaliah. They had been formally entrusted to Gedaliah, and the man who murdered him is now stealing them.

To cross over to the Ammonites. And the destination is the point. Ishmael is taking them to the Ammonites, to the king who had sent him to do the killing (40:14). This may never have been a bid for the throne of Judah. It looks like a foreign operation, and the remnant were the payment.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon. And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced. So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But. It is the first good word in the chapter.

Johanan the son of Kareah. And it is Johanan, the man who brought the warning Gedaliah would not believe, who had asked permission to deal with Ishmael quietly and been told he was a liar (40:14-16). He had every excuse to say he had told them so. Instead he raised his men and went after the column.

Helping those who doubted him. Being disbelieved is a real injury, and the test of a man is what he does for people who dismissed him once they are in trouble. Johanan passes it.

The great pool that is in Gibeon. The place is named because everyone knew it: the great pool at Gibeon, where Joab's and Abner's men had once fought a murderous tournament in David's day.

They rejoiced. It is the only gladness in the chapter, and it is the gladness of prisoners who look up and see who has come over the hill.

Held by force. The captives had been with Ishmael only for the few miles from Mizpah, and their loyalty was never his. The moment there was an alternative, it was obvious where they stood, which is usually true of people held by force. It is easy to forget, because people who are held by force can look as if they are willing.

Turned around and came back. No battle is described. The hostages simply turned around and walked to the rescue party, and Ishmael's operation collapsed, because the captives were people and not cargo, and they walked away from him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Intending to Go to Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael escapes to Ammon (v. 15). Johanan leads the recovered remnant to camp near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Frightened people walking back toward the country God had brought them out of.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites. Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon. And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Escaped from Johanan with eight men. He gets away to Ammon, where his paymaster is. He murdered a governor, seventy pilgrims and a garrison, and the chapter simply records that he escaped. There is no execution, no capture, no word of judgment pronounced over him in this book at all.

When wickedness escapes. Scripture is honest about this. Wickedness frequently walks away from the scene, and the reader who wants to see justice done before the story ends will not always find it. What we are given instead is the assurance that the account is kept by the God who said I am the one who knows, and I am witness (29:23).

Soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs. Read the list slowly: soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs. This is what was left of the people of God in the land of promise. Not a nation, but a column of survivors on a road, with their governor dead behind them.

Intending to go to Egypt. Their reasoning is not stupid: Babylon's governor and soldiers have been murdered, and a reprisal is coming. So: Egypt. Geruth Chimham, probably a lodging place named after the Chimham whom David took into his household (2 Sam 19:37-40), lay near Bethlehem on the road south.

Undoing the exodus. Their reasoning is sound as far as it goes, and it points them in the one direction God had forbidden. Egypt is where the story of this people began, and the whole shape of their existence is that God brought them out of it. To walk back in is to undo the exodus.

For they were afraid of them. And fear is what does it. Not appetite, not idolatry in any obvious form, but fear, with a plausible case attached. Gedaliah would not believe a warning and died of it; these men believe the evidence of their eyes and are about to make a worse mistake. Between trusting too easily and trusting only our own reckoning there is a third way, which is to ask God, and in the next chapter they do: that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do (42:3).

Near Bethlehem. It is the right question, asked by men who have already decided the answer. And the last picture the chapter leaves is a company of refugees encamped beside Bethlehem, facing south, afraid. And that is where, six centuries later, the answer to all of it would be born (Mic 5:2; Matt 2:6): the true Shepherd of Israel, who would not run from danger but go to meet it for his sheep.

41.title: Murder at Mizpah
41.overview: A few weeks after the fall of Jerusalem, Ishmael, a prince of the royal house, murders Gedaliah at his own table, with the Judeans and Babylonian soldiers at Mizpah (vv. 1-3). The next day he lures in eighty mourning pilgrims from the north and massacres seventy of them, throwing the bodies into King Asa's great cistern (vv. 4-9). He drives the rest of the people toward Ammon, until Johanan overtakes him at Gibeon and the captives walk free (vv. 10-14). Ishmael escapes, and the frightened survivors camp near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt (vv. 15-18).
41.theology: This is the darkest chapter of the aftermath, and Scripture tells it without softening. Betrayal at the table is one of the deepest wounds there is, and the Lord himself bore it knowingly (John 13:18). Hypocrisy appears here not as self-deception but as a tool, tears used to get near enough to kill. Ishmael escapes unpunished in this chapter, and the reckoning is left to the God who is witness (29:23). And fear backed by sensible-sounding reasons is what turns God's people back toward Egypt, beside the town where the true Shepherd would one day be born (Matt 2:6).
41.examples: The eighty pilgrims carrying flour and incense to a temple of ashes are a reminder that God's people are often more sincere than well taught, and deserve teaching rather than contempt. And Johanan, who raised his men for the very people who had called him a liar, shows what to do with the injury of being disbelieved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Whether It Is Good or Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole remnant asks Jeremiah to pray for guidance (vv. 1–3). He promises to keep nothing back (v. 4), and they swear to obey, whether it is good or bad (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: A perfect prayer and a total oath, from people who have already decided where they are going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the commanders of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near and said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Let our plea for mercy come before you, and pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant— because we are left with but a few, as your eyes see us— that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the least to the greatest. Everyone comes. Not a delegation this time, but the commanders, the officers, and all the people from the least to the greatest. After Mizpah there is nobody left who can afford to be indifferent.

Let our plea for mercy come before you. The request is beautifully put, and every part of it is right. They ask for prayer, they plead for mercy, they name their condition honestly, we are left with but a few, and they appeal to what the prophet can see with his own eyes.

The LORD your God. One phrase is a small warning light: the LORD your God. Not ours. Zedekiah's messengers had at least said the LORD our God (37:3); men who speak of God as someone else’s God are often keeping him at a distance in other ways too.

The way we should go. And there is the question, and it is the right question. Which way, and what to do. You could not improve on it as a prayer for guidance, and the tragedy of the chapter is that it was asked by men with their bags already packed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah the prophet said to them, "I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your request, and whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you." Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to us. Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard you. He agrees at once, and then makes one promise about himself: I will keep nothing back from you.

I will keep nothing back from you. Forty years of ministry stand behind that sentence. He had been beaten, put in stocks, dropped in a cistern and had his book burned for keeping nothing back, and he was too old and too tested to start editing now. A preacher who tells his people in advance that he will not trim the answer has given them the most useful thing he has.

A true and faithful witness against us. Inviting God to witness against them is the most solemn commitment available. Whether it is good or bad: they anticipate the possibility of an unwelcome answer and pledge obedience anyway. And their wording has improved: twice now it is the LORD our God.

Hollow words. Every word is correct and the whole thing is hollow, as chapter 43 will show within a day. There is a way of praying for guidance that is really a search for approval of a decision already made, and it can produce sincere-sounding oaths. The test of whether we meant whether it is good or bad only comes when the answer is bad.

How do I ask for guidance and mean it? Most of us have prayed their prayer, over a job offer, a move or a relationship we were already leaning into. Four marks of asking honestly. Name what you are hoping for. Tell God plainly which answer you want, so the wish is out in the open and not steering in the dark. Decide beforehand what would count as no. Settle what Scripture, a wise friend or a closed door would have to say for you to drop the plan, before you hear it. Ask someone who will keep nothing back. Find the person least likely to flatter you, and give them leave to say the unwelcome thing. Obey the part you already know. Most of God’s will is already written, and the remnant were told nothing here that Jeremiah had not been saying for years. None of this earns guidance. The Son prayed not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42) and obeyed when the answer was a cross; and the God who answered him works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — If You Will Remain in This Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After ten days the answer comes (vv. 7–9): stay, and God will build and plant them (v. 10). Their fear of Babylon is named and answered with his presence and mercy (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stay, and God will build and plant them, and deal with Nebuchadnezzar himself.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah. Then he summoned Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea for mercy before him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of ten days. Ten days of nothing.

The prophet waited. The prophet prayed and God did not answer for a week and a half, with a frightened camp waiting outside and a Babylonian reprisal expected any day. Jeremiah had to go out each morning with nothing to report.

Why God delayed. God is not on call. He answers according to his own timetable even when the request is urgent and the people are genuinely afraid, and the delay is not indifference. Ten days also gave the remnant ten days to examine what they actually wanted, and gave the oath time to be more than a mood.

All the people from the least to the greatest. He calls the same crowd back, all the people from the least to the greatest, because the answer belongs to everyone who asked, not to the leadership alone. He will not tell the leaders first and let them decide what the people hear.

To whom you sent me. He begins by reminding them that this was their idea. To whom you sent me. Whatever follows, they asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand. I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will build you up and not pull you down. Listen to the verbs, because they are the verbs of Jeremiah’s call. He was appointed to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10), and for forty years the first four had done the work. Here only the last two are used, with the destructive pair explicitly refused: built up and not pulled down, planted and not plucked up.

I relent of the disaster. And the reason given is staggering: for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. God speaks of turning from the harm with something like grief, not that he was wrong to send it, but that he takes no pleasure in it and is ready to deal kindly with them the moment they will stay put.

If you will remain in this land. The whole offer turns on one condition, and it is not a religious programme. It is geography: If you will remain in this land. Stay where God has put you.

Do not fear the king of Babylon. God names the fear precisely and says do not fear twice, because a frightened man needs the sentence repeated. The reason he gives is not a change in Nebuchadnezzar’s plans but his own presence: for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.

God with us. That promise of presence runs through the whole Bible, and it reaches its height in the child named Immanuel (which means, God with us) (Matt 1:23), who sent his frightened disciples out with the words I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20). The remedy for fear has always been a person, and in Christ that person has come.

That he may have mercy on you. Follow the chain. God will show them mercy, and the effect will be that the emperor shows them mercy. God speaks of the attitude of the most powerful man alive as something he will change in order to keep a promise to a small band of refugees.

Does God change his mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jer 18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alternative is quoted in their own voice, Egypt for peace and bread (vv. 13–14), and the answer turns it inside out: the sword and famine they fear will follow them there (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The two things they were running from were waiting at the destination.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you say, 'We will not remain in this land,' disobeying the voice of the LORD your God and saying, 'No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there,' then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: If you set your faces to enter Egypt and go to live there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We will not remain in this land. God quotes the sentence before they say it, and labels it: saying We will not remain in this land is disobeying the voice of the LORD your God. There will be no room afterwards to present the move as prudence rather than rebellion.

Or be hungry for bread. Their case is a good one: after a long siege, a murdered governor and a country of ashes, who would not want peace and bread? That is what makes this passage searching. The sin is not a craving for something wicked. It is a craving for peace and bread in a place God had forbidden. What they wanted was natural; where they meant to find it was forbidden. And Egypt was the obvious refuge: the one great power still outside Babylon’s grip, whose army had once drawn the Chaldeans away from Jerusalem during the siege (37:5), and where Judeans already lived (24:8).

The god called safety. Few idols are harder to see than this one, because it does not look like an idol. It looks like common sense. Who could object to a family wanting to be out of danger and sure of the next meal? Yet a great deal of modern life is quietly arranged around it: the job kept for its security long after it has hollowed us out, the risk never taken for a friend, the child shielded from every hardship until he can bear none. Augustine argued that sin is often not the love of bad things but the love of good things in the wrong order, so that a lesser good is given the place that belongs to God. Peace and bread are gifts. Made into the thing we must have at any cost, they become a master, and sooner or later every master demands obedience against God’s word. The remnant did not stop believing in God; they simply let fear decide. The gospel’s reversal is that real safety lies in walking toward the place God names, because the one who says I am with you walked into the worst danger of all for us, at the cross, and came out of the tomb alive.

We will go to the land of Egypt. And Egypt was forbidden by name. The law had said of the king that he must not cause the people to return to Egypt, because You shall never return that way again (Deut 17:16), and Isaiah had pronounced Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help (Isa 31:1). Egypt is the house of slavery they were brought out of. Walking back is not a change of address; it is a reversal of the exodus.

If you set your faces to enter Egypt. The phrase set your faces carries the whole problem. This is not drifting; it is a deliberate turning of the head in a chosen direction.

verseByVerse.quote: then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die. All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to live there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. They shall have no remnant or survivor from the disaster that I will bring upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their two reasons. The answer takes their two reasons and hands them back.

The sword that you fear shall overtake you. They were going to Egypt to escape war and hunger. God says the sword they fear will overtake them there, and the famine they dread will follow close after them: a picture of two pursuers outrunning a column on the road.

Nowhere to run. There is no safe country. If God has sent the thing a man is fleeing, no distance will get him away from it, and the only refuge available was obedience in a ruined land. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (Prov 14:12).

By the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. The threefold sentence that runs through the whole book, sword, famine and pestilence, falls one last time, now on those who survived it. And the closing phrase is the bitterest thing in the chapter: no remnant or survivor.

No remnant or survivor. These people are the remnant, the few survivors left. The word had been their identity and their comfort for two chapters. If they go down to Egypt, the remnant will have no remnant.

A door left open. Even this is not quite the last word. Two chapters later God allows that a few fugitives will get home (44:14, 28), and Scripture never closes the door on anyone who turns back from a wrong road: let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him (Isa 55:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Shall See This Place No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem's wrath will follow them to Egypt (v. 18). The warning is made formal (v. 19), their oath is read back to them, and the verdict falls on the place where you desire to go to live (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle ends by naming where they will die: the place they want to go.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You shall become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. You shall see this place no more. The LORD has said to you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day
verseByVerse.commentary:
As my anger and my wrath were poured out. God compares what will happen to them in Egypt with what his anger did to Jerusalem, and that should have ended the discussion. They had just watched what that looked like; the smoke was barely gone.

An execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. Then four words for their reputation, an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt, the same list pronounced over Jerusalem, now transferred to the refugees.

You shall see this place no more. And a short sentence that would fall hardest on anyone who loved the country: You shall see this place no more. Go, and you will never come back.

Do not go to Egypt. The instruction is reduced to five words so that nobody can claim it was ambiguous: Do not go to Egypt.

Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day. And Jeremiah puts his own testimony on record: Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day. He is establishing that the warning was given, plainly, on a particular day, in front of everyone. A faithful minister makes sure that if his people go wrong they cannot say they were not told.

verseByVerse.quote: that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, 'Pray for us to the LORD our God, and whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it.' And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you. Now therefore know for a certainty that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have gone astray at the cost of your lives. Their oath is read back to them, and its wording stings. You have gone astray: already, before a single step south. God treats the decision as taken, because it was taken before they ever asked.

Whatever the LORD our God says. And he quotes their promise exactly as they had worded it, calling him their own God: whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it. They had called him theirs and pledged obedience in advance. The words are now evidence.

I have this day declared it to you. Jeremiah has kept his side exactly, nothing held back, and the charge against them is total: not obedient in anything. They received a specific, urgent, gracious answer to the exact question they had asked. They had sworn in advance to obey it, and they obeyed none of it.

The place where you desire to go to live. And the oracle ends on a phrase that diagnoses the whole human problem: the place where you desire to go to live.

Not where they feared. That is where they will die. Not in the place they feared, but in the place they wanted. The destination chosen for safety, bread and quiet turns out to be the grave, and it is chosen freely, with a warning ringing in their ears and an oath still warm on their lips.

Why this chapter matters. Which is why this chapter is more than a piece of sixth-century politics. God gave them a plain word, named their fear, promised his presence, offered to build and plant them, and undertook to manage the emperor himself, and they preferred a country of their own choosing. The offer was If you will remain in this land, and remaining is generally harder than moving, because it requires trusting God rather than changing our circumstances.

Asking with the bags already packed. Every reader has asked for guidance with the bags already packed. The way back is not a better oath but the mercy this chapter itself offers, I relent of the disaster: Christ kept his Father's word perfectly where we have not, and his obedience is counted as ours (Rom 5:19). And the Spirit he gives is what makes a frightened heart able to stay where God has put it and trust the One who says I am with you.

42.title: Whether It Is Good or Bad
42.overview: The frightened survivors of Mizpah ask Jeremiah to seek God's guidance and swear to obey it, whether it is good or bad (vv. 1-6). After ten days the answer comes: stay in the land, and God will build and plant them and protect them from Babylon (vv. 7-12). But if they go to Egypt for peace and bread, the sword and famine they fear will follow them there (vv. 13-17), and Jeremiah warns them plainly that they have already chosen the place where they will die (vv. 18-22).
42.theology: There is a way of asking for guidance that is really a search for approval of what we have already decided, and it can produce faultless prayers and sincere oaths; the test of whether it is good or bad comes only when the answer is bad. Against that stands a God who answers in his own time, who relents of disaster and takes no pleasure in it, and whose answer to fear is not a change in the enemy's plans but his own presence, fulfilled in Immanuel (Matt 1:23). The sin here is not appetite for evil but a craving for peace and bread in a place God forbade, and its end is death in the very place they wanted.
42.examples: Most of us have asked God for guidance with the bags already packed: praying over a move, a job or a relationship we have in fact already chosen. The chapter does not answer that with scorn but with an offer. God still says to the frightened, Do not fear, twice, because frightened people need it twice, and he promises to be with those who stay where he has put them.

43.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them,<sup>2</sup>Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie.
