The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,'<sup>3</sup>but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."<sup>4</sup>So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah.<sup>5</sup>But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—<sup>6</sup>the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah.<sup>7</sup>And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:<sup>9</sup>"Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,<sup>10</sup>and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.<sup>11</sup>He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword.<sup>12</sup>I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace.<sup>13</sup>He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — You Are Telling a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The moment Jeremiah finishes, the leaders call him a liar and blame Baruch for the oracle (vv. 2–3). So they do not obey the voice of the LORD, and they gather the whole remnant, even those who had just come home from the nations (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: An oath to obey "whether it is good or bad" lasted exactly as long as the answer was welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them, Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,' but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jeremiah finished speaking. The narrator sets the record straight before anyone speaks: these were all these words of the LORD their God, and God had sent him with them.

Azariah the son of Hoshaiah. He is probably the Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah of 42:1; the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads Azariah in both places.

You are telling a lie. Ten days they waited for this answer. They swore an oath to obey it whether it is good or bad. Within a day of hearing it they call the prophet a liar.

The LORD our God did not send you. They do not say the message is hard, or ask for time, or admit they are afraid. They say God did not send it. When obedience becomes unbearable, the tempting move is not open rebellion but to decide that the word was never really God’s. Then there is nothing left to obey.

Johanan the son of Kareah. And Johanan is among them. The man who brought the true warning to Gedaliah and was called a liar for it (40:16) is now doing to Jeremiah exactly what was done to him.

Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us. Then the conspiracy theory, aimed at the scribe: the old prophet is being used by his secretary, and the message is really Baruch’s plan to hand them over to Babylon. The charge need not deny that Jeremiah is godly; it need only say that someone else is steering him. A word you cannot refute can still be set aside by explaining where it came from, and forty years of proven ministry were set aside with one accusation about the man holding the pen.

Explaining the speaker instead of answering him. We have become very good at this. Faced with a claim we dislike, we ask not whether it is true but where it came from: he only says that because of his upbringing, his class, his politics, his hurt. There is some truth in it, since motives do bend arguments. But C. S. Lewis noticed the trick and gave it a mocking name, Bulverism, after an imaginary inventor who discovered that you need not show a man is wrong if you assume he is and then explain how he came to be so silly. Lewis’s point was that it is a way of never having to think, and that it can be turned on anyone, including the person using it. The officers did exactly this. They could not refute forty years of fulfilled warnings, so they explained them away: Baruch is behind it. Religious people are not immune; it is a favourite way to dodge a sermon. The gospel offers a better way to hear a hard word. If God has already told me the worst about myself at the cross, and loved me there, I no longer need to discredit the messenger in order to survive the message.

verseByVerse.quote: So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah. But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—
verseByVerse.commentary:
To remain in the land of Judah. They had called it a lie; the narrator calls it what it is, did not obey the voice of the LORD, and names the command they broke: to remain in the land of Judah. Nothing was required of them but to stay where God had put them and let him build and plant them there (42:10). The command came with the promise already attached.

Who had returned to live in the land of Judah. And these were the people who had returned, home from Moab, Ammon and Edom when they heard there was a governor and a harvest (40:11-12). God had begun gathering them, in a small and real way, as he promised. Now they are taken out again by their own leaders. The gathering is undone by the people it had gathered.
verseByVerse.note: From here to the end of chapter 44, Jeremiah's ministry takes place in Egypt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everyone left in Judah goes down to Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and they arrive at Tahpanhes (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The two men who had told them not to go were carried along with them.

verseByVerse.quote: the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men, the women, the children, the princesses. The inventory is complete and it is heartbreaking: men, women, children, the royal daughters, and every single person the Babylonians had entrusted to Gedaliah. Whatever was left of Judah in Judah is on this road.

Also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. And then, at the end of the list, as if incidental: also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. The two men who had just been called a liar and a manipulator are taken along.

What his choice cost. He had been offered Babylon with a pension and had chosen his ruined country to stay with these people (40:4-6). This is what that choice cost him. He is an old man, and the last journey of his life is a forced march into the one country his whole message had warned against, in the company of men who had just disowned his ministry.

He goes with them. There is no lament recorded. He does not protest, and the text gives him no speech. He simply goes with them, which is the shape of his entire life: tied to a people who would not hear him and would not let him go.

For they did not obey the voice of the LORD. The reason is stated a second time in four verses: for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. The narrator is making sure no future reader mistakes this for an ordinary move to a new country.

They arrived at Tahpanhes. Tahpanhes was a frontier garrison town in the eastern delta, the first substantial place on the road in. And the place itself tells the story: the people God took out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm walked back in of their own accord.

What became of Jeremiah? Scripture does not say. He was last seen in Egypt, still preaching (ch. 44); later tradition, outside Scripture, says he died there, some accounts say at the hands of his own people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Tahpanhes Jeremiah buries stones in the pavement at Pharaoh's palace, where God will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: God lays a foundation in Pharaoh's forecourt for a throne that is coming whether Egypt likes it or not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes: "Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah, and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes. God speaks to him in Egypt.

God has not left him. That is not a small thing. Jeremiah had been dragged into a country where God had forbidden them to seek refuge, by men who denied that God had sent him, and the word of the LORD arrives there as it always had. He was disobedient in nothing, and God does not treat him as though he were. He remains a prophet on the wrong side of a border he never wanted to cross.

Take in your hands large stones. One more acted sign, a message from God performed as well as spoken, and after the yoke, the flask and the field, this one is characteristically odd: bury large stones in the wet mortar of the pavement outside Pharaoh's palace, and do it in the sight of the men of Judah.

Hidden but there. He is an old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pushing stones into mortar while his countrymen watch. The stones will be invisible within a day, which is the point: they are hidden, and they are still there.

I will set his throne above these stones. And the meaning lands hard. They came to Egypt to get away from Nebuchadnezzar, and God says he will set the man's throne on this very pavement, with his canopy spread over the spot. The buried stones are the foundation for a Babylonian throne in Pharaoh’s own doorway.

My servant. Once more the title appears that has run through this book: my servant (25:9; 27:6). The emperor is still an instrument, and the God who moves him is the God these refugees were running from: I will send and take him.

Providence at the destination. There is no hiding place from providence. You may cross a border to escape a man, and find that the one who commands him was waiting at the destination.

Did Nebuchadnezzar invade Egypt? A fragmentary Babylonian tablet records a campaign against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year, about 568/567 BC, against Pharaoh Amasis. How far into Egypt he went is not known, but the record fits Jeremiah’s word (and Ezek 29:17-20), which this commentary takes as fulfilled.
verseByVerse.note: Tahpanhes is usually identified with Tell Defenneh, where nineteenth-century excavators found a large brick platform in front of a fort; some linked it with this pavement, though that cannot be proved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — As a Shepherd Cleans His Cloak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Egypt itself is sentenced: its land struck, its temples burned, its obelisks broken (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge they chose receives the same sentence as the city they left.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword. I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace. He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He shall come and strike the land of Egypt. Egypt gets the sentence of Judah. The same three judgments, pestilence, captivity and the sword, follow them across the frontier, each person assigned to one of them, and the refuge turns out to be under the same verdict as the place they left.

I shall kindle a fire. Note who lights the fire: I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt. God says he will do it, and Nebuchadnezzar will carry it out. The gods that Judah had gone down to live among will be burned and carted off as loot by an army God sends.

As a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin. And then an image of startling contempt: he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin. A shepherd sitting in the sun picking lice out of his coat and flicking them away. That is the sack of one of the great old civilisations, described as delousing a garment, and the shepherd walks off afterwards in peace, unhurried, having lost nothing.

He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis. The last thing named is the obelisks of Heliopolis, the sun-god’s city, whose pillars were the most permanent objects in the world these people had fled into. Stone that had stood for a thousand years, broken.

What God has hidden. So the chapter ends where it began, with buried stones and standing ones. The obelisks that looked eternal come down; the stones an old prophet pushed into mortar mark where an emperor's throne will stand. What is visible is temporary, and what God has hidden is the thing that holds.

Out of Egypt I called my son. And this is not the last word on Egypt in Scripture. Six centuries later an angel would tell a carpenter to take a child down into Egypt to keep him alive from a king who wanted him dead, and then to bring him home again, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: Out of Egypt I called my son (Matt 2:15; Hos 11:1). Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and did not come back. The true Son went down in obedience, and came out, and made the road home for everyone who had taken the wrong one.

43.title: Down Into Egypt
43.overview:
Jeremiah has barely finished giving God's answer when the leaders call it a lie and blame Baruch for it. Against the plain command to stay, they march the whole remnant down to Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and arrive at the frontier town of Tahpanhes (vv. 1-7).

There God speaks to his prophet again. Jeremiah buries stones in the pavement at Pharaoh's palace and announces that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne on that very spot, burn the temples of Egypt's gods and break the obelisks of Heliopolis (vv. 8-13). The people fled from Babylon into the arms of the next country Babylon would strike.
43.theology:
The chapter shows how people refuse a word they cannot answer. They do not argue with it; they decide it is only a man’s word and explain where it came from (vv. 2-3). The sin itself is a failure to stay where God had put them, under a command that came with the promise already attached (42:10).

It also shows that there is no running from God's providence. The word reaches Jeremiah in a country he never chose, and the king the refugees fled is called God's servant and sent to the very door of their refuge (v. 10). Over it all stands the contrast the Gospels draw: Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and never came back, but the true Son went down in obedience and was called out (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15).
43.examples:
Think of someone who waits for counsel, promises in advance to take it, and then, once it is given, decides the adviser must have been got at by someone else. That is Johanan here: it is easier to blame the secretary than to obey the sermon.

Or think of an old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pressing stones into wet mortar while his countrymen watch. Within a day nothing can be seen. The thousand-year obelisks across the country look far more permanent, yet they are the things that fall, and the hidden stones are the things that hold.

44.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros,<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them,<sup>3</sup>because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.<sup>4</sup>Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!'<sup>5</sup>But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods.<sup>6</sup>Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.<sup>7</sup>And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant?<sup>8</sup>Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth?<sup>9</sup>Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?<sup>10</sup>They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah.<sup>12</sup>I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt.<sup>13</sup>I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence,<sup>14</sup>so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."<sup>15</sup>Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah:<sup>16</sup>"As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you.<sup>17</sup>But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.<sup>18</sup>But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine."<sup>19</sup>And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"<sup>20</sup>Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer:<sup>21</sup>"As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind?<sup>22</sup>The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day.<sup>23</sup>It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."<sup>24</sup>Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt.<sup>25</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows!<sup>26</sup>Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'<sup>27</sup>Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them.<sup>28</sup>And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.<sup>29</sup>This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm:<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Seen All the Disaster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes to the Judeans scattered across Egypt and begins with evidence they cannot dispute: the ruin of Jerusalem, caused by offerings to unknown gods, after God had persistently sent his prophets to plead with them (vv. 1–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The argument opens with a ruin they had walked through themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them, because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis. Four place names, and they tell a story on their own. The company that arrived together at Tahpanhes has spread — north to Migdol on the frontier, south to Memphis, and up the Nile into Pathros, which is upper Egypt. They are settling in, scattering through the country, making lives. A century later a Jewish garrison at Elephantine, far up the Nile in Pathros, had its own temple to the LORD, and its papyri suggest that other gods were honoured there beside him: the mixed worship this chapter confronts was slow to die.

You have seen. God begins with what is not in dispute. You have seen — not heard, not been told. These people had walked out through the rubble. Whatever else is arguable, the ruin is a fact they carry in their own memories.

The disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem. And he claims it: the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem. Babylon was only the instrument; the ruin was his doing.

That they knew not. The cause is stated in one word — idolatry — and there is a small devastating clause attached: gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.

Gods recently met. These were not ancestral deities with a long claim on the family. They were novelties, picked up from neighbours, unknown to the generations that had actually seen God act. A nation abandoned the God who brought it out of Egypt for gods it had only recently met.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!' But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods. Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet I persistently sent to you. The word that runs through the whole book appears again, persistently, and this time it comes with a cry that sounds like nothing else in Jeremiah.

Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! That is not the language of a law code. It is the cry of someone trying to stop a person he loves from doing something that will destroy them, and God puts it in his own mouth as the summary of four centuries of prophetic preaching. Generation after generation of warning, distilled to a single Oh.

But they did not listen or incline their ear. Two verbs of refusal, and they are the epitaph of the kingdom: did not listen, did not incline their ear. The second is worse than the first. To incline the ear is to lean in; they would not even turn their heads toward it.

As at this day. And as at this day is what the argument turns on. The evidence is in front of them now. God is not asking them to accept a theory about judgment; he is pointing at a country they can still see from where they stand, and asking them to read it correctly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Why Do You Commit This Great Evil Against Yourselves?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God describes their idolatry, taken up again in Egypt, as harm done to themselves (vv. 7–8); the evil of five groups, from their fathers down to their own wives, is listed as one continuous story, and none of them has humbled himself even to this day (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: From God's side, sin is a wound the sinner opens in his own household.

verseByVerse.quote: And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant? Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth? Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against yourselves. God describes their sin as committed against yourselves.

Idolatry as self-harm. It is the truest thing said about idolatry anywhere in the chapter. He has already told them it provokes him to anger, and here he describes it as self-mutilation, a knife taken to man and woman, infant and child, cutting away their own future. Sin is treason against God and self-destruction in the family, and the second is often what finally gets a person's attention.

The works of your hands. They made the thing they are worshipping. Paul's summary of the same exchange runs the same way: men who exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals (Rom 1:23).

Where you have come to live. And note where you have come to live. They had gone to Egypt for safety and immediately resumed the practice that had cost them their own country. A change of address does nothing to the heart that made the move.

Nobody exempt. Verse 9 lists the evil of five groups in one sentence. (The ESV notes that where the English has their wives after the kings, the Hebrew reads “his”.) Either way the list is comprehensive: fathers, kings, royal wives, the hearers themselves, their own wives. Nobody in the assembly is outside it, and the wives are named twice, which prepares for verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even to this day. One verse, three failures, and a phrase that should stop any reader: even to this day.

Everything they had seen. Consider what this day contains. The city burned. The temple gone. The king blinded after watching his sons die. A long famine, a governor murdered at his table, seventy pilgrims in a cistern, and a forced march into Egypt. If catastrophe by itself produced humility, these would be the humblest people alive.

They have not humbled themselves. They are not. They have not humbled themselves, nor have they feared. Suffering does not soften a heart on its own; it only reveals what the heart already was. The same fire hardens clay and melts wax, and Judah in Egypt is the proof.

Nor walked in my law and my statutes. And the third failure is the plainest: they have not walked in my law and my statutes, the law given to a people he had already brought out of Egypt. The charge is simply that nobody did them. No one ever has, fully (Eccl 7:20). That is why this book's hope rests on a new covenant with the law written on the heart (31:33), and on the one who walked in that law perfectly in our place, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him (Rom 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — They Shall All Be Consumed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets his face against those who set their faces toward Egypt: they will be punished there as Jerusalem was, and none will return, except some fugitives (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: They wanted Egypt for a while and Judah in the end, and are told they will have neither.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah. I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will set my face against you. Earlier in this book God had hidden his face from the city (33:5); here he turns it toward these people, and it is worse. An averted face means abandonment; a set face means deliberate opposition.

Answered exactly. The phrase is answered exactly. They set their faces toward Egypt (42:15), and God set my face against them. Two settings of the face in opposite directions, and only one of them can hold.

From the least to the greatest. And From the least to the greatest is the phrase used of the crowd that came asking for guidance and swore to obey (42:1, 8). The whole company that took the oath is the whole company under the sentence.

As I have punished Jerusalem. The comparison is the argument: as I have punished Jerusalem. They had seen what that looked like. Egypt will not be exempt.

To which they desire to return to dwell there. Here is the hidden assumption of the whole migration, exposed in one clause: to which they desire to return to dwell there. They never meant to stay in Egypt. The plan was to sit out the danger and go home afterwards — the reasoning of everyone who intends a short detour away from obedience and fully expects to come back.

Except some fugitives. They will not come back. And then, at the very end, three words that refuse to close the door completely: except some fugitives. A handful will straggle home. Even in this sentence God keeps a remnant of a remnant, and it matters that he says so, because the chapter is about to record the most direct refusal in the book and this clause is spoken before it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — We Will Not Listen to You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A great assembly, men and women together, refuses outright and vows to keep serving the queen of heaven, because in her days they prospered (vv. 15–18); the women add that their husbands approved (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: They read the ruin of Jerusalem as evidence that they had not sinned enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah: "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you. But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great assembly. The description is careful. The men knew what their wives were doing; the women are standing there; it is a great assembly. This is not a faction muttering. It is a congregation, organised, with the households aligned.

We will not listen to you. For forty years this people had not listened, but they had always said something else — that Jeremiah was a traitor, or mad, or Baruch's puppet, or that the LORD had not sent him. Here the pretence is dropped. They admit that the word was spoken in the name of the LORD, and refuse it anyway: we will not listen to you.

Unbelief out loud. It is one of the plainest sentences of unbelief in the Old Testament, and it is not the speech of ignorant people. They know what they are refusing, they mean it, and they say it together.

The queen of heaven. The queen of heaven was a pagan goddess of fertility and provision, probably Ishtar or Astarte, and this cult is not new. Jeremiah had described it decades earlier in Jerusalem: The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven (7:18). A whole family working together at it, which is exactly what is happening again here.

We had plenty of food, and prospered. And the argument they give is economic. When we served her, we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. It is the reasoning of a woman in Hosea: I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink (Hos 2:5) — and God's answer there is the answer here: she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil (Hos 2:8).

The god of what works. The argument from prosperity would be at home in any self-help shelf today. Do not ask whether a practice is true; ask whether it works. Does it lower my stress, help my marriage, grow the business, get me through the week? Spirituality chosen by results is now the ordinary kind, and it can look humble, because it makes no grand claims. But it puts us in charge. A god kept because he delivers is an employee, and he will be dismissed the day the results dip, which is exactly what these people say happened to the LORD under Josiah. And results are a poor judge, as the next verses show: read over one generation, the evidence pointed them exactly the wrong way. The God of the Bible will not be hired on those terms. He gives bread to people who never thank him for it, and in the end he gave himself, in what looked by every measure of results like the greatest failure in history, a man dying on a Roman cross. That failure is the one thing that has worked for sinners ever since.

Later misuse of the title. She was worshipped with cakes and drink offerings. Some Christians later gave the title to Mary; Scripture gives her no such title, and offerings and prayers to anyone but God are forbidden.
verseByVerse.note: This is the last time in the book that Jeremiah's hearers answer him, and their answer is the refusal itself.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine." And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
History upside down. This sentence is a reading of history, and it is exactly upside down.

Since we left off making offerings. What they are describing is most likely Josiah's reformation. The idols were cleared out, the high places (the hilltop shrines) pulled down, the queen of heaven’s cakes went off the family table, and then came Josiah’s death at Megiddo, Egyptian rule, Babylon, the siege, the famine and the fall. They have drawn the obvious conclusion from the sequence: the trouble started when the reform did.

Right facts, wrong cause. The facts are right; cause and effect are the wrong way round. And they are so nearly right that it is frightening. There is a way of reading events that is careful, based on what really happened, and completely wrong, because it leaves out the four centuries of patience that preceded the reform and the fact that the reform was too late and never reached the heart.

In everyday life. People still argue this way. Things went badly after I began to take God seriously, therefore taking God seriously was the mistake. The timeline is accurate and the verdict is a lie.

And the women said. The women now speak for themselves. (The ESV notes that the words And the women said are supplied from the Syriac; in the Hebrew the speech simply continues.)

A legal point. Their point is legal. Under the law a husband who heard his wife's vow and said nothing had confirmed it, and only by opposing it on the day he heard could he annul it (Num 30:6-8). So: our husbands knew, and never once forbade us. That is unanswerable as far as it goes, and it is an indictment of the men standing beside them, who had known all along (v. 15).

Shared blame. But look at what they are actually doing with the argument. They are not asking forgiveness or claiming they were pressured; they are establishing that the guilt is shared, as a reason to carry on. Spreading the blame feels like a defence, but it is in fact a confession, and Jeremiah’s reply goes, deliberately, to all the people, men and women (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah answers that God remembered those offerings and could bear them no longer (vv. 20–23). Their vow is handed back as a sentence, God's name will no more be spoken by them in Egypt, and the few survivors will know whose word stands; the sign is Pharaoh Hophra (vv. 24–30).
verseByVerse.theology: Two words have competed throughout this book, God’s and his opponents’, and the end shows which one holds.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer: "As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind? The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day. It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To all the people, men and women. He takes them at their word. They had argued that everybody was in it together, so he addresses everybody together.

Did not the LORD remember them? Two questions, and they go straight at the hole in the argument. They had said that in the days of the cakes there was plenty of food and no disaster — as though God had not noticed. Did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind?

Patience mistaken for approval. God's patience had been mistaken for God's approval. The years of prosperity were not evidence that he was pleased; they were the long stretch in which he sent prophet after prophet saying Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! Delay is not indifference, and every unpunished season is being remembered.

The LORD could no longer bear. The phrase implies that he had borne it for a very long time, and that there was a limit, and that the limit was reached. The desolation they keep pointing at is not the result of the reformation; it is the end of God's forbearance with the very practice they have resumed.

It is because you made offerings. The cause is stated outright: It is because. They had the cause of the disaster wrong, and Jeremiah corrects it. The disaster came because of the offerings, not because they stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. The address is almost a definition of what they have become: not Judah in Judah, but Judah in Egypt — a people identified by the place they should not be.

You and your wives have declared with your mouths. God quotes their oath back to them, and then says: do it.

Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! There is no sarcasm in it and no bluff. It is one of the most terrible things God says in the book, because it means God will no longer stand in their way. They have insisted on their vows for long enough; he stops arguing and lets them keep them.

Given up to their choice. Scripture knows this judgment elsewhere — God giving people up to what they have chosen. It is not that he has grown indifferent, but that pleading has an end, and being left alone with what you insisted on is the worst thing a person can be given.

For a tender conscience. A tender conscience may fear that this has happened to it. The fear itself is a good sign: those whom God has given up do not grieve over their sin or long for him. The door stays open for anyone who comes, for Christ has said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

By my great name. And here is the sentence. God swears by my great name that his name will never again be spoken by a Judean in Egypt.

As the Lord GOD lives. Weigh what is being removed. Not their lives first, but the words of their worship: the oath As the Lord GOD lives, the ordinary speech of a covenant people. They had gone on using his name while serving the queen of heaven, invoking him as a matter of habit, and he will not have his name in their mouths on those terms. It is possible to lose the right to say God's name while still saying it constantly.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them. And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs. This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm: Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am watching over them for disaster. The verb is the one from Jeremiah's first vision. God had shown him an almond branch and said he was watching over his word to perform it (1:12), and the same attentiveness that promised to build and plant in chapter 31 is here watching over them for disaster and not for good.

The same eye. It is the same eye, the same care, the same refusal to be distracted. That is a sobering thought about the character of God: his watchfulness is not automatically comfort. What it means for you depends on which side of his word you have placed yourself.

Few in number. A few will get home — few in number, the fugitives of verse 14 — and the reason given for their survival is not comfort but demonstration: so that everyone shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.

Whose word will stand, mine or theirs. That is the question the whole book has been asking since that first vision. Two words had been on offer in Jerusalem for forty years: Jeremiah's and everybody else's. Hananiah said two years; the queen of heaven's devotees said prosperity; the prophets of peace said no disaster would come. Each of those words could be tested by what happened, and each one failed.

Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt. The sign is aimed at the precise thing they trusted. They had come to Egypt for safety, and Hophra, whose army had once marched north and lifted the siege of Jerusalem for a time, is the man they were relying on. He will go the way Zedekiah went, and the comparison is spelled out so nobody can miss it: as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

Hophra’s end. And history records it. Hophra (the Greeks called him Apries) lost his throne to his general Amasis after an army revolt in about 570 BC, and within a few years he was dead, most likely killed trying to win it back, which is exactly into the hand of those who seek his life.

The last word to his people. So the last recorded words of Jeremiah to his own people end on a question rather than a curse: whose word will stand, mine or theirs. It is a question with an answer, and the answer is the reason this book exists. Every word spoken against Jerusalem stood; and that means the other words stand too — the everlasting love, the law written on the heart, the sins remembered no more, the shepherd who gathers, the Branch called The LORD is our righteousness. The God who kept the hard half of his word to the letter is the God who has promised the rest of it, and every one of those promises is kept in Christ: For all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Cor 1:20).

44.title: We Will Not Listen to You
44.overview:
This is Jeremiah's last recorded sermon, preached to Judeans now settled all over Egypt. God points to the ruin of Jerusalem they have seen with their own eyes and to its cause: the gods they served though he had pleaded with them persistently to stop. They have taken up the same worship in Egypt, and he warns that the refuge will share Jerusalem's sentence, with only a few fugitives returning (vv. 1-14).

A great assembly of men and women answers plainly: we will not listen to you. They will keep serving the queen of heaven, because in her days they prospered (vv. 15-19). Jeremiah replies that the disaster came because of those offerings, not because they stopped. God hands their vows back to them, swears that his name will no longer be on their lips, and gives the fall of Pharaoh Hophra as the sign of whose word will stand (vv. 20-30).
44.theology:
The chapter is a study of how a people can see God's judgment with their own eyes and still read it upside down. Suffering did not humble them (v. 10); God's long patience was mistaken for approval (vv. 21-22); and an accurate timeline was turned into a false verdict, as though the trouble began when the idols were removed (v. 18; Hos 2:5, 8).

Against that stands the faithfulness of God's word. His watchfulness is not automatically comfort: the eye that watched to build and plant can watch for disaster (v. 27; 1:12; 31:28). Yet because every hard word against Jerusalem stood, the promises of the same book stand too.
44.examples:
Some people say that things went badly from the time they began to take God seriously, so taking God seriously must have been the mistake. The women of Judah argued exactly that, and the timeline they gave was accurate. What they left out was four centuries of God's patience, and the fact that the reform never reached their hearts.

Others keep using God's name as a habit while their real trust lies elsewhere, the way the refugees went on saying As the Lord GOD lives while baking cakes for the queen of heaven. The chapter warns that it is possible to lose the right to say God's name while still saying it every day.

45.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch:<sup>3</sup>You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'<sup>4</sup>Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land.<sup>5</sup>And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dated to the year of the scroll Jehoiakim burned, this is God's word to the scribe by name, and it opens by quoting his own complaint back to him (vv. 1–3).
verseByVerse.theology: God repeats a tired man's private complaint to him, word for word, and it is not a rebuke.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch: You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Placed here on purpose. Five verses, addressed to one man, and they are placed here on purpose.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The date takes us back nearly twenty years, to the year Baruch wrote twenty-three years of sermons onto a scroll at Jeremiah's dictation (36:4) and watched the king cut it up and feed it to a brazier. But the book keeps this word until now, so that Jeremiah's words to his own people end not with a nation's refusal but with God bending down to one exhausted assistant.

To you, O Baruch. The solemn opening, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, which introduced oracles to kings, Babylon, Egypt and the nations, is used here to speak to a secretary, and it is to you, O Baruch. The God who commands the empires has a private message for the man holding the pen, and he uses his name. That is a word for anyone who has served in a supporting role and wondered whether anyone noticed the work.

Woe is me! God quotes him, and there is no reproach in the quotation. The LORD has added sorrow to my pain: he is not blaming circumstances but God, openly. I am weary with my groaning: worn out by his own complaining, which is a particular kind of exhaustion.

What Baruch had lost. He had reason. He came from a prominent family (his brother Seraiah, it seems, was a royal official, 51:59), and by attaching himself to Jeremiah he had chosen the losing side of every argument in Jerusalem. He saw his book burned, had to go into hiding, and was blamed as the sinister influence behind the prophet (43:3).

His master’s complaint too. And his master had said the same kind of thing: I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot (20:9). Serving God faithfully does not exempt a man from being worn out by it, and Scripture records the complaints of both of them without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows Baruch that his grief is part of God’s own tearing down of the whole land, tells him not to seek great things for himself, and promises him his life as a prize of war wherever he goes (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: Baruch is promised no career, no safety and no acclaim, only his life, wherever he ends up.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land. And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The larger picture. God begins not by consoling him but by showing him the larger picture.

What I have built I am breaking down. Baruch's own scroll had recorded Jeremiah's commission, to pluck up and break down, to build and to plant (1:10). Now God takes those verbs and applies them to himself, and the object is the whole land. God is not losing; he is demolishing, deliberately, his own work.

Not out of control. That puts Baruch’s grief in a different light. His pain was real, but the ruin around him had not got out of God’s control. It was a small part of something God was doing on purpose.

Do you seek great things for yourself? The question goes straight to what was wrong, and it is asked without contempt: do you seek great things for yourself? A man of his background, on the right side of the argument, might reasonably have looked for vindication and a future, and God names that hope and tells him to give it up. Not because ambition is always wicked, but because of the timing: this is not the hour for building a career. And the command comes wrapped in a gift: the God who tells him to want less is about to give him his life.

God’s way with the weary. God's way with his weary servants is often this: not a rebuke, but a clear-eyed account of what he is doing. Jeremiah himself had been answered the same way (12:5).

For every Christian. The New Testament says it to everyone. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness (Matt 6:33). The appointed time has grown very short (1 Cor 7:29-31). And a man who had thrown away far better prospects than Baruch's put it plainly: whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ (Phil 3:7). None of us lets go of great things for ourselves by resolve; it is the Spirit who shows us Christ as worth more than they are, and the one who never sought his own glory has already done that perfectly in our place.

What this looks like. Seeking great things for yourself is rarely a grand plan. It is usually quieter: the promotion you rehearse in your head at night, the need to be credited in the meeting, the sense that after all you have given up you are owed a future. Letting it go looks ordinary. Name the great thing. Tell God which hope you are holding, the title, the house, the recognition, as Baruch’s was named for him. Do the unseen task well. Baruch wrote the whole scroll out again after the first was burned; faithfulness in work nobody praises is the great thing given to most of us. Let someone else have the credit this week, and notice what it costs you. Hold your plans with an open hand, saying If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (Jas 4:15). We can do this without bitterness, because we have been given what Baruch was given and more: a life that is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:3), which no war and no disappointment can take.

I will give you your life as a prize of war. The promise is one Jeremiah had shouted across Jerusalem: go out to the Chaldeans and you will have your life as a prize of war (38:2). It was given personally to Ebed-melech, because you have put your trust in me (39:18). Now the scribe receives it.

In all places to which you may go. It is a soldier's phrase: the one thing you carry off the field. And it is exactly suited to a man about to be marched into Egypt against his will: in all places to which you may go. God does not promise him a destination he would choose. He promises to keep him in whatever place he ends up.

What Baruch was given. So the last word to Baruch is: the great things are not for you, and you will live. And we can see what he was given instead of a career. Much of what we possess of Jeremiah probably came through his hand. He wrote the burned scroll again, longer (36:32), and the book in which the new covenant stands came to us through his pen. That book has outlasted Jehoiakim, Babylon and Egypt, and is being read still.

A life no place can take. For a Christian the promise reaches further. Baruch was given his life in every place he might go; those who belong to Christ are given a life no place and no power can take. The one who said I do not seek my own glory (John 8:50) laid down his life and took it up again, and of his sheep he says, I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

45.title: A Word for Baruch
45.overview: This short word to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, dates from the year he first wrote the prophet's sermons on the scroll Jehoiakim burned (ch. 36), but the book places it here, after the last sermon to the people. God quotes Baruch's private complaint back to him without reproach (vv. 1-3), shows him that his grief is part of God’s own tearing down of the land, tells him not to seek great things for himself, and promises him his life in every place he may go (vv. 4-5).
45.theology:
God has private words for those who serve in supporting roles, and he uses their names (v. 2). Faithful service does not exempt anyone from exhaustion, and Scripture records Baruch's weariness, like his master's, without embarrassment (v. 3; 20:9).

God comforts Baruch here by showing him what God is doing, not by sympathy, and he answers his ambition not with shame but by telling him that this is not the hour for great things (vv. 4-5; Matt 6:33; 1 Cor 7:29-31; Phil 3:7). What he promises is not the destination his servant would choose but his keeping in every place the servant is taken (38:2; 39:18).
45.examples:
Picture a secretary who has spent twenty years writing down another man's unpopular words, watched the work cut up and burned, written it all out again, and been blamed for it by people who would not blame the prophet himself. Baruch's "woe is me" is the voice of every faithful assistant who has wondered whether anyone noticed.

God's reply is not a speech about his feelings. It tells him what God is doing, asks him to want less, and gives him one promise he can carry anywhere. Many weary Christians have found that the way through: not a better career, but the Lord's own company in the places they did not choose.

46.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations.<sup>2</sup>About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>3</sup>"Prepare buckler and shield, and advance for battle!<sup>4</sup>Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen! Take your stations with your helmets, polish your spears, put on your armor!<sup>5</sup>Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward. Their warriors are beaten down and have fled in haste; they look not back— terror on every side! declares the LORD.<sup>6</sup>"The swift cannot flee away, nor the warrior escape; in the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen.<sup>7</sup>"Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge?<sup>8</sup>Egypt rises like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He said, 'I will rise, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities and their inhabitants.'<sup>9</sup>Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! Let the warriors go out: men of Cush and Put who handle the shield, men of Lud, skilled in handling the bow.<sup>10</sup>That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes. The sword shall devour and be sated and drink its fill of their blood. For the Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.<sup>11</sup>Go up to Gilead, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you.<sup>12</sup>The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for warrior has stumbled against warrior; they have both fallen together."<sup>13</sup>The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt:<sup>14</sup>"Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes; say, 'Stand ready and be prepared, for the sword shall devour around you.'<sup>15</sup>Why are your mighty ones face down? They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down.<sup>16</sup>He made many stumble, and they fell, and they said one to another, 'Arise, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, because of the sword of the oppressor.'<sup>17</sup>Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, 'Noisy one who lets the hour go by.'<sup>18</sup>"As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea, shall one come.<sup>19</sup>Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! For Memphis shall become a waste, a ruin, without inhabitant.<sup>20</sup>"A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her.<sup>21</sup>Even her hired soldiers in her midst are like fattened calves; yes, they have turned and fled together; they did not stand, for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment.<sup>22</sup>"She makes a sound like a serpent gliding away; for her enemies march in force and come against her with axes like those who fell trees.<sup>23</sup>They shall cut down her forest, declares the LORD, though it is impenetrable, because they are more numerous than locusts; they are without number.<sup>24</sup>The daughter of Egypt shall be put to shame; she shall be delivered into the hand of a people from the north."<sup>25</sup>The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, said: "Behold, I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him.<sup>26</sup>I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old, declares the LORD.<sup>27</sup>"But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid.<sup>28</sup>Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Rising Like the Nile, and Fallen at Carchemish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracles concerning the nations open at Carchemish (vv. 1-2), where Nebuchadnezzar broke Pharaoh Neco in 605 BC. The poem begins as a mustering order and breaks off as the line collapses (vv. 3-6); Egypt's boast of rising like the Nile becomes the LORD's day of vengeance by the Euphrates, and there is no healing for her (vv. 7-12).
verseByVerse.theology: An army dresses for victory on the very field where God is holding a sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations. About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning the nations. A new section begins here, and it widens the horizon of the whole book. For forty-five chapters God has dealt chiefly with Judah; now come six chapters concerning the nations. (In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, these oracles stand after 25:13 and in a different order; the Hebrew text, which our English Bibles follow, places them here.) The God who judged his own people is not a local god whose rule stops at the borders of one hill country.

The fourth year of Jehoiakim. And the date matters: the fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605 BC. That is the year of the scroll (36:1), and Carchemish is the battle that made Babylon the master of the world.

About Egypt. Egypt comes first among the nations, and for a reason. Pharaoh Neco (Neco II) had marched north in 609 BC to prop up the failing Assyrians at Carchemish, killing Josiah at Megiddo on the way (2 Kgs 23:29). Four years later, at the same river crossing, Nebuchadnezzar, then still Babylon’s crown prince, routed Neco’s army and drove it back toward Egypt. Egypt was the power Judah’s politicians kept looking to for rescue (2:18, 36; 37:5–7), so this oracle is aimed as much at Judah’s hopes as at Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.note: Carchemish stood at a crossing of the upper Euphrates, on today's border between Turkey and Syria.

verseByVerse.quote: "Prepare buckler and shield, and advance for battle! Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen! Take your stations with your helmets, polish your spears, put on your armor! Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward. Their warriors are beaten down and have fled in haste; they look not back— terror on every side! declares the LORD. "The swift cannot flee away, nor the warrior escape; in the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prepare buckler and shield. The poem opens inside the Egyptian camp, and the voice is a drill sergeant's. Shields up, horses harnessed, helmets on, spears polished. It is all noise and confidence, and verse 5 will show that the voice is the LORD's, which should warn the reader that something ironic is coming.

Why have I seen it? The poem breaks off in the middle of the parade. Why have I seen it? The armour has only just been polished, and already the soldiers are running.

Terror on every side! And the phrase at the end is one Jeremiah had worn as a nickname. Terror on every side was what he cried and what his enemies called him (6:25; 20:3, 10). The thing he had suffered under is now pronounced over the army Judah was trusting in.

The swift cannot flee away. Speed and strength, the two things a soldier relies on, both fail, as Amos had said they would on the day of judgment (Amos 2:14–15). In the north by the river Euphrates names the place exactly: Carchemish lay hundreds of miles from the Nile, at the far edge of Egypt’s reach. The word stumbled will return as the last word of the whole poem (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge? Egypt rises like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He said, 'I will rise, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities and their inhabitants.' Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! Let the warriors go out: men of Cush and Put who handle the shield, men of Lud, skilled in handling the bow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rising like the Nile. The image is Egypt's own. The Nile flood was the source of everything she had, and the boast borrows its language: I will rise, I will cover the earth. The roll call that follows is Egypt’s allied and hired troops: Cush is the upper Nile (Nubia), Put probably Libya, and Lud probably the Lydians of Asia Minor, whose mercenaries served the pharaohs of this period.

Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! The second poem follows the pattern of the first: the boast and the battle orders come first (compare vv. 3–4), and the collapse follows. The orders are probably ironic, a summons to the slaughter the next verse describes. And there is irony in the boast too: the Nile rises every year, but it also goes down every year. A power that compares itself to the flood has chosen a picture of something that subsides.

verseByVerse.quote: That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes. The sword shall devour and be sated and drink its fill of their blood. For the Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts. The day of the LORD is the prophets’ name for the time when God steps in to judge (Amos 5:18; Zeph 1:14–16). Here it is a dated battle in 605 BC: the day of the LORD arrives in particular days of history, each a foretaste of the last one. A day of vengeance is not spite but the settling of accounts by the rightful judge (Deut 32:35).

The Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice. The battle is renamed. Egypt thought it was a campaign; God calls it a sacrifice, an act of his judgment, with himself as the one holding it. Isaiah had used the same terrible picture of a sword sated with blood at a sacrifice in Edom (Isa 34:6).

Is God bloodthirsty? The picture is meant to shock, but it is not delight in slaughter; God says he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11). It is the language of justice. Egypt had killed Josiah at Megiddo and ruled Judah by force (2 Kgs 23:29-35).

verseByVerse.quote: Go up to Gilead, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you. The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for warrior has stumbled against warrior; they have both fallen together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go up to Gilead, and take balm. Egypt is told to fetch balm, a healing ointment, from Gilead, where it came from. Jeremiah had once asked over his own people, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22). Judah's wound was called incurable too, and then God said I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal (30:17).

There is no healing for you. Here the sentence stops at the diagnosis: there is no healing for you. The difference between Judah and Egypt is not the severity of the wound. It is that one of them had a covenant, and a God who heals wounds he inflicted.

Warrior has stumbled against warrior. The poem ends where the first one ended (v. 6), with stumbling and falling. The picture is of a rout so crowded that soldiers trip over one another in flight, and the hired troops of verse 9 go down with the Egyptians they were paid to protect. Egypt wanted to cover the earth (v. 8); instead the earth is full of your cry, and her shame is known to every nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–19 — Noisy One Who Lets the Hour Go By
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second word concerns Nebuchadnezzar's coming against Egypt itself (v. 13), proclaimed in the very towns where the Judean refugees had settled (v. 14). The LORD thrusts the mighty down, the mercenaries break for home, Pharaoh is renamed, and Egypt is told to pack for exile (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The great power everyone trusted is renamed as all noise and no timing.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt: "Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes; say, 'Stand ready and be prepared, for the sword shall devour around you.' Why are your mighty ones face down? They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down. He made many stumble, and they fell, and they said one to another, 'Arise, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, because of the sword of the oppressor.' Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, 'Noisy one who lets the hour go by.' "As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea, shall one come. Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! For Memphis shall become a waste, a ruin, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol. Read the place names and remember who is living in them. Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes — the exact towns where the Judean refugees had settled (44:1). They fled to these cities to escape the sword, and the sword is being proclaimed over the streets they chose.

Because the LORD thrust them down. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "He does not stand" (v. 15), a single champion falling rather than many. Either way the cause is the same, and it is stated without decoration: the LORD thrust them down.

Let us go back to our own people. Egypt's army was full of foreign mercenaries, and here they break for home. Hired soldiers fight for pay and leave when the pay is not worth the risk, which is the lasting weakness of any strength that is merely bought.

Noisy one who lets the hour go by. Pharaoh is given a nickname, Noisy one who lets the hour go by, and it is devastating. He is all sound and no timing, a man who blusters while the moment passes him. The refugees in Egypt had staked their lives on Pharaoh (44:30), and God gives him a name that says he will not turn up.

As I live, declares the King. In a chapter full of pharaohs and emperors, only one is called King, and he swears by his own life: As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. Pharaoh is a noise that misses its moment; the King of all the armies of heaven and earth has never missed one.

The LORD of hosts. The title runs through this book like a signature, and it is easy to read past it. Hosts means armies: the stars, the angels, every power in heaven and on earth, all under one command. Egypt’s hired soldiers turned and fled (v. 21); the armies of the LORD do not desert. Elisha’s frightened servant was shown them once, when “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17). And when Isaiah heard the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), John tells us that he “saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41), meaning Jesus. Here is the wonder. On the night he was arrested, the Lord of those armies said he could ask his Father for “more than twelve legions of angels” (Matthew 26:53), and did not ask, so that he could be taken in our place. So when the news is loud with the noise of the powerful, pray the psalm the title belongs to: “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (Psalm 46:7).

Like Tabor among the mountains. And the invader will come like Tabor and Carmel: not a passing raid but something as fixed and unmissable as a mountain. So: Prepare yourselves baggage for exile. The country the refugees chose as a refuge is told to pack.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Beautiful Heifer and a Biting Fly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The pictures turn rural and dismissive: Egypt is a sleek heifer driven frantic by a fly from the north, her troops fattened calves, her forest felled by countless woodcutters. Judgment reaches Pharaoh, Egypt's gods and all who trust in him, and then, unexpectedly, Egypt is promised an afterward (vv. 20-26).
verseByVerse.theology: A superpower is reduced to livestock troubled by an insect, and is still given an afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: "A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her. Even her hired soldiers in her midst are like fattened calves; yes, they have turned and fled together; they did not stand, for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment. "She makes a sound like a serpent gliding away; for her enemies march in force and come against her with axes like those who fell trees. They shall cut down her forest, declares the LORD, though it is impenetrable, because they are more numerous than locusts; they are without number. The daughter of Egypt shall be put to shame; she shall be delivered into the hand of a people from the north." The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, said: "Behold, I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him. I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
