A beautiful heifer is Egypt. The imagery turns to the farmyard, and it is deliberately belittling. Egypt is a beautiful heifer — sleek, well fed, worth looking at — tormented by a biting fly. Anyone who has watched cattle in summer knows the picture: a huge animal made frantic by an insect it cannot reach.

Like fattened calves. Her professional soldiers are fattened calves, which is what you call an animal being prepared for slaughter rather than for work.

Like a serpent gliding away. Then three more pictures in quick succession: a snake sliding off through the grass, woodcutters swinging axes, and locusts beyond counting. Egypt's forest is called impenetrable and it comes down anyway.

Her gods and her kings. The list reaches past the politics to the religion — her gods — and then ends on a phrase that is aimed straight at the Judeans reading it: those who trust in him. They had trusted him. They are on the list. Amon of Thebes was the great god of Egypt’s southern capital, honoured as king of the gods, so the sentence strikes first at the head of Egypt’s religion.

Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited. And then one word that changes the mood: Afterward.

Not annihilation. Egypt will be inhabited again, as in the days of old. This is not an oracle of annihilation. The God who judges the nations has a future for them beyond the judgment, which is a remarkable thing to say about Egypt, the house of slavery.

How it was fulfilled. Egypt’s restoration after judgment came in history as it recovered under later rulers; Isaiah looks further, to Egypt worshipping the LORD (Isa 19:21–25), a hope that began to be fulfilled when Egyptians heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — But Fear Not, O Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by turning from Egypt to Israel, in words lifted from the Book of Consolation (30:10-11): God's servant need not fear, for he will save, discipline in just measure, and never make a full end of his people (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Egypt closes with the exact comfort once spoken to Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: "But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A repeated promise. The chapter turns, and anyone who has read chapter 30 will recognise every word. This is 30:10-11, repeated almost exactly, dropped here at the end of an oracle against Egypt.

Fear not, O Jacob my servant. Think about who first needed to hear it. Judeans living in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes, who had just been told that the sword would come to those streets. They are also told: fear not, O Jacob my servant. The same word that announces Egypt's ruin turns to the exiles trapped inside it and calls them God's servant.

For I am with you. And the comfort rests on God’s presence: for I am with you.

But of you I will not make a full end. Then the distinction the whole section rests on. The nations get a full end; Israel does not — but of you I will not make a full end. And the reason is not that Israel behaved better, which this book has spent forty-five chapters disproving. It is that God has bound himself to them by covenant, his sworn promise, and nothing else.

I will discipline you in just measure. Nor is the comfort soft. The same sentence promises discipline in just measure and adds I will by no means leave you unpunished. This is a father's measured hand, not an enemy's, and the difference between being disciplined and being ended is the difference between belonging to him and not.

The full end fell on him. For those in Christ the line runs deeper still. The full end that their sin deserved was not simply cancelled; it was borne by the one who was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people (Isa 53:8). What remains for God's children is a Father's discipline, never an enemy's wrath (Heb 12:6-11; Rom 8:1).

Judgment not the last word. So the first oracle against the nations closes on an unexpected note. Egypt is given an afterward; Israel is given a promise; and both come from the same God on the same page. Judgment on the nations is never the last word in this book, not even for Egypt, and never for the people he keeps.

46.title: Against Egypt
46.overview:
Here the oracles concerning the nations begin (chs. 46-51), and Egypt comes first. The opening poem stands at Carchemish in 605 BC, the battle that made Babylon master of the world: an army polishing its spears for a victory, collapsing in terror, and told there is no healing for its wound (vv. 1-12). A second poem carries the sword into Egypt itself, into the very towns where the Judean refugees had settled (vv. 13-26).

Yet the chapter does not end in ruin. Egypt, of all countries, is promised an afterward (v. 26), and the exiles living inside her are told not to fear, for God is with them and will not make a full end of them (vv. 27-28).
46.theology:
The God who judged Judah is not a local deity, and the nations that boast of what they will do (I will rise, I will cover the earth) find that he calls their battle his own sacrifice, his act of judgment (vv. 8, 10). Yet his judgment of the nations is not annihilation; Egypt is given an afterward (v. 26).

The chapter also marks the difference between Judah and Egypt. Both are wounded, but only one has a covenant and a God who heals what he has struck (v. 11; 30:17). Israel is spared a full end by that covenant, not by better behaviour, and its discipline is a father's, measured and purposeful (vv. 27-28).
46.examples:
Any power can look like the Nile in flood, rising to cover the earth. Jeremiah shows the same army polishing its spears and then fleeing, and the Pharaoh everyone was relying on renamed "Noisy one who lets the hour go by." It is a sobering picture for anyone tempted to trust a government, an employer or a market more than God.

It is also a comfort for those who live inside a world under judgment. The Judeans in Migdol and Memphis heard the sword proclaimed over their own streets, and in the same breath heard God call them his servant and say, I am with you.

47.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail.<sup>3</sup>At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands,<sup>4</sup>because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.<sup>5</sup>Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves?<sup>6</sup>Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still!<sup>7</sup>How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Waters Rising Out of the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza (v. 1). The invader is a flood out of the north, heard before it is seen, so terrible that fathers do not look back for their children, and every helper is cut off (vv. 2–4).
verseByVerse.theology: The flood comes out of the north, and fathers are too weak to turn round for their own children.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. "Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail. At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands, because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning the Philistines. Seven verses for a people who had been Israel's tormentors since the judges. Samson, Goliath, the ark carried into Ashdod, Saul's body hung on the wall at Beth-shan: the Philistines are woven through the whole earlier history, and here they are dealt with in a single short poem. This oracle names no crime, but other prophets do: Amos charged Gaza with carrying whole communities into exile to be sold (Amos 1:6), and Ezekiel spoke of their never-ending enmity (Ezek 25:15).

Before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. The dating is by an Egyptian raid on Gaza, which most likely belongs to the years around Carchemish (perhaps 609 or about 601 BC; the date is debated). The great powers are moving, and the small nations on the coast road are in the way.

Waters are rising out of the north. The invader is described as a flood, and the direction is the one this book has used from the beginning: out of the north. The boiling pot tilted from the north in chapter 1; the enemy from the north hung over Judah for twenty-five chapters. The same water that drowned Jerusalem now comes down the coast.

An overflowing torrent. A flood does not fight a city; it covers it, and there is nothing to fight back against. You hear the army before you see it.

So feeble are their hands. Then one image that does more than any casualty figure: men running who do not turn round for their own sons and daughters, and the reason given is not cowardice but collapse, so feeble are their hands. Scripture is not sneering here. It is telling the truth about what overwhelming force does to ordinary people.

Every helper that remains. Their allies to the north are cut off too: no help will come from Tyre or Sidon, because the same invader will reach them too.

The remnant of the coastland of Caphtor. And the Philistines are called the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor, Caphtor being their old homeland, the place Genesis names in the table of nations (Gen 10:14; compare Amos 9:7). They were sea people who had arrived from somewhere else centuries before. God knows where every nation came from, and the word remnant quietly says that they are already the leftovers of something larger.
verseByVerse.note: Caphtor is probably Crete, the Philistines’ ancestral home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–7 — Sword of the LORD, How Long?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gaza and Ashkelon mourn (v. 5). The poem pleads with the sword of the LORD to rest, and is answered that it cannot, because the LORD has given it a charge (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone begs the sword to stop, and is told who is holding it.

verseByVerse.quote: Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves? Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still! How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baldness has come upon Gaza. Two of the five Philistine cities are named, and the mourning takes the forms these people used: heads shaved, bodies cut. The gashing is the same practice the eighty pilgrims from Shechem and Shiloh had followed before Ishmael met them on the road (41:5), and the same that Israel was expressly forbidden: You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). What God prohibited in his own people was the ordinary way of grieving among their neighbours, and the question how long will you gash yourselves? is not mockery but a comment on futility. Cutting yourself changes nothing. Babylon’s own chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in 604 BC, plundered it and turned it into a heap of ruins.

Ah, sword of the LORD! Then the poet turns from the victims and speaks to the weapon. The tone is not triumph. It is the cry of a man who has watched too much of this. Jeremiah had wept over his own people's ruin, and he does not gloat over the ruin of Israel's old enemies either. Even the enemies of God's people are pitied by the man who has to announce their fall.

No cold talk of judgment. That rebukes anyone who speaks of God’s judgment coldly or with satisfaction. Anyone who can contemplate it without grief has not understood it.

How can it be quiet? The answer is not comfort: the sword cannot rest because it is under orders. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "you" where the English has "it", the poet still addressing the weapon directly. God has given it a charge and appointed it: this is not chaos but an order given, with a named target.

Not accidents. So one of the shortest oracles in this section makes the point the whole section exists to make. History is not a series of accidents in which the strong happen to eat the weak. There is a sword, and it is the LORD's, and it moves when he gives it a charge and rests when he says so.

The sword is at rest. And there is one more thing to say, standing where we do. A day came when the sword of the LORD was given a charge and did not fall on Ashkelon or on Judah. Zechariah had heard God say Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and Jesus took that verse to himself on the night he was betrayed (Zech 13:7; Matt 26:31). The sword fell on a man who had asked in a garden that his cup might pass from him, and who then put himself in its way, so that for everyone who is his the question How long till you are quiet? finally has its answer: the sword is at rest.

47.title: Against the Philistines
47.overview: A short oracle against the Philistines, Israel's old enemies since the days of the judges. The invader from the north comes down the coast like a flood, and the terror is so great that fathers flee without looking back for their children (vv. 1-4). Gaza and Ashkelon mourn, and the poet pleads with the sword of the LORD to rest, only to be told it cannot, because the LORD has given it a charge (vv. 5-7).
47.theology:
The flood from the north that covered Judah now covers the coastal plain: God's instruments are not reserved for one nation, and he knows where every nation came from (vv. 2, 4; 1:13-15; Gen 10:14). History is not chaos; it runs under God’s orders. The sword moves when he gives it a charge and rests when he says so (v. 7; Isa 34:5-6).

Yet the prophet does not gloat. He tells the truth about what terror does to ordinary people and pities even Israel's old tormentors (vv. 3, 6). Anyone who can think about God's judgment without grief has not understood it.
47.examples:
When news comes of a war far away, it is easy to read it either as random chaos or as the deserved fall of people we never liked. Jeremiah refuses both. The sword is the LORD's and is under orders, and the man who announces it still cries out, "How long?"

The father fleeing without turning back for his children is not mocked. Scripture lets us see what overwhelming force does to people, so that we feel it before we analyse it.

48.text: <sup>1</sup>Concerning Moab. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is taken; the fortress is put to shame and broken down;<sup>2</sup>the renown of Moab is no more. In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!' You also, O Madmen, shall be brought to silence; the sword shall pursue you.<sup>3</sup>"A voice! A cry from Horonaim, 'Desolation and great destruction!'<sup>4</sup>Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry.<sup>5</sup>For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; for at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distressed cry of destruction.<sup>6</sup>Flee! Save yourselves! You will be like a juniper in the desert!<sup>7</sup>For, because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials.<sup>8</sup>The destroyer shall come upon every city, and no city shall escape; the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken.<sup>9</sup>"Give wings to Moab, for she would fly away; her cities shall become a desolation, with no inhabitant in them.<sup>10</sup>"Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness, and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from bloodshed.<sup>11</sup>"Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.<sup>12</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I shall send to him pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces.<sup>13</sup>Then Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence.<sup>14</sup>"How do you say, 'We are heroes and mighty men of war'?<sup>15</sup>The destroyer of Moab and his cities has come up, and the choicest of his young men have gone down to slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts.<sup>16</sup>The calamity of Moab is near at hand, and his affliction hastens swiftly.<sup>17</sup>Grieve for him, all you who are around him, and all who know his name; say, 'How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.'<sup>18</sup>"Come down from your glory, and sit on the parched ground, O inhabitant of Dibon! For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you; he has destroyed your strongholds.<sup>19</sup>Stand by the way and watch, O inhabitant of Aroer! Ask him who flees and her who escapes; say, 'What has happened?'<sup>20</sup>Moab is put to shame, for it is broken; wail and cry! Tell it beside the Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.<sup>21</sup>"Judgment has come upon the tableland, upon Holon, and Jahzah, and Mephaath,<sup>22</sup>and Dibon, and Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim,<sup>23</sup>and Kiriathaim, and Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon,<sup>24</sup>and Kerioth, and Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near.<sup>25</sup>The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, declares the LORD.<sup>26</sup>"Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD, so that Moab shall wallow in his vomit, and he too shall be held in derision.<sup>27</sup>Was not Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves, that whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head?<sup>28</sup>"Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, O inhabitants of Moab! Be like the dove that nests in the sides of the mouth of a gorge.<sup>29</sup>We have heard of the pride of Moab— he is very proud— of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart.<sup>30</sup>I know his insolence, declares the LORD; his boasts are false, his deeds are false.<sup>31</sup>Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn.<sup>32</sup>More than for Jazer I weep for you, O vine of Sibmah! Your branches passed over the sea, reached to the Sea of Jazer; on your summer fruits and your grapes the destroyer has fallen.<sup>33</sup>Gladness and joy have been taken away from the fruitful land of Moab; I have made the wine cease from the winepresses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; the shouting is not the shout of joy.<sup>34</sup>"From the outcry at Heshbon even to Elealeh, as far as Jahaz they utter their voice, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. For the waters of Nimrim also have become desolate.<sup>35</sup>And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares the LORD, him who offers sacrifice in the high place and makes offerings to his god.<sup>36</sup>Therefore my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-hareseth. Therefore the riches they gained have perished.<sup>37</sup>"For every head is shaved and every beard cut off. On all the hands are gashes, and around the waist is sackcloth.<sup>38</sup>On all the housetops of Moab and in the squares there is nothing but lamentation, for I have broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares, declares the LORD.<sup>39</sup>How it is broken! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! So Moab has become a derision and a horror to all that are around him."<sup>40</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Behold, one shall fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Moab;<sup>41</sup>the cities shall be taken and the strongholds seized. The heart of the warriors of Moab shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains;<sup>42</sup>Moab shall be destroyed and be no longer a people, because he magnified himself against the LORD.<sup>43</sup>Terror, pit, and snare are before you, O inhabitant of Moab! declares the LORD.<sup>44</sup>He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For I will bring these things upon Moab, the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.<sup>45</sup>"In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stop without strength, for fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the house of Sihon; it has destroyed the forehead of Moab, the crown of the sons of tumult.<sup>46</sup>Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone, for your sons have been taken captive, and your daughters into captivity.<sup>47</sup>Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD." Thus far is the judgment on Moab.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Town after town falls until the renown of Moab is no more (vv. 1–5). Moab trusted in its works and treasures, and Chemosh goes into exile with his priests (vv. 6–9); the section ends with a hard word on doing the LORD's work with slackness (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Moab's national god is carried off into exile alongside the clergy who served him.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Moab. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is taken; the fortress is put to shame and broken down; the renown of Moab is no more. In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!' You also, O Madmen, shall be brought to silence; the sword shall pursue you. "A voice! A cry from Horonaim, 'Desolation and great destruction!' Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; for at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distressed cry of destruction. Flee! Save yourselves! You will be like a juniper in the desert! For, because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The destroyer shall come upon every city, and no city shall escape; the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken. "Give wings to Moab, for she would fly away; her cities shall become a desolation, with no inhabitant in them. "Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness, and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from bloodshed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Moab. Moab was the nation across the Dead Sea, close kin and old enemy. Genesis records the ugly beginning, when Lot's daughter bore a son and called his name Moab (Gen 19:37), and from then on they are neighbours, sometimes allies, mostly trouble.

Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! The poem moves through their towns like a casualty list, and it is full of proper names for a reason. These were real places with markets and families in them. Judgment in Scripture is rarely abstract.

Her little ones have made a cry. The sound that carries is a child's. Her little ones have made a cry: the detail a prophet includes when he is not enjoying his subject.

The ascent of Luhith. The ESV notes two things in verse 5: the Hebrew reads "weeping goes up with weeping", and the Septuagint has "heard the cry", comparing Isaiah 15:5. Isaiah had written the same scene a century before, with fugitives climbing the same road: at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping (Isa 15:5). Two prophets, the same hill, the same people stumbling up it.

You trusted in your works and your treasures. The indictment: you trusted in your works and your treasures. What you have made and what you have saved. It is the most respectable idolatry there is, and it needs no shrine.

Chemosh shall go into exile. And then the picture that exposes it: Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The national god of Moab is deported. A god who has to be carried into captivity by the men who served him is not a god; he is luggage. Moab’s own monument, the Moabite Stone set up by King Mesha at Dibon about 840 BC, credits Chemosh with Moab’s victories over Israel and boasts of taking Nebo and dragging the vessels of the LORD before Chemosh; Jeremiah names the same god and the same towns.

Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness. The curse on slackness is a hard word, spoken to the invading army, the Babylonians God had sent to judge Moab: to do his work half-heartedly would be to defy him. Why would God command bloodshed? Because here he acts as the judge of a nation whose guilt was full, and the army is only the officer who carries out his sentence; the verdict was his, not Babylon's. It is no warrant for violence today, for the church does God’s work with other weapons (2 Cor 10:4). But the principle beneath it reaches us: work God assigns is not to be done with slackness, whatever the task. For us the curse has already fallen elsewhere: Christ, who did his Father's work perfectly, became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), and the Spirit he gives is the one who makes us diligent in it now.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab's problem is comfort: settled on his dregs, never poured from vessel to vessel (v. 11). God will send pourers, Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was of Bethel, and the neighbours are told to mourn the broken scepter (vv. 12–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Wine left undisturbed keeps its taste; a nation never poured out keeps its sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I shall send to him pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces. Then Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence. "How do you say, 'We are heroes and mighty men of war'? The destroyer of Moab and his cities has come up, and the choicest of his young men have gone down to slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. The calamity of Moab is near at hand, and his affliction hastens swiftly. Grieve for him, all you who are around him, and all who know his name; say, 'How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.' "Come down from your glory, and sit on the parched ground, O inhabitant of Dibon! For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you; he has destroyed your strongholds. Stand by the way and watch, O inhabitant of Aroer! Ask him who flees and her who escapes; say, 'What has happened?' Moab is put to shame, for it is broken; wail and cry! Tell it beside the Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settled on his dregs. The picture comes out of a winery.

He has not been emptied from vessel to vessel. New wine was left to stand so the sediment, the dregs, would settle, and then it was poured off into another jar, and another, leaving the sediment behind. Wine that was never poured off kept its strength but also kept everything that should have been removed. It stayed exactly as it was.

Moab has been at ease from his youth. That is Moab. At ease from his youth, never carried into exile, never poured out, and therefore never changed. His taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.

Comfort is not favour. Judah had been poured from vessel to vessel until she hardly knew herself. Moab had been left alone on the shelf, and the text treats that as the worse condition. Undisturbed comfort is not the same as God's favour; it can be the reason a nation or a life never becomes anything different.

The world that abolished discomfort. Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World (1932) imagines a society that has finally solved unhappiness. Everyone is comfortable, entertained and pleasantly drugged, and nobody is ever poured from vessel to vessel. Near the end a young man raised outside that world refuses it: “I don’t want comfort. I want God, I want poetry, I want real danger, I want freedom, I want goodness.” Huxley saw that a life arranged wholly around ease would keep its taste and never change its scent, and that the price would be almost everything that makes a person grow. Our age has not built his world, but it often wishes for it: no friction, no waiting, no pain we cannot numb. Moab is the warning. Left undisturbed, he stayed exactly himself, and that was his tragedy. Scripture never tells us to go looking for suffering. It does tell us that God pours his people from jar to jar because he loves them too much to leave them on their dregs, and that his own Son poured out his soul to death for them (Isa 53:12), so that every pouring of theirs ends in joy.

I shall send to him pourers. So God sends pourers. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "their" where the English has "his". The pouring out that Moab never had is coming as an invasion, and this time the jars are broken as well as emptied.

Bethel, their confidence. Verse 13 is even-handed. Israel’s golden calf at Bethel is named in the same breath as Moab's Chemosh, and both are called their confidence. God does not flatter his own people by contrast.

We are heroes and mighty men of war. Moab’s boast, that its men are heroes and mighty warriors, is answered by events, and the oracle is signed by the one who answers it: declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. In a section full of nations and their kings, one King keeps signing the oracles, and every throne in them stands or falls at his word.

How the mighty scepter is broken. The neighbours are told to mourn, and the words given them are not gloating: How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff. Moab's greatness is acknowledged in the act of lamenting its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–33 — He Magnified Himself Against the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment runs through a roll-call of towns (vv. 21-24). Moab is made drunk because he magnified himself against the LORD and mocked Israel (vv. 25-27), and his pride is catalogued (vv. 28-30). Then the voice changes: Therefore I wail for Moab (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the sentence and then weeps over the country he is sentencing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Judgment has come upon the tableland, upon Holon, and Jahzah, and Mephaath, and Dibon, and Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, and Kiriathaim, and Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, and Kerioth, and Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, declares the LORD. "Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD, so that Moab shall wallow in his vomit, and he too shall be held in derision. Was not Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves, that whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head? "Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, O inhabitants of Moab! Be like the dove that nests in the sides of the mouth of a gorge. We have heard of the pride of Moab— he is very proud— of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know his insolence, declares the LORD; his boasts are false, his deeds are false. Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn. More than for Jazer I weep for you, O vine of Sibmah! Your branches passed over the sea, reached to the Sea of Jazer; on your summer fruits and your grapes the destroyer has fallen. Gladness and joy have been taken away from the fruitful land of Moab; I have made the wine cease from the winepresses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; the shouting is not the shout of joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment has come upon the tableland. Eleven towns in four verses, and then the sweep: all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The roll-call is slow on purpose. Somebody knew these places.

He magnified himself against the LORD. The charge is stated at last, and it is not the towns or the treasure: he magnified himself against the LORD. And the punishment fits the image of the chapter: the nation that was never poured out is now made to drink, and ends up in its own vomit. There is nothing dignified in the picture, which is the point about pride.

Was not Israel a derision to you? Here is the specific offence, and it is startling: Moab is being judged for mockery. Whenever Israel was humbled, Moab laughed and wagged your head. Zephaniah records the same charge — I have heard the taunts of Moab... how they have taunted my people, and the sentence comes in return for their pride (Zeph 2:8, 10). Nor was it only talk: under Jehoiakim, Moabite raiding bands joined the attacks on Judah (2 Kgs 24:2).

How we speak of another’s fall. God had sent the disaster on Judah himself, and he still holds the onlookers accountable for enjoying it. How we speak of another's downfall is noticed. The answer is not a stricter tongue alone but a new heart: those who have been shown mercy at their own lowest point learn to weep with others at theirs.

Be like the dove. The advice is to go and live like a bird in a cliff face, which is exactly what people did when nothing was left. And the gentleness of the image sits oddly beside the sentence, as though the one pronouncing it is watching a people he does not hate.

We have heard of the pride of Moab. Five words for the same thing, piled up: pride, loftiness, pride, arrogance, haughtiness. And then God's own assessment underneath the noise: his boasts are false, his deeds are false. The swagger had nothing behind it, and God had always known.

Therefore I wail for Moab. Then, without warning, the voice breaks. After such a charge we expect therefore to introduce a punishment; it introduces tears. The same God who has just catalogued Moab's arrogance and ordered him made drunk now mourns for him by name, and for the men of one particular town.

Gladness and joy have been taken away. Moab was famous for vineyards, and the picture is of harvest silenced. Treading grapes was noisy work, done with singing. Now there is shouting, and it is the shouting of battle, not of harvest joy.

I have made the wine cease. It is the LORD who says I have made the wine cease. He is not grieving over something that happened to him. He has brought this judgment himself, and he grieves over it. Both are true at once, which is as close as the Old Testament comes to explaining the tears of God. The fuller explanation comes in person, when Jesus, who would bear the judgment himself, wept over Jerusalem while he foretold its fall (Luke 19:41-44).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–47 — My Heart Moans Like a Flute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lament deepens, God's heart moaning like a flute (vv. 34-39); there is no escape from terror, pit and snare, and the old song of fire from Heshbon is sung again (vv. 40-46). Then the last line turns everything: Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab (v. 47).
verseByVerse.theology: After forty-six verses of ruin comes one word: Yet.

verseByVerse.quote: "From the outcry at Heshbon even to Elealeh, as far as Jahaz they utter their voice, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. For the waters of Nimrim also have become desolate. And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares the LORD, him who offers sacrifice in the high place and makes offerings to his god. Therefore my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-hareseth. Therefore the riches they gained have perished. "For every head is shaved and every beard cut off. On all the hands are gashes, and around the waist is sackcloth. On all the housetops of Moab and in the squares there is nothing but lamentation, for I have broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares, declares the LORD. How it is broken! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! So Moab has become a derision and a horror to all that are around him." For thus says the LORD: "Behold, one shall fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Moab; the cities shall be taken and the strongholds seized. The heart of the warriors of Moab shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains; Moab shall be destroyed and be no longer a people, because he magnified himself against the LORD. Terror, pit, and snare are before you, O inhabitant of Moab! declares the LORD. He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For I will bring these things upon Moab, the year of their punishment, declares the LORD. "In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stop without strength, for fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the house of Sihon; it has destroyed the forehead of Moab, the crown of the sons of tumult. Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone, for your sons have been taken captive, and your daughters into captivity. Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD." Thus far is the judgment on Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him who offers sacrifice in the high place. The cry runs across the whole map, and the religion goes with it. Worship at the high places, the hilltop shrines, stops, because there is nobody left to climb them.

My heart moans for Moab like a flute. Twice more the lament, and now with an instrument: my heart moans for Moab like a flute. The flute was played at funerals. God says his heart makes the sound of a funeral instrument over a pagan nation.

Isaiah’s lyre. Isaiah had written the same line with a different instrument — my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth (Isa 16:11) — the same town named in both. Two prophets, a century apart, given the same grief.

Every head is shaved. The mourning rites are the ones we have seen twice already in this book — shaved heads, cut beards, gashed hands (41:5; 47:5). And the vessel image returns one last time: not merely poured out now, but broken... like a vessel for which no one cares.

Terror, pit, and snare. Terror, pit and snare (vv. 43–44): three hazards in a row, arranged so that escaping one puts you into the next. It is the picture of a hunt, and it says what the whole chapter has been saying: nobody gets out of God’s judgment by running faster.

Fire came out from Heshbon. These two verses are a quotation. Centuries earlier, when Israel first came through this territory, the old Amorite victory song ran: For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon... Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! (Num 21:28-29). Jeremiah sings Moab's ancient defeat song back over Moab's final defeat. What happened to Moab then is happening again, and God has not forgotten the words.

Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days. The phrase is the one used of Israel herself (29:14; 30:3). It is spoken over the people of Chemosh, the nation that wagged its head at Jerusalem's funeral, the drunkard in his own vomit.

Ruth the Moabite. And it had already begun, quietly, long before. In the years of the judges a Moabite woman had followed her mother-in-law home to Bethlehem and said that Israel's God would be her God; and the neighbourhood women named her son Obed, who was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17). The line that runs to the Messiah has Moab in it, and Matthew names her in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5).

Thus far is the judgment on Moab. So the closing words, Thus far is the judgment on Moab, mark a limit in more than one sense. The judgment reaches this far and no further; and the God who wailed over a pagan country while sentencing it had a latter-day mercy in mind for it all along.

How was the promise kept? Moab was subdued by Babylon, probably about 582 BC, and afterwards disappears as a nation, so the promise looks beyond its ruin. Isaiah's oracle on Moab had already pointed to a throne set up in steadfast love in the tent of David (Isa 16:5), and the apostles saw that throne raised up when people from the nations were gathered to David's greater Son (Acts 15:16-17). The Greek translation of Jeremiah, shorter throughout, lacks verses 45-47; the ESV follows the Hebrew, which has them, and the hope they hold is taught in many other places.

48.title: Against Moab
48.overview:
Moab, Israel's close kin and old enemy across the Dead Sea, receives the longest oracle so far. Town after town falls, and Chemosh goes into exile with his priests (vv. 1-10). Moab's deeper trouble is undisturbed comfort, wine never poured from vessel to vessel (vv. 11-20). He is judged for magnifying himself against the LORD and for laughing at Israel's downfall, and then, unexpectedly, the voice pronouncing the sentence breaks into lament (vv. 21-39). There is no escaping by running, yet the last line promises that God will restore Moab's fortunes in the latter days (vv. 40-47).

Why are chapters about Moab and its neighbours in the Bible at all? Jeremiah was appointed a prophet to the nations (1:5, 10), and these oracles were spoken mostly in Judah's hearing. They told God's people that the LORD rules every nation and not only Israel; that the neighbours who mocked them would answer to him, so Judah need neither take revenge nor lean on alliances; and that pride is judged wherever it is found, Judah's included. They also end, again and again, in mercy, which is the first hint of the gospel that would go to all nations (Matt 28:19).
48.theology:
Moab's sins are respectable ones: trust in its own works and treasures, the complacency of a life never disturbed, and the pleasure of watching a neighbour fall (vv. 7, 11, 27). God names all three, and does not flatter Israel by contrast; Israel’s false worship at Bethel is named beside Moab’s god Chemosh (v. 13).

The chapter's deepest note is the grief of the judge. The same God who pronounces the sentence wails over Moab and grieves over what he himself has done (vv. 31-36). And his last word over this pagan enemy is restoration, a mercy already foreshadowed in Ruth the Moabitess, who stands in the line of David and of Christ (v. 47; Ruth 4:17).
48.examples:
It is possible to live a life like wine left on the shelf: never shaken, never poured out, keeping both its strength and its sediment. Moab's comfort was not a sign of God's favour but the reason it never changed. Christians who have been "poured from vessel to vessel" by loss or upheaval can take heart that God's disturbing is often his kindness.

The chapter also warns against the pleasure of seeing someone else humbled. Moab wagged its head at Judah's funeral, and God remembered it, though he had sent Judah's disaster himself.

49.text: <sup>1</sup>Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities?<sup>2</sup>Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD.<sup>3</sup>"Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials.<sup>4</sup>Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?'<sup>5</sup>Behold, I will bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, from all who are around you, and you shall be driven out, every man straight before him, with none to gather the fugitives.<sup>6</sup>"But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."<sup>7</sup>Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished?<sup>8</sup>Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Dedan! For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time when I punish him.<sup>9</sup>If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? If thieves came by night, would they not destroy only enough for themselves?<sup>10</sup>But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself. His children are destroyed, and his brothers, and his neighbors; and he is no more.<sup>11</sup>Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me."<sup>12</sup>For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink.<sup>13</sup>For I have sworn by myself, declares the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse, and all her cities shall be perpetual wastes."<sup>14</sup>I have heard a message from the LORD, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: "Gather yourselves together and come against her, and rise up for battle!<sup>15</sup>For behold, I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind.<sup>16</sup>The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD.<sup>17</sup>"Edom shall become a horror. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its disasters.<sup>18</sup>As when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were overthrown, says the LORD, no man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her.<sup>19</sup>Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?<sup>20</sup>Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman: Even the little ones of the flock shall be dragged away. Surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.<sup>21</sup>At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble; the sound of their cry shall be heard at the Red Sea.<sup>22</sup>Behold, one shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Bozrah, and the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains."<sup>23</sup>Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet.<sup>24</sup>Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor.<sup>25</sup>How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy?<sup>26</sup>Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed in that day, declares the LORD of hosts.<sup>27</sup>And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad."<sup>28</sup>Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down. Thus says the LORD: "Rise up, advance against Kedar! Destroy the people of the east!<sup>29</sup>Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!'<sup>30</sup>Flee, wander far away, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Hazor! declares the LORD. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you.<sup>31</sup>"Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone.<sup>32</sup>Their camels shall become plunder, their herds of livestock a spoil. I will scatter to every wind those who cut the corners of their hair, and I will bring their calamity from every side of them, declares the LORD.<sup>33</sup>Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste; no man shall dwell there; no man shall sojourn in her."<sup>34</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah.<sup>35</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might.<sup>36</sup>And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come.<sup>37</sup>I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life. I will bring disaster upon them, my fierce anger, declares the LORD. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them,<sup>38</sup>and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon is charged with squatting on Gad's inheritance (v. 1), so Israel will dispossess those who dispossessed him and Milcom will go into exile like Chemosh (vv. 2–5). Then, after five verses of ruin: But afterward (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Like Moab’s god Chemosh, Ammon’s god Milcom is carried off with his priests, and like Moab, Ammon is promised restoration after judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities? Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD. "Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials. Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?' Behold, I will bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, from all who are around you, and you shall be driven out, every man straight before him, with none to gather the fugitives. "But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning the Ammonites. Ammon was Moab's kinsman, descended from Lot's other son, born to his younger daughter and named Ben-ammi (Gen 19:38), and their territory lay east of the Jordan next to Gad's. In Jeremiah’s own day it was the Ammonite king Baalis who sent Ishmael to murder Gedaliah, and Ammon that sheltered the assassin afterwards (40:14; 41:15).

Has Israel no sons? The charge is occupation. When Assyria deported the northern tribes, Ammon moved into Gad's towns and stayed. God's questions are those of a landowner: Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? The tribe was gone, but its land still had an owner: it remained Israel’s inheritance from God.

Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad? The ESV notes that Milcom, the Ammonite god, may also be read "their king" here and in verse 3. Either reading makes the same point: Ammon took Gad’s land in the name of another lord, whether its god or its king.

Dispossess those who dispossessed him. The reversal is exact (dispossess those who dispossessed him), and God defends the inheritance of a tribe that had already been carried off for its own sins. When God disciplines his people, he does not hand their inheritance to anyone else.

Two gods deported. Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials (v. 3): Moab’s god Chemosh received the same sentence in 48:7. Two national gods are deported, and each needs its own priests to carry it.

Who will come against me? In verse 4 the ESV notes the Hebrew as “boast of your valleys, your valley flows”. What is clear is the confidence: good land, full treasuries, and the question Who will come against me?, which is the sentence every secure nation says just before the answer arrives.

But afterward. Five verses of judgment, and then afterward. That is, after the judgment God will restore them. It is the same pattern as Moab’s Yet (48:47) and Egypt’s (46:26), and it marks this whole section. God’s last word to the nations around Israel is not extinction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–22 — Though You Make Your Nest as High as the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom's wisdom fails and her hiding places are opened (vv. 7–11). If the less deserving drank the cup, Edom will not go unpunished (vv. 12–13); though she nests as high as the eagle, God will bring her down, for who can summon him? (vv. 14–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Edom trusts a fortress in a cliff, and God asks who could ever call him to court.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished? Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Dedan! For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time when I punish him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Edom. Edom is Esau, and the rivalry goes back to a womb: Two nations are in your womb... the older shall serve the younger (Gen 25:23). The Edomites were famous for their wisdom, and the oracle opens by asking where all that wisdom has gone. And Judah would remember a fresher grievance: when Jerusalem fell, Edom cheered and joined in the plunder (Ps 137:7; Obad 10-14).

O inhabitants of Dedan! Dedan was an Arabian trading people to the south-east, whose caravans passed through Edom (Isa 21:13; Ezek 27:20). They are told to turn back and hide in the depths, probably in caves or remote country, because the calamity of Esau is about to fall and anyone near him will be caught in it. The nation famous for counsel did not see its own ruin coming; its neighbours are warned before it is.
verseByVerse.note: Teman (v. 7) was a district of Edom named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11) and famous for its wise men; Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite (Job 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? If thieves came by night, would they not destroy only enough for themselves? But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself. His children are destroyed, and his brothers, and his neighbors; and he is no more. Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If grape gatherers came to you. Two pictures of ordinary loss. Harvesters always left gleanings on the vines (the law even required it, Lev 19:10; Deut 24:21), and thieves take only what they want and can carry. Edom’s ruin will be worse than either: nothing left over, nothing overlooked.

I have uncovered his hiding places. Edom's security was geography: canyons, cliffs and fortresses reached through slot gorges, the region of Petra. I have uncovered his hiding places is the end of that. There is no terrain God does not know.

Leave your fatherless children. Then comes an extraordinary verse in the middle of a judgment oracle (v. 11). To an enemy nation being stripped bare, God says: leave the orphans with me, and let the widows trust me. The God who defends widows and orphans in his law is the same God even here.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink. For I have sworn by myself, declares the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse, and all her cities shall be perpetual wastes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it. The deepest sentence in the chapter is about the cup, and its logic is: if even they, how much more you. The cup is the cup of wrath from chapter 25, which God handed round the nations beginning with Jerusalem (25:15-16). Judah had drunk it, and the phrase those who did not deserve to drink probably has her in view. Compared with Edom's guilt, God's own people were the less deserving party, and they drank anyway. So how shall Edom escape?

I have sworn by myself. God swears by himself because there is no one greater to swear by (Heb 6:13), and so binds himself to the sentence of verse 12. Bozrah was Edom’s chief city in the northern highlands, probably at modern Buseirah in Jordan. Four words pile up, a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse: Bozrah will become a name people use as a warning. Edom did fade as a nation after the Babylonian period; Arab peoples, later the Nabataeans, took over its land, and many Edomites moved into southern Judah, the later Idumea.

The innocent drank the cup. And the sentence reaches further than Edom, because there was one who truly did not deserve the cup and drank it to the bottom. In a garden he prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). So verse 12 warns and the cross comforts. If the innocent drank, the guilty cannot claim to be let off. And because the innocent drank, the guilty who hide in him need not drink it.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard a message from the LORD, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: "Gather yourselves together and come against her, and rise up for battle! For behold, I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind. The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An envoy has been sent among the nations. Jeremiah hears the LORD’s message, and the picture is of a herald going round the nations to raise a coalition: Gather yourselves together and come against her. Behind the movements of armies stands God’s summons. And the sentence is a reversal: I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind. A people proud of being great and feared will be made small and scorned.

You who live in the clefts of the rock. The ESV notes that the clefts of the rock may be read "of Sela", the place name behind Petra. And Obadiah has this passage almost word for word: The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock... Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down (Obad 3-4).

The horror you inspire. What deceived them was The horror you inspire. Being feared had convinced them they were safe. A reputation for being dangerous is no defence against God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Edom shall become a horror. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its disasters. As when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were overthrown, says the LORD, no man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom shall become a horror. The people who inspired horror (v. 16) become a sight that horrifies; the Hebrew words differ, but the reversal is plain. Passers-by hiss, a gesture of shock and contempt at a ruin, as Jeremiah had said they would over Jerusalem (19:8; compare 1 Kgs 9:8).

As when Sodom and Gomorrah. Sodom is Scripture’s standing example of a judgment so complete that nobody lives there again (Deut 29:23; Isa 13:19), and it was traditionally placed at the southern end of the Dead Sea, on Edom’s doorstep. No man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her: not even a traveller will stop for the night. The same words are spoken over Hazor (v. 33) and over Babylon (50:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman: Even the little ones of the flock shall be dragged away. Surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan. The jungle of the Jordan was the dense thicket along the river, where lions lived (compare 12:5). God pictures himself as a lion bursting out on a well-watered pasture and scattering flock and shepherds alike. I will appoint over her whomever I choose: Edom’s future rulers are God’s appointment, not Edom’s. The same words are used of Babylon (50:44).

For who is like me? The three questions of verse 19 are the heart of the whole section: For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? No one is like him, and the second question is the sharpest. God asks who could ever call him to court, and the silence that follows is the answer to every complaint that his judgments are unfair. There is no higher court to appeal to. That is not a refusal to hear our questions, for Jeremiah himself brought his complaints to God (12:1). It is a reminder of who the judge is.

Hear the plan that the LORD has made. Teman, proud of its counsel (v. 7), is told of a counsel it cannot match: the plan that the LORD has made and the purposes that he has formed. Even the little ones of the flock are dragged away, and the fold itself is appalled. The wise men had plans; God has a plan, and only his stands (Prov 19:21).

verseByVerse.quote: At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble; the sound of their cry shall be heard at the Red Sea. Behold, one shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Bozrah, and the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble. The crash of Edom is heard as far as the Red Sea, here its southern arm, the Gulf of Aqaba, where Edom’s ports had stood (1 Kgs 9:26). The whole country, from end to end, hears the cry.

One shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle. Edom had nested as high as the eagle’s (v. 16); now an eagle comes against her, the conqueror swooping on Bozrah. The same picture was used of Moab (48:40–41), with the same end: the warriors’ hearts become like the heart of a woman in her birth pains, helpless before what cannot be stopped. Height was Edom’s confidence, and God sends something that flies higher.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Damascus melts in panic though God calls her the city of my joy (vv. 23-27). Kedar's tents and camels are taken (vv. 28-30), and Hazor, a nation at ease with no gates or bars, becomes a waste (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: Walls are no defence, and having no walls at all is no defence either.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet. Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the sea that cannot be quiet. Syria now, and the image is a sea that will not settle. The picture is exact: like water that cannot stop moving, fear cannot settle or rest.

Hamath and Arpad are confounded. Hamath, on the Orontes, and Arpad, north of Aleppo, were Syrian cities north of Damascus; the bad news reaches them first and the panic runs south. Assyria had boasted of taking both a century earlier (Isa 10:9; 36:19). Then Damascus, the old capital of Aram that had fought Israel for generations, has become feeble: she turns to flee, seized by pains as of a woman in labor.

verseByVerse.quote: How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy? Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed in that day, declares the LORD of hosts. And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city of my joy. God calls a Gentile capital that. Damascus was ancient and beautiful, and its maker takes pleasure in it even while pronouncing its fall. Anyone who imagines the God of Israel is indifferent to the cities of the nations has not read this verse.

How is the famous city not forsaken. The line is hard; it probably means: why did the people not abandon the city while they could? They stayed, and so (therefore, v. 26) her young men shall fall in her squares. The same words are spoken over Babylon (50:30): the fate of the small capitals is the fate of the great one.

The strongholds of Ben-hadad. Amos had said the same, naming the same dynasty: I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad (Amos 1:4). The two prophets agree because one God speaks through both.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down. Thus says the LORD: "Rise up, advance against Kedar! Destroy the people of the east! Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!' Flee, wander far away, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Hazor! declares the LORD. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor. Now the Arab tribes of the desert; this Hazor is not the old Canaanite city in Galilee but a cluster of desert settlements, which Nebuchadnezzar raided probably about 599 BC. The inventory changes accordingly: not walls and gates but tents, curtains, flocks and camels. God's word reaches the nomads as precisely as the capitals, and it names what they actually own.

Terror on every side! And there is the phrase again, Terror on every side!, the words that had been Jeremiah's nickname (20:3, 10) and were pronounced over Egypt (46:5), now shouted after camel herds.

Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you. The people of the east is the old name for the desert tribes beyond the Jordan (Judg 6:3). They are told to wander far away and hide in the depths, as Dedan was (v. 8). The wording echoes what was said of Edom, the plan that the LORD has made (v. 20); here the plan is Nebuchadnezzar’s, but it is the LORD who declares it, so the king’s scheme is the means by which God’s word is done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone. Their camels shall become plunder, their herds of livestock a spoil. I will scatter to every wind those who cut the corners of their hair, and I will bring their calamity from every side of them, declares the LORD. Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste; no man shall dwell there; no man shall sojourn in her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That has no gates or bars. Hazor's defence was that it had nothing worth attacking: no gates or bars, living alone out in the desert where armies do not go.

Those who cut the corners of their hair. This was a desert custom of trimming the hair at the temples, forbidden to Israel (Lev 19:27) and used by Jeremiah as a name for these tribes (9:26; 25:23). God will scatter them to every wind and bring calamity from every side: the people whose safety was distance will find no direction left to flee. And Hazor is given the sentence Jerusalem had been given: a haunt of jackals (9:11; 10:22).

Three false securities. Set this beside Moab, who felt secure because he had never been disturbed or carried off (48:11), and Edom, whose security was a cliff. Here is a people who feel safe because no one notices them. All three fall. No arrangement of walls, wealth or remoteness can hide anyone from God, and the phrase a nation at ease has been a warning throughout these chapters rather than a compliment.

No promise for some. And note which oracles carry no promise of restoration. Egypt, Moab, Ammon and Elam are all promised restoration afterward; Damascus, Kedar and Hazor are not. God does not owe an explanation for the pattern, and the book does not offer one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elam, far east beyond Babylon, has its bow broken and is scattered to the four winds, and God sets his throne there (vv. 34-38). Then the last word: But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: God sets his throne in the farthest country named, and then promises it a future.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come. I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life. I will bring disaster upon them, my fierce anger, declares the LORD. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them, and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD. "But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Elam. Elam lay beyond Babylon, in what is now south-western Iran, one of the farthest nations named in the book, a country most Judeans would never see and had no dealings with.

I will break the bow of Elam. And their strength is identified precisely: the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. Elamite archers were famous. God names what a nation is actually proud of before he breaks it.

I will set my throne in Elam. Not a garrison or a governor, but a throne, in the most distant capital in the book. The claim is that the LORD of hosts governs there directly, and that its king holds his seat only by God’s leave.

I will restore the fortunes of Elam. And the chapter ends with a promise rather than a sentence of judgment. After Egypt (46:26), Moab (48:47) and Ammon (49:6), Elam is the fourth nation in these chapters told that judgment is not the end of its story.

Elamites at Pentecost. And on a day of Pentecost, when the Spirit fell and the crowd heard the mighty works of God each in his own language, Luke's list of the nationalities present begins: Parthians and Medes and Elamites (Acts 2:9). The restoration of Elam, promised through a prophet in a besieged city, turns up as men from Elam hearing the gospel in their own tongue.

49.title: Ammon, Edom, and the Nations Around
49.overview:
Four short oracles sweep round Judah's world. Ammon, which took over Gad's land, will lose it, and its god will go into exile (vv. 1-6). Edom, proud of its wisdom and its cliff fortresses, will be brought down from its eagle's nest, for no one can summon God to court (vv. 7-22). Damascus, the desert tribes of Kedar and Hazor fall in turn (vv. 23-33), and far-off Elam has its famous bow broken (vv. 34-39). Yet Ammon and Elam, like Egypt and Moab before them, are promised restoration.

Why does Judah need oracles about Ammon, Kedar and Elam? These names were the map of her whole world, near neighbours and far-off peoples alike, and the oracles say that no corner of it lay outside the LORD's rule. They also say his last word to many of these nations is mercy, which began to come true when Elamites heard the gospel at Pentecost.
49.theology:
No kind of security works against God, whether walls, wealth, a cliff, a fearsome reputation, or even having no gates at all (vv. 16, 31). He is the only judge, with no higher court to summon him (v. 19). Yet the same God tells a nation being stripped bare to leave its orphans with him (v. 11) and calls a Gentile capital the city of my joy (v. 25).

At the centre stands the cup. If those less deserving drank it, the guilty cannot claim to be let off; and because one wholly innocent drank it to the bottom, those who hide in him need not drink it (v. 12; 25:15-16; Matt 26:39).
49.examples:
Edom is the picture of a person whose safety lies in being feared: the sharp tongue, the reputation nobody wants to cross. The horror you inspire was exactly what deceived her. Hazor is the opposite, safe because no one notices her, and she falls too. Neither strength nor obscurity hides anyone from God.

Yet in the middle of Edom's sentence God says, leave your fatherless children with me. Even under judgment, the widow and the orphan can still be placed in his hands.

50.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet:<sup>2</sup>"Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.'<sup>3</sup>"For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation, and none shall dwell in it; both man and beast shall flee away.<sup>4</sup>"In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God.<sup>5</sup>They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.'<sup>6</sup>"My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains. From mountain to hill they have gone. They have forgotten their fold.<sup>7</sup>All who found them have devoured them, and their enemies have said, 'We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their habitation of righteousness, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.'<sup>8</sup>"Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as male goats before the flock.<sup>9</sup>For behold, I am stirring up and bringing against Babylon a gathering of great nations, from the north country. And they shall array themselves against her. From there she shall be taken. Their arrows are like a skilled warrior who does not return empty-handed.<sup>10</sup>Chaldea shall be plundered; all who plunder her shall be sated, declares the LORD.<sup>11</sup>"Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions,<sup>12</sup>your mother shall be utterly shamed, and she who bore you shall be disgraced. Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.<sup>13</sup>Because of the wrath of the LORD she shall not be inhabited but shall be an utter desolation; everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds.<sup>14</sup>Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD.<sup>15</sup>Raise a shout against her all around; she has surrendered; her bulwarks have fallen; her walls are thrown down. For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done.<sup>16</sup>Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land.<sup>17</sup>"Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones.<sup>18</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria.<sup>19</sup>I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan, and his desire shall be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead.<sup>20</sup>In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.<sup>21</sup>"Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you.<sup>22</sup>The noise of battle is in the land, and great destruction!<sup>23</sup>How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!<sup>24</sup>I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD.<sup>25</sup>The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans.<sup>26</sup>Come against her from every quarter; open her granaries; pile her up like heaps of grain, and devote her to destruction; let nothing be left of her.<sup>27</sup>Kill all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their punishment.<sup>28</sup>"A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple.<sup>29</sup>"Summon archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done.
