For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel.<sup>30</sup>Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed on that day, declares the LORD.<sup>31</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O proud one, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, for your day has come, the time when I will punish you.<sup>32</sup>The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up, and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all that is around him.<sup>33</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.<sup>34</sup>Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon.<sup>35</sup>"A sword against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her officials and her wise men!<sup>36</sup>A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed!<sup>37</sup>A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered!<sup>38</sup>A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols.<sup>39</sup>"Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations.<sup>40</sup>As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her.<sup>41</sup>"Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth.<sup>42</sup>They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon!<sup>43</sup>"The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor.<sup>44</sup>"Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?<sup>45</sup>Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.<sup>46</sup>At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Babylon Is Taken, Bel Is Put to Shame
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The news is to be published everywhere: Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame (v. 2), by a nation Out of the north (v. 3), the phrase that had long threatened Judah, now turned against Babylon. In the middle of it Israel and Judah come home together, weeping and seeking the LORD in an everlasting covenant (vv. 4–5), lost sheep led astray by their shepherds (vv. 6–7), and the call goes out to flee Babylon (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon, the enemy from the north that Judah feared, now faces an enemy from the north herself.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet: "Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.' "For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation, and none shall dwell in it; both man and beast shall flee away. "In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God. They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.' "My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains. From mountain to hill they have gone. They have forgotten their fold. All who found them have devoured them, and their enemies have said, 'We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their habitation of righteousness, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.' "Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as male goats before the flock. For behold, I am stirring up and bringing against Babylon a gathering of great nations, from the north country. And they shall array themselves against her. From there she shall be taken. Their arrows are like a skilled warrior who does not return empty-handed. Chaldea shall be plundered; all who plunder her shall be sated, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instrument on trial. For fifty chapters Babylon has been God’s instrument of judgment. God called Nebuchadnezzar my servant three times, put the yoke on Judah’s neck, and told the nations to submit. Now the instrument is put on trial herself.

Why so long. These two chapters, a hundred and ten verses, are the longest oracle in the book. It is so long because it answers the hardest question Jeremiah’s hearers faced: had God simply gone over to Babylon’s side?

Bel is put to shame. The instruction is to publish it and conceal it not. And what falls first is not the walls or the army, but Bel and Merodach, the gods. Isaiah had drawn the same scene: Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts (Isa 46:1). These are gods that have to be carried to safety on pack animals.

Out of the north. That phrase has been a threat since chapter 1: the boiling pot, the enemy from the north, the flood that covered Judah and the Philistines. Now it points at Babylon. Babylon does not decide where judgment falls. God does, and now he turns it on her.

The people of Israel and the people of Judah. In the middle of an oracle against an empire, this: both houses come home together, the northern tribes scattered for more than a century and Judah, in one company. And they come weeping, asking directions: They shall ask the way to Zion. People who had forgotten the road have to be told it, and their faces are turned toward it before their feet arrive. The covenant they ask for is the one promised in chapter 31, an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten, and it is asked for, not imposed. The God who scattered them has made them long for him.

Their shepherds have led them astray. In verse 6 God gives his diagnosis of the whole tragedy in two sentences, and he does not begin with the sheep’s foolishness. He begins with the shepherds, the kings, priests and prophets of chapter 23, who scattered my flock (23:2).

My people have been lost sheep. The sheep are still called my people, and still called lost. Isaiah puts both halves together and adds the remedy: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa 53:6).

Flee from the midst of Babylon. The same voice that said build houses and plant gardens in Babylon (29:5) now says leave, and the God who says it is the Redeemer who has broken their captors' grip (v. 34). Obedience does not mean always doing the same thing; it means doing what God says at each time. The people who had settled in for seventy years had to be told when the seventy years were up.

John hears it again. John hears that call again over a later Babylon: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Rev 18:4).

When was this fulfilled? It began when exiles of both kingdoms came home under Cyrus, but the everlasting covenant they ask for is the new covenant of 31:31-34, which Hebrews says Christ has brought in (Heb 8:6-13). In him the lost sheep of both houses, and of the nations too, become one flock under one shepherd (John 10:16).
verseByVerse.note: Bel (Marduk) and Merodach are names of Babylon’s chief god.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Hammer Punished, the Flock Restored
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plunderers who frolicked over God's heritage will see their mother shamed and Babylon made the last of the nations (vv. 11-13). She is punished because she sinned against the LORD, and must be done to as she has done (vv. 14-16). Israel, the sheep two lions mauled, will be brought back to pasture and its iniquity sought and not found (vv. 17-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Instruments are not exempt. God punishes the hammer he swung.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions, your mother shall be utterly shamed, and she who bore you shall be disgraced. Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert. Because of the wrath of the LORD she shall not be inhabited but shall be an utter desolation; everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds. Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD. Raise a shout against her all around; she has surrendered; her bulwarks have fallen; her walls are thrown down. For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done. Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land. "Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones. Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria. I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan, and his desire shall be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead. In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture. Babylon is pictured as livestock enjoying itself, a heifer kicking up its heels, stallions neighing. The pictures in these oracles keep cutting proud nations down to size: Egypt a heifer troubled by a fly, Moab wine left on its dregs, Babylon a frolicking herd. And the empire that was first among the nations will be the last of the nations, and the place will be desert.

She has sinned against the LORD. Here is the reason behind the whole chapter, and it answers the question of whether God has changed sides. Babylon is not being punished for defeating Judah; that was God's own doing. She is punished because she has sinned against the LORD, and the measure is do to her as she has done.

Accountable in God’s hand. An instrument used by God is still accountable for how it behaved in his hand. Babylon went beyond what God sent her to do: cruelty, pride, the temple burned, the plundering of God’s heritage for pleasure. Being useful to God is not the same as being righteous, and it excuses no one from judgment.

Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. Two empires are pictured as two lions over one sheep. Assyria devoured him; Babylon has gnawed his bones, the second predator working over what the first left behind.

As I punished the king of Assyria. Assyria is also the precedent. That empire had been God’s rod against the northern kingdom of Israel, and it fell: its capital Nineveh was destroyed within living memory. Babylon can read its own future in Assyria's ruins, and so can every power that thinks it is the exception.

I will restore Israel to his pasture. The sheep get pasture again — named pasture, Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim, Gilead, the good grazing country.

Sin in Judah, and none shall be found. And then a sentence that goes further than any restoration of land. Iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none. Someone will look for the sin and not find it, not because it was small, but because of the last clause: for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant, the survivors he keeps for himself. This is the promise of 31:34, that God will remember their sin no more, pictured as a search that finds nothing.

What it means for God to pardon. We tend to hear pardon as God being easygoing: the offence was not so bad, so he lets it go. This chapter will not let us think that. In the same breath God says of Babylon, “Repay her according to her deeds” (Jeremiah 50:29). He shrugs at no one’s sin. So how can Israel’s iniquity be sought and not found? Timothy Keller often pointed out, in The Reason for God, that real forgiveness is never free: when someone wrongs you, either you make them pay or you absorb the cost yourself, and to forgive is to bear it. God’s pardon is like that. The debt did not vanish; it was carried. The chapter names who carries it: Their Redeemer is strong (v. 34). That Redeemer came in person and paid with his life: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7). Our sin is worse than we like to admit, and the payment is greater than our sin. So when an old failure rises at night and accuses you, do not try to argue that it was small. Tell it where it went. If it was laid on Christ, the search comes back empty. See Forgiveness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The attack goes up against Merathaim and Pekod, "double rebellion" and "punishment" (v. 21). The hammer of the whole earth is broken in a snare Babylon never saw (vv. 22-27); word of vengeance for the temple reaches Zion, for she defied the Holy One of Israel and will not let his people go (vv. 28-33).
verseByVerse.theology: A district named Double Rebellion is caught in a snare it never saw.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you. The noise of battle is in the land, and great destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the land of Merathaim. Two Babylonian districts, and the ESV explains why these two are named: "Merathaim means double rebellion" and "Pekod means punishment". Real places on the map whose names, heard in Hebrew, spell out the charge and the verdict. The note on devoting also matters — "That is, set apart (devote) as an offering to the Lord (for destruction)" — the old language of holy war, now used against the empire that had carried out God's own judgment.

The noise of battle is in the land. A single line, like a shout from the field: the orders of verse 21 are already being carried out. Do all that I have commanded you makes the invader God’s servant, as Babylon had been before. In the prophets the command and the event often stand side by side, because what God commands is as good as done.

What of the command to kill and devote them to destruction? The Hebrew word, herem, means to hand something over wholly to God, here for destruction, as in the conquest of Canaan. It is God's sentence on an empire that had crushed nations, carried out by the armies he sent against Babylon: a judgment of that moment, not a pattern for believers, whose King said his servants do not fight for his kingdom (John 18:36). The Judge of all the earth may end a guilty power; no Christian may take up that sword in his name.
verseByVerse.note: Pekod was an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris, known from Assyrian records; Merathaim, "land of bitter waters", was probably a name for southern Babylonia near the Gulf.

verseByVerse.quote: How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hammer of the whole earth. Babylon's own oracle will say it more plainly still: You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces (51:20). A tool, and a tool can be broken by the hand that used it.

You did not know it. The snare was set, sprung and closed while the empire went about its business entirely unaware that anything had happened.

Judgment unnoticed. That is how judgment often comes to people who feel secure: the battle is lost before they notice anything. Belshazzar's feast was going on the night the city fell.

Because you opposed the LORD. The reason is given in one phrase. Babylon thought she was fighting Judah, Egypt and the rest; in fact she had picked a fight with God. Whoever contends with God is caught in the end, as the snare catches the bird that never saw it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans. Come against her from every quarter; open her granaries; pile her up like heaps of grain, and devote her to destruction; let nothing be left of her. Kill all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their punishment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has opened his armory. God keeps an armoury, and the weapons in it are nations. The invaders massing on the horizon think they are pursuing their own ambitions; in fact God has taken them out of his armoury.

Open her granaries. Babylon’s storehouses, filled from the harvests and plunder of many nations, are broken open, and the city itself is piled up like heaps of grain. Kill all her bulls probably means her young warriors, pictured as bulls (compare Ps 22:12; Isa 34:7), sent down to the slaughter. Their day has come: the day God had fixed (compare 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: "A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple. "Summon archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done. For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed on that day, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They flee and escape from the land of Babylon. Refugees running the other way — out of Babylon toward Zion, carrying news. And the news has a specific object: vengeance for his temple. The burning of that building was not overlooked.

The Holy One of Israel. The charge is pride, and the title used is the one that ties God to his people: the Holy One of Israel. Babylon had defied not an abstract deity but the God of the people she had plundered.

Repay her according to her deeds. The principle is justice in kind: Babylon is to receive what she gave. Revelation takes up these words over the last Babylon, the world city that persecutes the saints (Rev 18:6). The young men falling in her squares (v. 30) is the sentence already pronounced on Damascus (49:26).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am against you, O proud one, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, for your day has come, the time when I will punish you. The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up, and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all that is around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I am against you, O proud one. Babylon is now named by her sin: the Hebrew word for proud one stands as her name, like a title. I am against you is the most frightening thing God can say to anyone (compare 21:13; 51:25).

The proud one shall stumble and fall. Pride goes before a fall (Prov 16:18), and this fall has none to raise him up: no ally will lift her. The fire kindled in her cities answers the fire she set in Jerusalem (52:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. Both kingdoms are named together, the north carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and the south by Babylon: the whole family of Jacob held fast by its captors (compare v. 17). It is the plain complaint of the oppressed, and God himself states it.

They refuse to let them go. Any Israelite would hear the exodus in that phrase: Pharaoh, the hard-hearted king who would not release God’s people, and the God who took them out anyway. Babylon has made herself a second Egypt, and the next verse gives God’s answer: Their Redeemer is strong.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their Redeemer is strong (v. 34). Five swords and a drought fall on all that Babylon trusted, for she is mad over idols, and she becomes like Sodom (vv. 35-40). Her king's hands fall helpless, and the questions asked of Edom are asked of Babylon (vv. 41-46).
verseByVerse.theology: The captives do not have a lawyer; they have a Redeemer, and he takes the case himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon. "A sword against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her officials and her wise men! A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed! A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered! A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols. "Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations. As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her. "Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon! "The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor. "Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate. At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their Redeemer is strong. The word is Redeemer — the kinsman with the right and the duty to buy back what his relative had lost, the role Jeremiah himself played for a field at Anathoth (32:7). The captives have no rights and no one to speak for them. What they have is a relative with the power to free them.

He will surely plead their cause. He does not send a lawyer; he takes the case. Isaiah names him in the same breath: Our Redeemer — the LORD of hosts is his name — is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 47:4).

The Redeemer became a kinsman. That Redeemer at last became a kinsman in the full sense. The Son of God was born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal 4:4-5), and he shared our flesh and blood to free those held in slavery all their lives (Heb 2:14-15). The captives’ powerful relative turned out to be the LORD himself, and the price was his own life.

A sword against the Chaldeans. Five swords and a drought, hammered out one after another, and the list is a catalogue of everything Babylon trusted: administration, scholarship, divination, army, cavalry, treasury, and the canal system that made the land fertile.

A sword against the diviners. The diviners get a particular sentence — that they may become fools — and the diagnosis underneath it all is blunt: they are mad over idols. Not merely mistaken: mad.

As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks in Babylon here. The picture is a ruin with animals in it, measured against the oldest ruin in Scripture — Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24). John sees the same desolation over the last Babylon: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!... a haunt for every unclean bird (Rev 18:2).

His hands fell helpless. The words once used of Jerusalem under siege (6:24), and the labour pains of Edom's warriors (49:22), now fall on Babylon's king: his hands fell helpless. Every empire in this section ends in the same posture.

What shepherd can stand before me? Verse 44 repeats, almost unchanged, the words spoken over Edom a chapter earlier (49:19). The same three questions, For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?, silence the greatest nation as they silenced a small one.

I will appoint over her whomever I choose. Within a lifetime the appointment was made, and his name was Cyrus.

For the first readers. For the exiles who first read this chapter, the point was not the satisfaction of seeing an enemy fall. It was that the God who had used Babylon was not owned by Babylon: that the seventy years had an end written into them, that the shepherds who scattered the flock would answer for it, and that the people asking the way to Zion had a Redeemer strong enough to plead their cause against the hammer of the whole earth.

Did this come true? Babylon surrendered to Cyrus in 539 BC without a battle and stayed inhabited for centuries. The fulfilment came over time: it declined, was damaged by later kings, and became the ruin it is today. Prophecy often speaks of the end as if it were immediate. Revelation takes up Babylon as the name of every proud power that God will bring down (Rev 18).

50.title: Against Babylon
50.overview: The last and longest of the oracles against the nations (chs. 50-51) is spoken against Babylon, the empire God had used against Judah for fifty chapters. The instrument is now the defendant. Her gods are shamed and an enemy comes against her out of the north (vv. 1-3). Woven through the judgment is the homecoming of Israel and Judah together, weeping and seeking an everlasting covenant (vv. 4-20). The hammer of the whole earth is broken in a snare she never saw (vv. 21-33), because the captives' Redeemer is strong and pleads their cause himself (vv. 34-46).
50.theology:
This chapter answers the question the exiles must have asked: had God simply changed sides? He had not. Babylon is judged not for defeating Judah, which was his own doing, but for her pride and cruelty in doing it. Being useful to God excuses no one from judgment, and he alone decides where judgment falls (vv. 3, 14-15, 23).

Through it all runs a promise for the scattered flock. God blames the shepherds before the sheep (v. 6), searches for his people's iniquity and finds none because he has pardoned them (v. 20; 31:34), and stands as their Redeemer, the kinsman who takes their case himself (v. 34).
50.examples:
Some of the strongest powers in history have believed they were the exception, the hammer and never the anvil. Jeremiah tells Babylon to read her future in Nineveh's ruins; she did not, and the city fell while the feast went on.

For the believer, the comfort is personal. Those who have no rights and no one to speak for them are not left to plead their own case. Their Redeemer is strong, and the price of their freedom was his own life.

"My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea," let Jerusalem say.<sup>36</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry,<sup>37</sup>and Babylon shall become a heap of ruins, the haunt of jackals, a horror and a hissing, without inhabitant.<sup>38</sup>"They shall roar together like lions; they shall growl like lions' cubs.<sup>39</sup>While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD.<sup>40</sup>I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams and male goats.<sup>41</sup>"How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!<sup>42</sup>The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves.<sup>43</sup>Her cities have become a horror, a land of drought and a desert, a land in which no one dwells, and through which no son of man passes.<sup>44</sup>And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind:<sup>51</sup>'We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach; dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.'<sup>52</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will execute judgment upon her images, and through all her land the wounded shall groan.<sup>53</sup>Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.<sup>54</sup>"A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!<sup>55</sup>For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice. Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised,<sup>56</sup>for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay.<sup>57</sup>I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts.<sup>58</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Golden Cup That Made the Earth Drunk
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends a destroyer and winnowers against Babylon (vv. 1–4), for Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God (v. 5). Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand; balm is brought and she is not healed, and the Medes are stirred up as vengeance for his temple (vv. 6–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon was the cup that made the world drunk, but the LORD held her in his hand all along, and now he sets her down.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will stir up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai, and I will send to Babylon winnowers, and they shall winnow her, and they shall empty her land, when they come against her from every side on the day of trouble. Let not the archer bend his bow, and let him not stand up in his armor. Spare not her young men; devote to destruction all her army. They shall fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and wounded in her streets. For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. "Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad. Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been lifted up even to the skies. The LORD has brought about our vindication; come, let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God. "Sharpen the arrows! Take up the shields! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple. "Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon; make the watch strong; set up watchmen; prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon. O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut. The LORD of hosts has sworn by himself: Surely I will fill you with men, as many as locusts, and they shall raise the shout of victory over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai. The ESV notes that Leb-kamai is "A code name for Chaldea", a letter-substitution cipher. Why a cipher is used is not certain, since Babylon is named openly in the same verse; it may be wordplay, for read as it stands the name means something like heart of those who rise against me. Either way, Jeremiah is writing about an empire from inside its reach.

I will send to Babylon winnowers. And the picture is threshing. Winnowers toss grain into the wind so the chaff blows away; God says he will do that to Babylon and empty her land.

The exiles’ real question. Verse 5 is the pastoral heart of both chapters, and it answers the question the exiles were actually asking. Not: will Babylon fall? But: has God dropped us?

Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God. They had every appearance of being forsaken, with the city gone, the temple burned and the king blinded, and the verse denies it flatly.

Stubborn faithfulness. This is the faithfulness of God at its most stubborn: he has disciplined them, scattered them and burned his own house, and he has not let go of them for an hour.

Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand. An image of terrible beauty. Babylon was a golden cup, genuinely magnificent, and she was in the LORD's hand the whole time. He poured her out for the nations to drink, and the drinking drove them mad.

Intoxicating empires. Empires are intoxicating. Their wealth, art and confidence go to the heads of everyone around them. Yet the cup never held itself up: it was in the LORD’s hand.

Take balm for her pain. And then something unexpected: an attempt at nursing. Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. Somebody fetches medicine for the empire that burned the temple.

We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. The same balm of Gilead offered to Judah (8:22) and denied to Egypt (46:11) is brought to Babylon's bedside, and the verdict is that she could not be healed. Judgment here is not pictured as eagerness to destroy. It comes only after the cure has been tried and the patient is past healing.

The kings of the Medes. The nation God would use is named a generation before it arrived: the kings of the Medes. Isaiah had said the same — Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them (Isa 13:17) — and Daniel records the night it happened, when Darius the Mede received the kingdom (Dan 5:31).

The vengeance for his temple. And the stated motive is a building: the vengeance for his temple. The house Solomon built and the Chaldeans burned is on the charge sheet, which tells you that God does not shrug off what was done to the place where his name was.
verseByVerse.note: Leb-kamai is a code name for Chaldea (ESV note): read with the Hebrew alphabet reversed, it spells the word for Chaldeans.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A creation hymn sets the Maker of the earth against breathless idols (vv. 15–19). Then Babylon is told what she was, my hammer and weapon of war (v. 20), and that she will be repaid for the evil done in Zion and left a burnt mountain (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The tool is told what it was, just before it is put down.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is he who made the earth by his power. In the middle of a war oracle comes a hymn, the same hymn used earlier against the idols of Judah (10:12-13), repeated here against the idols of Babylon.

He makes lightning for the rain. Three of God’s qualities are named: power, wisdom, understanding. And then the weather, described as an operation: mist raised from the ends of the earth, lightning made for the rain, and the wind from his storehouses, as though God keeps weather in a warehouse and brings out what the day requires.

Established the world by his wisdom. Babylon was famous for its learning: astronomy, omens, the reading of the stars. The hymn answers that the wisdom which set the world in place and stretched out the heavens is the LORD’s (compare Prov 3:19). The exiles, surrounded by the temples and lore of the greatest city on earth, are reminded who made the sky the Babylonians studied.

verseByVerse.quote: Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no breath in them. Against that Creator, the craftsman. The contrast is between one who brings forth the wind and one who brings forth a statue, and the fatal lack is named exactly: there is no breath in them. The God who breathed into dust is set beside gods that cannot breathe at all.

At the time of their punishment they shall perish. Idols have their own day of judgment: when Babylon falls, her gods fall with her (50:2; 51:44, 47). Every man is stupid does not mean that idol-makers lack skill; the goldsmith is very skilful. It means that skill without the knowledge of God ends by worshipping its own work, and is put to shame by it.

The portion of Jacob. Israel's share, her allotted inheritance, is a person, and the sentence turns round and says Israel is his: the tribe of his inheritance. Each belongs to the other: the LORD is Israel’s, and Israel is the LORD’s.

He is the one who formed all things. And the one who formed all things has a name in the New Testament. John says of the Word who became flesh, All things were made through him (John 1:3, 14). The portion of Jacob, the Creator set against breathless idols, is the God who came to his people in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces; with you I destroy kingdoms; with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider; with you I break in pieces the chariot and the charioteer; with you I break in pieces man and woman; with you I break in pieces the old man and the youth; with you I break in pieces the young man and the young woman; with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With you I break in pieces. Nine times in four verses: with you I break in pieces. It is the rhythm of a hammer, and the list moves from cavalry to civilians to shepherds and ploughmen to the government.

You are my hammer and weapon of war. Read as a whole it is God's own account of what Babylon was: You are my hammer and weapon of war. Not a rival kingdom he failed to stop, but an implement he swung.

Who is the hammer? Interpreters differ. The verbs can be read as future, and some take the hammer to be Israel, or Cyrus, about to be swung against Babylon. This commentary follows the many who take it of Babylon herself, since the next verse turns at once to repay her, and 50:23 has already called Babylon the hammer of the whole earth.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD. "Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain. No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all the evil that they have done in Zion. And a hammer is accountable. For all the evil that they have done in Zion: the tool went beyond what it was sent to do, and the repayment will happen before your very eyes, so the exiles will see it.

O destroying mountain. Babylon sat on a flat plain, so destroying mountain describes her towering power, not her landscape. Her sentence is to be rolled down from the crags and left as a burnt mountain, a heap of burnt-out rubble.

No stone shall be taken from you for a corner. Then the detail that finishes it — No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation. Ruined cities were quarries for the next builders. This rubble will not even be worth carting away.

No stone for a foundation. The contrast is with Zion. Of Zion God had said, Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation (Isa 28:16), and the apostles saw that stone in Christ (1 Pet 2:4–6). Babylon’s rubble will never be built into anything; the stone God laid in Zion carries a building that is still rising.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Distant nations are summoned against Babylon, and her defence collapses from inside while runners carry the news to the king (vv. 27-33). Zion is given words for what Babylon did to her, and God answers that he will plead her cause, dry up Babylon's waters and give her rulers a feast that ends in endless sleep (vv. 34-40).
verseByVerse.theology: The city is taken while the messengers are still running to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up a standard on the earth; blow the trumpet among the nations; prepare the nations for war against her; summon against her the kingdoms, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; appoint a marshal against her; bring up horses like bristling locusts. Prepare the nations for war against her, the kings of the Medes, with their governors and deputies, and every land under their dominion. The land trembles and writhes in pain, for the LORD's purposes against Babylon stand, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz. Three little-known northern peoples, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, from the Armenian highlands, are called up to join the attack. And the cavalry comes up like bristling locusts: locusts in a bristling swarm (the Hebrew word is uncertain), a cavalry too many to count.

The LORD’s purposes against Babylon stand. These northern peoples had come under the power of the Medes, who are named next (v. 28; on the Medes see the note on v. 11). The trumpet and the standard gather them, but the one who musters them is God. Verse 29 says why the land trembles: not because of the armies, but because the LORD’s purposes against Babylon stand. Human plans rise and fall; his counsel stands (Isa 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting; they remain in their strongholds; their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken. One runner runs to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every side; the fords have been seized, the marshes are burned with fire, and the soldiers are in panic. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little while and the time of her harvest will come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting. The collapse is from the inside. They have not been beaten in the field — they have ceased fighting and gone indoors, and then their strength has failed. The bars of the gates are broken and the houses are burning.

One runner runs to meet another. A brilliant piece of reporting: couriers colliding on the road, each carrying worse news to the palace. By the time the king is told, his city is taken on every side. Anyone who has watched an institution fail will recognise the picture — the messages arriving faster than the leadership can hear them.

The fords have been seized. Babylon’s defences were water: the Euphrates ran through the city, and canals and marshes surrounded it. Seize the crossings and burn the reed-beds, and the defence is gone. The Greek historian Herodotus later told how Cyrus’ army entered the city by lowering the river and marching in along its bed (compare v. 36).

Like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden. A threshing floor was stamped hard and level before the harvest. The trampling Babylon now suffers prepares her for the harvest of judgment, when she will be threshed as she threshed others (compare the winnowers of v. 2). Yet a little while: the time is short, and it is fixed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me; he has made me an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out. The violence done to me and to my kinsmen be upon Babylon," let the inhabitant of Zion say. "My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea," let Jerusalem say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has rinsed me out. Now Zion is given a voice, and it is one of the most physical complaints in Scripture. Six verbs of being eaten: devoured, crushed, emptied, swallowed, and then the last indignity — he has rinsed me out, like a jar licked clean and set aside. The ESV notes that the phrase may be read "Or he has expelled me".

Honest complaint. God lets his people say exactly how bad it was. He does not tell them to tone it down.

My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea. Zion asks that the guilt for the violence and bloodshed be laid where it belongs. This is not private revenge but an appeal to the judge, the same appeal the martyrs make in Revelation (Rev 6:10), and it is left in God’s hands: Vengeance is mine (Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19). Telling God plainly what was done to us is part of how we leave it with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry, and Babylon shall become a heap of ruins, the haunt of jackals, a horror and a hissing, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will plead your cause. And the answer to that complaint is not a lecture but an advocate: I will plead your cause.

I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry. Babylon lived by water — the Euphrates and its canal network. Isaiah had put the same promise next to a name: God says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers', and says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose' (Isa 44:27-28).

Babylon shall become a heap of ruins. Every phrase of verse 37 had first been spoken over Jerusalem: a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals (9:11), a horror, a hissing (25:9, 18). The city that made Jerusalem a ruin is given Jerusalem’s sentence. That is how exactly God pleads his people’s cause.

verseByVerse.quote: "They shall roar together like lions; they shall growl like lions' cubs. While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD. I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams and male goats.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall roar together like lions. The Babylonians are pictured as lions growling over their prey, and the roar becomes the noise of their drinking party (v. 39). Then the picture turns: the lions are brought down like lambs to the slaughter (v. 40). The beasts of prey become the sacrificed flock, and a perpetual sleep is death, from which they will not wake.

While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast. A feast, wine, merriment, and then sleep. Daniel 5 records the night: a banquet, the vessels of the temple used for drinking, writing on the wall, and That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed (Dan 5:30). Babylon, who had made the nations drink, was handed a cup of her own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — Go Out of the Midst of Her, My People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The praise of the whole earth is taken and Bel made to give up what he swallowed (vv. 41-44). God's people are told to go out of her and not to faint at rumours (vv. 45-46); heaven and earth sing, and the escaped are told to remember the LORD and Jerusalem from far away (vv. 47-53).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are told to get out, and to take Jerusalem with them in their minds.

verseByVerse.quote: "How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves. Her cities have become a horror, a land of drought and a desert, a land in which no one dwells, and through which no son of man passes. And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. The nations shall no longer flow to him; the wall of Babylon has fallen. "Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land, when a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year, and violence is in the land, and ruler is against ruler. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the images of Babylon; her whole land shall be put to shame, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her. Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon, for the destroyers shall come against them out of the north, declares the LORD. Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, just as for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth. "You who have escaped from the sword, go, do not stand still! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind: 'We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach; dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.' "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will execute judgment upon her images, and through all her land the wounded shall groan. Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How Babylon is taken. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads Sheshach, "a code name for Babylon" — the same cipher used back in chapter 25, where Babylon drank last from the cup she had carried round (25:26). The code name returns for her funeral.

The praise of the whole earth. And the praise of the whole earth is not sarcasm. Babylon was admired everywhere, and the tone here is astonishment rather than gloating.

I will punish Bel in Babylon. Bel had swallowed the offerings and tribute of the world, and the temple vessels of Jerusalem with them. God will reach into the idol's mouth and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed — which is exactly what happened when Cyrus counted the bowls back out to a prince of Judah (Ezra 1:7-8).

Go out of the midst of her, my people! The call to leave comes again, and it rests on verse 5: a people not forsaken by their God is being called home, not driven out. Pastoral care is attached. There will be years of rumour before anything happens — a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year — coups, violence, ruler is against ruler. God tells them in advance not to let their hearts faint at each new report.

The last Babylon. John hears this same summons over the last Babylon: Come out of her, my people (Rev 18:4).

Shall sing for joy over Babylon. Creation sings. This is not human vindictiveness but the relief of a world that has been groaning, and the reason given is the dead: Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel. The psalmist by the canals had said it in grief, O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed (Ps 137:8), and here God answers him.

Is it right to rejoice when a city falls? The joy here is at the end of oppression and justice for the dead, and it belongs to God's judgment, not to private revenge. Christians still pray for their enemies (Matt 5:44) and leave vengeance with God (Rom 12:19); and they may rejoice, as heaven does in Revelation 19:1-2, when he puts an end to cruelty.

Remember the LORD from far away. Two instructions for survivors: Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind. Faith at a distance, with a city held in the memory — which is how most of God's people have lived ever since, remembering a place they are not in.

How do I remember the LORD from far away? The New Testament carries this over: Peter writes to Christians as elect exiles of the dispersion (1 Pet 1:1), and here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come (Heb 13:14). Remembering from far away is a habit more than a feeling. Keep a fixed time. Daniel, in Babylon itself, prayed three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10); give the LORD the first minutes of the day, before the news and the inbox. Keep the Lord’s Day with his people, the weekly reminder that you belong to another city. Let the other city shape the budget: give to the church and to the poor, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt 6:21). Talk about home at the table, so your children inherit the memory. And remember why there is a home to remember: the exiles thought of a city of stone, but Christ has gone ahead to prepare a place for us and promised to come again and take us to himself (John 14:2-3).

Though Babylon should mount up to heaven. The old ambition of Babel, still running: mount up to heaven. Isaiah had put the boast in the first person — I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high — and given the answer: But you are brought down to Sheol (Isa 14:13-15). Height is no defence when the destroyers come from me.
verseByVerse.note: Sheshach is a code name for Babylon (ESV note), formed the same way by reversing the alphabet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God of recompense silences Babylon and levels her broad wall (vv. 54-58). Then comes a last acted sign: Jeremiah sends the written oracle with Seraiah to be read in Babylon and sunk in the Euphrates with a stone, and the book records that the words of Jeremiah end here (vv. 59-64).
verseByVerse.theology: A book weighted with a stone and dropped in a river serves as the closing sermon of Jeremiah's book.

verseByVerse.quote: "A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans! For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice. Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised, for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire." The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster. Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon. And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: "When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words, and say, 'O LORD, you have said concerning this place that you will cut it off, so that nothing shall dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it shall be desolate forever.' When you finish reading this book, tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates, and say, 'Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more, because of the disaster that I am bringing upon her, and they shall become exhausted.'" Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stilling her mighty voice. A great city is a noise — markets, processions, armies, temple crowds — and God turns the volume off.

The LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. Recompense means repayment. It is one of the plainest statements in Scripture that God repays evil, and it is what makes the rest of the book bearable. A world in which the hammer is never put down is a world without justice.

The broad wall of Babylon. Babylon's walls were famous across the ancient world; Greek writers said they were wide enough to drive chariots along. They come down.

The peoples labor for nothing. And the last line is an epitaph for every empire: The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire. Decades of forced labour hauled brick for gates that will only feed the fire. Whatever is built without God is built for burning.

Isn’t history moving forward? Most of us were raised on the story of progress: each generation a little wiser and kinder than the last, history bending of its own accord toward the better. There is much to be thankful for, from anaesthetics to clean water. But the English philosopher John Gray, himself an atheist, has argued that faith in progress is Christian hope with God taken out, and that without God it is a myth: knowledge piles up, but human beings do not improve, and what one age gains another can lose. Babylon lived inside that myth. Her walls were a wonder of the world, her people laboured for decades to raise them, and the verdict is that the nations weary themselves only for fire. Jeremiah does not answer the myth with despair. He answers it with a different story, in which history does move toward an end, but not by our momentum. The broad wall falls; the city that is coming is the one whose designer and builder is God (Heb 11:10), and it was bought not by the labour of the peoples but by the work of the one who said, It is finished (John 19:30).

Was Babylon really levelled? Not in 539 BC: Cyrus took it with little fighting, and it remained a great city for a time. But over the following centuries it declined until it became the empty mound it is today, as Jeremiah said (50:39-40). Prophecy often shows the end of a long process in a single picture.

Seraiah the son of Neriah. (The Greek translation says Seraiah went from Zedekiah, that is, sent by him; either way he travelled on the king's business, probably in 594 or 593 BC.) Seraiah the son of Neriah — Baruch's brother, from the same family, and the quartermaster, a senior official travelling with the king to Babylon. The family that gave Jeremiah his scribe also gave him a courier into the enemy capital.

Jeremiah wrote in a book. So the prophet writes it down again — the man whose first scroll was burned and whose second was longer — and sends it a thousand kilometres to be read aloud in the city it condemns. A private reading, probably to nobody but God and one frightened official standing by a river.

Tie a stone to it. And there is the last acted sign recorded in the book, though it was performed years before he buried the stones at Tahpanhes (43:8-13). He had worn a yoke, smashed a flask, buried a loincloth and bought a field. Now, by proxy, a book is weighted with a stone and dropped into the Euphrates, and the words are spoken over the ripples: Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more.

A millstone into the sea. Some seven centuries later a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more" (Rev 18:21). The last book of the Bible repeats the gesture of an old man's courier at a riverbank.

Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

No grave, no vindication. Seven words to close forty years. No account of his death, no grave, no vindication scene — he is last seen in Egypt among people who would not hear him, and the book simply stops recording what he said.

What outlasted every power. And what he said outlasted every power in it. Jehoiakim burned the first scroll, and within a few years his son lost the throne after three months; Babylon is a mound in the desert; and the words thrown into the Euphrates with a stone tied to them float still. The man who asked God why he had ever been born (20:18) wrote the sentence about the law written on the heart and the sins remembered no more, and it is being read this morning in languages that did not exist when he dictated it.
verseByVerse.note: Zedekiah's journey to Babylon in his fourth year is not recorded elsewhere; it may have been to assure Nebuchadnezzar of his loyalty after the plotting of chapter 27.

51.title: A Stone in the Euphrates
51.overview:
The oracle against Babylon reaches its climax. God stirs up the Medes against the empire he had held like a golden cup, for his people have not been forsaken by their God (vv. 1-14). A creation hymn sets the Maker of all things against breathless idols, and Babylon is told she was only his hammer (vv. 15-26). Her defence collapses from inside, Zion's complaint is answered by God's promise to plead her cause, and his people are called to leave (vv. 27-53).

The chapter ends with a scene by a river. Jeremiah's written oracle is read aloud in Babylon and thrown into the Euphrates tied to a stone: Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more. With that, the words of Jeremiah end (vv. 54-64).
51.theology:
The exiles' real question was not whether Babylon would fall but whether God had dropped them, and the answer is flat: they have not been forsaken (v. 5). The empire that looked like their master was a cup in his hand and a hammer he swung, accountable for the evil it did beyond what God sent it to do (vv. 7, 20, 24).

God's judgment is not eagerness to destroy; balm was offered first (v. 9). His people are allowed to say exactly how much they have suffered, and he answers as their advocate (vv. 34-36). Because he is a God of recompense, the hammer is not swung for ever (v. 56), and whatever is built without him is built for burning (v. 58).
51.examples:
Anyone who has watched an institution fail will know the picture of the runners: one messenger after another arriving with worse news, until the leadership learns the city is already taken. Pride rarely sees its fall coming.

For believers living far from home, the chapter gives two instructions that have shaped God's people ever since: Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind. Faith often lives at a distance, holding to a city it cannot yet see (Heb 11:16).
