verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The appendix retells the fall in the plain prose of a court record: Zedekiah's evil reign and rebellion (vv. 1-3), the siege and famine (vv. 4-6), the breach, the flight and capture, and at Riblah his sons slaughtered before his eyes, his eyes put out, and prison till the day of his death (vv. 7-11).
verseByVerse.theology: After fifty-one chapters of warning, the fall is told as plain fact, and the facts prove Jeremiah right.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. And in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem, and laid siege to it. And they built siegeworks all around it. So the city was besieged till the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. On the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land. Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled and went out from the city by night by the way of a gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, and the Chaldeans were around the city. And they went in the direction of the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him. Then they captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he passed sentence on him. The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An appendix. The last chapter is an appendix, and it changes voice completely. After fifty-one chapters of poetry, lament, argument and tears, we get the flat prose of a court chronicle, running parallel to the end of 2 Kings. Since the previous chapter closed with Thus far are the words of Jeremiah (51:64), the appendix was probably added by another hand, many think Baruch's, to show that every word had come true.

The record. The preaching is over; here is the record, with dates and numbers.

He cast them out from his presence. Verse 3 gives two causes, and the order matters. What God did comes first, he cast them out from his presence, and then what the king did, Zedekiah’s rebellion. The chronicler will give the military details, but he will not let anyone think the army is the whole story.

In the ninth year of his reign. The dating is precise to the day, which is how you write about something you cannot forget. A siege of about a year and a half, roughly 588 to 586 BC, lies between those two dates, and the whole of it summarised in one clause: there was no food.

There was no food for the people of the land. Jeremiah lived through that on a loaf a day from the bakers' street until the bread ran out (37:21).

The army of the Chaldeans pursued the king. Zedekiah’s capture has already been told in chapter 39, and it is told again without one word of interpretation. There is no lament, no reproach, and no reminder that he could have surrendered and lived (38:17).

Put him in prison till the day of his death. One detail is added that chapter 39 left out: put him in prison till the day of his death. He had been promised that he would not die by the sword but in peace (34:4-5), and this is what that mercy looked like — years in a Babylonian cell, blind, and then a quiet end. God kept the promise exactly, and it was not what anybody would have pictured.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 52 closely follows 2 Kings 24:18–25:30.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — He Burned the House of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A month after the breach Nebuzaradan burns the house of the LORD and every great house, breaks down the walls and deports the people, leaving the poorest as vinedressers (vv. 12-16). Then a long inventory of the bronze carried off, down to the pillars' measurements and their pomegranates (vv. 17-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone lovingly records the temple’s beauty as it is broken up, and God has promised to bring it back (27:22).

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard, who served the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem. And he burned the house of the LORD, and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down. And all the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls around Jerusalem. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive some of the poorest of the people and the rest of the people who were left in the city and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, together with the rest of the artisans. But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen. And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and carried all the bronze to Babylon. And they took away the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the basins and the dishes for incense and all the vessels of bronze used in the temple service; also the small bowls and the fire pans and the basins and the pots and the lampstands and the dishes for incense and the bowls for drink offerings. What was of gold the captain of the guard took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver. As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze bulls that were under the sea, and the stands, which Solomon the king had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was beyond weight. As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, its circumference was twelve cubits, and its thickness was four fingers, and it was hollow. On it was a capital of bronze. The height of the one capital was five cubits. A network and pomegranates, all of bronze, were around the capital. And the second pillar had the same, with pomegranates. There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were a hundred upon the network all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He burned the house of the LORD. A month after the walls broke, the fire. And there it is, in seven words the earlier account did not write: he burned the house of the LORD.

The temple named at last. Chapter 39 listed the palace and the houses and the walls and did not clearly name the temple. Here the sentence is finally put down, first in the list, and the day is dated. Jewish tradition still fasts on the ninth of Ab for this.

Some of the poorest of the land. The poorest are left with the vines and the ploughs: the reversal noted in chapter 39, where those who owned nothing were given fields (39:10). It was an administrative decision, but it reads like a verdict on the rich.

The pillars of bronze. These are the exact items God had named twenty-five chapters earlier, when the popular prophets were promising the temple treasure would be back within two years: the pillars, the sea, the stands (27:19). They would go to Babylon and stay there until the day when I visit them (27:22). Here they go.

Which Solomon the king had made. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the sea in this verse. What the verse does carry is the name Solomon. This bronze was nearly four centuries old, made by the wisest king Israel had, and now it is scrap metal, so much of it that it is beyond weight.

As for the pillars. And then the strangest passage in the chapter: a detailed description of the pillars, measured in cubits (a cubit was about 18 inches, or 45 centimetres), with the thickness of the bronze given in fingers, and the pomegranates counted.

Recording beauty. Somebody wrote down how many pomegranates were cast on the capitals of Jachin and Boaz while they were being broken up and loaded onto carts. It is an act of love, the careful recording of a beautiful thing as it is destroyed, so that it would not be as though it had never existed.

Grief keeps inventories. And the God who let these things be taken had already spoken of a day when he would visit them (27:22).

On the tenth day of the month. Jeremiah dates the burning to the tenth day of the fifth month, Kings to the seventh (2 Kgs 25:8). Most likely the commander arrived on the seventh and the burning was done on the tenth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — So Judah Was Taken Into Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The senior men are executed at Riblah (vv. 24-27), and one flat sentence records the end: So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. The three deportations are counted, 4,600 in all (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: A nation's end is recorded as a headcount.

verseByVerse.quote: And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold; and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and seven men of the king's council, who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the midst of the city. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans; in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem 832 persons; in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Judeans 745 persons; all the persons were 4,600.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seraiah the chief priest. The leadership is collected by function: high priest, deputy priest, three doorkeepers, a general, seven counsellors, the conscription secretary, and sixty ordinary men.

Zephaniah the second priest. One name is quietly poignant. Zephaniah the second priest is the man who had read Shemaiah's hostile letter aloud to Jeremiah instead of acting on it (29:29), and whom Zedekiah twice sent to ask the prophet for prayer (21:1; 37:3). He was not an enemy. He goes to Riblah with the rest.

So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. One sentence for the end of a nation, and it is the sentence the whole book has been warning about since Jeremiah, as a young man, was called and shown an almond branch (1:11-12).

All the persons were 4,600. Three deportations, counted. And the totals are small — 4,600, perhaps adult men or heads of households rather than every person, but small in any reckoning.

Kings and Jeremiah compared. Do these figures contradict 2 Kings, which speaks of ten thousand taken in 597 BC (2 Kgs 24:14)? Probably not. This list dates events by Nebuchadnezzar's own years, one year earlier than Kings counts them (2 Kgs 24:12; 25:8), and it seems to count particular groups where Kings gives a round figure for everyone. The third deportation, about 582 BC, is recorded nowhere else. It was probably Babylon’s reprisal for the murder of Gedaliah (41:2-3), the reprisal the refugees had run to Egypt to escape (41:18). The Greek translation lacks verses 28-30 altogether.

What a remnant looks like. That is what a remnant, the few God keeps through judgment, looks like on paper. It is not a nation but a number, and a number low enough to be written in one line. Everything God had promised about restoration, the everlasting covenant, the Branch and the law written on the heart now rested on four thousand six hundred deportees and some vinedressers left behind.

God's purposes have often been carried by numbers that look like nothing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thirty-seven years into his captivity, Jehoiachin is released by the new king of Babylon, honoured above the other captive kings, and fed at the royal table for the rest of his life (vv. 31-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The book of the weeping prophet ends with a pardoned son of David eating dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison. And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, until the day of his death, as long as he lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the thirty-seventh year of the exile. And now, after everything, the book lifts.

Jehoiachin king of Judah. Thirty-seven years, bringing us to about 561 BC, is most of a lifetime. Jehoiachin is the Jeconiah of chapter 22, the young king carried off in 597, of whom God had said Write this man down as childless, with none of his offspring on David’s throne (22:30), and the good figs of chapter 24 went into exile with him. He has been in a Babylonian prison ever since.

Graciously freed Jehoiachin. The ESV notes that the Hebrew idiom behind graciously freed is "lifted up the head of", the phrase used of a man whose face is raised out of shame into favour. Somebody lifted the head of the last king of Judah. It was Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk), Nebuchadnezzar’s son, who reigned only about two years; a new king’s first year was a natural moment for such a release. Babylonian ration tablets from years earlier already list oil allotted to “Jehoiachin, king of the land of Judah” and his sons.

Four pictures of grace. Four things happen, and every one of them is a picture of grace.

He spoke kindly to him. These were rare kind words from a foreign king to a king of Judah. He is given a seat above the seats of the kings, honoured above other captive royalty for no stated reason. He put off his prison garments and was dressed otherwise. And he ate at the king's table every day of his life, on a regular allowance suited according to his daily needs.

Nothing deserved. Nothing is said about Jehoiachin deserving it. He had done what was evil, and a new emperor, for reasons of his own, raised his head, changed his clothes and sat him down to dinner. It is what happens to every sinner God pardons: summoned out of a cell, robes exchanged, seated at a table, and fed daily for life.

David’s line alive. And there is more here than a picture. The book ends this way because the line of David is alive. The house that was supposed to be finished has a living heir eating in Babylon, and Matthew's genealogy runs straight through him: Jeconiah, and then the generations to Joseph the husband of Mary (Matt 1:11-12). God had sworn that David's throne would be established forever (2 Sam 7:16), and in a Babylonian prison it looked like a promise that had died. This closing scene says it had not, and the angel's word to Mary says where it was going: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David... and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33).

According to his daily needs. So the last verse of the weeping prophet is an allowance of food for a pardoned king. No temple yet, no city yet, no Branch yet, but a son of David out of prison, at a table, with bread given him according to his daily needs, and many readers have heard in it the daily bread his greater Son taught his people to ask for (Matt 6:11).

Why the rest stands. Everything else in these fifty-two chapters came true to the letter: the siege, the famine, the breach, the blinded king, the burned house, the counted pomegranates. On the strength of that accuracy, the rest of what he wrote stands: an everlasting love, a new heart that God himself gives, a righteous Branch, a name over the city that reads The LORD is our righteousness, and sins that God has undertaken to remember no more.

Jeconiah and Jesus. But God said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (22:30), and Matthew traces Jesus through him (Matt 1:11–12). How do these fit? Jesus was Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father, but not his physical descendant; Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31), and many take Luke's list to give Mary's line. Others add that God later reversed the signet-ring sentence of 22:24 for Jeconiah's grandson Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23). Either way, the throne passed to a Son of David as God had promised.

52.title: A King at the Table
52.overview:
The book closes with an appendix in the flat prose of a court chronicle, closely matching the end of 2 Kings. It retells the fall of Jerusalem: Zedekiah blinded and imprisoned (vv. 1-11), the temple burned and its bronze carted off (vv. 12-23), the leaders executed and the deportations counted (vv. 24-30). Every word Jeremiah spoke against the city is shown to have come true.

Then, at the very end, the book lifts. Jehoiachin, the king of David's line who has spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison, is set free, given new clothes and a place at the king's table for life (vv. 31-34). The promise to David is not dead.
52.theology:
The appendix shows that God keeps his word exactly, though not always as we would picture it. God’s casting out of his people is named as the cause of the fall before Zedekiah’s rebellion (v. 3); Zedekiah's promised peaceful death meant years blind in a cell (v. 11; 34:4-5); and the temple vessels went to Babylon just as chapter 27 had said (27:19-22).

But the last word is grace. A remnant small enough to fit in one line carries all God's promises (v. 30), and a pardoned son of David sits at a king's table with nothing said about deserving it (vv. 31-34). The line of David is alive in Babylon and runs on to Christ (Matt 1:11-12).
52.examples:
When something precious is lost, people keep inventories: the photographs labelled, the recipes written down, the dates remembered. The clerk who counted the pomegranates on Solomon's pillars while they were broken up was doing the same thing, making sure that a beautiful thing would not vanish as though it had never been.

And when someone has spent years in the prison of their own failure, the end of this book is for them. Jehoiachin had done evil; a king lifted his head, changed his clothes and sat him down to dinner. That is what God does for every sinner he pardons.
